================================================================================
     STAGE 7: SECONDARY — GRADES 9-10 (Age ~14-16) — QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
     Algebra, geometry, proof
================================================================================

How to use this file (note for the parent / teacher)
----------------------------------------------------
- There are 43 topics (7.1 to 7.43, the same as in topic.txt), in six
  strands: Number systems (7.1-7.3), Algebra (7.4-7.18), Geometry
  (7.19-7.31), Trigonometry and vectors (7.32-7.36), Statistics and
  probability (7.37-7.40) and Reasoning (7.41-7.43). Each topic has:
    * WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN   the checklist of skills in that topic
    * PART A — DESCRIPTIVE        12 questions (D1-D12): real-life and
                                  board-exam style problems, worked
                                  examples, proofs and "explain why"
                                  questions, each with the answer and
                                  "Teacher explains" (the method step by
                                  step as a teacher shows it on the board,
                                  common mistakes, and a "Now you try"
                                  question)
    * PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY  12 questions (M1-M12): pure drills with
                                  answers. Most have many parts (a, b,
                                  c ...) so that EVERY case of this stage
                                  is practised — every factor-theorem and
                                  division type, every kind of quadratic,
                                  every circle theorem, every standard
                                  trigonometric value, every card and dice
                                  event, and so on — not just one example.
    * TEACHING TIPS               what to do if the student struggles, and
                                  how to make it harder
- In total: 516 descriptive + 516 mathematical questions, then a mixed
  revision test (equal descriptive and mathematical parts) and a readiness
  checklist for Stage 8.
- Level: this stage matches Class 9-10 board syllabuses (for example
  CBSE/ICSE in India, GCSE Higher in the UK) with some extension. Topics
  7.13-7.18 and 7.36 go a little beyond most Class 10 syllabuses and
  prepare for Stage 8.
- What is new in Stage 7: formal PROOF (Euclid, theorems with reasons,
  contradiction); real numbers and surds; polynomials and the factor
  theorem; QUADRATIC equations and parabolas; progressions; functions and
  graph transformations; coordinate geometry; circle theorems, tangents
  and similarity; TRIGONOMETRY; vectors; grouped-data statistics,
  standard deviation and probability; and first programming.
- Method: for each theorem, first explore it (measure, draw, use GeoGebra),
  then learn the proof, then apply it. For algebra, link symbols to graphs
  (Desmos) — every equation has a picture. Keep a "formula and theorem"
  notebook and a "mistakes I made" list.
- Proofs: write Statement / Reason in two columns, or full sentences with
  "because". Every step must follow from the previous ones or from a
  known fact.
- Do 60 minutes a day: 2-3 descriptive questions and 2-3 drills per
  session, plus weekly mixed revision of earlier topics. Before exams,
  practise full timed papers.
- Revise Stage 6 (A6.txt) whenever the student finds something difficult.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.1 — REAL NUMBERS: RATIONAL/IRRATIONAL, DECIMAL EXPANSIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The number families: N (natural) ⊂ W (whole) ⊂ Z (integers) ⊂ Q (rationals)
    ⊂ R (reals). A RATIONAL number can be written p/q with p, q integers and
    q ≠ 0. An IRRATIONAL number is a real number that cannot. Every real number
    is either rational or irrational, never both.
  - Decimal expansions: a rational number has a decimal that TERMINATES
    (7/8 = 0.875) or is NON-TERMINATING RECURRING (5/12 = 0.41(6), the block in
    brackets repeats for ever). An irrational number has a NON-TERMINATING
    NON-RECURRING decimal (√2 = 1.41421356..., π = 3.14159265...).
  - THE TERMINATING TEST: write p/q in LOWEST TERMS. The decimal terminates
    exactly when q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ (no prime factor other than 2 and 5), and then it
    has exactly max(m, n) decimal places: 7/80 = 7/(2⁴ × 5) = 0.0875 (4 places).
    Any other prime in q gives a recurring decimal.
  - PURE recurring (block starts at once, 3/7 = 0.(428571)) happens when q has
    no factor 2 or 5; MIXED recurring (some digits first, 7/30 = 0.2(3)) when q
    has 2 or 5 AND another prime. When dividing by q there are at most q − 1
    non-zero remainders, so a block of at most q − 1 digits must repeat.
  - Recurring decimal to p/q: let x = the decimal, multiply by powers of 10 so
    that the repeating tails line up, and subtract: x = 0.2(35),
    1000x − 10x = 235.3535... − 2.3535... = 233, so x = 233/990. Also 0.(9) = 1.
  - Between any two different real numbers there are infinitely many rationals
    (take the average) and infinitely many irrationals (write a non-recurring
    decimal between them).
  - Operations: rational ± × ÷ rational is rational (not ÷ 0);
    rational + irrational is ALWAYS irrational; non-zero rational × irrational
    is ALWAYS irrational; but irrational + irrational and
    irrational × irrational can be either: √2 + (3 − √2) = 3, √2 × √8 = 4,
    √2 + √3 and √2 × √3 = √6 are irrational.
  - Every real number is a point of the number line: locate decimals by
    SUCCESSIVE MAGNIFICATION and √x (x > 0) by the semicircle construction.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Sort into the families N, W, Z, Q, irrational and R: −7, 0, 11/3, √49, √50,
    0.3(18), 1.2020020002..., −√(16/9), π/4 and √12/√3.
    Answer: √49 = 7 and √12/√3 = √4 = 2: N, W, Z, Q, R. 0: W, Z, Q, R. −7: Z, Q,
    R. 11/3, 0.3(18) and −√(16/9) = −4/3: Q, R. √50, 1.2020020002... and π/4:
    irrational, R.
    Teacher explains: Picture the chain N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R: every natural number
    is whole, every whole number is an integer, every integer is rational
    (7 = 7/1) and every rational number is real, so list ALL the families a
    number belongs to. The irrationals form a separate box inside R. Step 1:
    SIMPLIFY first: √49 = 7, √12/√3 = √(12/3) = √4 = 2, −√(16/9) = −4/3. Step 2:
    decide. 50 is not a perfect square, so √50 = 5√2 is irrational.
    0.3(18) = 0.3181818... recurs, so it is rational (it is 7/22).
    1.2020020002... has a pattern, but the blocks of zeros keep growing, so no
    block REPEATS: irrational. π/4 is an irrational number divided by a non-zero
    rational, so it is irrational. Common mistakes: calling every number with a
    √ sign irrational, and calling every decimal with a pattern rational. Now
    you try: classify √0.09, ∛8 and 2 + √9. (0.3: Q, R; 2: N, W, Z, Q, R; 5: N,
    W, Z, Q, R)

D2. Without doing any long division, decide which of these have terminating
    decimal expansions: 13/3125, 17/8, 64/455, 15/1600, 29/343, 23/(2³ × 5²),
    129/(2² × 5⁷ × 7⁵), 6/15, 35/50, 77/210.
    Answer: Terminating: 13/3125, 17/8, 15/1600, 23/(2³ × 5²), 6/15, 35/50.
    Non-terminating recurring: 64/455, 29/343, 129/(2² × 5⁷ × 7⁵), 77/210.
    Teacher explains: THEOREM: if x = p/q is in LOWEST TERMS, then x has a
    terminating decimal exactly when the prime factorisation of q is 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ.
    Work in two steps. Step 1: cancel common factors. Step 2: factorise the
    denominator.
           13/3125     = 13/5⁵                    only 5s     T
           17/8        = 17/2³                    only 2s     T
           64/455      = 64/(5 × 7 × 13)          7 and 13    R
           15/1600     = 3/320 = 3/(2⁶ × 5)       only 2, 5   T
           29/343      = 29/7³                    7           R
           6/15        = 2/5                      only 5      T
           35/50       = 7/10 = 7/(2 × 5)         only 2, 5   T
           77/210      = 11/30 = 11/(2 × 3 × 5)   3           R
    Why it works: if q = 2³ × 5², multiply top and bottom by 5 to make the
    denominator 2³ × 5³ = 10³: 23/(2³ × 5²) = 115/1000 = 0.115. Only 2s and 5s
    can be 'topped up' to a power of 10. If q has another prime such as 3 or 7,
    no power of 10 is a multiple of q, so the division never stops (and it must
    recur). Common mistake: judging before cancelling: 6/15 has 3 in the
    denominator, but 6/15 = 2/5 = 0.4 terminates, while 77/210 = 11/30 still has
    the 3. In 129/(2² × 5⁷ × 7⁵), 129 = 3 × 43 cannot cancel the 7s. Now you
    try: 7/(2⁵ × 5⁴ × 3) and 21/(2⁵ × 5⁴ × 3). (the first recurs; the second is
    7/(2⁵ × 5⁴): it terminates)

D3. Write 17/8, 13/3125, 7/80 and 23/(2³ × 5²) as decimals by making the
    denominator a power of 10. How many decimal places does each have?
    Answer: 17/8 = 2.125 (3 places); 13/3125 = 0.00416 (5 places); 7/80 = 0.0875
    (4 places); 23/(2³ × 5²) = 0.115 (3 places).
    Teacher explains: Factorise the denominator and multiply top and bottom by
    whatever makes the numbers of 2s and 5s EQUAL:
           17/8    = 17/2³       = (17 × 5³)/(2³ × 5³) = 2125/10³ = 2.125
           13/3125 = 13/5⁵       = (13 × 2⁵)/(2⁵ × 5⁵) = 416/10⁵  = 0.00416
           7/80    = 7/(2⁴ × 5)  = (7 × 5³)/(2⁴ × 5⁴)  = 875/10⁴  = 0.0875
           23/200  = 23/(2³ × 5²) = (23 × 5)/(2³ × 5³) = 115/10³  = 0.115
    RULE: if p/q is in lowest terms and q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ, the decimal has exactly
    max(m, n) decimal places, because we need 10 to the power max(m, n) in the
    denominator. So 13/3125 needs 5 places: 0.00416 (count the zeros after the
    point too). Common mistake: writing 13/3125 = 0.416 by forgetting that the
    denominator is 10⁵, not 10³. Now you try: 11/40 and 3/250. (0.275, 3 places;
    0.012, 3 places)

D4. Divide 1 by 7 and 5 by 12. Explain why the decimals must recur, and why one
    is 'pure' and the other 'mixed'.
    Answer: 1/7 = 0.(142857) = 0.142857142857... (pure recurring);
    5/12 = 0.41(6) = 0.41666... (mixed recurring).
    Teacher explains: Long division of 1 ÷ 7, writing down each remainder:
           bring down   10  30  20  60  40  50  10 ...
           ÷ 7 gives     1   4   2   8   5   7   1 ...
           remainder     3   2   6   4   5   1   3 ...
    The remainder is always one of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (0 would mean the decimal
    stops, and 7 has no factor 2 or 5, so that never happens). After at most 6
    steps a remainder must come back, and from then on the digits repeat. Here
    the remainder 1 returns after 6 steps, so 1/7 = 0.(142857) with a block of 6
    digits. For 5 ÷ 12 the remainders are 2, 8, 8, 8, ... giving 0.41666...: two
    digits 4, 1 come BEFORE the repeating 6. The reason is 12 = 2² × 3: the 2²
    part produces max(2, 0) = 2 non-repeating digits, the 3 produces the
    recurring part. In general: q with no factor 2 or 5 gives PURE recurring; q
    with 2 or 5 and another prime gives MIXED recurring. Now you try: 3/7 and
    7/30. (0.(428571), pure; 0.2(3), mixed)

D5. Write 0.(7), 0.(47) and 2.(135) in the form p/q.
    Answer: 0.(7) = 7/9; 0.(47) = 47/99; 2.(135) = 79/37.
    Teacher explains: Let x = 0.777... Multiply by 10 (the block has 1 digit):
    10x = 7.777... Subtract: 10x − x = 7.777... − 0.777... = 7, so 9x = 7 and
    x = 7/9. For a 2-digit block multiply by 100:
           x    =  0.474747...
           100x = 47.474747...
           99x  = 47            so x = 47/99
    For 2.(135) multiply by 1000: 1000x = 2135.135135..., so 999x = 2133 and
    x = 2133/999 = 79/37 (divide top and bottom by 27). Or:
    2.(135) = 2 + 135/999 = 2 + 5/37 = 79/37. RULE: multiply by 10ᵏ where k is
    the number of digits in the block; the tails after the point are then
    identical and cancel. Check by dividing: 79 ÷ 37 = 2.135135... Common
    mistake: multiplying 0.(47) by 10, which gives 4.747..., whose tail is NOT
    the same as 0.4747... Now you try: 0.(18) and 3.(6). (2/11; 11/3)

D6. Write 0.2(35), 1.(27) and 0.12(3) in the form p/q.
    Answer: 0.2(35) = 233/990; 1.(27) = 14/11; 0.12(3) = 37/300.
    Teacher explains: For a MIXED recurring decimal first move the point to the
    START of the block, then past one whole block, and subtract:
           x = 0.2353535...
           10x   =   2.353535...     (point at the start of the block)
           1000x = 235.353535...     (point after one block)
           990x  = 233               so x = 233/990
           x = 0.12333...
           100x  =  12.333...
           1000x = 123.333...
           900x  = 111               so x = 111/900 = 37/300
    1.(27) is pure: 100x = 127.2727..., x = 1.2727..., so 99x = 126 and
    x = 126/99 = 14/11. SHORT RULE for checking: numerator = (all the digits up
    to the end of the first block) − (the digits before the block);
    denominator = one 9 for each block digit followed by one 0 for each
    non-repeating decimal digit: 0.2(35) = (235 − 2)/990,
    0.12(3) = (123 − 12)/900. Always simplify the fraction. Now you try: 0.3(2)
    and 1.1(45). (29/90; 63/55)

D7. Is 0.(9) = 0.999... exactly equal to 1, or just very close?
    Answer: It is exactly 1.
    Teacher explains: Proof 1 (algebra): let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999...,
    and 10x − x = 9, so 9x = 9 and x = 1. Proof 2: 1/3 = 0.333...; multiply by
    3: 3 × 1/3 = 1 and 3 × 0.333... = 0.999... Proof 3: if 0.(9) were less than
    1, the difference 1 − 0.(9) would be a positive number smaller than 0.1,
    0.01, 0.001, ... (smaller than every one of them), and the only such number
    is 0. So every terminating decimal has a second, recurring form ending in
    9s: 0.5 = 0.4(9), 2.4 = 2.3(9). This does not break the rule "rational means
    terminating or recurring"; it just means some rationals can be written both
    ways. Common mistake: thinking 0.999... is "the last number before 1" (there
    is no such number). Now you try: write 2.3(9) and 0.1(9) as terminating
    decimals. (2.4; 0.2)

D8. Find five rational numbers between 3/5 and 4/5, and the rational number
    exactly halfway between them.
    Answer: For example 19/30, 2/3, 7/10, 11/15, 23/30. Halfway: 7/10.
    Teacher explains: Method 1 (equivalent fractions): there is no whole number
    between 3 and 4, so multiply top and bottom by 6 (one more than the 5
    numbers we need): 3/5 = 18/30 and 4/5 = 24/30. Now 19/30, 20/30, 21/30,
    22/30, 23/30 lie between them; simplify: 19/30, 2/3, 7/10, 11/15, 23/30.
    Method 2 (average): the mean (a + b)/2 always lies between a and b:
    (3/5 + 4/5)/2 = (7/5)/2 = 7/10. Repeat with 3/5 and 7/10 to get 13/20, and
    so on for ever. So between any two rationals there are INFINITELY many
    rationals: the rationals are 'dense'. With decimals: 0.6 and 0.8 have 0.61,
    0.7, 0.75, 0.799 ... between them. Now you try: three rational numbers
    between −1 and −1/2. (for example −7/8, −3/4, −5/8)

D9. Find an irrational number between 1/7 and 2/7, a rational number between
    √2 and √3, and an irrational number between 0.1 and 0.12.
    Answer: For example 0.150150015000150000...; 1.5; 0.1101001000100001...
    Teacher explains: Step 1: write the given numbers as decimals.
    1/7 = 0.142857142857... and 2/7 = 0.285714285714... Step 2: build a decimal
    between them that NEVER terminates and NEVER repeats, for example
    0.15015001500015... (one more 0 each time). Any such decimal is irrational.
    For the second: √2 ≈ 1.414 and √3 ≈ 1.732, so 1.5 = 3/2 works (check:
    1.5² = 2.25 lies between 2 and 3). For the third: 0.11 lies between 0.1 and
    0.12, so make a non-recurring decimal starting 0.11...:
    0.1101001000100001... Another way: add a small irrational to a rational:
    0.1 + √2/100 = 0.114142... is irrational (rational + irrational) and lies
    between 0.1 and 0.12. Common mistake: writing 0.151515... which recurs, so
    it is rational. Now you try: an irrational number between 5/7 and 9/11.
    (5/7 = 0.(714285), 9/11 = 0.(81): for example 0.75075007500075...)

D10. Show 3.765 on the number line by successive magnification. Then describe
     where 4.2(6) lies, correct to 4 decimal places.
     Answer: 3.765 is the 5th mark between 3.76 and 3.77. 4.2(6) = 4.2666...
     lies between 4.2666 and 4.2667.
     Teacher explains: A decimal is located one digit at a time; each time we
     'zoom in' on one tenth of the previous interval.
           3 |----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----| 4
                3.1  3.2  3.3  3.4  3.5  3.6  3.7  3.8  3.9
         3.7 |----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----| 3.8
               3.71 3.72 3.73 3.74 3.75 3.76 3.77 3.78 3.79
        3.76 |----|----|----|----|----X----|----|----|----|----| 3.77
                                   3.765
     Step 1: 3.765 lies between 3 and 4; divide [3, 4] into 10 parts: it lies
     between 3.7 and 3.8. Step 2: divide [3.7, 3.8] into 10 parts: between 3.76
     and 3.77. Step 3: divide [3.76, 3.77] into 10 parts: 3.765 is the 5th mark
     (marked X). A terminating decimal needs only finitely many zooms. For a
     recurring decimal the zooming never ends, so we stop at the accuracy asked:
     4.2(6) = 4.26666... lies between 4.2666 and 4.2667 (4 zooms after 4 and 5).
     This is why every decimal, terminating or not, is a point of the line. Now
     you try: between which two hundredths does 5.3(7) lie? (5.37 and 5.38)

D11. The sum of two irrational numbers: always irrational? And the product?
     Classify (2 + √3) + (2 − √3), (2 + √3)(2 − √3), √2 + √3, √2 × √8, √2 × √3,
     5 + √2 and 3√7, and explain the rules.
     Answer: Rational: (2 + √3) + (2 − √3) = 4, (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 1,
     √2 × √8 = 4. Irrational: √2 + √3, √2 × √3 = √6, 5 + √2, 3√7.
     Teacher explains: Sum up what is ALWAYS true and what DEPENDS:
           rational ± rational           always rational
           rational × or ÷ rational      always rational (not ÷ 0)
           rational ± irrational         ALWAYS irrational
           non-zero rational × irrational ALWAYS irrational
           irrational ± irrational       either  (√2 − √2 = 0; √2 + √3)
           irrational × irrational       either  (√2 × √8 = 4; √2 × √3)
     Why is 5 + √2 irrational? Suppose 5 + √2 = r, a rational number. Then
     √2 = r − 5, and a rational minus a rational is rational, so √2 would be
     rational, which is false. So 5 + √2 is irrational. The same argument
     (divide by 3) shows 3√7 is irrational. To show that a rule is NOT always
     true, ONE counter-example is enough: (2 + √3) + (2 − √3) = 4 and
     (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1 show that two irrationals can give rationals.
     Now you try: classify (3 + √5) − (1 + √5), (3 + √5)(3 − √5), √5 × √20 and
     √5 + √20. (2, 4 and 10 are rational; √5 + √20 = 3√5 is irrational)

D12. Show how to locate √4.5 on the number line, and prove the construction
     works for √x, where x is any positive real number.
     Answer: Draw AB = 4.5 units and BC = 1 unit on a line, take the midpoint O
     of AC, draw a semicircle on AC, draw the perpendicular at B to meet it at
     D. Then BD = √4.5 ≈ 2.121.
                     .  .  .  .  .
                 .               D
               .                 |  .
               A----------O------B---C
               |<----- 4.5 ----->|<1>|
     Teacher explains: (The picture is not to scale.) Step 1: mark AB = 4.5
     units and extend by BC = 1 unit, so AC = 5.5. Step 2: bisect AC to find the
     midpoint O; OA = OC = 2.75. Step 3: with centre O and radius OC draw a
     semicircle. Step 4: at B draw a line perpendicular to AC, meeting the
     semicircle at D. Then BD = √4.5. PROOF for any x: AC = x + 1, so the radius
     is OD = (x + 1)/2 and OB = OC − BC = (x + 1)/2 − 1 = (x − 1)/2. Triangle
     OBD has a right angle at B, so by Pythagoras BD² = OD² − OB²
     = ((x + 1)/2)² − ((x − 1)/2)² = (4x)/4 = x, so BD = √x. Step 5: to put √x
     on the number line, let the line through A, B, C be the number line with B
     at 0 and draw an arc of radius BD with centre B; it cuts the line at √x.
     Common mistake: taking BC = x and AB = 1 and then measuring at the wrong
     point: the perpendicular must be at the point where the two lengths meet.
     Now you try: what does the same construction give with AB = 7 and BC = 1,
     and with AB = 3 and BC = 2? (√7; in general BD = √(AB × BC), so √6)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Write every family the number belongs to: N, W, Z, Q, irrational, R.
    a) −12      b) 0              c) 17               d) −5/8        e) √64
    f) √65      g) 0.(45)         h) 2.101001000...   i) −√(25/49)   j) π/3
    k) √0.49    l) ∛27            m) ∛9               n) (√7)²       o) √18/√2
    p) 3 + √5   q) 22/7           r) 0/9              s) −√100       t) √0.4
    u) 1.(9)    v) √2 × √2 × √2
    Answers: a) Z, Q, R   b) W, Z, Q, R   c) N, W, Z, Q, R   d) Q, R
             e) N, W, Z, Q, R   f) irrational, R   g) Q, R   h) irrational, R
             i) Q, R   j) irrational, R   k) Q, R   l) N, W, Z, Q, R
             m) irrational, R   n) N, W, Z, Q, R   o) N, W, Z, Q, R
             p) irrational, R   q) Q, R   r) W, Z, Q, R   s) Z, Q, R
             t) irrational, R   u) N, W, Z, Q, R   v) irrational, R

M2. Without dividing: write in lowest terms p/q, factorise q, and say T
    (terminating) or R (non-terminating recurring).
    a) 13/3125   b) 17/8           c) 64/455               d) 15/1600
    e) 29/343    f) 23/(2³ × 5²)   g) 129/(2² × 5⁷ × 7⁵)   h) 6/15
    i) 35/50     j) 77/210         k) 9/(2⁴ × 3)           l) 14/(2 × 5² × 7)
    m) 1/64      n) 3/48           o) 11/5⁵                p) 18/75
    q) 26/65     r) 49/140         s) 1/(2 × 3²)           t) 51/(2³ × 17)
    u) 7/12      v) 33/66
    Answers: a) 13/5⁵: T   b) 17/2³: T   c) 64/(5 × 7 × 13): R
             d) 3/(2⁶ × 5): T   e) 29/7³: R   f) 23/(2³ × 5²): T
             g) 129/(2² × 5⁷ × 7⁵): R   h) 2/5: T   i) 7/(2 × 5): T
             j) 11/(2 × 3 × 5): R   k) 3/2⁴: T   l) 1/5²: T   m) 1/2⁶: T
             n) 1/2⁴: T   o) 11/5⁵: T   p) 6/5²: T   q) 2/5: T
             r) 7/(2² × 5): T   s) 1/(2 × 3²): R   t) 3/2³: T   u) 7/(2² × 3): R
             v) 1/2: T

M3. Write as a terminating decimal and state the number of decimal places
    (max(m, n) when q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ).
    a) 3/8            b) 7/16   c) 13/125    d) 9/40          e) 21/(2³ × 5)
    f) 11/(2² × 5³)   g) 3/64   h) 17/25     i) 1/(2⁴ × 5²)   j) 27/250
    k) 49/500         l) 5/32   m) 123/625   n) 7/(2 × 5⁴)    o) 19/80
    p) 33/1024        q) 1/5    r) 3/2
    Answers: a) 0.375 (3)   b) 0.4375 (4)   c) 0.104 (3)   d) 0.225 (3)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: sort number cards into the nested family boxes; for the
  terminating test always write the two steps 'lowest terms' and 'factorise q'
  before deciding; do the long division 1 ÷ 7 on paper and watch the remainders
  return; convert recurring decimals with the x, 10x, 100x table and check by
  dividing. Harder: prove the terminating theorem in both directions; explain
  why the period of 1/p divides p − 1 (1/7: 6, 1/13: 6, 1/17: 16); find the
  100th digit of 1/7 (8, since 100 = 6 × 16 + 4); show that 0.(9) = 1 in three
  ways; construct √x for x = 2.5 and 9.3 accurately and measure.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.2 — EUCLID'S DIVISION LEMMA; FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ARITHMETIC
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - EUCLID'S DIVISION LEMMA: given positive integers a and b, there are UNIQUE
    whole numbers q (quotient) and r (remainder) with a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r < b.
    Example: 455 = 42 × 10 + 35. It is just
    'dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder' written carefully.
  - EUCLID'S DIVISION ALGORITHM for the HCF of a > b: divide a by b; if r = 0, b
    is the HCF; otherwise replace (a, b) by (b, r) and repeat. The last non-zero
    remainder (the last divisor) is the HCF. It works because
    HCF(a, b) = HCF(b, r): every common factor of a and b also divides
    r = a − bq, and every common factor of b and r also divides a = bq + r.
  - Using the lemma with b = 2, 3, 4, 6 ...: every integer is of the form 2q or
    2q + 1; 3q, 3q + 1 or 3q + 2; every odd integer is 4q + 1 or 4q + 3. By
    checking each case: the square of any integer is 3m or 3m + 1 (never
    3m + 2), and the square of any odd integer is 8m + 1.
  - FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ARITHMETIC (FTA): every composite number can be
    written as a product of primes, and this factorisation is UNIQUE apart from
    the order of the factors: 3825 = 3² × 5² × 17.
  - HCF = product of the SMALLEST power of each COMMON prime factor;
    LCM = product of the GREATEST power of EVERY prime factor that appears. For
    two numbers only: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b.
  - Consequences of the FTA: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a. This
    proves that √2, √3, √5, ... (√p for every prime p) are irrational; then
    2 + √3, 3√2, 5 − 2√3 are irrational too. Also 6ⁿ can never end in 0 (its
    only primes are 2 and 3, and ending in 0 needs a factor 5), and
    7 × 11 × 13 + 13 = 13 × 78 is composite.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. 455 laddoos are packed in boxes of 42. Write this as Euclid's division
    lemma. Then write the lemma for a = 17, b = 6; a = 81, b = 9; a = 5, b = 8.
    Answer: 455 = 42 × 10 + 35 (10 full boxes, 35 laddoos left over).
    17 = 6 × 2 + 5; 81 = 9 × 9 + 0; 5 = 8 × 0 + 5.
    Teacher explains: The lemma says: for positive integers a and b we can
    always find whole numbers q and r with a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r < b, and there
    is only ONE such pair. Think of sharing a objects into groups of b: q is the
    number of full groups, r is what is left, and r must be less than b
    (otherwise we could make another group). Check 455: 42 × 10 = 420 and
    455 − 420 = 35, which is less than 42. If b divides a exactly, r = 0
    (81 = 9 × 9 + 0). If a < b the quotient is 0 and r = a (5 = 8 × 0 + 5).
    Common mistake: writing 17 = 6 × 1 + 11; the equation is true but r = 11 is
    NOT less than 6, so it is not the division lemma. Now you try: write the
    lemma for a = 1000, b = 37 and for a = 36, b = 36. (1000 = 37 × 27 + 1;
    36 = 36 × 1 + 0)

D2. Use Euclid's division algorithm to find HCF(4052, 12,576). Why does the
    method work?
    Answer: HCF = 4.
    Teacher explains: Divide the larger number by the smaller, then keep
    dividing the last divisor by the last remainder until the remainder is 0.
    Write every step:
           12,576 = 4052 × 3 + 420
             4052 = 420 × 9 + 272
              420 = 272 × 1 + 148
              272 = 148 × 1 + 124
              148 = 124 × 1 + 24
              124 = 24 × 5 + 4
               24 = 4 × 6 + 0        remainder 0, so the HCF is 4
    Each line uses the divisor and remainder of the line above (they move
    DIAGONALLY one place left). WHY: from a = bq + r, any number that divides a
    and b also divides r = a − bq; and any number that divides b and r also
    divides a = bq + r. So (a, b) and (b, r) have exactly the same common
    factors, and HCF(a, b) = HCF(b, r). The numbers keep getting smaller, so we
    must reach remainder 0, and HCF(4, 0) = 4. Common mistakes: stopping at the
    first small remainder, or giving the last quotient (6) instead of the last
    divisor (4). Now you try: HCF(135, 225) and HCF(196, 38,220). (45; 196)

D3. A sweet-seller has 420 kaju barfis and 130 badam barfis. She wants to stack
    them so that each stack has the same number of barfis and only one kind,
    using as few stacks as possible. How many barfis in each stack? A band of 32
    marches behind a contingent of 616 soldiers in the same number of columns.
    What is the greatest number of columns?
    Answer: 10 barfis per stack (42 kaju stacks and 13 badam stacks). 8 columns.
    Teacher explains: 'Same number in each stack, fewest stacks' means the
    LARGEST number that divides both 420 and 130: the HCF.
           420 = 130 × 3 + 30
           130 = 30 × 4 + 10
            30 = 10 × 3 + 0      HCF(420, 130) = 10
    So each stack has 10 barfis: 420 ÷ 10 = 42 stacks of kaju and 130 ÷ 10 = 13
    stacks of badam, 55 stacks in all. For the parade: the number of columns
    must divide both 616 and 32, and we want the greatest: 616 = 32 × 19 + 8,
    32 = 8 × 4 + 0, so HCF = 8 columns (77 soldiers and 4 band members in each
    column). Key words: 'greatest', 'largest', 'maximum number that divides'
    point to the HCF; 'least', 'smallest', 'next time together' point to the
    LCM. Now you try: two ropes of 72 m and 120 m are cut into pieces of equal
    length with no waste. Find the greatest possible length. (HCF = 24 m)

D4. Find the HCF of 441, 567 and 693. Then find the largest number that divides
    245 and 1029 leaving remainder 5 in each case.
    Answer: HCF(441, 567, 693) = 63. The number is 16.
    Teacher explains: For three numbers find the HCF of two of them, then the
    HCF of that answer with the third number.
           567 = 441 × 1 + 126        693 = 63 × 11 + 0
           441 = 126 × 3 + 63
           126 = 63 × 2 + 0           so HCF(63, 693) = 63
           HCF(441, 567) = 63
    For the second question: if the number leaves remainder 5, then it divides
    245 − 5 = 240 and 1029 − 5 = 1024 EXACTLY, and it must be bigger than 5. So
    we need HCF(240, 1024):
           1024 = 240 × 4 + 64
            240 = 64 × 3 + 48
             64 = 48 × 1 + 16
             48 = 16 × 3 + 0         HCF = 16
    Check: 245 = 16 × 15 + 5 and 1029 = 16 × 64 + 5. Common mistake: finding
    HCF(245, 1029) and then subtracting 5. Now you try: the largest number that
    divides 70 and 125 leaving remainders 5 and 8. (HCF(65, 117) = 13)

D5. Show that every positive even integer is of the form 2q and every positive
    odd integer is of the form 2q + 1. Then show that every positive odd integer
    is of the form 4q + 1 or 4q + 3.
    Answer: Apply the division lemma with b = 2 and with b = 4.
    Teacher explains: Take any positive integer a and b = 2. By the lemma
    a = 2q + r with 0 ≤ r < 2, so r = 0 or r = 1. If r = 0, a = 2q is even; if
    r = 1, a = 2q + 1 is odd. Every integer is exactly one of these. Now take
    b = 4: a = 4q + r with r = 0, 1, 2 or 3.
           r = 0:  a = 4q        = 2(2q)         even
           r = 1:  a = 4q + 1                    odd
           r = 2:  a = 4q + 2    = 2(2q + 1)     even
           r = 3:  a = 4q + 3                    odd
    So an ODD integer can only be 4q + 1 or 4q + 3. Examples: 13 = 4 × 3 + 1,
    19 = 4 × 4 + 3. The method is always the same: choose b, list ALL the
    possible remainders 0, 1, ..., b − 1, and deal with every case. Common
    mistake: forgetting a case (for example r = 0). Now you try: show that every
    positive odd integer is of the form 6q + 1, 6q + 3 or 6q + 5. (6q, 6q + 2,
    6q + 4 are even)

D6. Show that the square of any positive integer is of the form 3m or 3m + 1 for
    some integer m.
    Answer: Every integer is 3q, 3q + 1 or 3q + 2; squaring each case gives 3m
    or 3m + 1.
    Teacher explains: By the lemma with b = 3, a = 3q, 3q + 1 or 3q + 2. Square
    each case and pull out a factor 3:
       a = 3q:      a² = 9q²                   = 3(3q²)              = 3m
       a = 3q + 1:  a² = 9q² + 6q + 1          = 3(3q² + 2q) + 1     = 3m + 1
       a = 3q + 2:  a² = 9q² + 12q + 3 + 1     = 3(3q² + 4q + 1) + 1 = 3m + 1
    In each case m is a whole number, so a² is always 3m or 3m + 1, never
    3m + 2. Check with numbers: 4² = 16 = 3 × 5 + 1, 6² = 36 = 3 × 12,
    8² = 64 = 3 × 21 + 1. A useful consequence: a number like 3m + 2 (for
    example 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, ...) can NEVER be a perfect square. Common
    mistake: in the last case writing 3(3q² + 4q) + 4 and stopping; the
    remainder must be less than 3. Now you try: show that the square of any
    integer is of the form 4m or 4m + 1. ((2q)² = 4q²;
    (2q + 1)² = 4(q² + q) + 1)

D7. Show that the square of any odd integer is of the form 8m + 1. Then show
    that the cube of any positive integer is of the form 9m, 9m + 1 or 9m + 8.
    Answer: (2q + 1)² = 4q(q + 1) + 1 and q(q + 1) is even, so it is 8m + 1. For
    cubes check a = 3q, 3q + 1, 3q + 2.
    Teacher explains: An odd integer is 2q + 1, so
    (2q + 1)² = 4q² + 4q + 1 = 4q(q + 1) + 1. Now q and q + 1 are consecutive
    integers, so one of them is even and q(q + 1) = 2k. Hence
    (2q + 1)² = 8k + 1. Check: 7² = 49 = 8 × 6 + 1, 9² = 81 = 8 × 10 + 1. For
    cubes use (x + y)³ = x³ + 3x²y + 3xy² + y³:
       a = 3q:     a³ = 27q³                  = 9(3q³)                = 9m
       a = 3q + 1: a³ = 27q³ + 27q² + 9q + 1  = 9(3q³ + 3q² + q) + 1  = 9m + 1
       a = 3q + 2: a³ = 27q³ + 54q² + 36q + 8 = 9(3q³ + 6q² + 4q) + 8 = 9m + 8
    Check: 4³ = 64 = 9 × 7 + 1, 5³ = 125 = 9 × 13 + 8, 6³ = 216 = 9 × 24. Now
    you try: is 8m + 3 ever the square of an odd number? (no: odd squares are
    always 8m + 1)

D8. Express 3825, 5005 and 7429 as products of primes. What does the Fundamental
    Theorem of Arithmetic say?
    Answer: 3825 = 3² × 5² × 17; 5005 = 5 × 7 × 11 × 13; 7429 = 17 × 19 × 23.
    Teacher explains: Divide repeatedly by primes, smallest first (2, 3, 5, 7,
    11, ...):
           3 | 3825            5 | 5005            17 | 7429
           3 | 1275            7 | 1001            19 |  437
           5 |  425           11 |  143            23 |   23
           5 |   85           13 |   13               |    1
          17 |   17              |    1
             |    1
    Tests help: 3825 has digit sum 18 (divisible by 3 and 9) and ends in 5. 7429
    has no prime factor below 17, so keep trying larger primes; you only need to
    try primes up to √7429 ≈ 86. THE FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ARITHMETIC: every
    composite number is a product of primes, and this product is UNIQUE apart
    from the order. Whether we start with 3825 = 25 × 153 or 3825 = 9 × 425, we
    always end with 3² × 5² × 17. This uniqueness is what makes HCF, LCM and the
    irrationality proofs work. Now you try: 5544 and 1001. (2³ × 3² × 7 × 11;
    7 × 11 × 13)

D9. Find the HCF and LCM of 96 and 404 by prime factorisation, and check that
    HCF × LCM = product of the numbers. Then find the HCF and LCM of 6, 72 and
    120.
    Answer: HCF(96, 404) = 4, LCM = 9696. HCF(6, 72, 120) = 6, LCM = 360.
    Teacher explains: Factorise, then line up the primes:
           96  = 2⁵ × 3
           404 = 2² × 101
           HCF = 2² = 4                    (smallest power of each COMMON prime)
           LCM = 2⁵ × 3 × 101 = 9696       (greatest power of EVERY prime)
    Check: 4 × 9696 = 38,784 and 96 × 404 = 38,784. This works for TWO numbers
    because each prime's smallest power and greatest power together use up
    exactly the powers in a and in b. For 6 = 2 × 3, 72 = 2³ × 3² and
    120 = 2³ × 3 × 5: HCF = 2 × 3 = 6 and LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360. But
    6 × 360 = 2160, while 6 × 72 × 120 = 51,840: for THREE numbers HCF × LCM is
    not the product. Common mistakes: using the greatest powers for the HCF, or
    leaving out a prime that appears in only one number from the LCM. Now you
    try: HCF and LCM of 336 and 54. (6; 3024)

D10. (a) HCF(306, 657) = 9. Find LCM(306, 657). (b) Sonia takes 18 minutes to
     drive once round a sports field and Ravi takes 12 minutes. They start
     together at the same point, in the same direction. After how many minutes
     do they meet again at the starting point?
     Answer: (a) 22,338. (b) After 36 minutes.
     Teacher explains: (a) For two numbers, LCM = (a × b) ÷ HCF
     = (306 × 657) ÷ 9 = 201,042 ÷ 9 = 22,338. It is easier to divide first:
     306 ÷ 9 = 34, so LCM = 34 × 657 = 22,338. (b) Sonia is at the start after
     18, 36, 54, ... minutes and Ravi after 12, 24, 36, ... minutes. They are
     there together at the COMMON multiples, and first at the LEAST common
     multiple: 18 = 2 × 3², 12 = 2² × 3, LCM = 2² × 3² = 36. Check: 36 ÷ 18 = 2
     rounds for Sonia and 36 ÷ 12 = 3 rounds for Ravi. Also: two numbers cannot
     have HCF 18 and LCM 380, because the HCF must always divide the LCM
     (380 ÷ 18 is not whole). Now you try: three traffic lights change every 48,
     72 and 108 seconds. They change together at 7 a.m. When next? (LCM = 432 s,
     at 7:07:12 a.m.)

D11. Prove that √2 is irrational. Use the same method to prove that √3 and
     √5 are irrational.
     Answer: Assume √p = a/b in lowest terms; then p divides a and p divides b,
     a contradiction.
     Teacher explains: First a THEOREM from the FTA: if a prime p divides a²,
     then p divides a. Reason: write a = p₁p₂...pₙ (primes); then
     a² = p₁²p₂²...pₙ², and by uniqueness the only primes in a² are p₁, ..., pₙ.
     If p divides a², p is one of them, so p divides a. Now the proof for √3 (by
     contradiction):
     Step 1: suppose √3 is rational: √3 = a/b where a, b are integers, b ≠ 0,
     and a, b are COPRIME (no common factor other than 1).
     Step 2: then b√3 = a, and squaring, 3b² = a². So 3 divides a², hence (by
     the theorem) 3 divides a. Write a = 3c.
     Step 3: then 3b² = 9c², so b² = 3c². So 3 divides b², hence 3 divides b.
     Step 4: now 3 divides both a and b, which contradicts 'coprime'. So the
     supposition is false and √3 is irrational. For √2 and √5 replace every 3 by
     2 or by 5. The proof needs p PRIME: for √4 Step 2 would say '4 divides a²,
     so 4 divides a', which is false (4 divides 36 but not 6), and indeed √4 = 2
     is rational. Now you try: which step fails if you try to 'prove' that √9 is
     irrational? (Step 2: 9 dividing a² does not make 9 divide a; √9 = 3)

D12. Given that √3 and √2 are irrational, prove that 2 + √3 and 3√2 are
     irrational. Then use the FTA to show that 6ⁿ can never end in the digit 0,
     and that 7 × 11 × 13 + 13 and 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 + 5 are composite.
     Answer: If 2 + √3 or 3√2 were rational, √3 or √2 would be rational. 6ⁿ has
     no prime factor 5. 7 × 11 × 13 + 13 = 13 × 78 and
     7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 + 5 = 5 × 1009.
     Teacher explains: Suppose 2 + √3 = a/b (a, b integers, b ≠ 0). Then
     √3 = a/b − 2 = (a − 2b)/b, a quotient of integers, so √3 would be rational:
     a contradiction. So 2 + √3 is irrational. Suppose 3√2 = a/b; then
     √2 = a/(3b), rational again: a contradiction. For 6ⁿ: a number ending in 0
     is divisible by 10 = 2 × 5, so 5 would appear in its prime factorisation.
     But 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ, and by UNIQUENESS no other primes can appear, so 5 does
     not divide 6ⁿ and 6ⁿ never ends in 0. (The same holds for 4ⁿ = 2²ⁿ, 12ⁿ,
     9ⁿ, but not for 15ⁿ × 2 or 20ⁿ.) For the last part take out the common
     factor: 7 × 11 × 13 + 13 = 13 × (77 + 1) = 13 × 78 = 1014, and
     7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 + 5 = 5 × (7 × 6 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 + 1) = 5 × 1009
     = 5045. Each has a factor other than 1 and itself, so each is composite.
     Now you try: prove 5 − 2√3 is irrational, and say whether 8ⁿ can end in 0.
     (√3 = (5 − r)/2 would be rational; no, 8ⁿ = 2³ⁿ has no factor 5)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: act out the division lemma with counters (share a counters into
  groups of b); write the Euclid steps in a column so that divisor and remainder
  visibly move one place left; build factor trees for numbers the student
  chooses and compare trees to see the same primes appear; say the irrationality
  proof aloud as five short steps. Harder: run Euclid's algorithm backwards to
  write the HCF as a combination (5 = HCF(210, 55) = 210 × 5 + 55 × (−19));
  prove there are infinitely many primes (Euclid: look at p₁p₂...pₙ + 1); show
  n³ − n is always divisible by 6; prove √2 + √3 is irrational; count the
  divisors of 3825 = 3² × 5² × 17 using (2 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 18.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.3 — SURDS AND RATIONALISATION; LAWS OF EXPONENTS FOR REAL NUMBERS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A SURD is an irrational root of a positive rational number, such as √2,
    √12 or ∛5. For positive a and b: √a × √b = √(ab) and √a ÷ √b = √(a/b). But
    √(a + b) is NOT √a + √b: √(9 + 16) = 5, while √9 + √16 = 7.
  - SIMPLEST FORM: take out the largest perfect-square factor:
    √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2, √180 = √(36 × 5) = 6√5. Use prime factors if unsure:
    72 = 2³ × 3², one 2 and one 3 come out of each pair.
  - LIKE surds (same number under the root, after simplifying) are added like
    like terms: 2√12 + 3√27 − √75 = 4√3 + 9√3 − 5√3 = 8√3. Unlike surds such as
    √2 + √3 cannot be combined.
  - IDENTITIES with surds: (√a + √b)² = a + b + 2√(ab),
    (√a − √b)² = a + b − 2√(ab), (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b,
    (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b.
  - RATIONALISING THE DENOMINATOR: 1/√a = √a/a (multiply top and bottom by √a);
    for 1/(a + √b) multiply by the CONJUGATE a − √b; for 1/(√a − √b) multiply by
    √a + √b. The denominator becomes rational.
  - LAWS OF EXPONENTS for a, b > 0 and rational m, n: aᵐ × aⁿ = a^(m + n);
    aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = a^(m − n); (aᵐ)ⁿ = a^(mn); aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ; a⁰ = 1; a^(−n) = 1/aⁿ;
    a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a (the nth root); a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ = ⁿ√(aᵐ). Here ^ means 'to
    the power'.
  - Evaluate a^(m/n) ROOT FIRST, then power: 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 2² = 4; a
    negative power means the reciprocal: 32^(−3/5) = 1/(⁵√32)³ = 1/8.
  - EXPONENTIAL EQUATIONS: write both sides as powers of the SAME base and
    equate the exponents: 2^(x + 1) = 32 = 2⁵, so x + 1 = 5 and x = 4.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Write in simplest form: √72, √50, √180, 3√48 and ∛54.
    Answer: √72 = 6√2; √50 = 5√2; √180 = 6√5; 3√48 = 12√3; ∛54 = 3∛2.
    Teacher explains: Look for the LARGEST perfect square that divides the
    number (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, ...), and use √(ab) = √a × √b:
           √72  = √(36 × 2) = √36 × √2 = 6√2
           √50  = √(25 × 2) = 5√2
           √180 = √(36 × 5) = 6√5
           3√48 = 3 × √(16 × 3) = 3 × 4√3 = 12√3
           ∛54  = ∛(27 × 2) = 3∛2         (for a cube root, a perfect CUBE)
    If you cannot see the square, use prime factors and take one number out for
    each PAIR: 180 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 2² × 3² × 5, so
    √180 = 2 × 3 × √5 = 6√5. Common mistake: using a square that is not the
    largest: √72 = √(4 × 18) = 2√18 is not finished, because √18 = 3√2 (so
    2√18 = 6√2). The number left under the root should have no square factor.
    Now you try: √98, √300 and 2√45. (7√2; 10√3; 6√5)

D2. Simplify 2√12 + 3√27 − √75 and √50 + √18 − √8. Is √2 + √3 = √5?
    Answer: 8√3; 6√2. No: √2 + √3 ≈ 3.146, but √5 ≈ 2.236.
    Teacher explains: Surds are added like algebra terms: 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2, just
    as 3x + 5x = 8x. But first SIMPLIFY each surd so you can see which are LIKE:
           2√12 + 3√27 − √75 = 2 × 2√3 + 3 × 3√3 − 5√3
                             = 4√3 + 9√3 − 5√3 = 8√3
           √50 + √18 − √8    = 5√2 + 3√2 − 2√2 = 6√2
    √2 and √3 are UNLIKE surds (like x and y) and cannot be combined:
    √2 + √3 stays as it is. Squaring shows the mistake: (√2 + √3)² = 5 + 2√6,
    not 5. Common mistake: adding the numbers under the roots: √8 + √2 = √10 is
    wrong; √8 + √2 = 2√2 + √2 = 3√2. Now you try: 5√8 − 3√18 + √32 and
    √20 + √45 − √5. (5√2; 4√5)

D3. Simplify √6 × √15, 3√2 × 4√6, √75 ÷ √3 and (6√20) ÷ (2√5).
    Answer: 3√10; 24√3; 5; 6.
    Teacher explains: MULTIPLY numbers outside the roots together and numbers
    inside the roots together, then simplify:
           √6 × √15     = √90 = √(9 × 10) = 3√10
           3√2 × 4√6    = 12√12 = 12 × 2√3 = 24√3
           √75 ÷ √3     = √(75/3) = √25 = 5
           (6√20) ÷ (2√5) = (6/2) × √(20/5) = 3 × √4 = 6
    A product or quotient of surds can be RATIONAL (√75 ÷ √3 = 5). Also
    √a × √a = a, so (3√2)² = 9 × 2 = 18, not 6√2 or 3 × 2. Common mistake:
    √a + √b = √(a + b) is false, but √a × √b = √(ab) is true (for positive a and
    b). Now you try: √10 × √15, (2√3)² and (√54) ÷ (√6). (5√6; 12; 3)

D4. Expand and simplify (√5 + √2)², (3 − √2)², (√7 + √3)(√7 − √3) and
    (2 + √3)(3 + √3). A square tile has side (√3 + 1) cm: find its area.
    Answer: 7 + 2√10; 11 − 6√2; 4; 9 + 5√3. Area = 4 + 2√3 cm² (about 7.46 cm²).
    Teacher explains: Use the algebra identities, treating each surd as a
    letter:
       (√5 + √2)² = (√5)² + 2 × √5 × √2 + (√2)² = 5 + 2√10 + 2 = 7 + 2√10
       (3 − √2)²  = 9 − 2 × 3 × √2 + 2 = 11 − 6√2
       (√7 + √3)(√7 − √3) = (√7)² − (√3)² = 7 − 3 = 4
       (2 + √3)(3 + √3)  = 6 + 2√3 + 3√3 + 3 = 9 + 5√3
    The third one is the most important: (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b is RATIONAL.
    This is the key to rationalising. For the tile: (√3 + 1)² = 3 + 2√3 + 1
    = 4 + 2√3 ≈ 4 + 3.464 = 7.464 cm². Common mistake: squaring each term
    separately, which gives only 5 + 2 = 7 and forgets the middle term 2√10. Now
    you try: (√6 − √2)² and (5 + 2√3)(5 − 2√3). (8 − 4√3; 13)

D5. Rationalise the denominators of 1/√7, 6/√3 and 5/(2√10). Why do we
    rationalise?
    Answer: 1/√7 = √7/7; 6/√3 = 2√3; 5/(2√10) = √10/4.
    Teacher explains: Multiply top AND bottom by the surd in the denominator
    (this is multiplying by 1, so the value does not change); √a × √a = a
    becomes a whole number:
           1/√7     = (1 × √7)/(√7 × √7)     = √7/7
           6/√3     = (6 × √3)/(√3 × √3)     = 6√3/3 = 2√3
           5/(2√10) = (5 × √10)/(2√10 × √10) = 5√10/20 = √10/4
    Why? Before calculators, dividing by 1.414... was hard, while
    √2/2 = 1.414.../2 = 0.707 is easy. Rationalised answers are also easier to
    compare and to add: 1/√2 + √2 = √2/2 + √2 = 3√2/2. For 5/(2√10) you only
    need to multiply by √10, not by 2√10. Common mistake: multiplying only the
    denominator. Now you try: 3/√6, 14/√7 and 1/(3√2). (√6/2; 2√7; √2/6)

D6. Rationalise 1/(2 + √3) and 3/(5 − √2).
    Answer: 1/(2 + √3) = 2 − √3; 3/(5 − √2) = (15 + 3√2)/23.
    Teacher explains: Multiplying by √3 would not help: (2 + √3)√3 = 2√3 + 3
    still has a surd. Instead multiply by the CONJUGATE, which has the opposite
    sign in the middle, and use (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²:
       1/(2 + √3) = (2 − √3)/((2 + √3)(2 − √3)) = (2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 2 − √3
       3/(5 − √2) = 3(5 + √2)/((5 − √2)(5 + √2)) = (15 + 3√2)/(25 − 2)
                  = (15 + 3√2)/23
    Check the first with decimals: 1/(2 + 1.732) = 1/3.732 ≈ 0.268 and
    2 − 1.732 = 0.268. The conjugate of a + √b is a − √b; the conjugate of
    a − √b is a + √b. Common mistake: (5 − √2)(5 + √2) = 25 − 4 (squaring 2
    instead of √2): (√2)² = 2, so it is 25 − 2 = 23. Now you try: 1/(3 + √5) and
    4/(√3 − 1). ((3 − √5)/4; 2√3 + 2)

D7. Rationalise 1/(√7 − √2) and (√5 + √3)/(√5 − √3).
    Answer: (√7 + √2)/5; 4 + √15.
    Teacher explains: The conjugate of √7 − √2 is √7 + √2, and
    (√7 − √2)(√7 + √2) = 7 − 2 = 5:
       1/(√7 − √2) = (√7 + √2)/((√7 − √2)(√7 + √2)) = (√7 + √2)/5
       (√5 + √3)/(√5 − √3) = (√5 + √3)²/(5 − 3) = (5 + 2√15 + 3)/2
                           = (8 + 2√15)/2 = 4 + √15
    In the second, the numerator gets multiplied too, so it becomes (√5 + √3)²,
    which must be expanded with its middle term. Always simplify at the end by
    dividing EVERY term by the common factor: (8 + 2√15)/2 = 4 + √15, not
    4 + 2√15. Check: (√5 + √3)/(√5 − √3) ≈ 3.968/0.504 ≈ 7.87, and
    4 + √15 ≈ 4 + 3.873 = 7.873. Now you try: 2/(√5 + √3) and
    (√3 + √2)/(√3 − √2). (√5 − √3; 5 + 2√6)

D8. Find rational numbers a and b such that (5 + 2√3)/(7 + 4√3) = a + b√3. Then,
    if x = 3 + 2√2, find x + 1/x and x² + 1/x².
    Answer: a = 11, b = −6. x + 1/x = 6 and x² + 1/x² = 34.
    Teacher explains: Rationalise the left side first;
    (7 + 4√3)(7 − 4√3) = 49 − 48 = 1:
       (5 + 2√3)(7 − 4√3) = 35 − 20√3 + 14√3 − 8 × 3 = 11 − 6√3
    So (5 + 2√3)/(7 + 4√3) = 11 − 6√3, and comparing with a + b√3, a = 11 and
    b = −6. We may compare 'rational part with rational part and √3 part with
    √3 part' because √3 is irrational. For x = 3 + 2√2: 1/x = 1/(3 + 2√2)
    = (3 − 2√2)/(9 − 8) = 3 − 2√2. So x + 1/x = 3 + 2√2 + 3 − 2√2 = 6. Then
    (x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x², so x² + 1/x² = 6² − 2 = 34. Common mistake:
    forgetting the middle term 2 when squaring x + 1/x. Now you try: if
    x = 2 + √3, find x + 1/x and x² + 1/x². (4; 14)

D9. Evaluate 64^(1/2), 125^(1/3), 8^(2/3), 32^(−3/5) and (81/16)^(−3/4).
    Answer: 8; 5; 4; 1/8; 8/27.
    Teacher explains: The denominator of the power is a ROOT, the numerator is a
    POWER, and a minus sign means 'take the reciprocal':
           a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a        a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ        a^(−n) = 1/aⁿ
           64^(1/2)      = √64 = 8
           125^(1/3)     = ∛125 = 5
           8^(2/3)       = (∛8)² = 2² = 4
           32^(−3/5)     = 1/32^(3/5) = 1/(⁵√32)³ = 1/2³ = 1/8
           (81/16)^(−3/4) = (16/81)^(3/4) = (⁴√(16/81))³ = (2/3)³ = 8/27
    Take the root FIRST: the numbers stay small (8^(2/3) as ∛64 also gives 4,
    but ∛(8²) is harder for bigger numbers). Why a^(1/2) = √a: by the law
    aᵐ × aⁿ = a^(m + n), a^(1/2) × a^(1/2) = a¹ = a, so a^(1/2) is the number
    whose square is a. Common mistakes: 8^(2/3) = 8 × 2/3, or 32^(−3/5) = −8. A
    negative power never makes the answer negative. Now you try: 27^(2/3),
    16^(−3/4) and (0.01)^(−1/2). (9; 1/8; 10)

D10. Simplify 2^(2/3) × 2^(1/3), (3^(1/3))⁶, 11^(1/2) ÷ 11^(1/4) and
     7^(1/2) × 8^(1/2). Then prove that
     (xᵃ/xᵇ)^(a + b) × (xᵇ/xᶜ)^(b + c) × (xᶜ/xᵃ)^(c + a) = 1 for x > 0.
     Answer: 2; 9; 11^(1/4); 56^(1/2) = 2√14. The product is x⁰ = 1.
     Teacher explains: The laws work for rational powers exactly as for
     whole-number powers:
     2^(2/3) × 2^(1/3)   = 2^(2/3 + 1/3) = 2¹ = 2       same base: ADD powers
     (3^(1/3))⁶          = 3^(6/3) = 3² = 9             power of power: MULTIPLY
     11^(1/2) ÷ 11^(1/4) = 11^(1/2 − 1/4) = 11^(1/4)    same base: SUBTRACT
     7^(1/2) × 8^(1/2)   = (7 × 8)^(1/2) = 56^(1/2)     same POWER: multiply
                         = √56 = 2√14                   the bases
     For the proof: xᵃ/xᵇ = x^(a − b), so the first factor is
     x^((a − b)(a + b)) = x^(a² − b²). Similarly the others are x^(b² − c²) and
     x^(c² − a²). Multiply by ADDING the powers:
     a² − b² + b² − c² + c² − a² = 0, and x⁰ = 1. Common mistake:
     2^(2/3) × 3^(2/3) = 6^(4/3); with DIFFERENT bases and the SAME power we
     multiply the bases and keep the power: 6^(2/3). Now you try:
     5^(1/2) × 5^(3/2) and (2^(3/4))^(8/3). (25; 4)

D11. Solve 2^(x + 1) = 32, 3^(2x − 1) = 243, 4ˣ = 8, 5^(x − 2) = 1/125 and
     9ˣ = 27^(x − 1).
     Answer: x = 4; x = 3; x = 3/2; x = −1; x = 3.
     Teacher explains: Write both sides as powers of the SAME base, then equate
     the powers (if aᵐ = aⁿ with a > 0, a ≠ 1, then m = n):
        2^(x + 1) = 2⁵              x + 1 = 5           x = 4
        3^(2x − 1) = 3⁵             2x − 1 = 5          x = 3
        4ˣ = 8:   2^(2x) = 2³       2x = 3              x = 3/2
        5^(x − 2) = 5⁻³             x − 2 = −3          x = −1
        9ˣ = 27^(x − 1):  3^(2x) = 3^(3x − 3)   2x = 3x − 3   x = 3
     For 4ˣ = 8 neither side is a power of the other, so go down to the common
     base 2. For 1/125 use a negative power: 1/125 = 5⁻³. Check: 2^(4 + 1) = 32,
     4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 8, 9³ = 729 = 27². Common mistake: (3²)ˣ = 3^(2 + x); the
     power of a power MULTIPLIES: 3^(2x). Now you try: 8^(x − 1) = 16 and
     (1/2)ˣ = 64. (3x − 3 = 4, x = 7/3; x = −6)

D12. A square plot of land has area 1800 m². Find its side in simplest surd
     form, its perimeter and its diagonal. Then decide which is bigger, √3 or
     ∛4.
     Answer: Side √1800 = 30√2 m ≈ 42.43 m; perimeter 120√2 m ≈ 169.7 m;
     diagonal 60 m exactly. ∛4 < √3.
     Teacher explains: Side = √1800 = √(900 × 2) = 30√2 m. Using √2 ≈ 1.414:
     30 × 1.414 ≈ 42.43 m. Perimeter = 4 × 30√2 = 120√2 ≈ 169.7 m. Diagonal
     (Pythagoras) = √(side² + side²) = √(1800 + 1800) = √3600 = 60 m: an
     irrational side can give a rational diagonal, because
     diagonal = side × √2 and 30√2 × √2 = 60. For fencing, the exact form
     120√2 m is best until the last step; round only at the end. To compare
     √3 = 3^(1/2) and ∛4 = 4^(1/3), raise both to the power 6 (the LCM of 2 and
     3) so the roots disappear: (3^(1/2))⁶ = 3³ = 27 and (4^(1/3))⁶ = 4² = 16.
     Since 16 < 27, ∛4 < √3. Check: ∛4 ≈ 1.587, √3 ≈ 1.732. Now you try: which
     is bigger, √2 or ∛3? (∛3: 2³ = 8 < 3² = 9)

    Answers: a) a = 11, b = −6   b) a = 8, b = 3   c) a = 2, b = −1
             d) a = 14/11, b = 5/11   e) a = 42/11, b = 0   f) a = 2, b = −1
             g) a = 3, b = 2   h) a = 0, b = 7/11   i) a = 11/7, b = 6/7
             j) a = 7, b = −4   k) a = −3, b = −2   l) a = 7/5, b = −2/5

M9. Evaluate (root first, then power; a negative power means the reciprocal).
    a) 64^(1/2)         b) 125^(1/3)    c) 8^(2/3)         d) 32^(−3/5)
    e) (81/16)^(−3/4)   f) 27^(2/3)     g) 16^(−3/4)       h) (0.01)^(−1/2)
    i) 16^(3/4)         j) 125^(−2/3)   k) 9^(−1/2)        l) (1/32)^(−2/5)

    q) 1000^(2/3)       r) 49^(3/2)     s) (0.008)^(1/3)   t) 81^(−5/4)
    u) (1/4)^(−3/2)     v) 32^(0.4)     w) 25^(1.5)        x) (1/8)^(−1/3)
    Answers: a) 8   b) 5   c) 4   d) 1/8   e) 8/27   f) 9   g) 1/8   h) 10
             i) 8   j) 1/25   k) 1/3   l) 4   m) 9   n) 5   o) 4/9   p) 25/16
             q) 100   r) 343   s) 1/5   t) 1/243   u) 8   v) 4   w) 125   x) 2

M10. Simplify using the laws of exponents; write the answer as a single power, a
     whole number or a surd.
     a) 2^(2/3) × 2^(1/3)     b) (3^(1/3))⁶
     c) 11^(1/2) ÷ 11^(1/4)   d) 7^(1/2) × 8^(1/2)

M11. Solve (write both sides as powers of the same base).
     a) 2^(x + 1) = 32           b) 3^(2x − 1) = 243   c) 4ˣ = 8
     d) 5^(x − 2) = 1/125        e) 9ˣ = 27^(x − 1)    f) 8^(x − 1) = 16
     g) (1/2)ˣ = 64              h) 2ˣ = 1             i) 10ˣ = 0.001
     j) 3^(x + 2) = 81           k) 25ˣ = 125          l) 2^(3x) = 4^(x + 1)
     m) 16ˣ = 1/8                n) 27ˣ = 9^(x + 1)    o) 5^(x + 1) = 25^(x − 1)
     p) (√2)ˣ = 8                q) 3ˣ × 9 = 3⁵        r) 2ˣ + 2ˣ = 64
     s) 4^(x + 1) = 32^(x − 1)   t) 6^(x − 3) = 1
     Answers: a) x = 4   b) x = 3   c) x = 3/2   d) x = −1   e) x = 3
              f) x = 7/3   g) x = −6   h) x = 0   i) x = −3   j) x = 2
              k) x = 3/2   l) x = 2   m) x = −3/4   n) x = 2   o) x = 3
              p) x = 6   q) x = 3   r) x = 5   s) x = 7/3   t) x = 3

M12. Given x, find 1/x (rationalise), then x + 1/x and x² + 1/x².
     a) x = 3 + 2√2   b) x = 2 + √3       c) x = √2 + 1   d) x = 5 + 2√6
     e) x = 4 − √15   f) x = (√5 + 1)/2   g) x = 3 − √8   h) x = 7 + 4√3
     i) x = 2 − √3    j) x = √3 + √2
     Answers:

       b) x + 1/x = 4; x² + 1/x² = 14
       c) x + 1/x = 2√2; x² + 1/x² = 6
       d) x + 1/x = 10; x² + 1/x² = 98
       e) x + 1/x = 8; x² + 1/x² = 62
       f) x + 1/x = √5; x² + 1/x² = 3
       g) x + 1/x = 6; x² + 1/x² = 34
       h) x + 1/x = 14; x² + 1/x² = 194
       i) x + 1/x = 4; x² + 1/x² = 14
       j) x + 1/x = 2√3; x² + 1/x² = 10

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep a list of the squares 1 to 20 on the desk for simplifying;
  treat √2 and √3 like the letters x and y when adding and expanding; for
  rationalising, say 'multiply by the conjugate, top and bottom' each time;
  check rationalised answers with a calculator; for powers, write the fraction
  as 'root over power' and always take the root first. Harder: rationalise
  1/(1 + √2 + √3) in two steps (answer (2 + √2 − √6)/4); explain why
  2^(1/2) × 2^(1/4) × 2^(1/8) × ... gets closer and closer to 2; solve
  2^(x + 3) + 2^(x + 1) = 320 (x = 5); simplify (√(x²y) × ∛(xy²)) as one power;
  compare ⁴√5, ∛3 and √2 by raising to the power 12.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.4 — POLYNOMIALS: DEGREE, ZEROS, REMAINDER THEOREM, FACTOR THEOREM
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A POLYNOMIAL in x is a sum of terms a·xⁿ where every power n is a WHOLE
    number (0, 1, 2, ...) and the coefficients a are real numbers:
    4x³ − 3x + √2 is a polynomial; √x + 1, 1/x + x and x^(3/2) are NOT.
  - The DEGREE is the highest power with a non-zero coefficient. Degree 1:
    LINEAR (ax + b); 2: QUADRATIC; 3: CUBIC; 4: QUARTIC (biquadratic). A
    non-zero constant such as 7 has degree 0; the ZERO polynomial 0 has no
    degree. By number of terms: MONOMIAL (1), BINOMIAL (2), TRINOMIAL (3).
  - VALUE: p(a) means 'put x = a': if p(x) = x² − 2x − 3 then
    p(−1) = 1 + 2 − 3 = 0. A ZERO of p is a number a with p(a) = 0. The zero of
    ax + b (a ≠ 0) is −b/a. A polynomial of degree n has AT MOST n zeros; a
    non-zero constant has none; every real number is a zero of the zero
    polynomial.
  - GRAPH: the zeros of p are the x-coordinates of the points where y = p(x)
    meets the x-axis. A line meets it once; a parabola 0, 1 or 2 times; a cubic
    curve 1, 2 or 3 times.
  - REMAINDER THEOREM: when p(x) is divided by (x − a), the remainder is p(a).
    Dividing by (x + a) = (x − (−a)) gives p(−a); dividing by (ax − b) gives
    p(b/a).
  - FACTOR THEOREM: (x − a) is a factor of p(x) exactly when p(a) = 0. Quick
    tests: if the coefficients add up to 0, (x − 1) is a factor; if p(−1) = 0,
    (x + 1) is a factor.
  - FACTORISING A CUBIC: try x = ±1, ±2, ±3, ... (divisors of the constant term,
    and fractions ±(divisor of constant)/(divisor of leading coefficient)) until
    p(a) = 0; divide by (x − a) to get a quadratic; factorise the quadratic by
    splitting the middle term. Check by expanding or by substituting.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Which of these are polynomials? Give the degree and the type of each
    polynomial: 4x² − 3x + 7, y³ + √2 y, 3√t + t√2, y + 2/y, x¹⁰ + y³ + t⁵⁰, 5,
    0, (x + 1)(x² − 4).
    Answer: Polynomials: 4x² − 3x + 7 (degree 2, quadratic trinomial), y³ + √2 y
    (degree 3, cubic binomial), x¹⁰ + y³ + t⁵⁰ (a polynomial in three
    variables), 5 (degree 0, constant), 0 (the zero polynomial, no degree),
    (x + 1)(x² − 4) = x³ + x² − 4x − 4 (degree 3, cubic). Not polynomials:
    3√t + t√2 and y + 2/y.
    Teacher explains: Check every power of the VARIABLE: it must be a whole
    number. √t = t^(1/2) has power 1/2, and 2/y = 2y⁻¹ has power −1, so those
    two expressions are not polynomials. A surd as a COEFFICIENT is fine: √2 y
    has power 1, and √2 is just a number. The degree is the HIGHEST power: for a
    product, multiply out first or add the degrees of the factors (1 + 2 = 3).
    5 = 5x⁰ has degree 0. The zero polynomial has no degree, because
    0 = 0x = 0x² = ... has no highest non-zero term. Common mistake: saying
    4x² − 3x + 7 has degree 7 (the constant is not a power). Now you try: are
    x² + 1/x² and x² − √5 x polynomials? (no; yes, degree 2)

D2. For p(x) = 5x − 4x² + 3 find p(0), p(−1) and p(2). Are 3 and −1 zeros of
    q(x) = x² − 2x − 3? Is 2 a zero?
    Answer: p(0) = 3, p(−1) = −6, p(2) = −3. q(3) = 0 and q(−1) = 0, so 3 and −1
    are zeros of q; q(2) = −3 ≠ 0, so 2 is not.
    Teacher explains: p(a) means: replace EVERY x by a, in brackets, and work
    out the value:
           p(0)  = 5(0) − 4(0)² + 3     = 3
           p(−1) = 5(−1) − 4(−1)² + 3   = −5 − 4 + 3 = −6
           p(2)  = 5(2) − 4(2)² + 3     = 10 − 16 + 3 = −3
    p(0) is always the constant term. For q: q(3) = 9 − 6 − 3 = 0 and
    q(−1) = 1 + 2 − 3 = 0, so both are zeros; q(2) = 4 − 4 − 3 = −3. Common
    mistake: −4(−1)² = +4: square FIRST, (−1)² = 1, then multiply by −4 to get
    −4. Brackets around negative numbers prevent this. Now you try: for
    r(x) = x³ − 2x + 1 find r(1), r(−2) and r(1/2). (0; −3; 1/8)

D3. Find the zeros of 2x + 5, 3x, x² − 5x + 6, x² − 9, x² + 4 and x³ − 4x. How
    many zeros can a polynomial of degree n have?
    Answer: −5/2; 0; 2 and 3; 3 and −3; none (no real zero); 0, 2 and −2. At
    most n.
    Teacher explains: A zero solves p(x) = 0.
           2x + 5 = 0          x = −5/2
           3x = 0              x = 0
           x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0      x = 2 or x = 3
           x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3) = 0           x = 3 or x = −3
           x² + 4 = 0          x² = −4: no real number works
           x³ − 4x = x(x − 2)(x + 2) = 0         x = 0, 2 or −2
    For a linear polynomial ax + b the zero is always −b/a. A product is 0 only
    when one of its factors is 0, so factorising finds zeros. A polynomial of
    degree n has at most n zeros (a quadratic at most 2, a cubic at most 3), but
    it may have fewer: x² + 4 has none, because x² + 4 ≥ 4 for every real x. 0
    is a zero exactly when the constant term is 0 (3x, x³ − 4x). Common mistake:
    saying x² − 9 has only the zero 3. Now you try: zeros of x² − 7x and 4x − 1.
    (0 and 7; 1/4)

D4. Draw the graph of y = x² − x − 6 for x from −3 to 4 and use it to read the
    zeros of x² − x − 6.
    Answer: The graph meets the x-axis at x = −2 and x = 3, so the zeros are −2
    and 3.
    Teacher explains: Make a table of values:
           x         −3   −2   −1    0    1    2    3    4
           y          6    0   −4   −6   −6   −4    0    6
    Plot the points (one row for every 2 units of y) and join them with a smooth
    U-shaped curve (a PARABOLA):
                     y
         6  *  .  .  |  .  .  .  *
         4  .  .  .  |  .  .  .  .
         2  .  .  .  |  .  .  .  .
         0 -+--*--+--+--+--+--*--+-- x
        −2  .  .  .  |  .  .  .  .
        −4  .  .  *  |  .  *  .  .
        −6  .  .  .  *  *  .  .  .
           −3 −2 −1  0  1  2  3  4
    The curve crosses the x-axis where y = 0, at (−2, 0) and (3, 0). So the
    zeros are the x-coordinates −2 and 3. Check by factorising:
    x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2). The graph also shows HOW MANY zeros: a parabola
    can cut the x-axis twice (as here), touch it once (y = (x − 2)², one zero 2)
    or miss it completely (y = x² + 1, no zero). A cubic always crosses at least
    once and at most three times. The value where the curve crosses the y-axis
    is p(0) = −6. Now you try: where does y = x² − 4 meet the axes? (x-axis at
    −2 and 2; y-axis at −4)

D5. Find the remainder when p(x) = x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 is divided by x + 1,
    x − 1/2, x and 5 + 2x, using the remainder theorem. Prove the theorem.
    Answer: p(−1) = 0; p(1/2) = 27/8; p(0) = 1; p(−5/2) = −27/8.
    Teacher explains: REMAINDER THEOREM: if p(x) is divided by (x − a), the
    remainder is p(a). So find the value of x that makes the divisor zero and
    substitute:
           x + 1 = 0     x = −1     p(−1)   = −1 + 3 − 3 + 1 = 0
           x − 1/2 = 0   x = 1/2    p(1/2)  = 1/8 + 3/4 + 3/2 + 1 = 27/8
           x = 0         x = 0      p(0)    = 1
           5 + 2x = 0    x = −5/2   p(−5/2) = −125/8 + 75/4 − 15/2 + 1
                                            = −27/8
    (p(x) = (x + 1)³, so p(−5/2) = (−3/2)³ = −27/8, a nice check.) PROOF: divide
    p(x) by (x − a). The divisor has degree 1, so the remainder r is a number:
    p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. Put x = a: p(a) = 0 × q(a) + r = r. For a divisor
    ax − b we get p(b/a) in the same way. Common mistake: substituting x = +1
    for the divisor x + 1: solve 'divisor = 0' first. Now you try: remainder of
    x³ − ax² + 6x − a divided by x − a. (5a)

D6. Find the remainder when 4x³ − 3x² + 2x − 4 is divided by x − 2, first by
    long division and then by the remainder theorem. Then find the remainder
    when x⁴ + x³ − 2x² + x + 1 is divided by x − 1.
    Answer: 20 both ways; 2.
    Teacher explains: Long division (divide the leading terms, multiply,
    subtract, bring down):
                 4x² + 5x + 12
               _______________________
       x − 2 ) 4x³ − 3x² +  2x −  4
               4x³ − 8x²                   4x³ ÷ x = 4x²
               ---------
                     5x² +  2x             subtract, bring down
                     5x² − 10x             5x² ÷ x = 5x
                     ---------
                           12x −  4
                           12x − 24        12x ÷ x = 12
                           --------
                                  20       remainder
    Remainder theorem: p(2) = 4(8) − 3(4) + 2(2) − 4 = 32 − 12 + 4 − 4 = 20.
    Same answer, much faster! Long division also gives the QUOTIENT
    4x² + 5x + 12; the theorem gives only the remainder. For the second:
    p(1) = 1 + 1 − 2 + 1 + 1 = 2 (at x = 1, p(1) is just the sum of the
    coefficients). Common mistake in long division: subtracting −8x² as −8x²
    instead of adding 8x²: −3x² − (−8x²) = 5x². Now you try: remainder of
    x³ − 6x² + 2x − 4 divided by 1 − 2x. (p(1/2) = −35/8)

D7. (a) When x³ + ax² − 5x + 6 is divided by x − 2, the remainder is 8. Find a.
    (b) The polynomials ax³ + 4x² + 3x − 4 and x³ − 4x + a leave the same
    remainder when divided by x − 3. Find a.
    Answer: (a) a = 1. (b) a = −1.
    Teacher explains: Use the remainder theorem to turn each fact into an
    EQUATION in a. (a) p(2) = 8 + 4a − 10 + 6 = 4a + 4. The remainder is 8, so
    4a + 4 = 8 and a = 1. Check: p(x) = x³ + x² − 5x + 6,
    p(2) = 8 + 4 − 10 + 6 = 8. (b) Remainder of the first:
    27a + 36 + 9 − 4 = 27a + 41. Remainder of the second: 27 − 12 + a = 15 + a.
    They are equal: 27a + 41 = 15 + a, so 26a = −26 and a = −1. Check: first
    −27 + 41 = 14, second 15 − 1 = 14. Common mistake: forgetting that a appears
    in BOTH polynomials in (b). Now you try: find k if x³ + kx² + 2x − 3 leaves
    remainder 5 when divided by x + 1. (−1 + k − 2 − 3 = 5, k = 11)

D8. Is x + 1 a factor of x³ + x² + x + 1? Of x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1? Is 2x + 1 a
    factor of 4x³ + 4x² − x − 1? State and prove the factor theorem.
    Answer: Yes (p(−1) = 0); no (p(−1) = 1); yes (p(−1/2) = 0).
    Teacher explains: FACTOR THEOREM: x − a is a factor of p(x) if and only if
    p(a) = 0.
       x³ + x² + x + 1:        p(−1) = −1 + 1 − 1 + 1 = 0           factor
       x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1:   p(−1) = 1 − 1 + 1 − 1 + 1 = 1        not a factor
       4x³ + 4x² − x − 1:      p(−1/2) = −1/2 + 1 + 1/2 − 1 = 0     factor
    (2x + 1 = 0 gives x = −1/2.) PROOF: by the remainder theorem
    p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + p(a). If p(a) = 0, then p(x) = (x − a)q(x), so x − a is
    a factor. Conversely, if x − a is a factor, p(x) = (x − a)q(x), and putting
    x = a gives p(a) = 0. Indeed x³ + x² + x + 1 = (x + 1)(x² + 1) and
    4x³ + 4x² − x − 1 = (2x + 1)(2x² + x − 1) = (2x + 1)(2x − 1)(x + 1). Now you
    try: is x − 3 a factor of x³ − 3x² + 4x − 12? (p(3) = 27 − 27 + 12 − 12 = 0:
    yes)

D9. (a) Find k if x − 2 is a factor of x³ − 3x² + kx − 10. (b) Find a and b if
    x − 1 and x + 2 are both factors of x³ + ax² + bx − 6.
    Answer: (a) k = 7. (b) a = 4, b = 1.
    Teacher explains: A factor gives value ZERO, so each factor gives an
    equation. (a) p(2) = 8 − 12 + 2k − 10 = 2k − 14 = 0, so k = 7. Check:
    x³ − 3x² + 7x − 10 at x = 2: 8 − 12 + 14 − 10 = 0. (b) Two factors give two
    equations:
           p(1)  = 1 + a + b − 6 = 0          a + b = 5
           p(−2) = −8 + 4a − 2b − 6 = 0       4a − 2b = 14, so 2a − b = 7
    Add: 3a = 12, a = 4, then b = 1. So p(x) = x³ + 4x² + x − 6, and in fact
    p(x) = (x − 1)(x + 2)(x + 3): the third factor comes from comparing constant
    terms, (−1)(2)(c) = −6 gives c = 3. Common mistake: using p(2) for the
    factor x + 2. Now you try: find k if x + 1 is a factor of
    2x³ + kx² − 3x − 4. (−2 + k + 3 − 4 = 0, k = 3)

D10. Factorise x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120.
     Answer: (x − 1)(x − 10)(x − 12).
     Teacher explains: Step 1: look for a zero among the divisors of the
     constant term 120: ±1, ±2, ±3, ±4, ±5, ±6, ±8, ±10, ... Try x = 1 first:
     p(1) = 1 − 23 + 142 − 120 = 0 (the coefficients add up to 0). So x − 1 is a
     factor. Step 2: divide by x − 1 (or compare coefficients):
                   x² − 22x + 120
                _________________________
        x − 1 ) x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120
                x³ −   x²
                ----------
                    − 22x² + 142x
                    − 22x² +  22x
                    -------------
                              120x − 120
                              120x − 120
                              ----------
                                       0
     Step 3: factorise the quadratic: two numbers with product 120 and sum −22
     are −10 and −12, so x² − 22x + 120 = (x − 10)(x − 12). So
     x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120 = (x − 1)(x − 10)(x − 12). Check at x = 2:
     8 − 92 + 284 − 120 = 80 and (1)(−8)(−10) = 80. Now you try: factorise
     x³ − 2x² − x + 2. ((x − 1)(x + 1)(x − 2))

D11. Factorise x³ + 13x² + 32x + 20 and 2y³ + y² − 2y − 1.
     Answer: (x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 10); (y − 1)(y + 1)(2y + 1).
     Teacher explains: For x³ + 13x² + 32x + 20 all the terms are positive, so a
     POSITIVE x can never give 0: try negatives. p(−1) = −1 + 13 − 32 + 20 = 0,
     so x + 1 is a factor. Compare coefficients instead of long division:
     x³ + 13x² + 32x + 20 = (x + 1)(x² + bx + 20). The x² terms: 13 = b + 1, so
     b = 12. Then x² + 12x + 20 = (x + 2)(x + 10). For 2y³ + y² − 2y − 1:
     coefficients 2 + 1 − 2 − 1 = 0, so y − 1 is a factor; or group:
        2y³ + y² − 2y − 1 = y²(2y + 1) − 1(2y + 1) = (2y + 1)(y² − 1)
                          = (2y + 1)(y − 1)(y + 1)
     When the leading coefficient is not 1, zeros may be FRACTIONS ±c/d, with c
     dividing the constant term and d dividing the leading coefficient; here
     y = −1/2 is a zero. Always finish by factorising the quadratic completely.
     Now you try: factorise x³ − 3x² − 9x − 5 and 3x³ − x² − 3x + 1.
     ((x + 1)²(x − 5); (x − 1)(x + 1)(3x − 1))

D12. A closed box has volume x³ + 6x² + 11x + 6 cm³, and each edge is a linear
     expression in x with whole-number coefficients. Find expressions for the
     edges, and the volume when x = 4.
     Answer: The edges are (x + 1), (x + 2) and (x + 3) cm; when x = 4 the box
     is 5 × 6 × 7 cm and the volume is 210 cm³.
     Teacher explains: Factorise the volume polynomial. All coefficients are
     positive, so try x = −1: p(−1) = −1 + 6 − 11 + 6 = 0, so x + 1 is a factor.
     Then x³ + 6x² + 11x + 6 = (x + 1)(x² + 5x + 6) = (x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 3). The
     three factors are the three edges (length × breadth × height = volume). For
     x = 4: 5 × 6 × 7 = 210 cm³. Check directly: p(4) = 64 + 96 + 44 + 6 = 210.
     This is the everyday meaning of 'factor': the volume is built by
     MULTIPLYING the edges. The factorisation is unique, so there is no other
     set of such edges (apart from order). Now you try: a rectangle has area
     25a² − 35a + 12. Find expressions for its sides. ((5a − 3) and (5a − 4))

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Is it a polynomial in one variable? If yes, give its degree.
    a) 4x² − 3x + 7   b) y³ + √2 y       c) 3√t + t√2         d) y + 2/y
    e) 5              f) x^(1/2) + 1     g) √3 x² − 2         h) 1/x² + 3
    i) 7x⁴ − x        j) 0               k) x(x − 1)(x + 2)   l) (x + 1)/2
