TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: write a₁, b₁, c₁, a₂, b₂, c₂ in a small table before comparing
  ratios or cross-multiplying; draw both lines in Desmos to SEE 'intersecting,
  parallel, coincident'; for word problems write 'Let x = ...' with units, one
  equation per sentence, and check the answer in the original words; for
  1/x-type equations always write 'u = 1/x' on its own line. Harder: derive the
  cross-multiplication formula by eliminating y from the general pair; find all
  k for which kx + y = 1, x + ky = 1 has no solution, one solution, infinitely
  many; solve three equations in three unknowns (x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2,
  2x + y − z = 1); a boat problem where the answer shows the boat cannot go
  upstream (stream faster than the boat).


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.9 — QUADRATIC EQUATIONS: FACTORISATION, COMPLETING THE SQUARE, QUADRATIC
            FORMULA
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A QUADRATIC EQUATION has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0 (standard
    form). Its solutions are called ROOTS. A quadratic equation has at most TWO
    real roots. A number is a root exactly when it makes the equation true:
    substitute it to CHECK.
  - ZERO PRODUCT RULE: if p × q = 0 then p = 0 or q = 0. So FIRST make one side
    0, then factorise: (x − 3)(x + 5) = 0 gives x = 3 or x = −5. Never divide
    both sides by x: you lose the root x = 0.
  - FACTORISATION: x² + bx + c: two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.
    ax² + bx + c: split the middle term using two numbers that multiply to a × c
    and add to b. Special cases: x² − 49 = (x + 7)(x − 7); 3x² = 12x gives
    3x(x − 4) = 0.
  - COMPLETING THE SQUARE: x² + bx = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)². To solve
    x² + 6x − 7 = 0: (x + 3)² − 9 − 7 = 0, (x + 3)² = 16, x + 3 = ±4, x = 1 or
    −7. If a ≠ 1, divide every term by a first. Remember the ± when taking a
    square root.
  - QUADRATIC FORMULA (proved by completing the square): the roots of
    ax² + bx + c = 0 are x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a). Write a, b, c WITH their
    signs first. Simplify surds (√20 = 2√5) and cancel common factors; give
    decimals to 2 d.p. when asked.
  - Which method? Factorise when the numbers are friendly; the formula ALWAYS
    works; completing the square gives the vertex form (topic 7.11) and the
    proof of the formula.
  - EQUATIONS REDUCIBLE TO QUADRATICS: clear fractions by multiplying by the LCD
    (x + 1/x = 10/3 gives 3x² − 10x + 3 = 0); substitute u = x² in
    x⁴ − 13x² + 36 = 0. Reject any value that makes a denominator zero.
  - WORD PROBLEMS: choose the unknown, write the other quantities using it, form
    the equation, bring it to standard form, solve, REJECT roots that make no
    sense (negative lengths, ages, speeds) and check in the story.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Solve (x − 3)(x + 5) = 0 and 2x(x − 7) = 0. Explain the zero product rule.
    Riya solves x² = 7x by dividing both sides by x and gets x = 7. What has she
    lost?
    Answer: x = 3 or x = −5; x = 0 or x = 7. Riya has lost the root x = 0.
    Teacher explains: If two numbers multiply to give 0, at least one of them
    MUST be 0 (if neither were 0, their product could not be 0). So:
        (x − 3)(x + 5) = 0
        x − 3 = 0   or   x + 5 = 0
            x = 3   or       x = −5
        2x(x − 7) = 0
        2x = 0   or   x − 7 = 0
         x = 0   or       x = 7
    Check x = −5: (−5 − 3)(−5 + 5) = (−8) × 0 = 0. For x² = 7x, bring everything
    to one side: x² − 7x = 0, x(x − 7) = 0, x = 0 or 7. Dividing by x is only
    allowed when x ≠ 0, so it throws away the root x = 0. Check: 0² = 7 × 0 is
    true. Common mistake: solving (x − 3)(x + 5) = 12 as x − 3 = 12 or
    x + 5 = 12. The rule works ONLY with 0 on one side. Now you try:
    (2x + 1)(x − 4) = 0 and 5x² = 20x. (x = −1/2 or 4; x = 0 or 4)

D2. Solve by factorisation: x² − 5x − 14 = 0 and x² + 9x + 20 = 0. Verify each
    root by substitution.
    Answer: x² − 5x − 14 = (x − 7)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 7 or x = −2.
    x² + 9x + 20 = (x + 4)(x + 5) = 0, so x = −4 or x = −5.
    Teacher explains: For x² − 5x − 14 we need two numbers with product −14 and
    sum −5. The product is negative, so the signs differ; the bigger number
    takes the sign of the middle term: −7 and +2.
        x² − 5x − 14 = 0
        (x − 7)(x + 2) = 0
        x = 7   or   x = −2
        check x = 7:   7² − 5 × 7 − 14 = 49 − 35 − 14 = 0
        check x = −2:  (−2)² − 5 × (−2) − 14 = 4 + 10 − 14 = 0
    For x² + 9x + 20: product +20, sum +9, so both numbers are positive: 4 and
    5. (x + 4)(x + 5) = 0 gives x = −4 or x = −5. Check x = −5:
    25 − 45 + 20 = 0. Notice the roots have the OPPOSITE signs to the numbers in
    the brackets. Common mistake: writing x = 4 and x = 5. Now you try:
    x² − 11x + 24 = 0 and x² + 3x − 40 = 0. (x = 3 or 8; x = −8 or 5)

D3. Solve 6x² − x − 2 = 0 by splitting the middle term. Check one root.
    Answer: 6x² − x − 2 = (3x − 2)(2x + 1) = 0, so x = 2/3 or x = −1/2.
    Teacher explains: a × c = 6 × (−2) = −12. We need two numbers with product
    −12 and sum −1: −4 and +3. Split −x into −4x + 3x and group:
        6x² − x − 2 = 0
        6x² − 4x + 3x − 2 = 0
        2x(3x − 2) + 1(3x − 2) = 0
        (3x − 2)(2x + 1) = 0
        3x − 2 = 0  or  2x + 1 = 0
            x = 2/3  or      x = −1/2
    Check x = 2/3: 6 × 4/9 − 2/3 − 2 = 8/3 − 2/3 − 2 = 2 − 2 = 0. When a ≠ 1 the
    roots are usually fractions: from (3x − 2) = 0 we get x = 2/3, NOT x = 2.
    Common mistake: stopping at (3x − 2)(2x + 1) and reading off x = 2 and
    x = −1. Now you try: 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0 and 4x² − 4x − 3 = 0. (x = 1/2 or −3;
    x = 3/2 or −1/2)

D4. Solve x(x + 3) = 40 and (x + 2)(x − 3) = 14. Arjun writes "x = 40 or
    x + 3 = 40" for the first one. What is wrong?
    Answer: x = 5 or x = −8; x = 5 or x = −4. Arjun used the zero product rule
    when the right-hand side was 40, not 0.
    Teacher explains: The zero product rule only works for a product equal to
    ZERO. Expand, bring everything to one side, then factorise:
        x(x + 3) = 40            (x + 2)(x − 3) = 14
        x² + 3x − 40 = 0         x² − x − 6 − 14 = 0
        (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0       x² − x − 20 = 0
        x = −8 or x = 5          (x − 5)(x + 4) = 0
                                 x = 5 or x = −4
    Check: 5 × 8 = 40 and (−8) × (−5) = 40; (5 + 2)(5 − 3) = 7 × 2 = 14 and
    (−4 + 2)(−4 − 3) = (−2) × (−7) = 14. Arjun's x = 40 gives 40 × 43 = 1,720,
    not 40. Also: x² − 9 = 0 needs x = ±3 (TWO roots), and 2x² = 50 gives
    x² = 25, x = ±5. Now you try: x(x − 2) = 35 and (x − 1)(x + 4) = 6. (x = 7
    or −5; x = 2 or −5)

D5. Solve x² + 6x − 7 = 0 by completing the square. Use a square diagram to
    explain the method. Then solve x² + 4x − 1 = 0 the same way.
    Answer: x = 1 or x = −7; x = −2 ± √5 ≈ 0.24 or −4.24.
    Teacher explains: Think of x² + 6x as a square x by x plus a strip 6 by x.
    Cut the strip in half and put one half on each side of the square:
              x      3
           +------+----+
         x |  x²  | 3x |
           +------+----+
         3 |  3x  | 9  |  <- the missing corner
           +------+----+
    The big square is (x + 3)², but the corner 9 was not in x² + 6x, so
    x² + 6x = (x + 3)² − 9. Half of the x-coefficient is 3, and we subtract
    3² = 9.
        x² + 6x − 7 = 0          x² + 4x − 1 = 0
        (x + 3)² − 9 − 7 = 0     (x + 2)² − 4 − 1 = 0
        (x + 3)² = 16            (x + 2)² = 5
        x + 3 = ±4               x + 2 = ±√5
        x = 1 or x = −7          x = −2 ± √5
    Check x = 1: 1 + 6 − 7 = 0. For the second, √5 ≈ 2.236, so x ≈ 0.24 or
    x ≈ −4.24. Common mistakes: forgetting the ± (it gives only ONE root), and
    writing (x + 6)² instead of halving 6. Now you try: x² − 8x + 12 = 0 and
    x² − 2x − 2 = 0. (x = 2 or 6; x = 1 ± √3)

D6. Solve 2x² − 5x + 1 = 0 by completing the square. Give exact roots and roots
    to 2 decimal places.
    Answer: x = (5 ± √17)/4 ≈ 2.28 or 0.22.
    Teacher explains: Step 1: make the x²-coefficient 1 by dividing EVERY term
    by 2. Step 2: half of −5/2 is −5/4, and (5/4)² = 25/16.
        2x² − 5x + 1 = 0
        x² − (5/2)x + 1/2 = 0
        (x − 5/4)² − 25/16 + 1/2 = 0
        (x − 5/4)² = 25/16 − 8/16 = 17/16
        x − 5/4 = ±√17/4
        x = (5 ± √17)/4
    With √17 ≈ 4.123: x ≈ (5 + 4.123)/4 ≈ 2.28 and x ≈ (5 − 4.123)/4 ≈ 0.22.
    Check the sum: 2.28 + 0.22 = 2.5 = 5/2, which is −b/a. Common mistakes:
    dividing only the x² term by 2; halving −5 instead of −5/2; writing
    √(17/16) = √17/16 (it is √17/4). Now you try: 3x² + 6x − 1 = 0.
    (x = (−3 ± 2√3)/3 ≈ 0.15 or −2.15)

D7. Prove the quadratic formula: the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) are
    x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a).
    Answer: Complete the square on the general equation; the steps are below.
    The formula gives real roots only when b² − 4ac ≥ 0.
    Teacher explains: Do exactly what we did with numbers, but with letters:
        ax² + bx + c = 0
        x² + (b/a)x + c/a = 0                 (divide by a ≠ 0)
        (x + b/(2a))² − b²/(4a²) + c/a = 0    (half of b/a is b/(2a))
        (x + b/(2a))² = b²/(4a²) − c/a
        (x + b/(2a))² = (b² − 4ac)/(4a²)      (common denominator 4a²)
        x + b/(2a) = ±√(b² − 4ac)/(2a)        (needs b² − 4ac ≥ 0)
        x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a)
    The step with ± is the key: a positive number has TWO square roots. The
    quantity b² − 4ac under the root is called the DISCRIMINANT (topic 7.10): if
    it is negative, there is no real square root and no real root. Check the
    formula on x² − 5x + 6 = 0: a = 1, b = −5, c = 6, b² − 4ac = 25 − 24 = 1,
    x = (5 ± 1)/2 = 3 or 2, the same as factorising (x − 2)(x − 3). Common
    mistake: writing −b ± √(b² − 4ac) over 2a with the fraction line only under
    the root. Now you try: use the formula on x² + 2x − 15 = 0. (a = 1, b = 2,
    c = −15, b² − 4ac = 64, x = 3 or −5)

D8. Use the quadratic formula to solve 3x² − 4x − 2 = 0 and x² − 6x + 4 = 0.
    Simplify the surds.
    Answer: x = (2 ± √10)/3 ≈ 1.72 or −0.39; x = 3 ± √5 ≈ 5.24 or 0.76.
    Teacher explains: Write a, b, c WITH their signs, then work out b² − 4ac
    separately:
        3x² − 4x − 2 = 0:  a = 3, b = −4, c = −2
        b² − 4ac = (−4)² − 4 × 3 × (−2) = 16 + 24 = 40
        x = (4 ± √40)/6 = (4 ± 2√10)/6 = (2 ± √10)/3
        x² − 6x + 4 = 0:   a = 1, b = −6, c = 4
        b² − 4ac = 36 − 16 = 20
        x = (6 ± √20)/2 = (6 ± 2√5)/2 = 3 ± √5
    Simplify √40 = √(4 × 10) = 2√10, then divide EVERY term on top by the common
    factor 2. With √10 ≈ 3.162: (2 + 3.162)/3 ≈ 1.72 and (2 − 3.162)/3 ≈ −0.39.
    Common mistakes: −b = −4 (it is +4 because b is −4); writing (−4)² as −16;
    cancelling only one term: (4 ± 2√10)/6 is NOT 4 ± √10/3. Now you try:
    x² + 4x − 3 = 0 and 2x² − 2x − 1 = 0. (x = −2 ± √7; x = (1 ± √3)/2)

D9. Solve (i) x + 1/x = 10/3, (ii) 1/x − 1/(x + 2) = 1/4 (x ≠ 0, −2), (iii)
    x⁴ − 13x² + 36 = 0.
    Answer: (i) x = 3 or 1/3; (ii) x = 2 or −4; (iii) x = ±2 or ±3.
    Teacher explains: These are not quadratic at first sight, but they BECOME
    quadratic. (i) Multiply every term by the LCD 3x:
        3x² + 3 = 10x  →  3x² − 10x + 3 = 0  →  (3x − 1)(x − 3) = 0
    so x = 1/3 or 3. Check: 3 + 1/3 = 10/3. (ii) Multiply by 4x(x + 2):
        4(x + 2) − 4x = x(x + 2)
        8 = x² + 2x  →  x² + 2x − 8 = 0  →  (x + 4)(x − 2) = 0
    x = −4 or 2. Neither makes a denominator zero, so both are allowed. Check
    x = 2: 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4. (iii) Put u = x²: u² − 13u + 36 = 0,
    (u − 4)(u − 9) = 0, u = 4 or 9, so x² = 4 or x² = 9 and x = ±2, ±3 (four
    roots, because the equation has degree 4). Common mistakes: multiplying only
    some terms by the LCD; forgetting to go back from u to x. Now you try:
    x − 1/x = 3/2 and x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0. (x = 2 or −1/2; x = ±1, ±2)

D10. A rectangular vegetable plot is 5 m longer than it is wide and its area is
     84 m². Find its length and width. Then: a square lawn has a path 2 m wide
     all round it; the lawn and path together cover 196 m². Find the side of the
     lawn.
     Answer: Width 7 m, length 12 m. The lawn has side 10 m.
     Teacher explains: Let the width be w m. Then the length is (w + 5) m and
         w(w + 5) = 84
         w² + 5w − 84 = 0
         (w + 12)(w − 7) = 0
         w = −12 or w = 7
     A width cannot be negative, so REJECT w = −12. Width 7 m, length 12 m.
     Check: 7 × 12 = 84 and 12 − 7 = 5. For the lawn, let its side be s m. The
     path adds 2 m on EACH side, so the outer square has side s + 4:
     (s + 4)² = 196, s + 4 = ±14, s = 10 or s = −18. Reject −18: the side is
     10 m. Check: 14 × 14 = 196. Common mistake: adding only 2 to the side (the
     path is on both sides). Now you try: the length of a rectangle is 3 cm more
     than twice its width and its area is 90 cm². Find its sides.
     (w(2w + 3) = 90 gives w = 6: 6 cm by 15 cm)

D11. The product of two consecutive odd positive integers is 143. Find them.
     Then: a father is 25 years older than his son and the product of their ages
     is 350. Find their ages.
     Answer: 11 and 13. The son is 10 and the father is 35.
     Teacher explains: Consecutive odd integers differ by 2: call them n and
     n + 2.
         n(n + 2) = 143
         n² + 2n − 143 = 0
         (n + 13)(n − 11) = 0
         n = 11  (reject −13: not positive)
     The integers are 11 and 13 (11 × 13 = 143). To factorise, look for two
     numbers with product −143 and difference 2: 13 and 11. For the ages, let
     the son be s years old; the father is s + 25:
         s(s + 25) = 350
         s² + 25s − 350 = 0
         (s + 35)(s − 10) = 0
         s = 10  (reject −35)
     Son 10, father 35; 10 × 35 = 350. Common mistake: calling the odd numbers n
     and n + 1 (those are consecutive integers, one odd and one even). Now you
     try: the sum of the squares of two consecutive natural numbers is 313; and
     two numbers differ by 3 and their product is 108. (12 and 13; 9 and 12, or
     −12 and −9)

D12. A train travels 360 km at a uniform speed. If the speed had been 5 km/h
     more, it would have taken 1 hour less. Find the speed of the train.
     Answer: 40 km/h.
     Teacher explains: Let the speed be v km/h. Time = distance ÷ speed, so the
     usual time is 360/v hours and the faster time is 360/(v + 5) hours. The
     faster time is 1 hour LESS:
         360/v − 360/(v + 5) = 1
         360(v + 5) − 360v = v(v + 5)      (× v(v + 5))
         1,800 = v² + 5v
         v² + 5v − 1,800 = 0
         (v + 45)(v − 40) = 0
         v = 40  (reject −45: a speed is positive)
     Check: 360 ÷ 40 = 9 h and 360 ÷ 45 = 8 h, which is 1 hour less. To
     factorise v² + 5v − 1,800, look for factors of 1,800 that differ by 5:
     45 × 40. If you cannot see them, use the formula:
     b² − 4ac = 25 + 7,200 = 7,225 = 85², v = (−5 ± 85)/2 = 40 or −45. Common
     mistake: writing 360/(v + 5) − 360/v = 1 (the slower time is the BIGGER
     one). Now you try: a plane left 30 minutes late; to reach a city 1,500 km
     away on time it flew 100 km/h faster than usual. Find its usual speed.
     (1500/v − 1500/(v + 100) = 1/2 gives v = 500 km/h)

M8. Write down a, b and c, then solve with the quadratic formula. Simplify
    surds; give decimals to 2 d.p.
    a) x² − 3x − 10 = 0   b) x² + 4x + 2 = 0    c) x² − 2x − 1 = 0
    d) 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0   e) 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0   f) 3x² + 5x + 1 = 0
    g) x² + 6x + 4 = 0    h) 5x² − 2x − 1 = 0   i) x² − x − 3 = 0
    j) 4x² + 4x − 1 = 0   k) 2x² + 7x + 4 = 0   l) 3x² − x − 1 = 0
    m) x² + 8x + 13 = 0   n) 6x² + x − 1 = 0    o) x² + 5x + 5 = 0
    p) 2x² − x − 4 = 0
    Answers: a) a = 1, b = −3, c = −10; x = −2, 5
             b) a = 1, b = 4, c = 2; x = −2 ± √2 ≈ −0.59, −3.41
             c) a = 1, b = −2, c = −1; x = 1 ± √2 ≈ 2.41, −0.41
             d) a = 2, b = 3, c = −5; x = −5/2, 1
             e) a = 2, b = −4, c = −3; x = (2 ± √10)/2 ≈ 2.58, −0.58
             f) a = 3, b = 5, c = 1; x = (−5 ± √13)/6 ≈ −0.23, −1.43
             g) a = 1, b = 6, c = 4; x = −3 ± √5 ≈ −0.76, −5.24
             h) a = 5, b = −2, c = −1; x = (1 ± √6)/5 ≈ 0.69, −0.29
             i) a = 1, b = −1, c = −3; x = (1 ± √13)/2 ≈ 2.30, −1.30
             j) a = 4, b = 4, c = −1; x = (−1 ± √2)/2 ≈ 0.21, −1.21
             k) a = 2, b = 7, c = 4; x = (−7 ± √17)/4 ≈ −0.72, −2.78
             l) a = 3, b = −1, c = −1; x = (1 ± √13)/6 ≈ 0.77, −0.43
             m) a = 1, b = 8, c = 13; x = −4 ± √3 ≈ −2.27, −5.73
             n) a = 6, b = 1, c = −1; x = −1/2, 1/3
             o) a = 1, b = 5, c = 5; x = (−5 ± √5)/2 ≈ −1.38, −3.62
             p) a = 2, b = −1, c = −4; x = (1 ± √33)/4 ≈ 1.69, −1.19

M9. Solve with the formula. Simplify the surds fully and cancel common factors.
    If there are no real roots, say so.
    a) x² − 2x − 2 = 0     b) x² + 6x + 3 = 0     c) x² − 8x + 8 = 0
    d) 2x² − 8x + 5 = 0    e) 3x² + 6x + 2 = 0    f) −x² + 4x + 1 = 0
    g) 9x² − 6x − 1 = 0    h) 4x² + 12x + 7 = 0   i) x² + x + 1 = 0
    j) 2x² − 3x + 4 = 0    k) x² − 10x + 25 = 0   l) 5x² − 3 = 0

    p) (x − 3)² = 2x
    Answers: a) x = 1 ± √3 ≈ 2.73, −0.73   b) x = −3 ± √6 ≈ −0.55, −5.45
             c) x = 4 ± 2√2 ≈ 6.83, 1.17   d) x = (4 ± √6)/2 ≈ 3.22, 0.78
             e) x = (−3 ± √3)/3 ≈ −0.42, −1.58   f) x = 2 ± √5 ≈ 4.24, −0.24
             g) x = (1 ± √2)/3 ≈ 0.80, −0.14   h) x = (−3 ± √2)/2 ≈ −0.79, −2.21
             i) no real roots   j) no real roots   k) x = 5 (twice)
             l) x = ±√15/5 ≈ 0.77, −0.77   m) x = (1 ± √13)/3 ≈ 1.54, −0.87
             n) x = −1 ± √2 ≈ 0.41, −2.41   o) x = (1 ± √7)/2 ≈ 1.82, −0.82
             p) x = 4 ± √7 ≈ 6.65, 1.35

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always make one side zero before factorising; list the factor
  pairs of c with their sums; use the formula when factorising takes longer than
  a minute; write a, b, c with signs in a little table; check every root by
  substituting it back. For completing the square, draw the square-and-strips
  picture every time until the rule "halve b, square it, subtract it" is
  automatic. Harder: solve x² − 2(a + b)x + 4ab = 0 for x in terms of a and b
  (x = 2a or 2b); solve √(x + 7) = x − 5 and reject the false root (x = 9; x = 2
  fails); solve 1/(a + b + x) = 1/a + 1/b + 1/x (x = −a or −b); find two
  consecutive even numbers whose squares add to 340 (12, 14 or −14, −12); a
  two-digit number is 4 times the sum of its digits and 3 times the product of
  its digits: find it (24).


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.10 — NATURE OF ROOTS AND DISCRIMINANT
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - For ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) the DISCRIMINANT is D = b² − 4ac. It is the
    number under the square root in the formula x = (−b ± √D)/(2a), so it
    DISCRIMINATES (tells apart) the kinds of roots without solving.
  - D > 0: two DISTINCT (different) real roots, (−b + √D)/(2a) and
    (−b − √D)/(2a). D = 0: two EQUAL real roots (one repeated root),
    x = −b/(2a). D < 0: NO real roots, because a negative number has no real
    square root.
  - "Real roots" means D ≥ 0 (distinct OR equal). "Distinct real roots" means
    D > 0. "No real roots" means D < 0.
  - RATIONAL or IRRATIONAL: when a, b, c are rational and D > 0, the roots are
    rational exactly when D is a PERFECT SQUARE (of a rational number);
    otherwise they involve a surd. A perfect-square D also means the quadratic
    factorises with rational numbers.
  - GRAPH: the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 are the x-intercepts of
    y = ax² + bx + c. D > 0: the parabola CUTS the x-axis twice; D = 0: it
    TOUCHES the x-axis once (at its vertex); D < 0: it does not meet the x-axis.
  - FINDING k: write a, b, c in terms of k (keep the signs and brackets), form
    D, then solve D = 0, D ≥ 0, D > 0 or D < 0 as the question asks. If k is in
    the x²-coefficient, remember that a ≠ 0 (so k cannot make a zero).
  - Proving roots are always real: show that D is a square or a sum of squares
    plus something positive, for example D = (a − b)² + 4 > 0.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Explain why the number b² − 4ac decides whether ax² + bx + c = 0 has two,
    one or no real roots. Illustrate with x² − 6x + 5 = 0, x² − 6x + 9 = 0 and
    x² − 6x + 13 = 0.
    Answer: The roots are (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a). If b² − 4ac > 0 the ± gives
    two different values; if it is 0 both values are −b/(2a); if it is negative
    there is no real square root. The three equations have D = 16, 0, −16: roots
    1 and 5; 3 (repeated); no real roots.
    Teacher explains: Look at the formula: everything is an ordinary number
    EXCEPT √D. Work out D for each equation (a = 1, b = −6 in all three):
        x² − 6x + 5 = 0:   D = 36 − 20 = 16 > 0   x = (6 ± 4)/2 = 5 or 1
        x² − 6x + 9 = 0:   D = 36 − 36 = 0        x = (6 ± 0)/2 = 3, 3
        x² − 6x + 13 = 0:  D = 36 − 52 = −16 < 0  √(−16) is not real
    Completing the square shows the same thing: x² − 6x + 13 = (x − 3)² + 4, and
    (x − 3)² + 4 is at least 4, so it can never be 0. Common mistake: saying
    "D = 0 means no roots". D = 0 means ONE repeated root (two equal roots). Now
    you try: find D and the nature of the roots of x² + 2x + 3 = 0 and
    x² + 2x − 3 = 0. (D = −8, no real roots; D = 16, two distinct real roots)

D2. Find the discriminant and state the nature of the roots of (i)
    2x² − 3x + 5 = 0, (ii) 4x² − 12x + 9 = 0, (iii) 3x² − 2x − 4 = 0. Find the
    roots when they are real.
    Answer: (i) D = −31: no real roots. (ii) D = 0: equal roots, x = 3/2
    (twice). (iii) D = 52: two distinct irrational roots, x = (1 ± √13)/3.
    Teacher explains: Write a, b, c with signs, then substitute carefully, using
    brackets for negative numbers:
        (i)   a = 2, b = −3, c = 5:   D = (−3)² − 4 × 2 × 5 = 9 − 40 = −31
        (ii)  a = 4, b = −12, c = 9:  D = 144 − 144 = 0
              x = −b/(2a) = 12/8 = 3/2
        (iii) a = 3, b = −2, c = −4:  D = 4 − 4 × 3 × (−4) = 4 + 48 = 52
              x = (2 ± √52)/6 = (2 ± 2√13)/6 = (1 ± √13)/3
    In (ii), 4x² − 12x + 9 = (2x − 3)², a perfect square, which is why the roots
    are equal. In (iii), c is negative, so −4ac is POSITIVE and D is bigger than
    b². Common mistakes: writing (−3)² as −9, and forgetting that −4 × 3 × (−4)
    is +48. Now you try: 5x² + 2x + 1 = 0 and 9x² + 6x + 1 = 0. (D = −16, no
    real roots; D = 0, x = −1/3 twice)

D3. Both 6x² − x − 2 = 0 and x² − 2x − 4 = 0 have two distinct real roots.
    Without solving, decide which one has rational roots and which has
    irrational roots. Explain the rule.
    Answer: 6x² − x − 2 = 0 has D = 49 = 7², a perfect square: rational roots
    (2/3 and −1/2). x² − 2x − 4 = 0 has D = 20, not a perfect square: irrational
    roots (1 ± √5).
    Teacher explains: The roots are (−b ± √D)/(2a). With whole-number a, b, c,
    the only part that can be irrational is √D.
        6x² − x − 2:  D = 1 + 48 = 49,  √49 = 7    x = (1 ± 7)/12
                      x = 8/12 = 2/3  or  x = −6/12 = −1/2
        x² − 2x − 4:  D = 4 + 16 = 20,  √20 = 2√5  x = (2 ± 2√5)/2
                      x = 1 ± √5
    So: D a perfect square (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...) gives rational roots and
    the quadratic FACTORISES: 6x² − x − 2 = (3x − 2)(2x + 1). D positive but not
    a perfect square gives a pair of surd roots p ± √q (they come in CONJUGATE
    pairs). This is a quick test of whether it is worth trying to factorise. Now
    you try: rational or irrational roots? 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0 and x² + 3x − 1 = 0.
    (D = 49, rational; D = 13, irrational)

D4. Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 16 = 0 has equal roots, and find
    the roots. Then do the same for 2x² + kx + 3 = 0.
    Answer: k = 8 (root −4) or k = −8 (root 4). For the second, k = ±2√6, with
    roots x = ∓√6/2.
    Teacher explains: Equal roots means D = 0. Here a = 1, b = k, c = 16:
        D = k² − 4 × 1 × 16 = k² − 64 = 0
        k² = 64,  k = ±8
        k = 8:  x² + 8x + 16 = (x + 4)² = 0, x = −4 (twice)
        k = −8: x² − 8x + 16 = (x − 4)² = 0, x = 4 (twice)
    The repeated root is always x = −b/(2a) = −k/2. For 2x² + kx + 3 = 0:
    D = k² − 24 = 0, k² = 24, k = ±√24 = ±2√6. The root is
    −k/(2a) = −k/4 = ∓2√6/4 = ∓√6/2. Common mistake: giving only k = 8; k² = 64
    has TWO square roots. Now you try: x² − kx + 25 = 0 and 3x² + kx + 12 = 0
    have equal roots. (k = ±10; k = ±12)

D5. Find k if kx² − 6x + 1 = 0 has equal roots. Then find k if x² − 5x + k = 0
    has equal roots. Why must k ≠ 0 in the first equation?
    Answer: k = 9 (root x = 1/3); k = 25/4 (root x = 5/2). If k = 0 the first
    equation becomes −6x + 1 = 0, which is not quadratic.
    Teacher explains: First equation: a = k, b = −6, c = 1.
        D = (−6)² − 4 × k × 1 = 36 − 4k = 0,  k = 9
        9x² − 6x + 1 = (3x − 1)² = 0,  x = 1/3 (twice)
    Second equation: a = 1, b = −5, c = k: D = 25 − 4k = 0, so k = 25/4 and
    x² − 5x + 25/4 = (x − 5/2)², root 5/2. A quadratic needs a ≠ 0. With k = 0
    the first equation is LINEAR and has exactly one root x = 1/6, but it is not
    a quadratic with "equal roots". So whenever k is in the x²-coefficient,
    write the condition k ≠ 0 in your answer. Now you try: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 and
    4x² − 12x + k = 0 have equal roots. (k = 4; k = 9)

D6. For what values of k does x² − 4x + k = 0 have (i) two distinct real roots,
    (ii) equal roots, (iii) real roots, (iv) no real roots?
    Answer: D = 16 − 4k. (i) k < 4, (ii) k = 4, (iii) k ≤ 4, (iv) k > 4.
    Teacher explains: D = (−4)² − 4 × 1 × k = 16 − 4k. Now turn each condition
    into an inequality in k:
        (i)   D > 0:  16 − 4k > 0,  16 > 4k,  k < 4
        (ii)  D = 0:  16 − 4k = 0,  k = 4
        (iii) D ≥ 0:  16 − 4k ≥ 0,  k ≤ 4
        (iv)  D < 0:  16 − 4k < 0,  k > 4
    Check with numbers: k = 3 gives x² − 4x + 3 = (x − 1)(x − 3), two roots;
    k = 5 gives D = −4, no real roots. "Real roots" includes the equal case, so
    (iii) uses ≤. Common mistake: when dividing an inequality by a NEGATIVE
    number the sign turns round: −4k > −16 gives k < 4. Now you try: for which k
    does 2x² + 3x + k = 0 have real roots? (9 − 8k ≥ 0, k ≤ 9/8)

D7. Find the values of k for which (k + 1)x² − 2(k − 1)x + 1 = 0 has equal
    roots.
    Answer: k = 0 or k = 3.
    Teacher explains: Take a, b, c WITH their brackets: a = k + 1,
    b = −2(k − 1), c = 1.
        D = [−2(k − 1)]² − 4(k + 1)(1)
          = 4(k − 1)² − 4(k + 1)
          = 4(k² − 2k + 1) − 4k − 4
          = 4k² − 12k
          = 4k(k − 3)
        D = 0:  k = 0 or k = 3
    Check: a = k + 1 is not 0 for either value, so both are allowed. k = 0:
    x² + 2x + 1 = (x + 1)², root −1. k = 3: 4x² − 4x + 1 = (2x − 1)², root 1/2.
    The equation for k itself is a quadratic here, so we may get two values.
    Common mistake: writing [−2(k − 1)]² as −4(k − 1)²; squaring always gives a
    positive coefficient. Now you try: (k − 12)x² + 2(k − 12)x + 2 = 0 has equal
    roots; find k. (D = 4(k − 12)(k − 14), k = 14; reject k = 12 because then
    a = 0)

D8. Sketch y = x² − 4x + 3, y = x² − 4x + 4 and y = x² − 4x + 5. Link the number
    of x-intercepts to the discriminant.
    Answer: D = 4, 0 and −4. The first graph cuts the x-axis at 1 and 3, the
    second touches it at 2, the third does not meet it.
    Teacher explains: The x-intercepts are where y = 0, which are exactly the
    real roots of x² − 4x + c = 0. All three graphs have the same shape and axis
    x = 2; increasing c lifts the graph up.
        y = x² − 4x + 3 (D = 4 > 0): cuts twice at (1, 0) and (3, 0)
                 y
          5   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
          4   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
          3   .  *  .  .  .  *  .
          2   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
          1   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
          0 --+--+--*--+--*--+--+-x
         −1   .  |  .  *  .  .  .
         −2   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
         −3   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
         −4   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
             −1  0  1  2  3  4  5
        y = x² − 4x + 4 (D = 0): touches at (2, 0)
                 y
          5   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
          4   .  *  .  .  .  *  .
          3   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
          2   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
          1   .  |  *  .  *  .  .
          0 --+--+--+--*--+--+--+-x
         −1   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
             −1  0  1  2  3  4  5
        y = x² − 4x + 5 (D = −4 < 0): lowest point (2, 1), no x-intercepts
                 y
          5   .  *  .  .  .  *  .
          4   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
          3   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
          2   .  |  *  .  *  .  .
          1   .  |  .  *  .  .  .
          0 --+--+--+--+--+--+--+-x
         −1   .  |  .  .  .  .  .
             −1  0  1  2  3  4  5
    For a < 0 the parabola opens DOWN, but the rule is the same: D > 0 two
    crossings, D = 0 one touching point, D < 0 none. Now you try: how many times
    does y = 2x² + x + 1 meet the x-axis? And y = −x² + 6x − 9? (D = −7: never;
    D = 0: touches once at (3, 0))

D9. Prove that the equation (x − a)(x − b) = 1 has two distinct real roots for
    all real numbers a and b. Also prove that x² + px − 1 = 0 has real roots for
    every p.
    Answer: D = (a − b)² + 4 > 0 and D = p² + 4 > 0, so both always have two
    distinct real roots.
    Teacher explains: Expand and write in standard form first:
        (x − a)(x − b) = 1
        x² − (a + b)x + ab − 1 = 0
        D = (a + b)² − 4(ab − 1)
          = a² + 2ab + b² − 4ab + 4
          = a² − 2ab + b² + 4
          = (a − b)² + 4
    A square is never negative, so (a − b)² ≥ 0 and D ≥ 4 > 0. Hence there are
    always two distinct real roots. For x² + px − 1 = 0:
    D = p² − 4(1)(−1) = p² + 4 ≥ 4 > 0. In fact whenever a and c have OPPOSITE
    signs, −4ac > 0 and the roots are real and distinct. The proof strategy:
    write D as a square plus a positive number. Now you try: show that
    x² + kx + k² + 1 = 0 has no real roots for any k.
    (D = k² − 4k² − 4 = −3k² − 4 < 0)

D10. Is it possible to design a rectangular park with perimeter 80 m and area
     400 m²? If so, find its length and breadth. What about area 500 m²?
     Answer: Area 400 m²: yes, exactly one way, a 20 m by 20 m square. Area 500
     m²: impossible (D < 0).
     Teacher explains: Perimeter 80 m means length + breadth = 40 m. Let the
     length be x m; the breadth is (40 − x) m.
         x(40 − x) = 400
         40x − x² = 400
         x² − 40x + 400 = 0
         D = 1,600 − 1,600 = 0   equal roots: x = 40/2 = 20
     So the park is 20 m by 20 m (a square is a special rectangle). For 500 m²:
     x² − 40x + 500 = 0 has D = 1,600 − 2,000 = −400 < 0, so no such park
     exists. In fact 400 m² is the LARGEST area with perimeter 80 m (topic
     7.11). The discriminant answers "is it possible?" questions without
     solving. Now you try: can two numbers have sum 10 and product 30? And sum
     10 and product 21? (x² − 10x + 30 = 0, D = −20: no; x² − 10x + 21 = 0,
     D = 16: yes, 3 and 7)

D11. A ball is thrown up so that its height after t seconds is h = 20t − 5t²
     metres. Can it reach a height of 25 m? 20 m? 15 m? Use the discriminant.
     Answer: 25 m: no (D < 0). 20 m: yes, exactly once, at t = 2 s (D = 0), so
     20 m is the greatest height. 15 m: yes, twice, at t = 1 s (going up) and
     t = 3 s (coming down).
     Teacher explains: Set h equal to the height and bring to standard form:
         h = 25: 5t² − 20t + 25 = 0   D = 400 − 500 = −100 < 0
         h = 20: 5t² − 20t + 20 = 0   D = 400 − 400 = 0
         h = 15: 5t² − 20t + 15 = 0   D = 400 − 300 = 100 > 0
     D < 0 means the height is never 25 m. D = 0 means the ball is at 20 m at
     just one moment, t = 20/10 = 2 s: this is the top of its flight. D > 0
     gives two moments: 5(t² − 4t + 3) = 5(t − 1)(t − 3) = 0, t = 1 or 3. In
     real problems two roots often mean "on the way up and on the way down". Now
     you try: h = 30t − 5t². What is the greatest height? (5t² − 30t + H = 0 has
     D = 900 − 20H = 0 when H = 45 m)

D12. For which values of k does kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 have two distinct real roots?
     For which natural numbers k does x² − 5x + k = 0 have rational roots?
     Answer: k < 4 and k ≠ 0. Rational roots for k = 4 (roots 1, 4) and k = 6
     (roots 2, 3).
     Teacher explains: First equation: a = k, b = 4, c = 1, D = 16 − 4k. D > 0
     gives k < 4. But k = 0 makes the equation 4x + 1 = 0, which is not
     quadratic, so the answer is k < 4, k ≠ 0 (for example k = −2 or k = 3
     work). Second equation: D = 25 − 4k. Real roots need k ≤ 25/4, so the
     natural numbers to try are k = 1 to 6:
         k      1    2    3    4    5    6
         D     21   17   13    9    5    1
         square? no  no   no  yes   no  yes
     k = 4: x² − 5x + 4 = (x − 1)(x − 4); k = 6: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). A
     table is the safest way to search. Common mistake: forgetting the condition
     k ≠ 0 when k multiplies x². Now you try: for which k does kx² − 2x + 3 = 0
     have no real roots? (4 − 12k < 0: k > 1/3)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make a three-column table a | b | c before every calculation, with
  signs and brackets; practise (−b)² and −4ac with negative c until it is
  automatic; draw the three pictures (cuts, touches, misses) and label them
  D > 0, D = 0, D < 0; for k problems write the condition in words first ("equal
  roots, so D = 0"). Harder: show that if a, b, c are rational and a + b + c = 0
  then ax² + bx + c = 0 has rational roots (x = 1 is a root); prove that
  (a² + b²)x² + 2(ac + bd)x + c² + d² = 0 has no real roots unless ad = bc
  (D = −4(ad − bc)²); find all k for which BOTH x² − kx + 9 = 0 and
  x² − 6x + k = 0 have real roots (k ≤ −6 or 6 ≤ k ≤ 9).


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.11 — QUADRATIC FUNCTIONS AND PARABOLAS: VERTEX FORM, AXIS OF SYMMETRY,
             MAX/MIN
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The graph of a QUADRATIC FUNCTION y = ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0) is a PARABOLA. If
    a > 0 it opens UP (a "U", with a lowest point, a MINIMUM); if a < 0 it opens
    DOWN (a "cap", with a highest point, a MAXIMUM). The bigger |a| is, the
    narrower the parabola.
  - The turning point is the VERTEX. Its x-coordinate is h = −b/(2a); put h into
    the function to get its y-coordinate k. Example: y = 2x² − 8x + 3 has
    h = 8/4 = 2 and k = 8 − 16 + 3 = −5, vertex (2, −5).
  - VERTEX FORM: y = a(x − h)² + k has vertex (h, k). Get it by completing the
    square: x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4. Watch the sign: (x + 2)² means h = −2.
  - AXIS OF SYMMETRY: the vertical line x = h through the vertex. Points with
    the same y-value are mirror images in it, so the axis is halfway between
    them (also halfway between the two x-intercepts).
  - INTERCEPTS: y-intercept (0, c), found by putting x = 0. x-intercepts: solve
    ax² + bx + c = 0 (two, one or none, decided by the discriminant, topic
    7.10).
  - MAXIMUM/MINIMUM and RANGE: for a > 0 the minimum value is k (when x = h) and
    the range is y ≥ k; for a < 0 the maximum value is k and the range is y ≤ k.
    The domain is all real x.
  - SKETCHING: (1) direction of opening, (2) y-intercept, (3) x-intercepts, (4)
    vertex and axis, (5) the mirror image of the y-intercept, then a smooth
    symmetric U through the points (never a V with a sharp point).
  - WRITING THE EQUATION: from the vertex (h, k) and one more point use
    y = a(x − h)² + k and find a; from the x-intercepts p and q and one more
    point use y = a(x − p)(x − q).
  - OPTIMISATION: write the quantity (area, height, profit) as a quadratic in
    one variable, then its vertex gives the greatest or least value.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Make a table of values for y = x² − 2x − 3 for x = −2 to 4 and plot the
    graph. Describe its shape and read off the vertex, the axis of symmetry and
    the intercepts.
    Answer: y = 5, 0, −3, −4, −3, 0, 5. A U-shaped parabola with vertex (1, −4),
    axis x = 1, y-intercept (0, −3) and x-intercepts (−1, 0) and (3, 0).
    Teacher explains: Work out each y with brackets for negative x: x = −2 gives
    (−2)² − 2 × (−2) − 3 = 4 + 4 − 3 = 5.
        x   −2   −1    0    1    2    3    4
        y    5    0   −3   −4   −3    0    5
                    y
          5   *  .  |  .  .  .  *
          4   .  .  |  .  .  .  .
          3   .  .  |  .  .  .  .
          2   .  .  |  .  .  .  .
          1   .  .  |  .  .  .  .
          0 --+--*--+--+--+--*--+-x
         −1   .  .  |  .  .  .  .
         −2   .  .  |  .  .  .  .
         −3   .  .  *  .  *  .  .
         −4   .  .  |  *  .  .  .
             −2 −1  0  1  2  3  4
    The y-values go down and then come back up in MIRROR pairs (0 and 2 both
    give −3; −1 and 3 both give 0). The mirror line is x = 1, and the lowest
    point (1, −4) is the vertex. Join the points with a smooth curve, not
    straight segments, and not a sharp V at the bottom. Common mistake:
    (−2)² − 2 × (−2) − 3 worked as −4 + 4 − 3. Now you try: table for
    y = x² − 4x + 3 for x = 0 to 4 and its vertex. (3, 0, −1, 0, 3; vertex
    (2, −1))

D2. Find the vertex of y = 2x² − 8x + 3 and of y = −x² − 4x + 1 using
    h = −b/(2a). Say whether each vertex is a maximum or a minimum point.
    Answer: (2, −5), a minimum point (a = 2 > 0); (−2, 5), a maximum point
    (a = −1 < 0).
    Teacher explains: The formula h = −b/(2a) is the x-value halfway between the
    two roots (−b ± √D)/(2a), so it is the axis of symmetry.
        y = 2x² − 8x + 3:   a = 2, b = −8
        h = −(−8)/(2 × 2) = 8/4 = 2
        k = 2 × 2² − 8 × 2 + 3 = 8 − 16 + 3 = −5
        y = −x² − 4x + 1:   a = −1, b = −4
        h = −(−4)/(2 × (−1)) = 4/(−2) = −2
        k = −(−2)² − 4 × (−2) + 1 = −4 + 8 + 1 = 5
    a > 0 gives a U, so the vertex is the LOWEST point; a < 0 gives a cap, so
    the vertex is the HIGHEST point. Common mistakes: forgetting the minus in
    −b/(2a); working out −(−2)² as +4 (the square is done first: −(4) = −4). Now
    you try: vertex of y = x² + 6x + 1 and of y = −3x² + 6x + 2. ((−3, −8)
    minimum; (1, 5) maximum)

D3. Write y = −x² + 6x − 5 and y = 2x² + 12x + 13 in vertex form a(x − h)² + k
    by completing the square. State the vertex and the greatest or least value
    of y.
    Answer: y = −(x − 3)² + 4: vertex (3, 4), greatest value 4.
    y = 2(x + 3)² − 5: vertex (−3, −5), least value −5.
    Teacher explains: When a ≠ 1, take a out of the x² and x terms FIRST:
        y = −x² + 6x − 5              y = 2x² + 12x + 13
          = −(x² − 6x) − 5              = 2(x² + 6x) + 13
          = −[(x − 3)² − 9] − 5         = 2[(x + 3)² − 9] + 13
          = −(x − 3)² + 9 − 5           = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 13
          = −(x − 3)² + 4               = 2(x + 3)² − 5
    Why is 4 the greatest value of −(x − 3)² + 4? Because (x − 3)² ≥ 0, so
    −(x − 3)² ≤ 0 and y ≤ 4, with y = 4 only when x = 3. Similarly 2(x + 3)² ≥ 0
    gives y ≥ −5. Common mistakes: 2[(x + 3)² − 9] + 13 written as
    2(x + 3)² − 9 + 13 (the −9 must be multiplied by 2 too), and reading the
    vertex of (x + 3)² as x = 3. Now you try: vertex form of y = x² − 10x + 21
    and y = −2x² − 4x + 1. ((x − 5)² − 4; −2(x + 1)² + 3)

D4. A parabola passes through (1, 7) and (5, 7). Find its axis of symmetry. If
    it is y = x² − 6x + 12, find the point symmetric to its y-intercept. Another
    parabola crosses the x-axis at −1 and 5: find its axis.
    Answer: Axis x = 3; the y-intercept (0, 12) has mirror image (6, 12). The
    second axis is x = 2.
    Teacher explains: Points at the SAME height on a parabola are mirror images
    in the axis, so the axis is exactly halfway between them:
        axis:  x = (1 + 5)/2 = 3
        y-intercept of x² − 6x + 12: (0, 12)
        0 is 3 to the left of the axis, so its mirror is 3 to the right:
        x = 3 + 3 = 6, and check: 6² − 6 × 6 + 12 = 36 − 36 + 12 = 12
    Also −b/(2a) = 6/2 = 3, which agrees. The x-intercepts are also a mirror
    pair at height 0, so for −1 and 5 the axis is x = (−1 + 5)/2 = 2. Symmetry
    halves the work when you make a table: once you know one side of the axis,
    copy the values to the other side. Common mistake: taking the difference
    (5 − 1)/2 = 2 instead of the midpoint. Now you try: y = 2x² + 8x − 1 passes
    through (0, −1); find its axis and the mirror image of (0, −1). (x = −2;
    (−4, −1))

D5. Sketch y = x² − 4x − 5, showing the intercepts, the vertex and the axis of
    symmetry. State the range.
    Answer: Opens up; y-intercept (0, −5); x-intercepts (−1, 0) and (5, 0);
    vertex (2, −9); axis x = 2; range y ≥ −9.
    Teacher explains: Follow the five steps:
        1. a = 1 > 0: opens UP (minimum point)
        2. x = 0:  y = −5, so (0, −5)
        3. y = 0:  x² − 4x − 5 = (x − 5)(x + 1) = 0, x = 5 or −1
        4. h = 4/2 = 2, k = 4 − 8 − 5 = −9: vertex (2, −9), axis x = 2
        5. mirror of (0, −5) in x = 2 is (4, −5)
                    y
          7   *  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  *
          6   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
          5   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
          4   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
          3   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
          2   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
          1   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
          0 --+--*--+--+--+--+--+--*--+-x
         −1   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
         −2   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
         −3   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
         −4   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
         −5   .  .  *  .  .  .  *  .  .
         −6   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
         −7   .  .  |  .  .  .  .  .  .
         −8   .  .  |  *  .  *  .  .  .
         −9   .  .  |  .  *  .  .  .  .
             −2 −1  0  1  2  3  4  5  6
    Check: the axis x = 2 is halfway between −1 and 5. The lowest value of y is
    −9, so the RANGE is y ≥ −9 (every value from −9 upwards is reached, some
    twice). In vertex form y = (x − 2)² − 9. Now you try: sketch
    y = −x² + 2x + 8: intercepts, vertex and range. ((0, 8), (−2, 0), (4, 0),
    vertex (1, 9), range y ≤ 9)

D6. For y = −2x² + 4x + 6 find the maximum value, the value of x where it
    occurs, the range and the x-intercepts.
    Answer: Maximum 8 at x = 1; range y ≤ 8; x-intercepts (−1, 0) and (3, 0).
    Teacher explains: Complete the square (or use −b/(2a) = −4/(−4) = 1):
        y = −2(x² − 2x) + 6
          = −2[(x − 1)² − 1] + 6
          = −2(x − 1)² + 8
    Because −2(x − 1)² is never positive, y ≤ 8, and y = 8 only at x = 1. So the
    maximum is 8 and the range is y ≤ 8 (all real numbers up to 8). For the
    intercepts: −2x² + 4x + 6 = 0, divide by −2: x² − 2x − 3 = 0,
    (x − 3)(x + 1) = 0. Common mistakes: giving the maximum as x = 1 (that is
    WHERE it happens; the maximum VALUE is y = 8), and writing the range as
    y ≥ 8 for a parabola that opens down. Now you try: minimum value and range
    of y = 3x² + 12x + 7. (−5 at x = −2; y ≥ −5)

D7. Compare the graphs of y = x², y = 2x², y = (1/2)x² and y = −x². What does
    the number a in y = ax² do?
    Answer: All have vertex (0, 0) and axis x = 0. y = 2x² is narrower
    (steeper), y = (1/2)x² is wider, and y = −x² is the reflection of y = x² in
    the x-axis (it opens down).
    Teacher explains: A table shows the effect of a at once:
        x                −2    −1     0     1     2
        y = x²            4     1     0     1     4
        y = 2x²           8     2     0     2     8
        y = (1/2)x²       2   1/2     0   1/2     2
        y = −x²          −4    −1     0    −1    −4
    Every y-value of 2x² is DOUBLE that of x², so the graph rises twice as fast:
    narrower. (1/2)x² rises half as fast: wider. −x² has every y-value turned to
    its negative: the same shape upside down. So: the SIGN of a gives the
    direction (up or down) and the SIZE |a| gives the width (bigger |a|,
    narrower). a never changes the vertex of y = ax² (it is (0, 0) for all of
    them). Now you try: which is narrowest: y = 3x², y = −5x², y = 0.2x²? Which
    open down? (−5x² is narrowest; only −5x² opens down)

D8. A parabola has vertex (2, −3) and passes through (4, 5). Find its equation
    in vertex form and in the form ax² + bx + c.
    Answer: y = 2(x − 2)² − 3 = 2x² − 8x + 5.
    Teacher explains: Start with the vertex form, which already contains the
    vertex; only a is unknown:
        y = a(x − 2)² − 3
        through (4, 5):  5 = a(4 − 2)² − 3
                         5 = 4a − 3
                         a = 2
        y = 2(x − 2)² − 3 = 2(x² − 4x + 4) − 3 = 2x² − 8x + 5
    Check with the point: 2 × 16 − 8 × 4 + 5 = 32 − 32 + 5 = 5. Check the
    vertex: −b/(2a) = 8/4 = 2. Since a = 2 > 0 the vertex is a minimum. Common
    mistake: y = a(x + 2)² − 3 for vertex (2, −3); the bracket is (x − h). Now
    you try: vertex (−1, 4), through (1, −4).
    (y = −2(x + 1)² + 4 = −2x² − 4x + 2)

D9. A parabola crosses the x-axis at x = −1 and x = 5 and passes through
    (0, −10). Find its equation and its vertex.
    Answer: y = 2(x + 1)(x − 5) = 2x² − 8x − 10; vertex (2, −18).
    Teacher explains: If p and q are the roots, then (x − p)(x − q) is a factor,
    so the equation is y = a(x − p)(x − q) ("intercept form"):
        y = a(x + 1)(x − 5)
        through (0, −10):  −10 = a(1)(−5) = −5a,  a = 2
        y = 2(x + 1)(x − 5) = 2(x² − 4x − 5) = 2x² − 8x − 10
        axis: x = (−1 + 5)/2 = 2
        vertex: y = 2(3)(−3) = −18, so (2, −18)
    The three forms of a quadratic each show something: standard form shows the
    y-intercept, vertex form shows the vertex, intercept form shows the
    x-intercepts. Common mistake: y = a(x − 1)(x + 5) for roots −1 and 5 (signs
    reversed). Now you try: x-intercepts 2 and 6, through (4, 8).
    (y = −2(x − 2)(x − 6), vertex (4, 8))

D10. A farmer has 40 m of fencing to make a rectangular pen against a long
     straight wall (the wall is one side, so only three sides need fencing).
     What is the largest possible area?
     Answer: 200 m², with the two sides from the wall 10 m long and the side
     parallel to the wall 20 m long.
     Teacher explains: Let each side from the wall be x m. The fence left for
     the side parallel to the wall is (40 − 2x) m.
                 wall
           ==================
           |                |
           x                x
           |                |
           +----------------+
                40 − 2x
         A = x(40 − 2x) = −2x² + 40x
           = −2(x² − 20x) = −2[(x − 10)² − 100] = −2(x − 10)² + 200
     a = −2 < 0, so the vertex is a MAXIMUM: A is largest when x = 10, and then
     A = 200. The pen is 10 m by 20 m. Check two nearby values: x = 9 gives
     9 × 22 = 198 and x = 11 gives 11 × 18 = 198, both smaller. The sensible
     domain is 0 < x < 20 (lengths must be positive). Common mistake: using 4
     sides (x(20 − x)), which ignores the wall. Now you try: with 60 m of
     fencing and the wall as one side, find the largest area. (x = 15,
     15 × 30 = 450 m²)

D11. A cricket ball is hit so that its height after t seconds is
     h = 2 + 20t − 5t² metres. Find the greatest height and when it is reached,
     when the ball is 17 m high, and when it lands.
     Answer: Greatest height 22 m at t = 2 s. It is 17 m high at t = 1 s and
     t = 3 s. It lands at t = (10 + √110)/5 ≈ 4.10 s.
     Teacher explains: Complete the square:
         h = −5t² + 20t + 2
           = −5(t² − 4t) + 2
           = −5[(t − 2)² − 4] + 2
           = −5(t − 2)² + 22
     So the maximum height is 22 m at t = 2 s. For h = 17: −5t² + 20t + 2 = 17
     gives 5t² − 20t + 15 = 0, t² − 4t + 3 = 0, t = 1 or 3 (going up and coming
     down, symmetric about t = 2). It lands when h = 0: 5t² − 20t − 2 = 0,
     t = (20 ± √440)/10 = (10 ± √110)/5; the negative root means "before the
     hit" and is rejected, so t ≈ 4.10 s. Common mistake: starting the graph at
     the origin; at t = 0 the ball is already 2 m up. Now you try:
     h = 30t − 5t². Greatest height, and time in the air? (45 m at t = 3 s; 6 s)

D12. A cinema charges ₹200 a ticket and sells 500 tickets a show. For every ₹10
     reduction in price it sells 50 more tickets. What price gives the greatest
     income? Then: find two numbers whose sum is 20 and whose product is as
     large as possible.
     Answer: Price ₹150 (750 tickets), income ₹112,500. The numbers are 10 and
     10 (product 100).
     Teacher explains: Let n be the number of ₹10 reductions. Price = 200 − 10n;
     tickets = 500 + 50n.
         R = (200 − 10n)(500 + 50n)
           = 100,000 + 10,000n − 5,000n − 500n²
           = −500n² + 5,000n + 100,000
           = −500(n − 5)² + 112,500
     The maximum is at n = 5: price 200 − 50 = ₹150, tickets 500 + 250 = 750,
     income 150 × 750 = ₹112,500. Check n = 4: 160 × 700 = 112,000 and n = 6:
     140 × 800 = 112,000 (equal, symmetric about n = 5). For the numbers: x and
     20 − x, product P = x(20 − x) = −(x − 10)² + 100, so the largest product is
     100 when both are 10. Common mistake: stopping at n = 5 and forgetting to
     answer the question asked (the PRICE). Now you try: sum 30, largest
     product? (15 × 15 = 225)

             g) x = −6   h) x = −4   i) x = 3/2   j) x = −1/2   k) x = 4
             l) x = 5/2   m) x = −5   n) x = 3/2   o) x = 1/2   p) x = 3/2

M9. Find the equation y = a(x − h)² + k of the parabola with the given vertex
    through the given point.
    a) vertex (2, −3), through (4, 5)     b) vertex (1, 4), through (3, −4)
    c) vertex (0, 2), through (1, 5)      d) vertex (−3, 0), through (−1, 8)
    e) vertex (−1, −5), through (1, 3)    f) vertex (4, 6), through (2, −2)

    i) vertex (−2, 7), through (0, 3)     j) vertex (3, 1), through (4, 4)
    k) vertex (−4, −8), through (−2, 0)   l) vertex (1, −1), through (5, 7)
    m) vertex (6, 0), through (4, −1)     n) vertex (−1, 3), through (1, 5)
    Answers: a) y = 2(x − 2)² − 3   b) y = −2(x − 1)² + 4   c) y = 3x² + 2
             d) y = 2(x + 3)²   e) y = 2(x + 1)² − 5   f) y = −2(x − 4)² + 6
             g) y = −3x²   h) y = (1/2)(x − 5)² − 2   i) y = −(x + 2)² + 7
             j) y = 3(x − 3)² + 1   k) y = 2(x + 4)² − 8
             l) y = (1/2)(x − 1)² − 1   m) y = −(1/4)(x − 6)²
             n) y = (1/2)(x + 1)² + 3

M10. Find the equation in the form y = a(x − p)(x − q) (or a(x − p)² when it
     touches the axis).
     a) x-intercepts −1 and 5, through (0, −10)

     Answers: a) y = 2(x + 1)(x − 5)   b) y = −2(x − 2)(x − 6)

              h) y = −(x + 2)²   i) y = −(x + 5)(x − 1)   j) y = 3(x − 2)(x − 7)

M11. Complete the table of values: give y for the listed x-values, in order.
     a) y = x² − 2x − 3; x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
     b) y = x² + 4x; x = −5, −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1

M12. The point lies on the parabola. Find its mirror image in the axis of
     symmetry.
     a) y = x² − 4x + 1;  (0, 1)         b) y = x² − 4x + 1;  (5, 6)
     c) y = x² + 6x;  (1, 7)             d) y = −x² + 2x + 3;  (−1, 0)
     e) y = −x² + 2x + 3;  (3, 0)        f) y = 2x² − 12x + 13;  (1, 3)

     i) y = −(x − 1)² + 9;  (−2, 0)      j) y = x² − 9;  (−3, 0)
     k) y = x² − 9;  (4, 7)              l) y = 3x² + 12x + 7;  (0, 7)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make a table of values and plot on squared paper first; mark the
  mirror pairs with the same colour; always find the vertex with −b/(2a) AND by
  completing the square until both agree; say "a positive, smile, minimum; a
  negative, frown, maximum". Harder: find the equation of the parabola through
  (0, 3), (1, 0) and (3, 0) (y = x² − 4x + 3); show that the vertex of
  y = x² + bx + c lies on y = c − x² as b varies; prove that of all rectangles
  with perimeter 36 cm the square has the greatest area
  (A = x(18 − x) = 81 − (x − 9)²); a shop sells 100 kites a day at ₹50 and 2
  fewer for each ₹5 rise: find the best price (₹150, income ₹9,000).


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.12 — ARITHMETIC PROGRESSIONS: NTH TERM, SUM OF N TERMS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - An ARITHMETIC PROGRESSION (AP) is a list of numbers in which each term is
    got by ADDING the same fixed number to the previous term. That fixed number
    is the COMMON DIFFERENCE d = t₂ − t₁ = t₃ − t₂ = ... It can be positive,
    negative, zero or a fraction. First term: a (or t₁).
  - To TEST for an AP, check that EVERY difference t(k+1) − t(k) is the same,
    not just the first one: 1, 4, 9, 16 is not an AP.
  - nTH TERM: tₙ = a + (n − 1)d (the first term, plus (n − 1) steps of d). For
    3, 7, 11, ...: tₙ = 3 + (n − 1) × 4 = 4n − 1. An AP's nth term is always
    LINEAR in n, and d is the coefficient of n.
  - Using tₙ: find any term; decide whether a number is a term (n must be a
    positive whole number); find the NUMBER OF TERMS of a finite AP,
    n = (l − a)/d + 1 where l is the last term; the nth term FROM THE END is
    l − (n − 1)d.
  - Two facts give a and d: write two equations, e.g. a + 2d = 12 and
    a + 9d = 40, subtract to get d. Three terms in AP are best written a − d, a,
    a + d; the middle one is the average of its neighbours (b = (a + c)/2).
  - SUM OF THE FIRST n TERMS: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2 (a + l). Proof:
    write the sum forwards and backwards and add; each pair adds to a + l and
    there are n pairs.
  - Special sums: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2; 1 + 3 + 5 + ... (n odd
    numbers) = n²; 2 + 4 + ... (n even numbers) = n(n + 1). Also tₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁.
  - To find n from a sum, Sₙ = given value leads to a QUADRATIC in n (topic
    7.9); keep only positive whole-number roots and check which make sense.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Which of these are arithmetic progressions? Give d when it is. (i) Priya's
    savings: ₹100, ₹150, ₹200, ₹250, ... (ii) 1, 4, 9, 16, ... (iii) −3, −1, 1,
    3, ... (iv) 10, 7, 4, 1, ... (v) 5, 5, 5, ... (vi) 2, 4, 8, 16, ...
    Answer: (i) AP, d = 50; (ii) not an AP; (iii) AP, d = 2; (iv) AP, d = −3;
    (v) AP, d = 0; (vi) not an AP.
    Teacher explains: Find EVERY difference "next minus previous":
        (i)   150 − 100 = 50, 200 − 150 = 50, 250 − 200 = 50    AP
        (ii)  4 − 1 = 3, 9 − 4 = 5, 16 − 9 = 7                 not AP
        (iii) −1 − (−3) = 2, 1 − (−1) = 2, 3 − 1 = 2           AP
        (iv)  7 − 10 = −3, 4 − 7 = −3, 1 − 4 = −3              AP
        (v)   5 − 5 = 0 each time                              AP
        (vi)  4 − 2 = 2, 8 − 4 = 4                             not AP
    A decreasing AP has a NEGATIVE d. A constant list is an AP with d = 0. (vi)
    grows by MULTIPLYING by 2 each time: that is a geometric progression (topic
    7.18). Common mistakes: subtracting the wrong way round (10 − 7 = 3 gives
    d = +3 for a decreasing list), and checking only the first difference. Now
    you try: 1/2, 1, 3/2, 2, ... and 0.3, 0.6, 1.2, ... (AP with d = 1/2; not an
    AP)

D2. Find the 20th term of 3, 7, 11, 15, ... and a formula for the nth term.
    Explain why tₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
    Answer: t₂₀ = 79; tₙ = 4n − 1.
    Teacher explains: Each step ADDS d. To get from t₁ to t₂ is 1 step, to t₃ is
    2 steps, so to tₙ is (n − 1) steps:
        t₁ = a
        t₂ = a + d
        t₃ = a + 2d
        t₄ = a + 3d          (the number of d's is one less than n)
        tₙ = a + (n − 1)d
        here a = 3, d = 4:
        t₂₀ = 3 + 19 × 4 = 3 + 76 = 79
        tₙ = 3 + (n − 1) × 4 = 3 + 4n − 4 = 4n − 1
    Check with n = 4: 4 × 4 − 1 = 15. Notice tₙ = 4n − 1 is linear in n and the
    coefficient 4 is d; so the points (n, tₙ) lie on a straight line. Common
    mistake: t₂₀ = 3 + 20 × 4 = 83 (one step too many). Now you try: the 15th
    term and the nth term of 10, 7, 4, ... (t₁₅ = 10 + 14 × (−3) = −32;
    tₙ = 13 − 3n)

D3. Which term of the AP 3, 8, 13, 18, ... is 183? Is 301 a term of this AP?
    Answer: 183 is the 37th term. 301 is not a term.
    Teacher explains: Set tₙ equal to the number and solve for n; n must be a
    POSITIVE WHOLE number:
        a = 3, d = 5:   tₙ = 3 + (n − 1) × 5 = 5n − 2
        5n − 2 = 183   →   5n = 185   →   n = 37
        5n − 2 = 301   →   5n = 303   →   n = 60.6   not whole
    Check: t₃₇ = 3 + 36 × 5 = 183. For 301: t₆₀ = 298 and t₆₁ = 303, so 301
    falls between two terms. Another way: every term is 3 more than a multiple
    of 5 (ends in 3 or 8), and 301 does not. Now you try: which term of 21, 18,
    15, ... is −81? Is 0 a term? (tₙ = 24 − 3n: n = 35; yes, n = 8)

D4. The 3rd term of an AP is 12 and the 10th term is 40. Find the first term,
    the common difference and the 20th term.
    Answer: a = 4, d = 4, t₂₀ = 80.
    Teacher explains: Write both facts with tₙ = a + (n − 1)d and subtract to
    remove a:
        t₁₀:  a + 9d = 40
        t₃:   a + 2d = 12
        subtract:  7d = 28,  d = 4
        then a + 2 × 4 = 12,  a = 4
        t₂₀ = 4 + 19 × 4 = 80
    Shortcut: from the 3rd to the 10th term is 7 steps, and the value rises by
    40 − 12 = 28, so d = 28 ÷ 7 = 4. The AP is 4, 8, 12, 16, ... Common mistake:
    t₃ = a + 3d. Now you try: t₅ = 19 and t₁₂ = 47; find a, d and t₃₀. (d = 4,
    a = 3, t₃₀ = 119)

D5. The AP 3, 8, 13, ..., 253 is finite. How many terms does it have? Find its
    12th term from the end.
    Answer: 51 terms; the 12th term from the end is 198.
    Teacher explains: Number of terms: the last term l = 253 is tₙ, so
        3 + (n − 1) × 5 = 253
        (n − 1) × 5 = 250,  n − 1 = 50,  n = 51
    From the END, read the AP backwards: 253, 248, 243, ... This is an AP with
    first term l = 253 and common difference −5, so its 12th term is
        253 + 11 × (−5) = 253 − 55 = 198
    Check another way: the 12th from the end of 51 terms is the
    (51 − 12 + 1) = 40th from the start: 3 + 39 × 5 = 198. Common mistakes:
    n = 250 ÷ 5 = 50 (forgetting the "+ 1": there is one more term than steps,
    like fence posts), and 253 − 12 × 5. Now you try: how many two-digit numbers
    are divisible by 7? (14, 21, ..., 98: n = 13)

D6. Fill in the blanks so that 5, __, __, 26 is an AP. Then: three numbers in AP
    have sum 24 and product 440. Find them.
    Answer: 5, 12, 19, 26. The numbers are 5, 8, 11 (or 11, 8, 5).
    Teacher explains: From the first to the fourth term is 3 steps:
    3d = 26 − 5 = 21, so d = 7 and the missing terms are 12 and 19. For the
    three numbers use the SYMMETRIC form a − d, a, a + d, so that d cancels in
    the sum:
        (a − d) + a + (a + d) = 3a = 24,   a = 8
        (8 − d) × 8 × (8 + d) = 440
        64 − d² = 55,   d² = 9,   d = ±3
    d = 3 gives 5, 8, 11 and d = −3 gives 11, 8, 5: the same numbers. Check:
    5 + 8 + 11 = 24 and 5 × 8 × 11 = 440. The middle term of three in AP is the
    AVERAGE of the outer two: 8 = (5 + 11)/2. Common mistake: calling them a,
    a + d, a + 2d, which gives messier equations. Now you try: for what x are
    2x, x + 10, 3x + 2 in AP? (x + 10 = (2x + 3x + 2)/2 gives x = 6: 12, 16, 20)

D7. Find 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 100 by pairing (young Gauss's method). Use the same
    idea to prove Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d].
    Answer: 5,050. The proof is below.
    Teacher explains: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add column by
    column:
        S =   1 +  2 +  3 + ... + 100
        S = 100 + 99 + 98 + ... +   1
        2S = 101 + 101 + 101 + ... + 101     (100 columns)
        2S = 100 × 101 = 10,100,   S = 5,050
    For any AP with first term a, last term l = a + (n − 1)d and n terms:
        Sₙ = a + (a + d) + ... + (l − d) + l
        Sₙ = l + (l − d) + ... + (a + d) + a
        2Sₙ = n(a + l)
        Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]
    Every column adds to a + l because one term goes up by d while the other
    goes down by d. Use n/2 (a + l) when you know the last term and n/2
    [2a + (n − 1)d] when you know d. Now you try: 1 + 2 + ... + 50 and
    1 + 2 + ... + 1,000. (1,275; 500,500)

D8. Find the sum of the first 20 terms of 2, 7, 12, ... Then find the sum
    7 + 10 + 13 + ... + 97.
    Answer: S₂₀ = 990; 7 + 10 + ... + 97 = 1,612.
    Teacher explains: First sum: a = 2, d = 5, n = 20:
        S₂₀ = 20/2 × [2 × 2 + 19 × 5] = 10 × [4 + 95] = 10 × 99 = 990
    Second sum: we know the last term, but not n. Find n first:
        7 + (n − 1) × 3 = 97,  (n − 1) × 3 = 90,  n = 31
        S = 31/2 × (7 + 97) = 31/2 × 104 = 31 × 52 = 1,612
    Check the first with the other formula: t₂₀ = 2 + 19 × 5 = 97, and
    20/2 × (2 + 97) = 990. Common mistakes: using n = 30 in the second sum, and
    multiplying only 2a by n/2. Now you try: the sum of the first 15 terms of
    20, 17, 14, ... and of the odd numbers 1 + 3 + ... + 99.
    (15/2 × [40 − 42] = −15; 2,500)

D9. How many terms of the AP 54, 51, 48, ... must be taken so that their sum is
    513? Explain the double answer.
    Answer: n = 18 or n = 19. The 19th term is 0, so adding it does not change
    the sum.
    Teacher explains: a = 54, d = −3. Put Sₙ = 513 and get a quadratic in n:
        n/2 × [108 + (n − 1)(−3)] = 513
        n(108 − 3n + 3) = 1,026
        n(111 − 3n) = 1,026
        3n² − 111n + 1,026 = 0
        n² − 37n + 342 = 0
        (n − 18)(n − 19) = 0,   n = 18 or n = 19
    Both are positive whole numbers, so both are valid.
    t₁₉ = 54 + 18 × (−3) = 0: the sum of 19 terms equals the sum of 18 terms
    plus 0. Always ask whether each root makes sense: a negative or fractional n
    is rejected. Now you try: how many terms of 24, 21, 18, ... make 78?
    (n² − 17n + 52 = 0: n = 4 or 13; t₁₃ = −12, so terms 5 to 13 add up to 0)

D10. Show that the sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)/2, the sum of
     the first n odd numbers is n² and the sum of the first n even numbers is
     n(n + 1). Draw a picture for the odd numbers.
     Answer: Use Sₙ = n/2 (a + l): (a, l) = (1, n), (1, 2n − 1), (2, 2n). So the
     sums are n(n + 1)/2, n², n(n + 1).
     Teacher explains: Naturals: a = 1, l = n, Sₙ = n/2 (1 + n). Odds: the nth
     odd number is 1 + (n − 1) × 2 = 2n − 1, so Sₙ = n/2
     (1 + 2n − 1) = n/2 × 2n = n². Evens: l = 2n, Sₙ = n/2 (2 + 2n) = n(n + 1).
     The odd numbers build squares by adding L-shapes:
         1        1 + 3      1 + 3 + 5      1 + 3 + 5 + 7
         #        # o        # o x          # o x +
                  o o        o o x          o o x +
                             x x x          x x x +
                                            + + + +
         1 = 1²   4 = 2²     9 = 3²         16 = 4²
     Also the evens are double the naturals:
     2 + 4 + ... + 2n = 2(1 + 2 + ... + n) = n(n + 1). Now you try: find
     1 + 3 + 5 + ... + 39 and 2 + 4 + ... + 100. (20 odd numbers: 400; 50 even
     numbers: 2,550)

D11. Ravi saves ₹50 in the first month, ₹70 in the second, ₹90 in the third, and
     so on. In which month does he save ₹290? How much has he saved in total
     after one year?
     Answer: In the 13th month. ₹1,920 after 12 months.
     Teacher explains: The monthly savings form an AP with a = 50 and d = 20.
         tₙ = 50 + (n − 1) × 20 = 290
         (n − 1) × 20 = 240,  n − 1 = 12,  n = 13
         S₁₂ = 12/2 × [2 × 50 + 11 × 20] = 6 × [100 + 220] = 6 × 320
             = 1,920
     Check: in month 12 he saves 50 + 11 × 20 = ₹270, and
     12/2 × (50 + 270) = 6 × 320 = 1,920. Keep the two questions apart: "how
     much in month n" is tₙ; "how much altogether" is Sₙ. Common mistake:
     answering the second question with t₁₂ = 270. Now you try: a taxi charges
     ₹30 for the first km and ₹12 for each extra km. What is the fare for 10 km?
     (30 + 9 × 12 = ₹138)

D12. A school hall has 25 rows of seats. The first row has 20 seats and each row
     has 2 more than the row in front. How many seats are in the last row and in
     the hall? Then: logs are stacked with 20 in the bottom row, 19 in the next,
     18 in the next, and so on. In how many rows are 200 logs placed, and how
     many logs are in the top row?
     Answer: Last row 68 seats; 1,100 seats in all. The logs need 16 rows with 5
     logs in the top row.
     Teacher explains: Seats: a = 20, d = 2, n = 25: t₂₅ = 20 + 24 × 2 = 68, and
     S₂₅ = 25/2 × (20 + 68) = 25 × 44 = 1,100. Logs: a = 20, d = −1:
         n/2 × [40 + (n − 1)(−1)] = 200
         n(41 − n) = 400
         n² − 41n + 400 = 0
         (n − 16)(n − 25) = 0
     n = 25 would need t₂₅ = 20 − 24 = −4 logs in the top row, which is
     impossible (the rows 17 to 25 would have 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, ...), so REJECT
     it. n = 16 rows, top row t₁₆ = 20 − 15 = 5 logs. Always test both roots in
     the story. Now you try: a stadium has 30 seats in the first row and 3 more
     in each row; how many rows hold 1,170 seats in all? (n/2 (57 + 3n) = 1,170:
     n = 20)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Is it an AP? If yes, give d.
    a) 3, 7, 11, 15, ...           b) 2, 6, 18, 54, ...
    c) 10, 6, 2, −2, ...           d) 1, 4, 9, 16, ...
    e) −5, −2, 1, 4, ...           f) 1/2, 1, 3/2, 2, ...
    g) 7, 7, 7, 7, ...             h) 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2, ...
    i) 1, 3, 6, 10, ...            j) −1, −3, −5, −7, ...
    k) 1/3, 2/3, 1, 5/3, ...       l) √2, 2√2, 3√2, 4√2, ...
    m) 2, 5, 9, 14, ...            n) 100, 75, 50, 25, ...
    o) 3/4, 1/2, 1/4, 0, ...       p) 1, −1, 1, −1, ...
    q) √3, 2√3, 3√3, 4√3, ...      r) −10, −15/2, −5, −5/2, ...
    s) 4, 4.5, 5.5, 7, ...         t) 1.5, 3.1, 4.7, 6.3, ...
    Answers: a) yes, d = 4   b) no   c) yes, d = −4   d) no   e) yes, d = 3
             f) yes, d = 1/2   g) yes, d = 0   h) yes, d = 0.3   i) no
             j) yes, d = −2   k) no   l) yes, d = √2   m) no   n) yes, d = −25
             o) yes, d = −1/4   p) no   q) yes, d = √3   r) yes, d = 5/2   s) no
             t) yes, d = 1.6

M2. Write the first four terms of the AP.
    a) a = 3, d = 4        b) a = 10, d = −3      c) a = −2, d = 5
    d) a = 1/2, d = 1/4    e) a = 0, d = −7       f) a = 4, d = 0
    g) a = −1.5, d = 0.5   h) a = 20, d = −4      i) tₙ = 5n − 2
    j) tₙ = 3n + 4         k) tₙ = 10 − 2n        l) tₙ = (n + 1)/2
    m) tₙ = −4n            n) Sₙ = n² + 2n        o) Sₙ = 3n² − n
    p) Sₙ = n(n + 1)/2     q) Sₙ = 4n − n²        r) Sₙ = 2n² + 3n
    Answers: a) 3, 7, 11, 15   b) 10, 7, 4, 1   c) −2, 3, 8, 13
             d) 1/2, 3/4, 1, 5/4   e) 0, −7, −14, −21   f) 4, 4, 4, 4
             g) −1.5, −1, −0.5, 0   h) 20, 16, 12, 8   i) 3, 8, 13, 18
