TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always go back to the picture "distance on the number line":
  |x − 3| = 5 means "5 steps from 3", |x − 3| < 5 means "fewer than 5 steps from
  3"; walk it out on a floor number line; insist that the absolute value is
  isolated before splitting into cases; check every answer by substituting;
  sketch the V graph and a horizontal line to see how many solutions to expect.
  Harder: solve |x − 1| + |x − 5| = 6 (every x from 1 to 5) and
  |x − 1| + |x − 5| = 10 (x = −2 or x = 8) by the distance idea; solve
  |x² − 5| = 4 (x = ±1, ±3); prove the triangle inequality |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|
  by squaring; graph y = |x² − 4|; find the values of k for which |x − 2| = kx
  has exactly one solution.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.17 — EXPONENTIAL GROWTH AND DECAY (INTRODUCTION)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - An EXPONENTIAL function has the form y = a × bˣ (written y = a·bˣ), with
    a > 0 and b > 0, b ≠ 1. a is the INITIAL VALUE (the value when x = 0) and b
    is the FACTOR by which y is MULTIPLIED each time x goes up by 1.
  - b > 1: exponential GROWTH (y = 500 × 2ˣ). 0 < b < 1: exponential DECAY
    (y = 800 × 0.5ˣ). The factor b is the key, not the initial value.
  - LINEAR change ADDS the same amount each step (constant DIFFERENCE);
    EXPONENTIAL change MULTIPLIES by the same factor each step (constant RATIO).
    Test a table by working out differences and ratios.
  - PERCENTAGE change as a MULTIPLIER: an increase of r% multiplies by
    (1 + r/100); a decrease of r% multiplies by (1 − r/100). +5% is × 1.05, −20%
    is × 0.8, +100% is × 2. After n equal periods: A = P(1 ± r/100)ⁿ.
  - Successive percentages MULTIPLY, they do not add: +10% twice
    is × 1.1 × 1.1 = × 1.21, a 21% increase; +20% then −20% is × 0.96, a 4%
    decrease.
  - HALF-LIFE T: the time for a decaying quantity to halve. Amount after time t:
    A = A₀ × (1/2)^(t/T). DOUBLING TIME d: N = N₀ × 2^(t/d).
  - RULE OF 72: at r% growth per period the doubling time is ABOUT 72 ÷ r
    periods (8% a year: about 9 years). It is an estimate only.
  - GRAPHS of y = a·bˣ: they pass through (0, a), are always above the x-axis,
    rise (b > 1) or fall (0 < b < 1) ever more steeply or ever more gently, and
    get closer and closer to the x-axis without touching it (the ASYMPTOTE
    y = 0). y = 2ˣ and y = (1/2)ˣ are mirror images in the y-axis.
  - Negative x means going BACK in time: y = 100 × 2ˣ gives y = 50 at x = −1. To
    undo a growth, DIVIDE by the multiplier (not subtract the percentage).
  - Exponential growth always overtakes linear growth in the end, however big
    the linear step. Give answers exactly, or say clearly how they are rounded
    (≈ 29,386.56, to the nearest paisa).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A culture starts with 500 bacteria and the number doubles every hour. Make a
    table for the first 6 hours, write a formula, and find when the number first
    passes 100,000.
    Answer: N = 500 × 2ᵗ (t in hours). After 6 hours N = 32,000. It passes
    100,000 between t = 7 (64,000) and t = 8 (128,000), so during the 8th hour.
    Teacher explains: "Doubles every hour" means MULTIPLY by 2 each hour:
            t (hours)   0     1      2      3      4       5       6
            N         500  1,000  2,000  4,000  8,000  16,000  32,000
    Each number is 2 times the one before, so after t hours we have multiplied
    by 2 t times: N = 500 × 2ᵗ. Check: 500 × 2⁶ = 500 × 64 = 32,000. Keep
    doubling: 500 × 2⁷ = 64,000 and 500 × 2⁸ = 128,000. So 100,000 is passed
    between 7 and 8 hours. Here a = 500 is the starting number and b = 2 is the
    growth factor. Common mistake: writing N = 500 × 2 × t (linear, 500, 1,000,
    1,500, ...), which ADDS 1,000 each hour instead of doubling. Now you try:
    300 cells triple every day. How many after 4 days? (300 × 3⁴ = 24,300)

D2. The population of a town is 80,000 and grows by 5% each year. Find the
    population after 1, 2 and 3 years. Why is the answer after 3 years not
    80,000 + 15%?
    Answer: 84,000; 88,200; 92,610. Adding 15% would give 92,000, which is too
    small.
    Teacher explains: A 5% increase keeps 100% and adds 5%, so the new value is
    105% of the old: MULTIPLY by 1.05.
            after 1 year:  80,000 × 1.05 = 84,000
            after 2 years: 84,000 × 1.05 = 88,200
            after 3 years: 88,200 × 1.05 = 92,610
    In one step: 80,000 × 1.05³ = 92,610. Each year the 5% is taken of a BIGGER
    population (4,000, then 4,200, then 4,410), so the increase itself grows.
    That is what makes growth exponential. 80,000 + 15% = 80,000 × 1.15 = 92,000
    would treat all three increases as 4,000. General formula:
    P = 80,000 × 1.05ⁿ after n years. Common mistake: multiplying by 0.05 (that
    gives only the increase) or by 1.5 (that is +50%). Now you try: 12,000 fish
    increase by 10% a year. How many after 2 years? (12,000 × 1.1² = 14,520)

D3. A scooter costs ₹90,000. Its value falls by 20% every year (depreciation).
    Find its value after 3 years. After how many whole years is it first worth
    less than half its price?
    Answer: ₹46,080 after 3 years. After 4 years (₹36,864) it is first below
    ₹45,000.
    Teacher explains: A 20% decrease leaves 80% of the value: MULTIPLY by 0.8
    each year.
            year      0        1        2        3        4
            value  90,000   72,000   57,600   46,080   36,864
    So V = 90,000 × 0.8ⁿ, and after 3 years
    90,000 × 0.8³ = 90,000 × 0.512 = 46,080. Half the price is 45,000. After 3
    years the value is still above 45,000; after 4 years 90,000 × 0.8⁴ = 36,864
    is below. This is exponential DECAY: the factor 0.8 is less than 1. Note
    that the value falls by 18,000, then 14,400, then 11,520: smaller and
    smaller amounts, because 20% is taken of a smaller value each time. It never
    reaches zero. Common mistake: subtracting 20% of the ORIGINAL price every
    year (18,000 a year), which would make the scooter worthless after 5 years.
    Now you try: a laptop bought for ₹50,000 loses 10% a year. Value after 2
    years? (50,000 × 0.9² = ₹40,500)

D4. A laboratory has 800 mg of a radioactive substance whose half-life is 5
    years. How much is left after 5, 10, 15 and 20 years? Write a formula. After
    how long are only 25 mg left?
    Answer: 400, 200, 100 and 50 mg. A = 800 × (1/2)^(t/5). 25 mg are left after
    25 years.
    Teacher explains: HALF-LIFE is the time for half of the substance to decay.
    Every 5 years the amount is multiplied by 1/2:
            t (years)    0     5    10    15    20    25
            A (mg)     800   400   200   100    50    25
    In t years there are t/5 half-lives, so A = 800 × (1/2)^(t/5). Check t = 20:
    20/5 = 4 half-lives and 800 × (1/2)⁴ = 800 ÷ 16 = 50. For 25 mg:
    800 ÷ 25 = 32 = 2⁵, so we need 5 half-lives: 5 × 5 = 25 years. Carbon-14,
    used to date ancient wood and bones, has a half-life of about 5,730 years.
    Common mistake: thinking that after two half-lives everything has gone
    (half + half = whole). After two half-lives a QUARTER remains. Now you try:
    640 g, half-life 3 days. How much after 12 days? (4 half-lives:
    640 ÷ 16 = 40 g)

D5. Say whether each is growth or decay and give the initial value and the
    factor: (a) y = 3 × 2ˣ (b) y = 100 × 0.9ˣ (c) y = 5 × (1/3)ˣ. Then find the
    formula for the tables: (d) x = 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y = 4, 12, 36, 108; (e)
    x = 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y = 200, 150, 112.5, 84.375.
    Answer: (a) growth, a = 3, b = 2; (b) decay, a = 100, b = 0.9 (10% less each
    step); (c) decay, a = 5, b = 1/3; (d) y = 4 × 3ˣ; (e) y = 200 × 0.75ˣ (25%
    decay).
    Teacher explains: In y = a × bˣ, putting x = 0 gives y = a × 1 = a, the
    initial value. The base b decides growth (b > 1) or decay (0 < b < 1). From
    a TABLE: the value at x = 0 is a, and the RATIO of consecutive values is b:
            (d)  12 ÷ 4 = 3,   36 ÷ 12 = 3,   108 ÷ 36 = 3       b = 3
            (e)  150 ÷ 200 = 0.75,  112.5 ÷ 150 = 0.75,  84.375 ÷ 112.5 = 0.75
    All the ratios must be EQUAL for the rule to be exponential. For (e),
    0.75 = 1 − 0.25, a 25% decrease each step. Common mistake: using the
    DIFFERENCES (8, 24, 72 in (d)); differences that are all equal show a LINEAR
    rule, not an exponential one. Also, 3 × 2ˣ is not 6ˣ: the power acts only on
    the 2. Now you try: x = 0, 1, 2 gives y = 50, 10, 2. Formula?
    (y = 50 × (1/5)ˣ, decay)

D6. A job offers two salary schemes, both starting at ₹20,000 a month. Scheme A:
    a rise of ₹2,000 every year. Scheme B: a rise of 8% every year. Compare the
    salaries over 10 years. When does B overtake A?
    Answer: B is behind for the first 6 years but ahead from year 7 onwards
    (₹34,276.49 against ₹34,000), and the gap then keeps widening.
    Teacher explains: A is LINEAR: 20,000 + 2,000n. B is EXPONENTIAL:
    20,000 × 1.08ⁿ. Table (B to the nearest paisa):
            year n     A (₹)       B (₹)
              1       22,000     21,600.00
              3       26,000     25,194.24
              5       30,000   ≈ 29,386.56
              6       32,000   ≈ 31,737.49
              7       34,000   ≈ 34,276.49
              8       36,000   ≈ 37,018.60
             10       40,000   ≈ 43,178.50
    At first 8% of 20,000 is only 1,600, less than 2,000. But 8% of a growing
    salary keeps growing, while A's rise stays 2,000 for ever. By year 10 B's
    rise is about ₹3,200 a year. This is always true: exponential growth (b > 1)
    beats linear growth in the long run, however large the linear step is.
    Common mistake: judging from the first few years only. Now you try: which is
    bigger after 20 years, 100 + 50n or 100 × 1.2ⁿ? (A: 1,100; B: 100 × 1.2²⁰ ≈
    3,833.76, so B)

D7. (a) After a 25% increase a shirt costs ₹500. What was the price before? (b)
    A village's population grew by 10% a year for 2 years to 12,100. What was it
    2 years ago? (c) For P = 10,000 × 1.1ᵗ, what does t = −1 mean?
    Answer: (a) ₹400. (b) 10,000. (c) One year BEFORE the start:
    P = 10,000 ÷ 1.1 ≈ 9,090.91.
    Teacher explains: To go FORWARD we multiply by the multiplier, so to go BACK
    we DIVIDE by it.
            (a)  original × 1.25 = 500,   original = 500 ÷ 1.25 = 400
            (b)  original × 1.1² = 12,100, original = 12,100 ÷ 1.21 = 10,000
    Check (a): 400 × 1.25 = 500. Common mistake: taking 25% off ₹500, giving
    500 × 0.75 = 375. That is wrong because the 25% was worked out on the OLD
    price (₹400), not on ₹500. In (c) a negative power means going back in time:
    1.1⁻¹ = 1/1.1, so P = 10,000 ÷ 1.1 ≈ 9,090.91 (to 2 d.p.), the population
    one year before t = 0. The exponential formula works for negative and
    fractional t as well. Now you try: after a 20% fall a phone costs ₹12,000.
    Original price? (12,000 ÷ 0.8 = ₹15,000)

D8. Make tables of values of y = 2ˣ and y = (1/2)ˣ for x = −3 to 3 and sketch
    both graphs on one grid. Describe their shapes.
                       y
          8   B  .  .  |  .  .  A
          7   .  .  .  |  .  .  .
          6   .  .  .  |  .  .  .
          5   .  .  .  |  .  .  .
          4   .  B  .  |  .  A  .
          3   .  .  .  |  .  .  .
          2   .  .  B  |  A  .  .
          1   .  .  .  *  .  .  .
          0 --+--+--+--+--+--+--+-x
             −3 −2 −1  0  1  2  3
            (A: y = 2ˣ, B: y = (1/2)ˣ, *: (0, 1) on both; points with y < 1
             are too close to the axis to show on this grid)
    Answer: y = 2ˣ: 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 4, 8. y = (1/2)ˣ: 8, 4, 2, 1, 1/2, 1/4,
    1/8. Both pass through (0, 1), stay above the x-axis, and are mirror images
    in the y-axis. 2ˣ rises, (1/2)ˣ falls.
    Teacher explains: Use 2⁻ⁿ = 1/2ⁿ: 2⁻³ = 1/8, 2⁻² = 1/4, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁰ = 1.
            x          −3    −2    −1    0    1     2     3
            2ˣ         1/8   1/4   1/2   1    2     4     8
            (1/2)ˣ     8     4     2     1    1/2   1/4   1/8
    Features of y = bˣ: (i) it passes through (0, 1) because b⁰ = 1; (ii) y is
    ALWAYS POSITIVE, so the graph never touches or crosses the x-axis; (iii) for
    b > 1 it rises, slowly at first and then ever more steeply; for 0 < b < 1 it
    falls, steeply at first and then ever more gently; (iv) at one side it gets
    closer and closer to the x-axis: the x-axis (y = 0) is an ASYMPTOTE. Since
    (1/2)ˣ = 2⁻ˣ, the second graph is the first one reflected in the y-axis.
    Common mistake: joining the points with straight lines; the graph is a
    smooth curve. Now you try: where does y = 5 × 3ˣ cross the y-axis, and does
    it rise or fall? ((0, 5); rises)

D9. Priya invests money at 8% per year compound interest. Use the Rule of 72 to
    estimate how long it takes to double, and check. Do the same for a
    population growing at 3% a year.
    Answer: About 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years (1.08⁹ ≈ 1.999, almost exactly double). About
    72 ÷ 3 = 24 years (1.03²⁴ ≈ 2.03).
    Teacher explains: The doubling time does NOT depend on the starting amount:
    ₹1,000 and ₹100,000 (1 lakh) both double in the same time at the same rate,
    because we only need (1.08)ⁿ = 2. The RULE OF 72 gives a quick estimate:
    doubling time ≈ 72 ÷ (rate in %). Check by multiplying out:
            1.08⁹  ≈ 1.999     (just under 2: doubled in about 9 years)
            1.08¹⁰ ≈ 2.159     (definitely doubled after 10 whole years)
            1.03²³ ≈ 1.974,   1.03²⁴ ≈ 2.033
    The rule works well for rates from about 2% to 15%; for big rates it is
    rougher (at 36%, 72 ÷ 36 = 2 years, but 1.36² = 1.8496, and it takes 3 whole
    years). Once you know the doubling time, the growth is easy to picture: at
    8%, ₹10,000 becomes about ₹20,000 in 9 years, ₹40,000 in 18 years and
    ₹80,000 in 27 years. Common mistake: 8% for 9 years is NOT 72% (simple
    interest thinking); compounding gives about 100%. Now you try: estimate the
    doubling time at 6% a year. (72 ÷ 6 = 12 years; 1.06¹² ≈ 2.01)

D10. (a) A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. Is it back where it
     started? (b) A share rises 10% in each of two years. Is that a 20% rise?
     (c) Salt water loses 50% of its volume and then 50% of what is left. Is it
     all gone?
     Answer: (a) No: it is 4% lower (× 0.96). (b) No: it is a 21% rise (× 1.21).
     (c) No: a quarter (25%) is left.
     Teacher explains: Successive percentage changes MULTIPLY their multipliers:
              (a)  × 1.2 × 0.8 = × 0.96      so 100 → 120 → 96
              (b)  × 1.1 × 1.1 = × 1.21      so 100 → 110 → 121
              (c)  × 0.5 × 0.5 = × 0.25      so 100 → 50 → 25
     In (a) the 20% fall is taken of a BIGGER number (120), so it removes 24,
     more than the 20 added. The order does not matter: × 0.8 × 1.2 is
     also × 0.96. In (b) the second 10% is taken of 110, giving an extra 1%
     (interest on interest). Common mistake: adding and subtracting the
     percentages as if they were all taken of the same amount. A shop's "20%
     off, then a further 10% off" is × 0.8 × 0.9 = × 0.72, a 28% discount, not
     30%. Now you try: a population falls 10% and then rises 10%. Overall
     change? (× 0.9 × 1.1 = × 0.99, a 1% fall)

D11. (a) A forest has 2,000 deer. Two years later it has 2,420. Assuming a
     constant yearly growth factor, find the yearly percentage growth. (b) A
     sample of 64 g of a radioactive isotope decays to 4 g in 12 days. Find its
     half-life.
     Answer: (a) 10% a year. (b) 3 days.
     Teacher explains: (a) Let the yearly factor be b. Then
             2,000 × b² = 2,420
                     b² = 2,420 ÷ 2,000 = 1.21
                      b = 1.1         (b is positive; 1.1² = 1.21)
     A factor of 1.1 is 110%, a 10% increase per year. Check:
     2,000 × 1.1 = 2,200 and 2,200 × 1.1 = 2,420. Common mistake: dividing the
     total increase of 21% by 2 to get 10.5%. (b) Count the halvings: 64 → 32 →
     16 → 8 → 4, that is 4 half-lives. So 4 half-lives = 12 days and one
     half-life is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 days. Or with the formula: 64 × (1/2)^(12/T) = 4,
     so (1/2)^(12/T) = 1/16 = (1/2)⁴, 12/T = 4 and T = 3. Now you try: 5,000
     grows to 7,200 in 2 years. Yearly factor? (b² = 1.44, b = 1.2: 20% a year)

D12. A patient is given 400 mg of a medicine. Each hour the body removes 30% of
     the amount present. Find the amount after 1, 2, 3 and 4 hours and write a
     formula. When does it first fall below 100 mg? Will it ever reach 0? Spot
     the mistake in: "30% an hour, so after 4 hours 120% is gone."
     Answer: 280, 196, 137.2 and 96.04 mg; A = 400 × 0.7ᵗ. It first falls below
     100 mg between the 3rd and 4th hour (96.04 mg at 4 hours). It never reaches
     exactly 0. The 120% argument is wrong.
     Teacher explains: Removing 30% leaves 70%, so the multiplier is 0.7.
             t (h)      0      1      2      3        4
             A (mg)   400    280    196    137.2    96.04
     Check: 400 × 0.7⁴ = 400 × 0.2401 = 96.04. Each hour the body removes 30% of
     a SMALLER amount (120, then 84, then 58.8, then 41.16 mg), so the amount
     decreases more and more slowly. Mathematically 400 × 0.7ᵗ is always
     positive: the graph approaches the t-axis but never meets it (in practice
     the amount becomes too small to measure). The 120% argument wrongly takes
     30% of the ORIGINAL 400 mg every hour; with a constant factor it can never
     go below zero. Doctors use this decay to decide how often a dose must be
     repeated. Now you try: 1,000 mg, 20% removed each hour. Amount after 3
     hours? (1,000 × 0.8³ = 512 mg)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: act it out with rice grains on a chessboard (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) or
  by folding paper in half again and again; always write the MULTIPLIER first
  (+5% is × 1.05, −20% is × 0.8) and build a table step by step before using the
  formula; test tables with "difference or ratio?"; use a calculator's power key
  and say how you rounded. Harder: show that the doubling time at r% is log
  2 ÷ log(1 + r/100) and compare it with 72/r; find the continuous growth
  formula A = Pe^(rt) as the limit of compounding more and more often; model a
  real data set (India's population, COVID-19 cases, a cooling cup of tea) with
  y = a·bˣ in a spreadsheet; explain why the Rule of 72 works (ln 2 ≈ 0.693, and
  72 has many factors).


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.18 — GEOMETRIC SEQUENCES (INTRODUCTION)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A GEOMETRIC SEQUENCE (geometric progression, GP) is a list of numbers in
    which each term is the previous term MULTIPLIED by the same number r, the
    COMMON RATIO: 3, 6, 12, 24, ... (r = 2). Test: t₂ ÷ t₁ = t₃ ÷ t₂ = ... (the
    first term a and r are not 0).
  - r can be a fraction (81, 27, 9, ...: r = 1/3, the terms shrink) or negative
    (2, −6, 18, −54, ...: r = −3, the signs alternate). Compare an arithmetic
    sequence (topic 7.12), where the same number is ADDED.
  - The nth term is aₙ = a × rⁿ⁻¹: to reach the nth term from the first we
    multiply by r only (n − 1) times. 10th term of 3, 6, 12, ...:
    3 × 2⁹ = 1,536.
  - To find n, set a × rⁿ⁻¹ equal to the given term and match powers
    (3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 96 gives 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 32 = 2⁵, n = 6). If no whole n works, the number
    is not a term.
  - From two terms: aₘ ÷ aₖ = rᵐ⁻ᵏ. For example a₆ ÷ a₃ = r³. Then find a.
  - SUM of the first n terms: Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) (neat when r > 1), or
    Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) (neat when r < 1); if r = 1, Sₙ = na. Proof: write Sₙ
    and rSₙ, and subtract: nearly all terms cancel.
  - SUM TO INFINITY: when −1 < r < 1 (|r| < 1), rⁿ gets closer and closer to 0
    and the sum approaches S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 there is no sum to
    infinity. 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = 1.
  - A RECURRING DECIMAL is an infinite GP:
    0.777... = 7/10 + 7/100 + ... = (7/10)/(1 − 1/10) = 7/9. This proves every
    recurring decimal is a fraction (topic 7.1).
  - Compound interest amounts P(1 + i), P(1 + i)², P(1 + i)³, ... form a GP with
    r = 1 + i. Regular savings add up to a geometric SERIES.
  - Three numbers a, b, c are in GP when b² = ac; b = √(ac) (b > 0) is the
    GEOMETRIC MEAN of a and c (geometric mean of 4 and 9 is 6).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Which of these are geometric sequences? Give the common ratio of each one
    that is. (a) 3, 6, 12, 24, ... (b) 81, 27, 9, 3, ... (c) 2, −6, 18, −54, ...
    (d) 5, 10, 15, 20, ... (e) 1, 4, 9, 16, ... (f) 7, 7, 7, 7, ...
    Answer: (a) GP, r = 2; (b) GP, r = 1/3; (c) GP, r = −3; (d) not a GP
    (arithmetic, d = 5); (e) not a GP (square numbers); (f) GP, r = 1 (also
    arithmetic, d = 0).
    Teacher explains: The test is the RATIO of each term to the one before. It
    must be the SAME every time:
            (a)  6 ÷ 3 = 2,       12 ÷ 6 = 2,        24 ÷ 12 = 2:      r = 2
            (b)  27 ÷ 81 = 1/3,   9 ÷ 27 = 1/3,      3 ÷ 9 = 1/3:      r = 1/3
            (c)  −6 ÷ 2 = −3,     18 ÷ (−6) = −3,    −54 ÷ 18 = −3:    r = −3
            (d)  10 ÷ 5 = 2,      15 ÷ 10 = 1.5:     not equal
            (e)  4 ÷ 1 = 4,       9 ÷ 4 = 2.25:      not equal
    In (b) the ratio is a FRACTION, so the terms get smaller: multiplying by 1/3
    is the same as dividing by 3. In (c) the ratio is NEGATIVE, so the signs
    alternate. (d) has a common DIFFERENCE (it is arithmetic, topic 7.12), not a
    common ratio. Common mistake: dividing the wrong way round (3 ÷ 6 = 1/2 in
    (a)); always divide a term by the term BEFORE it. Now you try: 800, 80, 8,
    0.8, ... and 1, −1, 1, −1, ... (r = 1/10; r = −1)

D2. Find a formula for the nth term of 3, 6, 12, 24, ... and use it to find the
    10th term. Why is the power n − 1 and not n?
    Answer: aₙ = 3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹; the 10th term is 3 × 2⁹ = 1,536.
    Teacher explains: Write each term as the first term times powers of r:
            a₁ = 3             = 3 × 2⁰
            a₂ = 3 × 2         = 3 × 2¹
            a₃ = 3 × 2 × 2     = 3 × 2²
            a₄ = 3 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 3 × 2³
    The power is always ONE LESS than the term number, because the first term
    has not been multiplied at all. So aₙ = a × rⁿ⁻¹ = 3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹. For n = 10:
    3 × 2⁹ = 3 × 512 = 1,536. Check by listing: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, 192, 384,
    768, 1,536. Common mistakes: using 3 × 2¹⁰ = 3,072 (the 11th term), and
    writing (3 × 2)ⁿ⁻¹ = 6ⁿ⁻¹; the power acts ONLY on r. Now you try: the 8th
    term of 5, 15, 45, ... (5 × 3⁷ = 10,935)

D3. Find the 8th term of 64, −32, 16, −8, ... and the 7th term of 1/9, 1/3, 1,
    3, ...
    Answer: −1/2 and 81.
    Teacher explains: First find r, then use aₙ = a × rⁿ⁻¹.
            64, −32, 16, ...:   r = −32 ÷ 64 = −1/2
            a₈ = 64 × (−1/2)⁷ = 64 × (−1/128) = −1/2
            1/9, 1/3, 1, ...:   r = (1/3) ÷ (1/9) = 3
            a₇ = (1/9) × 3⁶ = 729/9 = 81
    With a NEGATIVE ratio, an odd power is negative and an even power is
    positive: (−1/2)⁷ is negative, so the 8th term is negative (even-numbered
    terms are negative here: −32, −8, ...). Check by listing: 64, −32, 16, −8,
    4, −2, 1, −1/2. Always put a negative or fractional r in BRACKETS: −1/2⁷
    would mean −(1/128), and forgetting the brackets loses the sign pattern. Now
    you try: the 6th term of 2, −6, 18, ... (2 × (−3)⁵ = −486)

D4. Which term of 3, 6, 12, ... is 1,536? Is 1,000 a term of this sequence?
    Which term of 128, 64, 32, ... is 1/4?
    Answer: 1,536 is the 10th term. 1,000 is not a term. 1/4 is the 10th term of
    the second sequence.
    Teacher explains: Put the nth term equal to the number and solve for n:
            3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 1,536
               2ⁿ⁻¹ = 512 = 2⁹
              n − 1 = 9,  so  n = 10
    For 1,000: 3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 1,000 gives 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 1,000/3, which is not even a whole
    number, so it cannot be a power of 2. The terms jump from 768 (9th) to 1,536
    (10th) and miss 1,000. For the second sequence r = 1/2:
            128 × (1/2)ⁿ⁻¹ = 1/4
                 (1/2)ⁿ⁻¹ = 1/512 = (1/2)⁹,  so n − 1 = 9 and n = 10
    Common mistake: stopping at n − 1 = 9 and answering 9. Now you try: which
    term of 2, 6, 18, ... is 1,458? (2 × 3ⁿ⁻¹ = 1,458 gives 3ⁿ⁻¹ = 729 = 3⁶, so
    the 7th)

D5. The 3rd term of a GP is 12 and the 6th term is 96. Find the first term, the
    common ratio and the 10th term. Then do the same for a GP with 2nd term 6
    and 5th term −162.
    Answer: a = 3, r = 2, a₁₀ = 1,536. Second GP: a = −2, r = −3, a₁₀ = 39,366.
    Teacher explains: Write both terms with the formula and DIVIDE to remove a:
            a × r⁵ = 96
            a × r² = 12
            divide:  r³ = 96 ÷ 12 = 8,  so r = 2
            then     a × 2² = 12,  so a = 3
    From the 3rd term to the 6th we multiply by r three times, which is why we
    get r³. Then a₁₀ = 3 × 2⁹ = 1,536. Second GP:
            a × r⁴ = −162,   a × r = 6
            r³ = −162 ÷ 6 = −27,  so r = −3   (a cube root can be negative)
            a × (−3) = 6,  so a = −2
            a₁₀ = −2 × (−3)⁹ = −2 × (−19,683) = 39,366
    Check: −2, 6, −18, 54, −162: the 5th term is −162. Common mistake: when the
    gap is even, for example r² = 9, there are TWO possible ratios, 3 and −3;
    give both. Now you try: a₂ = 10 and a₄ = 40. (r² = 4: r = 2, a = 5 or
    r = −2, a = −5)

D6. Prove that the sum of the first n terms of a GP is Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1)
    when r ≠ 1. Use it to find 3 + 6 + 12 + ... to 10 terms.
    Answer: S₁₀ = 3(2¹⁰ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 3 × 1,023 = 3,069.
    Teacher explains: Write the sum, then multiply every term by r and write it
    one place to the right:
             Sₙ = a + ar + ar² + ... + arⁿ⁻¹
            rSₙ =     ar + ar² + ... + arⁿ⁻¹ + arⁿ
    Subtract the first line from the second. Everything in the middle cancels:
            rSₙ − Sₙ = arⁿ − a
            Sₙ(r − 1) = a(rⁿ − 1)
            Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1)       (we may divide because r ≠ 1)
    When r < 1 it is neater to use the same formula multiplied top and bottom by
    −1: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). If r = 1 all terms equal a and Sₙ = na. For
    3 + 6 + 12 + ...: a = 3, r = 2, n = 10, so S₁₀ = 3(1,024 − 1)/1 = 3,069.
    Check the start: S₃ = 3(8 − 1) = 21 = 3 + 6 + 12. Common mistake: using rⁿ⁻¹
    in the sum formula; the nth TERM has rⁿ⁻¹, the SUM of n terms has rⁿ. Now
    you try: 2 + 6 + 18 + ... to 6 terms. (2(3⁶ − 1)/2 = 728)

D7. A message is sent to 4 people on day 1. On each following day, everyone who
    received it the day before forwards it to 4 NEW people. How many new people
    receive it on day 5, and how many have received it altogether after 5 days?
    (The legend of the chessboard: 1 grain on the first square, 2 on the second,
    4 on the third, ... How many grains on all 64 squares?)
    Answer: 1,024 new people on day 5; 1,364 altogether. Chessboard:
    2⁶⁴ − 1 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains.
    Teacher explains: New people each day: 4, 16, 64, 256, 1,024: a GP with
    a = 4 and r = 4, so day n has 4ⁿ new people and day 5 has 4⁵ = 1,024. The
    total is a geometric SERIES:
            S₅ = 4 + 16 + 64 + 256 + 1,024 = 1,364
            by formula: S₅ = 4(4⁵ − 1)/(4 − 1) = 4 × 1,023/3 = 1,364
    Check by adding: 4 + 16 = 20, + 64 = 84, + 256 = 340, + 1,024 = 1,364. By
    day 12 the new people alone would number 4¹² = 16,777,216: this is why
    rumours and viruses spread so fast. Chessboard: a = 1, r = 2, n = 64:
    S₆₄ = 1(2⁶⁴ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 2⁶⁴ − 1, about 18 billion billion grains, far
    more rice than the whole world grows in a century. Common mistake: finding
    only the LAST term (day 5) when the question asks for the TOTAL. Now you
    try: a chain starts with 1 person, who tells 3 people; each tells 3 new
    people, and so on. Total told in the first 6 rounds, counting the first
    person? (1 + 3 + ... + 3⁵ = (3⁶ − 1)/2 = 364)

D8. A ball is dropped from a height of 10 m. After each bounce it rises to 3/5
    of the height it fell from. Find the total distance it has travelled when it
    hits the ground for the 4th time. What total distance does it travel if it
    bounces for ever?
    Answer: 33.52 m at the 4th landing; 40 m in all.
    Teacher explains: The heights of the bounces are 6, 3.6, 2.16, ... m: a GP
    with a = 6 and r = 3/5 = 0.6. Each bounce is travelled TWICE (up and down),
    but the first drop of 10 m only once:
            drop 10, up 6, down 6, up 3.6, down 3.6, up 2.16, down 2.16
            distance = 10 + 2(6 + 3.6 + 2.16) = 10 + 2 × 11.76 = 33.52 m
    With the sum formula:
    6 + 3.6 + 2.16 = 6(1 − 0.6³)/(1 − 0.6) = 6 × 0.784/0.4 = 11.76. For ever:
    since |r| < 1, the bounces add up to the sum to infinity
    6/(1 − 0.6) = 6/0.4 = 15, so the total is 10 + 2 × 15 = 40 m. An infinite
    number of bounces covers a FINITE distance! Common mistake: forgetting that
    each bounce is up AND down, or doubling the first drop too. Now you try:
    dropped from 16 m, rebounding to 1/2 of the height. Total distance for ever?
    (16 + 2 × 8/(1 − 1/2) = 48 m)

D9. Explain why 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 + ... = 1. Then find the sum to infinity
    of 8 − 4 + 2 − 1 + ... Why does 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... have no sum to infinity?
    Answer: 1; 16/3; its partial sums grow without limit.
    Teacher explains: Picture a square of area 1. Shade half, then half of what
    is left (1/4), then half of what is left (1/8), and so on. The shaded area
    gets as close to 1 as we like but never goes past it. By formula,
    Sₙ = (1/2)(1 − (1/2)ⁿ)/(1 − 1/2) = 1 − (1/2)ⁿ; as n grows, (1/2)ⁿ shrinks
    towards 0, so Sₙ approaches 1. In general, if |r| < 1 then rⁿ → 0 and
            S∞ = a/(1 − r)
    For 8 − 4 + 2 − 1 + ...: a = 8, r = −1/2, so
    S∞ = 8/(1 − (−1/2)) = 8/(3/2) = 16/3. The partial sums 8, 4, 6, 5, 5.5,
    5.25, ... swing above and below 16/3 = 5.333... and close in on it. For
    1 + 2 + 4 + ..., r = 2 and 2ⁿ grows without limit, so there is no sum to
    infinity. (The formula would give 1/(1 − 2) = −1, which is nonsense: this is
    exactly why the condition |r| < 1 matters.) Now you try: S∞ of
    27 + 9 + 3 + 1 + ... (27/(1 − 1/3) = 40.5)

D10. Use geometric series to write 0.777... and 0.2454545... as fractions.
     Explain why 0.999... = 1.
     Answer: 0.777... = 7/9; 0.2454545... = 27/110;
     0.999... = 9/10 ÷ (1 − 1/10) = 1.
     Teacher explains: A recurring decimal is an infinite GP:
             0.777... = 0.7 + 0.07 + 0.007 + ...   a = 7/10, r = 1/10
                      = (7/10)/(1 − 1/10) = (7/10)/(9/10) = 7/9
     For 0.2454545..., the 2 does not repeat, so keep it apart:
             0.2454545... = 0.2 + (0.045 + 0.00045 + 0.0000045 + ...)
             the bracket: a = 45/1000, r = 1/100
             its sum: (45/1000)/(99/100) = 45/990 = 1/22
             total = 1/5 + 1/22 = 22/110 + 5/110 = 27/110
     Check with division: 27 ÷ 110 = 0.24545... Finally
     0.999... = 0.9 + 0.09 + ... = (9/10)/(9/10) = 1. It is not "just below" 1;
     it is another way of writing 1, because the sum to infinity is the number
     the partial sums 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, ... approach. Common mistake: using
     r = 1/10 for a block of TWO repeating digits; the block 45 repeats every
     two places, so r = 1/100. Now you try: 0.363636... (36/99 = 4/11)

D11. Rahul deposits ₹10,000 at 10% per year compound interest. Show that the
     amounts after 1, 2, 3, ... years form a GP. Then: he saves ₹1,000 at the
     START of each year for 5 years at 10% compound interest. How much has he at
     the end of the 5th year?
     Answer: 11,000, 12,100, 13,310, ... is a GP with r = 1.1. The savings plan
     gives ₹6,715.61.
     Teacher explains: Each year the amount is multiplied by 1.1, so the amounts
     are 10,000 × 1.1ⁿ: a GP with first term 11,000 and ratio 1.1. After n
     years: aₙ = 11,000 × 1.1ⁿ⁻¹ = 10,000 × 1.1ⁿ. For the savings plan, look at
     each deposit separately at the end of year 5:
             1st ₹1,000 (5 years' interest):  1,000 × 1.1⁵
             2nd ₹1,000 (4 years):            1,000 × 1.1⁴
             ...
             5th ₹1,000 (1 year):             1,000 × 1.1
             total = 1,000(1.1 + 1.1² + 1.1³ + 1.1⁴ + 1.1⁵)
     The bracket is a GP with a = 1.1, r = 1.1, n = 5:
             1.1(1.1⁵ − 1)/(1.1 − 1) = 1.1 × 0.61051/0.1 = 6.71561
     So the total is ₹6,715.61. He paid in ₹5,000, so ₹1,715.61 is interest.
     Recurring deposits, SIPs and loan EMIs are all calculated with geometric
     series. Common mistake: giving every deposit 5 years of interest. Now you
     try: ₹2,000 at the start of each year for 3 years at 5%: amount at the end
     of year 3? (2,000(1.05 + 1.05² + 1.05³) = ₹6,620.25)

D12. (a) Find the geometric mean of 4 and 9, and insert two numbers between 3
     and 81 so that the four numbers are in GP. (b) For which values of k are
     k − 1, k + 3, 3k + 1 (in this order) in GP?
     Answer: (a) 6; 9 and 27. (b) k = 5 (4, 8, 16) or k = −1 (−2, 2, −2).
     Teacher explains: (a) If a, b, c are in GP then b/a = c/b, so b² = ac. For
     4, b, 9: b² = 36, b = 6 (the geometric mean is taken positive; −6 also
     gives a GP). For 3, __, __, 81: 3 × r³ = 81, r³ = 27, r = 3, so the numbers
     are 9 and 27. (b) Use b² = ac:
             (k + 3)² = (k − 1)(3k + 1)
             k² + 6k + 9 = 3k² − 2k − 1
             0 = 2k² − 8k − 10 = 2(k² − 4k − 5) = 2(k − 5)(k + 1)
             k = 5  or  k = −1
     Check: k = 5 gives 4, 8, 16 (r = 2); k = −1 gives −2, 2, −2 (r = −1). Both
     work. Compare with the ARITHMETIC mean of 4 and 9, (4 + 9)/2 = 6.5; for
     positive numbers the geometric mean is never bigger than the arithmetic
     mean. Common mistake: using b = (a + c)/2, which is the condition for an
     AP. Now you try: insert 3 positive geometric means between 2 and 32. (4,
     8, 16)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Is the sequence geometric? If so give the common ratio r.
    a) 3, 6, 12, 24, ...               b) 81, 27, 9, 3, ...
    c) 2, −6, 18, −54, ...             d) 5, 10, 15, 20, ...
    e) 1, 4, 9, 16, ...                f) 7, 7, 7, 7, ...
    g) 1000, 100, 10, 1, ...           h) 1, −1, 1, −1, ...
    i) 64, −32, 16, −8, ...            j) 2, 4, 8, 14, ...
    k) 1/2, 1, 2, 4, ...               l) −3, −6, −12, −24, ...
    m) 10, 5, 5/2, 5/4, ...            n) 0, 0, 0, 0, ...
    o) 4, 6, 9, 27/2, ...              p) 1, 2, 3, 5, ...
    q) −1, 3, −9, 27, ...              r) 0.2, 0.04, 0.008, 0.0016, ...
    s) 100, 90, 80, 70, ...            t) 2/3, 4/9, 8/27, 16/81, ...
    Answers: a) GP, r = 2   b) GP, r = 1/3   c) GP, r = −3

             o) GP, r = 3/2   p) not a GP   q) GP, r = −3   r) GP, r = 0.2
             s) not a GP (AP, d = −10)   t) GP, r = 2/3

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always write out the first five terms before using a formula; say
  the ratio aloud ("times 2", "times minus a half"); put negative and fractional
  ratios in brackets; keep a table "term number n | power of r" to see why the
  power is n − 1; check sums by adding the first few terms. Harder: prove the
  sum formula and the sum to infinity carefully; show that
  1 + r + r² + ... + rⁿ⁻¹ = (rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) gives the factorisation of xⁿ − 1;
  find the total area of the Koch snowflake or the Sierpinski triangle; work out
  a loan EMI with a geometric series; investigate Zeno's paradox of Achilles and
  the tortoise.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.19 — EUCLID'S AXIOMS AND POSTULATES; THE IDEA OF PROOF
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Euclid of Alexandria (about 300 BCE) collected the geometry of his time in
    the ELEMENTS (13 books). He started from a few DEFINITIONS, AXIOMS and
    POSTULATES and DEDUCED 465 propositions (theorems) from them, step by step.
    This way of building mathematics is called the AXIOMATIC method.
  - Some terms must be left UNDEFINED (point, line, plane), because every
    definition uses other words, and the chain has to start somewhere. Euclid's
    descriptions: a point is that which has no part; a line is breadthless
    length; the ends of a line are points; a surface has length and breadth
    only.
  - AXIOMS (Euclid's "common notions") are used throughout mathematics: (1)
    Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another. (2) If
    equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal. (3) If equals are
    subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal. (4) Things which coincide
    with one another are equal to one another. (5) The whole is greater than the
    part. (6) Things which are double of the same things are equal to one
    another. (7) Things which are halves of the same things are equal to one
    another.
  - POSTULATES are assumptions about GEOMETRY: (1) A straight line may be drawn
    from any one point to any other point. (2) A terminated line (a segment) can
    be produced indefinitely. (3) A circle can be drawn with any centre and any
    radius. (4) All right angles are equal to one another. (5) If a straight
    line falling on two straight lines makes the interior angles on the same
    side of it taken together less than two right angles, then the two lines, if
    produced indefinitely, meet on that side.
  - Axiom 5.1 (a modern form of Postulate 1): given two distinct points, there
    is a UNIQUE (exactly one) line through them. From it we PROVE: two distinct
    lines cannot have more than one point in common.
  - PLAYFAIR'S AXIOM: through a point not on a given line there is EXACTLY ONE
    line parallel to the given line. It is EQUIVALENT to Postulate 5, and so
    are: the angles of every triangle add up to 180°; two intersecting lines
    cannot both be parallel to the same line.
  - A THEOREM is a statement PROVED from axioms, postulates, definitions and
    earlier theorems. A PROOF is a chain of statements, each justified by a
    REASON. A CONJECTURE is a statement believed true but not yet proved:
    checking many examples is NOT a proof, and one COUNTEREXAMPLE disproves a
    general statement.
  - A system of axioms must be CONSISTENT (it must be impossible to prove both a
    statement and its opposite). For 2,000 years people tried to prove Postulate
    5 from the other four and failed: it is INDEPENDENT. Denying it gives
    non-Euclidean geometries (on a sphere the angles of a triangle add up to
    MORE than 180°).
  - Why Euclid matters: the Elements taught the world HOW to prove. Earlier
    geometry, such as the Sulba Sutras of India (rules for building fire altars)
    and Egyptian surveying, gave correct rules; Euclid showed WHY they must be
    true.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A student tries to define a "point" as "a dot", a "dot" as "a very small
    spot", and a "spot" as "a small mark at a point". What goes wrong? What did
    Euclid do instead, and what do we do today?
    Answer: The definitions go round in a circle: "point" is finally defined
    using "point". Some terms must be left UNDEFINED. Euclid DESCRIBED them ("a
    point is that which has no part"); today point, line and plane are accepted
    as undefined terms, and we use them through the axioms.
    Teacher explains: Every definition uses other words, which need their own
    definitions, and so on. Either we go on for ever or we go round in a circle,
    as the student did. So mathematics starts with a few UNDEFINED terms whose
    meaning comes from how they are used. Euclid gave descriptions:
            1. A point is that which has no part.
            2. A line is breadthless length.
            3. The ends of a line are points.
            4. A straight line lies evenly with the points on itself.
            5. A surface is that which has length and breadth only.
    These descriptions use "part", "breadth" and "length", which are themselves
    not defined, so they are really pictures in words. A pencil dot has a size,
    and a pencil line has a width: they are only MODELS of a point and a line.
    Next come the DEFINED terms, which are built from undefined ones: "a line
    segment is the part of a line between two points", "a circle is the set of
    points at a fixed distance from a fixed point". Now you try: which of these
    can be defined using simpler terms: angle, point, triangle? (angle and
    triangle; point is undefined)

D2. Write Euclid's seven axioms (common notions) and give an example of each,
    using numbers or line segments.
    Answer: (1) equal to the same thing, (2) equals added, (3) equals
    subtracted, (4) things that coincide, (5) whole greater than part, (6)
    doubles, (7) halves; examples below.
    Teacher explains: The axioms are about QUANTITIES in general, not only
    geometry, and they are the rules we use every time we solve an equation.
            1. Equal to the same thing:  a = 5 and b = 5, so a = b
            2. Equals added:            x = y, so x + 3 = y + 3
            3. Equals subtracted:       x + 7 = 12 = 5 + 7, so x = 5
            4. Coincide:                if AB fits exactly on PQ, AB = PQ
            5. Whole > part:            if B is between A and C, AC > AB
            6. Doubles:                 AB = CD, so 2AB = 2CD
            7. Halves:                  2x = 2y, so x = y
    Axiom 4 is the basis of "superposition": to compare two figures, imagine
    placing one on top of the other. Axiom 5 looks obvious for lengths and
    areas, but mathematicians later found that it fails for INFINITE sets: the
    even numbers are "part" of the whole numbers, yet they can be paired off one
    to one with them. Common mistake: thinking axioms are "guesses". They are
    the agreed STARTING POINTS; nothing is proved without them. Now you try:
    which axiom gives "if 2x = 18 then x = 9"? (Axiom 7: halves of equals are
    equal)

D3. State Euclid's five postulates and draw a picture for the fifth.
                     t
                      \
            l ---------\------.
                       a\       ` - .
                         \            ` - .
                          \                 ` - .
            m ------------\------------------------P-----
                          b\
                            \
            (a + b < 180°: l and m meet at P, on the side of a and b)
    Answer: (1) A straight line may be drawn from any point to any other point.
    (2) A terminated line can be produced indefinitely. (3) A circle can be
    drawn with any centre and any radius. (4) All right angles are equal to one
    another. (5) If a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the
    interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, the two lines,
    if produced indefinitely, meet on that side.
    Teacher explains: Postulates 1 to 3 describe what a perfect RULER (unmarked
    straight edge) and COMPASS can do: join two points, extend a segment, draw a
    circle. Postulate 4 says a right angle is the same size everywhere, so it
    can be used as a standard unit of angle. Postulate 5 is different: it is
    long and not "self-evident", and it talks about what happens far away, where
    we cannot check. In the picture, the transversal t cuts l and m, and the
    interior angles a and b are on the same side of t. If a + b < 180°, then l
    and m are tilted towards each other on that side and must meet there. If
    a + b = 180°, they never meet: they are PARALLEL. Common mistake: thinking
    the lines meet on the side where the angles are BIGGER; they meet where the
    interior angles add up to LESS than 180°. Now you try: interior angles 88°
    and 89° on one side of a transversal. Do the lines meet? (yes, on that side:
    88 + 89 = 177 < 180)

D4. Name the axiom used in each step. (a) If x + 5 = 12, then x = 7. (b) ∠A = ∠B
    and ∠B = ∠C, so ∠A = ∠C. (c) If AB = PQ, then 2AB = 2PQ. (d) The area of a
    square is greater than the area of one of the two triangles cut off by its
    diagonal. (e) If x − 4 = 6, then x = 10.
    Answer: (a) Axiom 3; (b) Axiom 1; (c) Axiom 6; (d) Axiom 5; (e) Axiom 2.
    Teacher explains: Match the ACTION to the axiom:
            (a)  x + 5 = 12 = 7 + 5; subtract 5 from both     Axiom 3
            (b)  ∠A and ∠C both equal the same thing, ∠B      Axiom 1
            (c)  doubles of equal things                      Axiom 6
            (d)  the triangle is a part of the square         Axiom 5
            (e)  add 4 to both sides: x − 4 + 4 = 6 + 4       Axiom 2
    Every "rule" you learned for solving equations ("do the same to both sides")
    is one of these axioms. In (a) we subtract the same number from two equal
    quantities, so the results are equal. Common mistake in (e): saying Axiom 3
    because the equation contains a minus sign. What matters is what we DO: here
    we ADD 4. Now you try: which axiom gives "∠1 + ∠2 = 90° and ∠3 + ∠2 = 90°,
    so ∠1 + ∠2 = ∠3 + ∠2", and which then gives ∠1 = ∠3? (Axiom 1, then Axiom 3)

D5. C is a point between A and B such that AC = BC. Prove that AC = ½AB. Then
    explain why every line segment has only ONE midpoint.
            A ----------------- C ----------------- B
    Answer: AC + AC = BC + AC = AB, so 2AC = AB and AC = ½AB. If a segment had
    two midpoints C and D, then AC = ½AB = AD, so C and D would coincide.
    Teacher explains: Write the proof as Statement / Reason:
            Statement                    Reason
            AC = BC                      given
            AC + AC = BC + AC            Axiom 2 (equals added to equals)
            BC + AC = AB                 Axiom 4 (BC + AC coincides with AB)
            2AC = AB                     Axiom 1 (both equal BC + AC)
            AC = ½AB                     Axiom 7 (halves of equals are equal)
    For the uniqueness, suppose C and D are BOTH midpoints of AB. By what we
    just proved, AC = ½AB and AD = ½AB, so AC = AD (Axiom 1). Two points on the
    ray AB at the same distance from A must be the same point; otherwise one of
    AC, AD would be a PART of the other and so smaller (Axiom 5). So C = D. This
    is a proof by CONTRADICTION: assume the opposite and reach something
    impossible. Common mistake: "it is obvious from the figure". A figure shows
    one case; the proof must work for every segment. Now you try: if AB = 12 cm
    and C is its midpoint, which axiom gives 2AC = 12 cm when AC = 6 cm? (Axiom
    6, or read the proof backwards)

D6. Euclid's Proposition 1: construct an equilateral triangle on a given segment
    AB, and prove that it is equilateral. Which postulate is really missing from
    the proof?
                         C
                        / \
                       /   \         circle 1: centre A, radius AB
                      /     \        circle 2: centre B, radius BA
                    A ------- B      C is where the circles meet
    Answer: Draw circle 1 (centre A, radius AB) and circle 2 (centre B, radius
    BA); let C be a point where they meet; join CA and CB. Then AC = AB (radii
    of circle 1) and BC = AB (radii of circle 2), so AC = BC = AB. The missing
    step: nothing in the postulates says that the two circles MUST meet.
    Teacher explains: The proof with reasons:
            Statement                    Reason
            draw circle, centre A, AB    Postulate 3
            draw circle, centre B, BA    Postulate 3
            join C to A and C to B       Postulate 1
            AC = AB                      radii of the same circle (definition)
            BC = AB                      radii of the same circle (definition)
            AC = BC                      Axiom 1 (both equal AB)
            so AC = AB = BC: ΔABC is equilateral
    The gap: the picture makes it OBVIOUS that the circles cross, but "obvious
    from the picture" is not a reason. Two thousand years later David Hilbert
    (1899) added extra axioms (about "betweenness" and "continuity") to close
    such gaps. This is how mathematics improves: every step must rest on a
    stated assumption. Now you try: which postulate lets us draw BC in a
    triangle once B and C are marked? (Postulate 1)

D7. Prove the theorem: two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in
    common.
                 l
                  \      m
                   \    /
                    \  /
                     \/
                     /\ P
                    /  \
    Answer: Suppose two distinct lines l and m had two common points P and Q.
    Then two different lines would pass through P and Q, which contradicts Axiom
    5.1 (exactly one line through two distinct points). So they have at most one
    common point.
    Teacher explains: This is a proof by CONTRADICTION:
            Step 1  Assume the opposite: l ≠ m, and both pass through two
                    points P and Q (P ≠ Q).
            Step 2  Axiom 5.1: through P and Q there is ONLY ONE line.
            Step 3  So l and m are the same line, which contradicts l ≠ m.
            Step 4  The assumption is false: l and m share at most one point.
    So two distinct lines either meet in exactly ONE point (intersecting lines)
    or have NO common point (parallel lines, if they are in the same plane). The
    proof uses only Axiom 5.1; it does not depend on the drawing. Common
    mistake: "I drew two lines and they met only once" is an EXPERIMENT, not a
    proof. Now you try: how many lines can pass through (i) one given point,
    (ii) two given distinct points? (infinitely many; exactly one)

D8. Points A, B, C, D lie on a line in this order, and AC = BD. Prove that
    AB = CD. If AC = BD = 12 cm and BC = 5 cm, find AB and CD.
            A ---------- B ---------- C ---------- D
    Answer: AB + BC = BC + CD, and subtracting BC gives AB = CD. With the
    numbers: AB = CD = 12 − 5 = 7 cm.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                    Reason
            AC = AB + BC                 B lies between A and C
            BD = BC + CD                 C lies between B and D
            AC = BD                      given
            AB + BC = BC + CD            Axiom 1 (both equal AC = BD)
            AB = CD                      Axiom 3 (subtract BC from both)
    Numbers: AB = AC − BC = 12 − 5 = 7 cm and CD = BD − BC = 12 − 5 = 7 cm. The
    two segments AC and BD overlap in BC; removing the SAME overlap from equal
    segments leaves equal pieces. The reverse is also true: if AB = CD then
    AC = BD (add BC to both: Axiom 2). Common mistake: writing "AB = CD because
    they look equal". Now you try: A, B, C, D in order on a line with
    AB = CD = 4 cm and BC = 9 cm. Find AC and BD. (13 cm each, Axiom 2)

D9. A transversal cuts lines l and m. The interior angles on one side are 85°
    and 90°. Using Postulate 5, do l and m meet? On which side? State Playfair's
    axiom and explain how it is related to Postulate 5.
    Answer: 85° + 90° = 175° < 180°, so l and m meet on that side. Playfair's
    axiom: through a point not on a line there is exactly one line parallel to
    it. It is equivalent to Postulate 5: either one can be proved from the other
    (with the other axioms).
    Teacher explains: On the other side of the transversal the interior angles
    are 180° − 85° = 95° and 180° − 90° = 90°, which add up to 185° > 180°. So
    the lines SPREAD APART on that side and come together on the first side:
            side 1:  85° + 90° = 175° < 180°   → the lines meet on side 1
            side 2:  95° + 90° = 185° > 180°   → they do not meet on side 2
            both 90° and 90° (sum 180°)        → parallel, they never meet
    Playfair's version is easier to picture: take a line l and a point P not on
    it. Draw the line through P that makes interior angles adding up to 180°
    with l; it is parallel. Postulate 5 says that ANY other line through P makes
    a sum less than 180° on one side, so it meets l. Hence there is exactly ONE
    parallel through P. Common mistake: thinking that "meet" must be visible on
    the page; the lines may meet a kilometre away. Now you try: interior angles
    100° and 80° on one side. (sum 180°: parallel)

D10. Explain why the fifth postulate was so famous. Give two statements
     equivalent to it, and describe a geometry in which it is false.
     Answer: Mathematicians tried for about 2,000 years to prove it from the
     other postulates and failed; in the 1800s it was shown to be independent.
     Equivalent statements: Playfair's axiom; the angle sum of every triangle is
     180°. On a SPHERE there are no parallel "straight lines" (great circles),
     and a triangle can have three right angles.
     Teacher explains: Postulate 5 is longer and less obvious than the others,
     so many (Ptolemy, the Persian poet-mathematician Omar Khayyam, Saccheri)
     tried to deduce it from Postulates 1 to 4. Every "proof" secretly used a
     statement equivalent to it, such as:
             - through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel
             - the angles of any triangle add up to 180°
             - two intersecting lines cannot both be parallel to the same line
             - two triangles can have the same angles but different sizes
     In the 1820s Lobachevsky and Bolyai (and Gauss) built consistent geometries
     in which Postulate 5 is FALSE. On the surface of the Earth take the North
     Pole N and two points A and B on the equator, a quarter of the way round
     from each other. The "straight lines" are great circles. ΔNAB has angles of
     90° at A, at B and at N:
             angle sum = 90° + 90° + 90° = 270° > 180°
     So the angle sum depends on which postulates we accept. Einstein's theory
     of gravity uses non-Euclidean geometry. Common mistake: "Euclid's geometry
     is wrong". It is correct for flat surfaces, and a very good approximation
     for everyday sizes. Now you try: on a sphere, can two great circles be
     parallel? (no: any two great circles meet, in two points)

D11. Mark n points on a circle and join every pair with a chord (no three chords
     through one point inside). Count the regions for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Guess
     the number for n = 6. Is your guess right? What does this teach about
     proof?
             n          1    2    3    4    5    6
             regions    1    2    4    8   16    ?
     Answer: The pattern 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 suggests 32 for n = 6, but careful
     counting gives only 31. A pattern from examples is only a CONJECTURE; it
     must be proved.
     Teacher explains: Most people guess "it doubles" and expect 32. Draw six
     points carefully (not equally spaced, so that no three chords meet at one
     point) and count: 31 regions. The correct formula is
             regions = 1 + C(n, 2) + C(n, 4)
             n = 5:  1 + 10 + 5  = 16
             n = 6:  1 + 15 + 15 = 31
     (C(n, 2) counts chords and C(n, 4) counts crossing points.) This is the
     difference between INDUCTIVE reasoning (guessing a rule from examples;
     useful for discovering) and DEDUCTIVE reasoning (deriving a result from
     axioms by logic; the only way to be SURE). Euclid's method is deductive. A
     statement becomes a THEOREM only when it has a proof; until then it is a
     CONJECTURE, and one COUNTEREXAMPLE (n = 6 here) is enough to destroy it.
     Now you try: the claim "n² + 1 is odd for every whole number n" holds for
     n = 0 and n = 2. Find a counterexample. (n = 1: 1 + 1 = 2 is even)

D12. A "mini-geometry" has three axioms: (A) there are exactly 3 points; (B) any
     two points lie on exactly one line; (C) every line contains exactly 2
     points. Is the system consistent? How many lines are there? What happens if
     we add (D) "there are exactly 2 lines"?
     Answer: It is consistent: the three corners of a triangle with its three
     sides satisfy (A), (B) and (C), so there are 3 lines. Adding (D) makes the
     system inconsistent, because (A), (B), (C) force 3 lines.
     Teacher explains: A system of axioms is CONSISTENT if no contradiction can
     be proved from it. One way to show consistency is to find a MODEL, an
     example that obeys every axiom:
             points P, Q, R        lines {P, Q}, {Q, R}, {P, R}
     Check: exactly 3 points (A); each pair of points is on exactly one of the
     lines (B); each line has exactly 2 points (C). Now COUNT: each line is
     fixed by its pair of points, and there are C(3, 2) = 3 pairs, so there must
     be exactly 3 lines. Axiom (D) says 2, so the system (A) to (D) proves "3
     lines" and "2 lines": a CONTRADICTION, so it is inconsistent and useless.
     Euclid's axioms have a model too (coordinate geometry, topic 7.29: points
     are pairs (x, y)), so they are consistent as long as arithmetic is. Common
     mistake: thinking that more axioms always make a better system; they must
     not contradict each other, and ideally none should be provable from the
     others (INDEPENDENCE). Now you try: with (A) replaced by "exactly 4
     points", how many lines? (C(4, 2) = 6)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make a wall chart of the 7 axioms and 5 postulates with a small
  picture or equation for each; when solving any equation, say which axiom each
  step uses; use a ruler and compass to act out Postulates 1 to 3; draw two
  lines with interior angles 85° and 90° on a long sheet and extend them to see
  where they meet. Harder: read Proposition 1 of Book I of the Elements and list
  every hidden assumption; prove that Playfair's axiom implies the angle sum of
  a triangle is 180° (using alternate angles); make a triangle on a football
  with string along great circles and measure its angles; invent a small axiom
  system (for example 4 points, every line has 2 points) and find a model;
  research Baudhayana's Sulba Sutra and compare its rules with Euclid's proofs.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.20 — LINES AND ANGLES THEOREMS (FORMAL PROOFS)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - LINEAR PAIR AXIOM: if a ray stands on a line, the two adjacent angles it
    forms add up to 180°. CONVERSE (also taken as an axiom): if two adjacent
    angles add up to 180°, their outer arms form a straight line.
  - VERTICALLY OPPOSITE ANGLES THEOREM: when two lines intersect, the vertically
    opposite angles are equal. Proof: both angles make a linear pair with the
    same angle between them.
  - A transversal cutting two lines makes 8 angles: CORRESPONDING pairs (same
    position at each crossing), ALTERNATE INTERIOR pairs (between the lines,
    opposite sides of the transversal), CO-INTERIOR pairs (between the lines,
    same side), and alternate exterior pairs.
  - CORRESPONDING ANGLES AXIOM: if a transversal cuts two PARALLEL lines, each
    pair of corresponding angles is equal. Its CONVERSE axiom: if a pair of
    corresponding angles is equal, the lines are parallel.
  - Theorems proved from these: with parallel lines, ALTERNATE interior angles
    are equal and CO-INTERIOR angles add up to 180°. Converses: equal alternate
    angles, or co-interior angles adding up to 180°, prove the lines parallel.
  - Lines which are parallel to the same line are parallel to each other (l ∥ m
    and m ∥ n give l ∥ n).
  - ANGLE SUM THEOREM: the angles of a triangle add up to 180° (draw the
    parallel to one side through the opposite vertex). EXTERIOR ANGLE THEOREM:
    an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
  - A formal proof is written as STATEMENT / REASON. Every statement needs a
    reason: given, linear pair axiom, vertically opposite angles, corresponding
    angles (l ∥ m), alternate angles (l ∥ m), co-interior angles (l ∥ m), angle
    sum of a triangle, and so on. Name the parallel lines in the reason.
  - In algebraic angle problems first decide HOW the angles are related (equal
    or adding up to 180°), then write and solve the equation, and finally check
    that every angle is positive.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. State the linear pair axiom and its converse. A ray OC stands on the line AB
    with ∠AOC = 3x° and ∠BOC = (2x + 20)°. Find x and both angles. Then:
    ∠POQ = 118° and ∠QOR = 62° are adjacent angles. What can you say about P, O
    and R?
                          C
                         /
                        /
            A ---------O----------- B
    Answer: x = 32; ∠AOC = 96°, ∠BOC = 84°. P, O and R lie on a straight line.
    Teacher explains: The linear pair axiom: if a ray stands on a line, the sum
    of the two adjacent angles so formed is 180°. So
            Statement                        Reason
            ∠AOC + ∠BOC = 180°               linear pair axiom
            3x + 2x + 20 = 180               substitute
            5x = 160, x = 32                 solve
            ∠AOC = 3 × 32 = 96°,  ∠BOC = 2 × 32 + 20 = 84°
    Check: 96 + 84 = 180. The CONVERSE: if the sum of two adjacent angles is
    180°, the non-common arms form a line. Since 118° + 62° = 180°, the arms OP
    and OR form one straight line: P, O, R are COLLINEAR. We use the converse
    whenever we must PROVE that three points are in a line. Common mistake:
    applying the axiom to angles that are not ADJACENT, or not on a straight
    line. Now you try: ∠AOC = (4x − 10)° and ∠BOC = (x + 40)° form a linear
    pair. (x = 30: 110° and 70°)

D2. Prove that if two lines intersect, the vertically opposite angles are equal.
    Lines AB and CD cross at O and ∠AOC = 40°. Find the other three angles.
                A           D
                  \       /
                    \   /
                      O
                    /   \
                  /       \
                C           B
    Answer: ∠AOC = ∠BOD and ∠AOD = ∠BOC. Here ∠BOD = 40°, ∠AOD = ∠BOC = 140°.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                        Reason
            ∠AOC + ∠AOD = 180°               linear pair (ray OA stands on CD)
            ∠AOD + ∠BOD = 180°               linear pair (ray OD stands on AB)
            ∠AOC + ∠AOD = ∠AOD + ∠BOD        both equal 180° (Axiom 1)
            ∠AOC = ∠BOD                      subtract ∠AOD (Axiom 3)
    In the same way ∠AOD = ∠BOC. Numbers: ∠BOD = ∠AOC = 40° (vertically
    opposite); ∠AOD = 180° − 40° = 140° (linear pair); ∠BOC = ∠AOD = 140°
    (vertically opposite). Check: 40 + 140 + 40 + 140 = 360, the angles round a
    point. Common mistake: calling ADJACENT angles (such as ∠AOC and ∠AOD)
    vertically opposite. Vertically opposite angles share only the vertex, and
    their arms are opposite rays. Now you try: two lines cross and one angle is
    3 times another. Find all four angles. (45°, 135°, 45°, 135°)

D3. Rays OE and OF bisect the angles ∠AOC and ∠BOC of a linear pair. Prove that
    ∠EOF = 90°. Find ∠EOF when ∠AOC = 70°.
                   E        C
                    \      /       F
                     \    /    .-'
                      \  /  .-'
            A ----------O------------- B
    Answer: ∠EOF = ½∠AOC + ½∠BOC = ½ × 180° = 90° always; with ∠AOC = 70°:
    35° + 55° = 90°.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                              Reason
            ∠AOC + ∠BOC = 180°                     linear pair axiom
            ∠EOC = ½∠AOC                           OE bisects ∠AOC
            ∠COF = ½∠BOC                           OF bisects ∠BOC
            ∠EOF = ∠EOC + ∠COF                     OC lies inside ∠EOF
                 = ½(∠AOC + ∠BOC) = ½ × 180° = 90°
    With numbers: ∠BOC = 180° − 70° = 110°, so ∠EOC = 35° and ∠COF = 55°, and
    ∠EOF = 35° + 55° = 90°. The proof shows WHY the answer does not depend on
    the size of ∠AOC. The same idea proves that the bisectors of two co-interior
    angles between parallel lines meet at 90°. Common mistake: halving only one
    of the angles. Now you try: the bisectors of vertically opposite angles:
    what angle do they make? (180°: they form one straight line)

D4. Using the corresponding angles axiom, prove that when a transversal cuts two
    parallel lines, the alternate interior angles are equal. State the converse.
                              t
                             /
                        1   /  2
            l -------------P-------------------------
                      3   /  4
                         /
                    5   /  6
            m ---------Q-----------------------------
                  7   /  8
                     /
    Answer: With l ∥ m: ∠3 = ∠6 and ∠4 = ∠5. Converse: if a pair of alternate
    interior angles is equal, the lines are parallel.
    Teacher explains: In the figure the transversal t cuts l at P and m at Q. We
    prove ∠4 = ∠5 (the other pair is similar):
            Statement               Reason
            ∠1 = ∠5                 corresponding angles (l ∥ m)
            ∠1 = ∠4                 vertically opposite angles
            ∠4 = ∠5                 both equal ∠1 (Axiom 1)
    For the CONVERSE, suppose ∠4 = ∠5. Since ∠1 = ∠4 (vertically opposite),
    ∠1 = ∠5. These are corresponding angles, so by the converse of the
    corresponding angles axiom, l ∥ m. Notice the pattern of a proof: we may use
    ONLY the axiom and theorems proved before. Once this theorem is proved, it
    can be used as a reason in later proofs ("alternate angles, l ∥ m"). Common
    mistake: writing "alternate angles" as a reason when the lines are not known
    to be parallel. Now you try: prove ∠3 = ∠6 in the same way. (∠2 = ∠6
    corresponding; ∠2 = ∠3 vertically opposite)

D5. Prove that the co-interior angles ∠4 and ∠6 in the figure add up to 180°
    when l ∥ m. Then decide whether l ∥ m when ∠3 = 105° and ∠5 = 75°.
                              t
                             /
                        1   /  2
            l -------------P-------------------------
                      3   /  4
                         /
                    5   /  6
            m ---------Q-----------------------------
                  7   /  8
                     /
    Answer: ∠4 + ∠6 = 180°. Yes: ∠3 + ∠5 = 180°, so l ∥ m (converse of the
    co-interior theorem).
    Teacher explains:
            Statement               Reason
            ∠4 + ∠2 = 180°          linear pair axiom (on line l)
            ∠2 = ∠6                 corresponding angles (l ∥ m)
            ∠4 + ∠6 = 180°          substitute ∠6 for ∠2
    CONVERSE: if co-interior angles add up to 180°, the lines are parallel.
    Proof: from ∠3 + ∠5 = 180° and ∠3 + ∠1 = 180° (linear pair) we get ∠5 = ∠1;
    they are corresponding angles, so l ∥ m. In the numbers, ∠3 and ∠5 are both
    between l and m and on the SAME side of t (co-interior), and
    105° + 75° = 180°, so l ∥ m. If ∠5 had been 70°, the sum would be 175°, and
    by Postulate 5 the lines would meet on that side. Common mistake: deciding
    "parallel" because two angles are EQUAL; for co-interior angles equality is
    not the test (unless both are 90°). Now you try: ∠4 = 98° and ∠6 = 88°.
    Parallel? (no: 186° ≠ 180°)

D6. In the figure l ∥ m and ∠1 = 118°. Find the other seven angles, giving a
    reason for each.
                              t
                             /
                        1   /  2
            l -------------P-------------------------
                      3   /  4
                         /
                    5   /  6
            m ---------Q-----------------------------
                  7   /  8
                     /
    Answer: ∠1 = ∠4 = ∠5 = ∠8 = 118°; ∠2 = ∠3 = ∠6 = ∠7 = 62°.
    Teacher explains: Work outwards from the angle you know, one reason at a
    time:
            Angle   Value   Reason
            ∠2      62°     linear pair with ∠1 (180 − 118)
            ∠4      118°    vertically opposite ∠1
            ∠3      62°     vertically opposite ∠2
            ∠5      118°    corresponding to ∠1 (l ∥ m)
            ∠6      62°     alternate to ∠3 (l ∥ m)
            ∠8      118°    vertically opposite ∠5
            ∠7      62°     linear pair with ∠8
    With two parallel lines and a transversal there are only TWO different
    sizes, and they add up to 180°: 118° + 62° = 180°. The four "big" angles are
    1, 4, 5, 8 and the four "small" angles are 2, 3, 6, 7. Check with
    co-interior angles: ∠4 + ∠6 = 118° + 62° = 180°. Common mistake: using
    corresponding angles when the lines are NOT given parallel. Now you try: l ∥
    m and ∠7 = 55°. Find ∠1 and ∠2. (∠1 = 125°, ∠2 = 55°)

D7. AB ∥ CD, and E is a point between the lines, as shown. ∠ABE = 40° and
    ∠CDE = 35°. Find ∠BED and prove the general result.
            A ------------------------------ B
                                           /
                                         /
                                       /
                                     E
                                       \
                                         \
                                           \
            C ------------------------------ D
    Answer: ∠BED = 40° + 35° = 75°. In general ∠BED = ∠ABE + ∠CDE.
    Teacher explains: The trick is to draw a NEW line: through E draw EF
    parallel to AB, with F on the same side as A and C. Since AB ∥ CD, also EF ∥
    CD (lines parallel to the same line are parallel).
            Statement                      Reason
            EF ∥ AB, EF ∥ CD               construction; lines parallel to AB
            ∠BEF = ∠ABE = 40°              alternate angles (EF ∥ AB)
            ∠FED = ∠CDE = 35°              alternate angles (EF ∥ CD)
            ∠BED = ∠BEF + ∠FED = 75°       EF lies inside ∠BED
    If instead E lies on the OTHER side of BD (so that the figure looks like a
    "C"), the construction gives co-interior angles, and
    ∠ABE + ∠BED + ∠EDC = 360°. Always draw the extra parallel line and look at
    which pairs of angles appear. Common mistake: trying to find ∠BED with the
    angle sum of a triangle when there is no triangle in the figure. Now you
    try: ∠ABE = 52° and ∠BED = 90° in the same figure. Find ∠CDE. (38°)

D8. Prove that two lines which are both parallel to a third line are parallel to
    each other. Then: l ∥ m and m ∥ n; a transversal makes an angle of 65° with
    l. What angles does it make with m and n?
            t cuts l, m, n at P, Q, R; ∠1, ∠2, ∠3 are corresponding angles
            at P, Q and R
    Answer: If l ∥ m and n ∥ m, then l ∥ n. The transversal makes 65° (and 115°)
    with m and with n.
    Teacher explains: Draw a transversal t that cuts all three lines, and take
    corresponding angles ∠1, ∠2, ∠3 at the three crossings.
            Statement               Reason
            ∠1 = ∠2                 corresponding angles (l ∥ m)
            ∠3 = ∠2                 corresponding angles (n ∥ m)
            ∠1 = ∠3                 Axiom 1
            l ∥ n                   converse of the corresponding angles axiom
    Numbers: all three corresponding angles are 65°, and the angles next to them
    are 180° − 65° = 115°. This theorem is why the lines of an exercise book,
    all drawn parallel to the top edge, are parallel to each other, and why the
    rails of a railway track, each parallel to the centre line, never meet. It
    is also equivalent to Playfair's axiom (topic 7.19). Common mistake:
    assuming the result in the proof ("l ∥ n because they look parallel"). Now
    you try: l ∥ m, m ∥ n, and a transversal is perpendicular to l. What angle
    does it make with n? (90°)

D9. Write formal proofs of (a) the angle sum theorem for ΔABC and (b) the
    exterior angle theorem. Then find the angles if ∠A = 58° and the exterior
    angle ∠ACD = 121°.
            X ------------- A ------------- Y
                          /   \
                        /       \
                      /           \
                    B --------------- C ----------- D
    Answer: (a) ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°. (b) ∠ACD = ∠A + ∠B. With the numbers:
    ∠B = 121° − 58° = 63° and ∠ACB = 180° − 121° = 59°.
    Teacher explains: (a) Through A draw XY ∥ BC.
            Statement                        Reason
            ∠XAB = ∠B                        alternate angles (XY ∥ BC)
            ∠YAC = ∠ACB                      alternate angles (XY ∥ BC)
            ∠XAB + ∠BAC + ∠YAC = 180°        angles on the line XY
            ∠B + ∠BAC + ∠ACB = 180°          substitute
    (b) BC is produced to D.
            ∠ACD + ∠ACB = 180°               linear pair axiom
            ∠A + ∠B + ∠ACB = 180°            angle sum theorem (a)
            ∠ACD = ∠A + ∠B                   both equal 180° − ∠ACB
    Numbers: ∠B = ∠ACD − ∠A = 121° − 58° = 63°; ∠ACB = 180° − 121° = 59°. Check:
    58 + 63 + 59 = 180. The proof of (a) needs a parallel line, so it rests on
    Postulate 5 (on a sphere it fails). A consequence of (b): an exterior angle
    is greater than each interior opposite angle. Common mistake: in (b) adding
    the interior angle NEXT to the exterior angle. Now you try: interior
    opposite angles 47° and 68°. Exterior angle? (115°)

D10. A transversal cuts two parallel lines AB and CD at P and Q. PR bisects ∠APQ
     and QS bisects ∠DQP (a pair of alternate interior angles). Prove that PR ∥
     QS.
             A ------------------P-------------------- B
                               / |
                             /   |
                           R     |     S
                                 |   /
                                 | /
             C ------------------Q-------------------- D
             (PR bisects ∠APQ, QS bisects ∠DQP)
     Answer: ∠RPQ = ½∠APQ = ½∠DQP = ∠SQP, and these are alternate angles for the
     lines PR and QS with transversal PQ, so PR ∥ QS.
     Teacher explains:
             Statement                      Reason
             ∠APQ = ∠DQP                    alternate angles (AB ∥ CD)
             ½∠APQ = ½∠DQP                  Axiom 7 (halves of equals)
             ∠RPQ = ∠SQP                    PR and QS are the bisectors
             PR ∥ QS                        converse: equal alternate angles
     The key is to see a NEW pair of lines (PR and QS) with the SAME transversal
     PQ, and to recognise ∠RPQ and ∠SQP as alternate angles for them. For
     example, if ∠APQ = 70°, then ∠DQP = 70°, and ∠RPQ = ∠SQP = 35°. Common
     mistake: forgetting to say WHICH lines are parallel in each reason; here
     two different pairs of lines are involved. Now you try: prove that the
     bisectors of a pair of CORRESPONDING angles are parallel. (halves of equal
     corresponding angles are equal corresponding angles)

D11. In the figure l ∥ m. Find x in each case: (a) ∠1 = (3x + 10)° and
     ∠5 = (5x − 30)°; (b) ∠3 = (2x + 15)° and ∠6 = (4x − 25)°; (c)
     ∠4 = (3x + 20)° and ∠6 = (2x + 10)°.
                               t
                              /
                         1   /  2
             l -------------P-------------------------
                       3   /  4
                          /
                     5   /  6
             m ---------Q-----------------------------
                   7   /  8
                      /
     Answer: (a) x = 20 (both 70°); (b) x = 20 (both 55°); (c) x = 30 (110° and
     70°).
     Teacher explains: FIRST name the relationship, THEN write the equation:
             (a)  ∠1, ∠5 corresponding: equal     3x + 10 = 5x − 30,  x = 20
             (b)  ∠3, ∠6 alternate: equal         2x + 15 = 4x − 25,  x = 20
             (c)  ∠4, ∠6 co-interior: sum 180°    3x + 20 + 2x + 10 = 180,
                                                  5x = 150,  x = 30
     Check (a): 3 × 20 + 10 = 70 and 5 × 20 − 30 = 70. Check (c):
     3 × 30 + 20 = 110 and 2 × 30 + 10 = 70; 110 + 70 = 180. Always check that
     each angle is POSITIVE and less than 180°: a solution giving a negative
     angle means the relationship was misread. Common mistake: setting
     co-interior angles EQUAL. In (c) that would give 3x + 20 = 2x + 10,
     x = −10, and the angles would be −10°: impossible. Now you try:
     ∠2 = (5x − 5)° and ∠7 = (3x + 25)° with l ∥ m. (alternate exterior, equal:
     x = 15, both 70°)

D12. (a) Prove that if the arms of ∠ABC are parallel to the arms of ∠DEF (BA ∥
     ED and BC ∥ EF, pointing the same way), then ∠ABC = ∠DEF. (b) What if one
     pair of arms points the opposite way?
                       A           D
                      /           /
                     /           /
                    B ----------G---------- C
                               /
                              E ---------- F
             (BA ∥ ED, BC ∥ EF; the line DE meets BC at G)
     Answer: (a) Let the line DE meet BC at G. ∠ABC = ∠DGC (corresponding, BA ∥
     GD) and ∠DGC = ∠DEF (corresponding, BC ∥ EF), so ∠ABC = ∠DEF. (b) Then the
     angles are SUPPLEMENTARY (they add up to 180°).
     Teacher explains:
             Statement                Reason
             ∠ABC = ∠DGC              corresponding (BA ∥ GD, transversal BC)
             ∠DGC = ∠DEF              corresponding (GC ∥ EF, transversal DE)
             ∠ABC = ∠DEF              Axiom 1
     For (b), if EF points the opposite way, the angle at E is the angle next to
     ∠DEF on the line, so it equals 180° − ∠ABC. For example, an angle of 65°
     whose arms are parallel to the arms of another angle: the other angle is
     65° or 115°. This is useful in problems with rulers, set squares and
     parallel bars (such as a parallel ruler or a folding gate). Common mistake:
     forgetting the second possibility. Now you try: the arms of ∠P are
     perpendicular to the arms of ∠Q (not parallel). Are they equal or
     supplementary? (either, depending on the directions: for example 40° and
     40°, or 40° and 140°)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY

    g) 179°     h) 120°     i) 64°      j) 108°     k) 37.5°    l) 142.5°

             n) 120°   o) 179.5°   p) 81°   q) 30°   r) 107°   s) 167.75°
             t) 80°

M3. Lines AB and CD intersect at O. Find all four angles (and x).
    a) ∠AOC = 40°

    f) ∠AOC = 179°
    g) ∠AOC = 72°
    h) ∠AOC = 22.5°
    i) ∠AOC = 115°
    j) ∠AOC = 60°
    k) ∠AOC = (2x + 10)°, ∠BOD = (3x − 20)°
    l) ∠AOC = (4x)°, ∠AOD = (x + 30)°
    m) ∠AOD = (5x − 20)°, ∠BOC = (3x + 40)°
    n) ∠AOC = (x + 50)°, ∠BOC = (2x + 10)°

M4. Three lines AB, CD, EF pass through O; going round O the rays are in the
    order OA, OC, OE, OB, OD, OF. Find the other four angles.
    a) ∠AOC = 50°, ∠COE = 60°       b) ∠AOC = 40°, ∠COE = 70°
    c) ∠AOC = 90°, ∠COE = 30°       d) ∠AOC = 25°, ∠COE = 45°
    e) ∠AOC = 60°, ∠COE = 60°       f) ∠AOC = 100°, ∠COE = 35°
    g) ∠AOC = 15°, ∠COE = 75°       h) ∠AOC = 80°, ∠COE = 80°
    i) ∠AOC = 37.5°, ∠COE = 52.5°   j) ∠AOC = 120°, ∠COE = 30°
    k) ∠AOC = 10°, ∠COE = 10°       l) ∠AOC = 44°, ∠COE = 91°
    Answers:
      a) ∠EOB = 70°, ∠BOD = 50°, ∠DOF = 60°, ∠FOA = 70°
      b) ∠EOB = 70°, ∠BOD = 40°, ∠DOF = 70°, ∠FOA = 70°
