TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: colour the eight angles of the transversal figure in two colours
  (the four big ones and the four small ones); trace a "Z" for alternate angles,
  an "F" for corresponding angles and a "C" (or "U") for co-interior angles;
  always write the reason next to each step and name the parallel lines; check
  every answer with "two sizes that add up to 180°". Harder: prove the converses
  carefully; prove that the sum of the angles of a pentagon is 540° using
  parallel lines; find a formula for the zigzag with n bends between two
  parallel lines; prove that the bisectors of the interior angles of a
  parallelogram form a rectangle; investigate which of these theorems fail on a
  sphere.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.21 — TRIANGLE THEOREMS: CONGRUENCE, INEQUALITIES IN A TRIANGLE
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Two triangles are CONGRUENT (≅) when all three pairs of sides and all three
    pairs of angles are equal. The order of the letters shows the matching: ΔABC
    ≅ ΔPQR means A ↔ P, B ↔ Q, C ↔ R, so AB = PQ, ∠B = ∠Q, and so on. CPCT:
    corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal.
  - SAS CONGRUENCE RULE (taken as an AXIOM): two sides and the INCLUDED angle of
    one triangle equal to two sides and the included angle of the other. Euclid
    "proved" it by moving one triangle onto the other (superposition), which his
    postulates do not justify, so today it is an axiom.
  - Theorems proved from SAS: ASA (two angles and the included side), AAS (two
    angles and any corresponding side; the third angles are then equal too), SSS
    (three sides), RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and one side). SSA and AAA are
    NOT congruence rules.
  - ISOSCELES TRIANGLE THEOREM: angles opposite equal sides are equal (proof:
    the bisector of the apex angle gives two triangles congruent by SAS).
    CONVERSE: sides opposite equal angles are equal (proof by AAS). So an
    equilateral triangle has three 60° angles.
  - INEQUALITIES: in a triangle the angle opposite the LONGER side is LARGER,
    and (converse) the side opposite the LARGER angle is LONGER. So the longest
    side faces the largest angle, and in a right triangle the hypotenuse is the
    longest side.
  - TRIANGLE INEQUALITY: the sum of any two sides of a triangle is GREATER than
    the third side (a + b > c). Equivalently the difference of two sides is LESS
    than the third. So the third side x of a triangle with sides a and b
    satisfies |a − b| < x < a + b.
  - To test three lengths, check only that the two SHORTER ones add up to MORE
    than the longest. 3, 4, 8: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8, not a triangle; 5, 5, 10:
    5 + 5 = 10, not a triangle (the points would be in a line).
  - The perpendicular from a point to a line is the SHORTEST segment from the
    point to the line (every other segment is the hypotenuse of a right
    triangle).
  - Writing a congruence proof: name the two triangles, give three pairs of
    equal parts with a REASON each (given, common side, vertically opposite
    angles, alternate angles, ...), state the rule, then use CPCT.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. In ΔABC, AB = AC and AD bisects ∠A, meeting BC at D. Prove that BD = CD and
    AD ⊥ BC. Why is SAS taken as an axiom rather than proved?
                        A
                      / | \
                    /   |   \
                  /     |     \
                /       |       \
              B---------D---------C
    Answer: ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SAS, so BD = CD and ∠ADB = ∠ADC; since these two
    angles make a linear pair, each is 90°. SAS cannot be proved from Euclid's
    axioms and postulates without "moving" figures, so it is accepted as an
    axiom.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = AC                     given
            ∠BAD = ∠CAD                 AD bisects ∠A (given)
            AD = AD                     common side
            ΔABD ≅ ΔACD                 SAS rule
            BD = CD                     CPCT
            ∠ADB = ∠ADC                 CPCT
            ∠ADB + ∠ADC = 180°          linear pair axiom
            ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°           each is half of 180°
    The included angle is the angle BETWEEN the two sides used: ∠BAD lies
    between AB and AD, and ∠CAD between AC and AD. Euclid proved SAS by picking
    up one triangle and placing it on the other, but none of his postulates says
    that a figure can be moved without changing its shape. So modern geometry
    (Hilbert) takes SAS as an AXIOM and proves the other rules from it. Common
    mistake: using an angle that is not between the two sides (SSA), which is
    not a valid rule. Now you try: what else follows from ΔABD ≅ ΔACD? (∠B = ∠C:
    the base angles are equal)

D2. Prove the ASA rule from the SAS axiom: if ∠B = ∠E, BC = EF and ∠C = ∠F in
    ΔABC and ΔDEF, then ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF.
                    A                        D
                   / \                      / \
                  /   \                   P/   \     (P on ED with EP = BA,
                 /     \                  /     \     used if AB ≠ DE)
                B ------ C               E ------ F
    Answer: If AB = DE, the triangles are congruent by SAS. If AB ≠ DE, say
    AB < DE, mark P on ED with EP = AB; then ΔABC ≅ ΔPEF by SAS, so
    ∠PFE = ∠ACB = ∠DFE, which is impossible because P ≠ D. The case AB > DE is
    the same. So AB = DE and ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF.
    Teacher explains: There are three cases, and two of them lead to a
    CONTRADICTION.
            Case 1  AB = DE: with ∠B = ∠E and BC = EF, SAS gives ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF.
            Case 2  AB < DE: take P on ED with EP = AB.
                    In ΔABC and ΔPEF: AB = PE, ∠B = ∠E, BC = EF, so they are
                    congruent (SAS), and ∠ACB = ∠PFE (CPCT).
                    But ∠ACB = ∠DFE (given), so ∠PFE = ∠DFE.
                    This is impossible: P is between E and D, so ∠PFE is only a
                    PART of ∠DFE (the whole is greater than the part).
            Case 3  AB > DE: the same argument with a point on BA.
    Only Case 1 is possible, so the triangles are congruent. This is typical of
    how theorems are built: a new rule (ASA) is proved from an axiom (SAS) and
    earlier results. The side BC is INCLUDED between the two angles at B and C.
    Now you try: in ΔABC and ΔPQR, ∠A = ∠P = 50°, AB = PQ = 6 cm, ∠B = ∠Q = 70°.
    Congruent? (yes, ASA)

D3. Line l is the bisector of an angle ∠A and B is any point on l. BP and BQ are
    perpendiculars from B to the arms of ∠A. Prove that ΔAPB ≅ ΔAQB and hence
    BP = BQ.
                               .-P
                         .-'
                   .-'
            A---------------------B--------l
                   '-.
                         '-.
                               '-Q
    Answer: ∠APB = ∠AQB = 90°, ∠PAB = ∠QAB and AB is common, so ΔAPB ≅ ΔAQB by
    AAS; hence BP = BQ (CPCT): B is equally far from the two arms.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            ∠APB = ∠AQB = 90°           BP and BQ are perpendiculars (given)
            ∠PAB = ∠QAB                 l bisects ∠A (given)
            AB = AB                     common side
            ΔAPB ≅ ΔAQB                 AAS rule
            BP = BQ                     CPCT
    AAS: two angles and a side that is NOT between them. It follows from ASA,
    because if two angles are equal the third angles are equal too (angle sum
    180°), and then the side IS between two known angles. The result is
    important: every point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from its
    arms. That is why the centre of the circle that touches all three sides of a
    triangle (the incentre) lies on the angle bisectors. Common mistake: calling
    this RHS; RHS needs the HYPOTENUSE and one SIDE, and here we know only one
    side (AB, which is the hypotenuse) and an angle. Now you try: if BP = 4 cm,
    how far is B from AQ? (4 cm)

D4. Prove that the angles opposite the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are
    equal, and prove the converse. Then: (a) AB = AC and ∠B = 70°; find ∠A. (b)
    In ΔPQR, ∠Q = ∠R = 45° and PQ = 6 cm; find PR.
                        A
                      / | \
                    /   |   \
                  /     |     \
                /       |       \
              B---------D---------C
    Answer: If AB = AC then ∠B = ∠C; conversely, if ∠B = ∠C then AB = AC. (a)
    ∠A = 40°. (b) PR = 6 cm.
    Teacher explains: THEOREM. Draw the bisector AD of ∠A. ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SAS
    (AB = AC, ∠BAD = ∠CAD, AD common), so ∠B = ∠C (CPCT). CONVERSE. Suppose
    ∠B = ∠C. Again draw the bisector AD:
            Statement                   Reason
            ∠B = ∠C                     given
            ∠BAD = ∠CAD                 AD bisects ∠A
            AD = AD                     common side
            ΔABD ≅ ΔACD                 AAS rule
            AB = AC                     CPCT
    (a) ∠C = ∠B = 70°, so ∠A = 180° − 70° − 70° = 40°. (b) ∠Q = ∠R, so the sides
    OPPOSITE them are equal: PR (opposite ∠Q) = PQ (opposite ∠R) = 6 cm. Also
    ∠P = 90°. A consequence: all three angles of an equilateral triangle are
    equal, so each is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. Common mistake: matching the equal angles
    with the wrong sides; the equal angles are at the ends of the BASE, opposite
    the equal sides. Now you try: in ΔXYZ, XY = XZ and ∠X = 80°. Find ∠Y. (50°)

D5. In ΔABC, AB = AC. D and E are points on BC with BD = CE. Prove that AD = AE
    and ∠ADE = ∠AED.
                            A
                         / / \ \
                      /   /   \   \
                   /     /     \     \
                /       /       \       \
              B--------D---------E--------C
    Answer: ΔABD ≅ ΔACE by SAS (AB = AC, ∠B = ∠C, BD = CE), so AD = AE; then
    ΔADE is isosceles and ∠ADE = ∠AED.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = AC                     given
            ∠ABD = ∠ACE                 angles opposite equal sides AB, AC
            BD = CE                     given
            ΔABD ≅ ΔACE                 SAS rule
            AD = AE                     CPCT
            ∠ADE = ∠AED                 angles opposite equal sides in ΔADE
    Notice the chain: the isosceles theorem gives an angle for the congruence,
    and the congruence gives two equal sides for another use of the isosceles
    theorem. Also ∠BAD = ∠CAE (CPCT). If instead we are told BE = CD, subtract
    DE from both (BE − DE = CD − DE) to get BD = CE, and the proof is the same.
    Common mistake: trying ΔABE and ΔACD without first checking which parts are
    known. Now you try: in the same figure, if ∠BAD = 20° and ∠B = 50°, find
    ∠ADE. (exterior angle of ΔABD: 20° + 50° = 70°)

D6. ΔABC and ΔDBC are on the same base BC, with A and D on the same side of BC,
    AB = AC and DB = DC. Prove that ΔABD ≅ ΔACD and that the line AD bisects
    ∠BAC. If AD produced meets BC at P, show that AP is the perpendicular
    bisector of BC.
                      A
                     /|\
                    / | \
                   /  D  \
                  / /   \ \
                 //       \\
                B-----P-----C
    Answer: ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SSS, so ∠BAD = ∠CAD. Then ΔABP ≅ ΔACP by SAS, so
    BP = CP and ∠APB = ∠APC = 90°.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = AC                     given
            DB = DC                     given
            AD = AD                     common side
            ΔABD ≅ ΔACD                 SSS rule
            ∠BAD = ∠CAD                 CPCT: AD bisects ∠BAC
    Now in ΔABP and ΔACP: AB = AC, ∠BAP = ∠CAP (just proved), AP common, so ΔABP
    ≅ ΔACP (SAS). Hence BP = CP and ∠APB = ∠APC; these form a linear pair, so
    each is 90°. SSS is the rule behind rigid frames: three fixed lengths allow
    only ONE triangle. Both A and D are equidistant from B and C, and the proof
    shows that such points lie on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Common
    mistake: using "AD bisects ∠A" in the first congruence; that is what we must
    PROVE. Now you try: why does the proof still work if D is on the OTHER side
    of BC? (SSS does not need D to be inside; AB = AC, DB = DC and AD common
    still hold)

D7. In ΔABC the altitudes BE (to AC) and CF (to AB) are equal. Prove that the
    triangle is isosceles. Then: two equal 5 m ladders lean against a vertical
    wall and both reach 4 m high. Show that their feet are equally far from the
    wall.
                     A
                    / \
                 F /   \ E
                  /     \
                 B ------ C
            (BE ⊥ AC, CF ⊥ AB)
    Answer: ΔBCE ≅ ΔCBF by RHS, so ∠BCE = ∠CBF, that is ∠C = ∠B, and AB = AC.
    Ladders: the two right triangles are congruent by RHS, and each foot is 3 m
    from the wall.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            ∠BEC = ∠CFB = 90°           BE and CF are altitudes
            BC = CB                     common side (the hypotenuse)
            BE = CF                     given
            ΔBEC ≅ ΔCFB                 RHS rule
            ∠ECB = ∠FBC                 CPCT, so ∠C = ∠B
            AB = AC                     sides opposite equal angles
    RHS: Right angle, Hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) and one
    other Side. It works only for right triangles. Ladders: wall and ground meet
    at 90°, the hypotenuses (ladders) are equal (5 m), the heights are equal (4
    m), so the triangles are congruent by RHS and the feet are equally far from
    the wall: √(5² − 4²) = √9 = 3 m. Common mistake: using RHS with the two
    LEGS; that is SAS (the right angle is between the legs). Now you try: two
    right triangles have hypotenuse 13 cm and one leg 12 cm. Are they congruent?
    (yes, RHS; the other legs are both 5 cm)

D8. Prove: if two sides of a triangle are unequal, the angle opposite the longer
    side is larger. Then order the angles of ΔABC with AB = 5 cm, BC = 7 cm and
    CA = 9 cm.
                      A
                     / \
                    /    \  D      (AC > AB; D on AC with AD = AB)
                   /    .  \
                  /  .       \
                 B ------------ C
    Answer: If AC > AB then ∠ABC > ∠ACB. For the triangle: ∠B > ∠A > ∠C.
    Teacher explains: Suppose AC > AB. Mark D on AC with AD = AB and join BD.
            Statement                        Reason
            AD = AB                          construction
            ∠ABD = ∠ADB                      angles opposite equal sides (ΔABD)
            ∠ADB > ∠ACB                      exterior angle of ΔBDC at D is
                                             greater than the interior ∠C
            ∠ABC > ∠ABD                      ∠ABD is a part of ∠ABC
            ∠ABC > ∠ABD = ∠ADB > ∠ACB        so ∠ABC > ∠ACB
    Numbers: each angle is OPPOSITE the side that does not touch it. ∠B is
    opposite CA = 9 (longest), ∠A is opposite BC = 7, and ∠C is opposite AB = 5
    (shortest). So ∠B > ∠A > ∠C. Common mistake: taking the angle AT the end of
    the longest side; the largest angle is ACROSS from the longest side. Now you
    try: in ΔPQR, PQ = 8, QR = 6, RP = 10. Which angle is largest? (∠Q, opposite
    RP)

D9. Prove the converse: the side opposite the larger angle is longer. Deduce
    that the hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle and that the
    perpendicular is the shortest segment from a point to a line. Then order the
    sides of ΔABC with ∠B = 50° and ∠C = 70°.
    Answer: If ∠B > ∠C then AC > AB. For the triangle ∠A = 60°, so AB > BC > CA.
    Teacher explains: Proof by contradiction. Suppose ∠B > ∠C. There are only
    three possibilities for AC and AB:
            AC = AB:  then ∠B = ∠C (isosceles theorem): false
            AC < AB:  then ∠B < ∠C (the theorem of D8): false
            AC > AB:  the only possibility left
    In a right triangle the right angle is the LARGEST angle (the other two add
    up to 90°), so the side opposite it, the hypotenuse, is the longest side. If
    PM ⊥ l and N is any other point on l, then ΔPMN is right-angled at M, so PN
    (the hypotenuse) > PM: the perpendicular is the shortest distance. For the
    numbers: ∠A = 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°. Largest angle ∠C = 70° is opposite AB;
    ∠A = 60° is opposite BC; smallest ∠B = 50° is opposite CA:
            ∠C > ∠A > ∠B   so   AB > BC > CA
    Common mistake: forgetting to find the THIRD angle, which may be the
    largest. Now you try: ∠P = 35° and ∠Q = 100° in ΔPQR. Longest side?
    (PR, opposite ∠Q)

D10. Prove that the sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third
     side. Can a triangle have sides (a) 4, 7, 12 cm; (b) 5, 7, 12 cm; (c) 6, 7,
     12 cm?
                          D
                         / \
                        /    \      (BA produced to D with AD = AC)
                       A       \
                      /  \       \
                     B ----------- C
     Answer: AB + AC > BC for every triangle. (a) No: 4 + 7 = 11 < 12. (b) No:
     5 + 7 = 12, the points would be in a straight line. (c) Yes:
     6 + 7 = 13 > 12.
     Teacher explains: Produce BA to D so that AD = AC, and join CD.
             Statement                        Reason
             ∠ADC = ∠ACD                      AD = AC (isosceles ΔACD)
             ∠BCD > ∠ACD = ∠BDC               ∠ACD is a part of ∠BCD
             BD > BC                          side opposite the larger angle
             BA + AD > BC                     BD = BA + AD
             AB + AC > BC                     AD = AC
     The same works for each pair of sides. For a TEST it is enough to check
     that the two SHORTER sides add up to MORE than the longest; the other two
     sums are then automatically bigger. In (b) the sum is EQUAL, so the
     "triangle" is flat: this is the case of three points in a line (a
     degenerate triangle). This is also why a straight road is the shortest
     route between two towns: going via a third town is longer. Common mistake:
     checking only one sum, such as 4 + 12 > 7, and concluding "yes". Now you
     try: can 2.5, 3.5, 5.5 be sides? (yes: 2.5 + 3.5 = 6 > 5.5)

D11. Village A is 6 km from village B, and B is 10 km from village C
     (straight-line distances). What can the distance AC be? If AC is a whole
     number of kilometres and A, B, C are not in a line, how many values are
     possible? An isosceles triangle has two sides 4 cm and 9 cm. Find the third
     side.
     Answer: 4 km < AC < 16 km; 11 whole-number values (5 to 15). The third side
     of the isosceles triangle is 9 cm.
     Teacher explains: The triangle inequality works both ways. With sides 6 and
     10 and third side x:
             x < 6 + 10 = 16          (sum of the other two sides)
             x > 10 − 6 = 4           (difference of the other two sides)
             so 4 < x < 16: whole numbers 5, 6, 7, ..., 15
             that is 15 − 5 + 1 = 11 values
     If the villages ARE in a line, AC can also be exactly 4 km (A between B and
     C) or 16 km (B between A and C). For the isosceles triangle the third side
     is 4 or 9. Test both:
             4, 4, 9:  4 + 4 = 8 < 9      impossible
             4, 9, 9:  4 + 9 = 13 > 9     possible
     So the sides are 4, 9, 9 cm and the perimeter is 22 cm. Common mistake:
     counting 4 and 16 as possible values (the inequalities are STRICT for a
     real triangle). Now you try: two sides are 7 cm and 3 cm. Range for the
     third side, and how many whole-number values? (4 < x < 10: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9,
     so 5 values)

D12. O is any point inside ΔABC. Prove that (a) AB + AC > OB + OC and (b)
     OA + OB + OC > half the perimeter of ΔABC.
                         A
                        / \
                       /   \
                      /  O  \ D      (BO produced meets AC at D)
                     /        \
                    B -------- C
     Answer: (a) Produce BO to meet AC at D; AB + AD > BD = BO + OD and
     OD + DC > OC; adding gives AB + AC > OB + OC. (b) OA + OB > AB,
     OB + OC > BC, OC + OA > CA; adding gives 2(OA + OB + OC) > AB + BC + CA.
     Teacher explains: (a)
             Statement                        Reason
             AB + AD > BD = BO + OD           triangle inequality in ΔABD
             OD + DC > OC                     triangle inequality in ΔODC
             AB + AD + OD + DC > BO + OD + OC add the two inequalities
             AB + AC > OB + OC                AD + DC = AC; take OD from both
     (b) Use the triangle inequality in the three small triangles OAB, OBC, OCA
     and add:
             (OA + OB) + (OB + OC) + (OC + OA) > AB + BC + CA
             2(OA + OB + OC) > perimeter
     Example: in an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm with O at the centre,
     OA = OB = OC ≈ 3.46 cm, so OA + OB + OC ≈ 10.39 cm, which is more than 9 cm
     (half the perimeter 18 cm) and less than 12 cm (AB + AC). Inequalities can
     be ADDED side by side, just like equations (but not subtracted). Common
     mistake: using "=" where the triangle inequality gives only ">". Now you
     try: prove that the sum of the two diagonals of a quadrilateral ABCD is
     less than its perimeter. (AC < AB + BC and AC < AD + DC; similarly for BD;
     add)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY

M1. The given parts of ΔABC and ΔPQR are equal (A ↔ P, B ↔ Q, C ↔ R). Which rule
    proves ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS or RHS? Or is it not enough?
    a) AB = PQ, BC = QR, CA = RP         b) AB = PQ, ∠B = ∠Q, BC = QR
    c) AB = PQ, CA = RP, ∠A = ∠P         d) AB = PQ, BC = QR, ∠A = ∠P
    e) ∠B = ∠Q, BC = QR, ∠C = ∠R         f) ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q, AB = PQ
    g) ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q, BC = QR         h) ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q, ∠C = ∠R
    i) AB = PQ, CA = RP, ∠B = ∠Q = 90°   j) CA = RP, BC = QR, ∠C = ∠R
    k) CA = RP, ∠A = ∠P, ∠C = ∠R         l) AB = PQ, ∠B = ∠Q, ∠C = ∠R
    m) CA = RP, BC = QR, ∠A = ∠P         n) CA = RP, AB = PQ, ∠B = ∠Q
    o) CA = RP, BC = QR, ∠B = ∠Q = 90°   p) BC = QR, AB = PQ, ∠C = ∠R = 90°
    q) AB = PQ, BC = QR, ∠C = ∠R = 90°   r) CA = RP, ∠B = ∠Q, ∠C = ∠R
    s) BC = QR, CA = RP, ∠C = ∠R = 90°   t) AB = PQ, BC = QR, ∠B = ∠Q = 90°
    u) AB = PQ, ∠C = ∠R                  v) BC = QR, ∠A = ∠P, ∠C = ∠R
    Answers:
      a) SSS
      b) SAS
      c) SAS
      d) not enough (SSA)
      e) ASA

      i) RHS
      j) SAS

      n) not enough (SSA)
      o) RHS
      p) RHS
      q) RHS
      r) AAS
      s) SAS
      t) SAS
      u) not enough
      v) AAS

M7. Sides of ΔABC are given (cm). Write the angles in order of size, largest
    first.
    a) AB = 5, BC = 7, CA = 9         b) AB = 8, BC = 6, CA = 10
    c) AB = 4, BC = 4, CA = 5         d) AB = 7, BC = 7, CA = 7
    e) AB = 10, BC = 12, CA = 11      f) AB = 3, BC = 9, CA = 7
    g) AB = 6, BC = 5, CA = 6         h) AB = 2.5, BC = 3.5, CA = 4.5
    i) AB = 13, BC = 12, CA = 5       j) AB = 9, BC = 9, CA = 2
    k) AB = 15, BC = 8, CA = 17       l) AB = 6, BC = 11, CA = 6
    m) AB = 20, BC = 21, CA = 29      n) AB = 4, BC = 3, CA = 5
    o) AB = 1.2, BC = 1.5, CA = 1.1   p) AB = 100, BC = 99, CA = 98
    q) AB = 7, BC = 10, CA = 7        r) AB = 12, BC = 12, CA = 13
    Answers:
      a) ∠B > ∠A > ∠C
      b) ∠B > ∠C > ∠A
      c) ∠B > ∠C = ∠A
      d) ∠C = ∠A = ∠B
      e) ∠A > ∠B > ∠C
      f) ∠A > ∠B > ∠C
      g) ∠C = ∠B > ∠A
      h) ∠B > ∠A > ∠C
      i) ∠C > ∠A > ∠B
      j) ∠C = ∠A > ∠B
      k) ∠B > ∠C > ∠A
      l) ∠A > ∠C = ∠B
      m) ∠B > ∠A > ∠C
      n) ∠B > ∠C > ∠A
      o) ∠A > ∠C > ∠B
      p) ∠C > ∠A > ∠B
      q) ∠A > ∠C = ∠B
      r) ∠B > ∠C = ∠A

M8. Two angles of ΔABC are given. Find ∠A and write the sides in order of
    length, longest first.
    a) ∠B = 50°, ∠C = 70°       b) ∠B = 90°, ∠C = 30°
    c) ∠B = 45°, ∠C = 45°       d) ∠B = 60°, ∠C = 60°
    e) ∠B = 100°, ∠C = 40°      f) ∠B = 35°, ∠C = 100°
    g) ∠B = 80°, ∠C = 50°       h) ∠B = 30°, ∠C = 30°
    i) ∠B = 20°, ∠C = 120°      j) ∠B = 65°, ∠C = 65°
    k) ∠B = 72°, ∠C = 36°       l) ∠B = 55°, ∠C = 70°
    m) ∠B = 89°, ∠C = 2°        n) ∠B = 40°, ∠C = 100°
    o) ∠B = 37.5°, ∠C = 52.5°   p) ∠B = 110°, ∠C = 35°
    q) ∠B = 25°, ∠C = 90°       r) ∠B = 60°, ∠C = 75°
    Answers:
      a) ∠A = 60°; AB > BC > CA
      b) ∠A = 60°; CA > BC > AB
      c) ∠A = 90°; BC > CA = AB
      d) ∠A = 60°; BC = CA = AB
      e) ∠A = 40°; CA > BC = AB
      f) ∠A = 45°; AB > BC > CA
      g) ∠A = 50°; CA > BC = AB
      h) ∠A = 120°; BC > CA = AB
      i) ∠A = 40°; AB > BC > CA
      j) ∠A = 50°; CA = AB > BC
      k) ∠A = 72°; BC = CA > AB
      l) ∠A = 55°; AB > BC = CA
      m) ∠A = 89°; BC = CA > AB
      n) ∠A = 40°; AB > BC = CA
      o) ∠A = 90°; BC > AB > CA
      p) ∠A = 35°; CA > BC = AB
      q) ∠A = 65°; AB > BC > CA
      r) ∠A = 45°; AB > CA > BC

M9. Use the isosceles theorem or its converse (equal sides ↔ equal angles). Find
    x, the sides and the perimeter (cm).
    a) AB = AC; AB = 2x + 3, AC = 5x − 9, BC = x + 5
    b) AB = AC; AB = 3x − 1, AC = x + 7, BC = 2x
    c) equilateral; AB = 4x − 6, BC = 2x + 4, CA = y
    d) ∠B = ∠C; AB = 3x + 2, AC = 4x − 3, BC = 2x + 1
    e) ∠A = ∠C; AB = 6x − 5, BC = 3x + 7, CA = 5x − 4
    f) AB = AC; AB = x + 12, AC = 3x, BC = x + 3
    g) ∠A = ∠B; BC = 7x − 10, CA = 4x + 5, AB = 3x
    h) equilateral; AB = 5x − 3, BC = 3x + 5, CA = 2y + 1
    i) AB = AC; AB = 2.5x, AC = x + 6, BC = x
    j) ∠B = ∠C = 60°; AB = 8x − 1, BC = 5x + 11
    k) AB = AC; AB = 4x + 1, AC = 2x + 9, BC = 6x − 10
    l) ∠A = ∠C; AB = 10 − x, BC = 2x + 1, CA = x + 4
    Answers:
      a) x = 4; sides 11, 9, 11; perimeter 31
      b) x = 4; sides 11, 8, 11; perimeter 30
      c) x = 5; sides 14, 14, 14; perimeter 42 (y = 14)
      d) x = 5; sides 17, 11, 17; perimeter 45
      e) x = 4; sides 19, 19, 16; perimeter 54
      f) x = 6; sides 18, 9, 18; perimeter 45
      g) x = 5; sides 15, 25, 25; perimeter 65
      h) x = 4; sides 17, 17, 17; perimeter 51 (y = 8)
      i) x = 4; sides 10, 4, 10; perimeter 24
      j) x = 4; sides 31, 31, 31; perimeter 93
      k) x = 4; sides 17, 14, 17; perimeter 48
      l) x = 3; sides 7, 7, 7; perimeter 21

M10. Lengths in cm. Are the triangles congruent? If yes, give the rule and the
     congruence with the letters in the correct order.
     a) ΔABC: AB = 5, BC = 7, ∠B = 50°;  ΔPQR: PQ = 5, QR = 7, ∠Q = 50°
     b) ΔABC: AB = 5, BC = 7, ∠B = 50°;  ΔPQR: QR = 5, RP = 7, ∠R = 50°
     c) ΔABC: AB = 6, BC = 8, CA = 9;  ΔPQR: PQ = 9, QR = 8, RP = 6
     d) ΔABC: ∠A = 40°, ∠B = 60°, AB = 7;  ΔPQR: ∠P = 40°, ∠Q = 60°, PQ = 7
     e) ΔABC: ∠A = 40°, ∠B = 60°, BC = 7;  ΔPQR: ∠Q = 40°, ∠R = 60°, RP = 7
     f) ΔABC: ∠A = 40°, ∠B = 60°, BC = 7;  ΔPQR: ∠P = 40°, ∠Q = 60°, RP = 7
     g) ΔABC: AB = 8, CA = 6, ∠B = 40°;  ΔPQR: PQ = 8, RP = 6, ∠Q = 40°
     h) ΔABC: ∠A = 50°, ∠B = 60°, ∠C = 70°;  ΔPQR: ∠P = 50°, ∠Q = 60°, ∠R = 70°
     i) ΔABC: ∠B = 90°, CA = 13, AB = 5;  ΔPQR: ∠Q = 90°, RP = 13, PQ = 5
     j) ΔABC: ∠C = 90°, AB = 10, BC = 6;  ΔPQR: ∠P = 90°, QR = 10, PQ = 6
     k) ΔABC: AB = 4, BC = 5, CA = 6;  ΔPQR: PQ = 4, QR = 6, RP = 5
     l) ΔABC: AB = 5, ∠B = 70°, BC = 6;  ΔPQR: PQ = 6, ∠Q = 70°, QR = 5
     m) ΔABC: AB = 5, ∠B = 70°, BC = 6;  ΔPQR: PQ = 5, ∠Q = 70°, RP = 6
     n) ΔABC: ∠A = 30°, ∠C = 80°, AB = 9;  ΔPQR: ∠Q = 30°, ∠P = 80°, PR = 9
     Answers:
       a) yes, SAS: ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR
       b) yes, SAS: ΔABC ≅ ΔQRP
       c) yes, SSS: ΔABC ≅ ΔPRQ
       d) yes, ASA: ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR
       e) yes, AAS: ΔABC ≅ ΔQRP
       f) no: the sides are different
       g) cannot say (SSA is not a rule)
       h) cannot say (AAA is not a rule)
       i) yes, RHS: ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR
       j) yes, RHS: ΔABC ≅ ΔRQP
       k) yes, SSS: ΔABC ≅ ΔQPR
       l) yes, SAS: ΔABC ≅ ΔRQP
       m) cannot say (SSA is not a rule)
       n) no: the sides are different

M11. True or false?
     a) SAS is taken as an axiom.
     b) ASA can be proved using SAS.
     c) SSA is a valid congruence rule.
     d) AAA proves that two triangles are congruent.
     e) RHS applies only to right triangles.
     f) In ΔABC, if AB = AC then ∠B = ∠C.
     g) In ΔABC, if ∠B = ∠C then AB = AC.
     h) Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.
     i) The longest side is opposite the largest angle.
     j) The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle.
     k) A triangle can have sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm.
     l) A triangle can have sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm.
     m) The difference of two sides is less than the third side.
     n) The perpendicular is the shortest segment from a point to a line.
     o) Two triangles with equal areas are congruent.
     p) Congruent triangles have equal areas.
     q) A triangle can have two obtuse angles.
     r) If ∠A = 100° in ΔABC, then BC is the longest side.
     s) If AB > AC in ΔABC, then ∠C > ∠B.
     t) If AB > AC in ΔABC, then ∠B > ∠C.
     Answers: a) true   b) true   c) false   d) false   e) true   f) true
              g) true   h) true   i) true   j) true   k) false   l) false
              m) true   n) true   o) false   p) true   q) false   r) true
              s) true   t) false

M12. Find x and the angles of ΔABC, then write the sides in order of length,
     longest first.
     a) ∠A = (2x + 10)°, ∠B = 3x°, ∠C = (x + 20)°
     b) ∠A = x°, ∠B = 2x°, ∠C = 3x°
     c) ∠A = (4x − 10)°, ∠B = (3x + 5)°, ∠C = (x + 25)°
     d) ∠A = 2x°, ∠B = 2x°, ∠C = x°
     e) ∠A = 5x°, ∠B = 3x°, ∠C = x°
     f) ∠A = (x + 40)°, ∠B = (x + 20)°, ∠C = x°
     g) ∠A = (3x + 15)°, ∠B = (2x + 5)°, ∠C = (x + 10)°
     h) ∠A = 6x°, ∠B = (x + 10)°, ∠C = (x + 50)°
     i) ∠A = x°, ∠B = x°, ∠C = 4x°
     j) ∠A = (2x + 10)°, ∠B = (3x − 10)°, ∠C = (2x + 5)°
     k) ∠A = 7x°, ∠B = 2x°, ∠C = 3x°
     l) ∠A = (x + 30)°, ∠B = 2x°, ∠C = (3x − 30)°
     m) ∠A = (5x − 20)°, ∠B = (2x + 20)°, ∠C = 2x°
     n) ∠A = 3x°, ∠B = 4x°, ∠C = 5x°
     Answers:
       a) x = 25; ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 75°, ∠C = 45°; CA > BC > AB
       b) x = 30; ∠A = 30°, ∠B = 60°, ∠C = 90°; AB > CA > BC
       c) x = 20; ∠A = 70°, ∠B = 65°, ∠C = 45°; BC > CA > AB
       d) x = 36; ∠A = 72°, ∠B = 72°, ∠C = 36°; BC = CA > AB
       e) x = 20; ∠A = 100°, ∠B = 60°, ∠C = 20°; BC > CA > AB
       f) x = 40; ∠A = 80°, ∠B = 60°, ∠C = 40°; BC > CA > AB
       g) x = 25; ∠A = 90°, ∠B = 55°, ∠C = 35°; BC > CA > AB
       h) x = 15; ∠A = 90°, ∠B = 25°, ∠C = 65°; BC > AB > CA
       i) x = 30; ∠A = 30°, ∠B = 30°, ∠C = 120°; AB > BC = CA
       j) x = 25; ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 65°, ∠C = 55°; CA > BC > AB
       k) x = 15; ∠A = 105°, ∠B = 30°, ∠C = 45°; BC > AB > CA
       l) x = 30; ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 60°, ∠C = 60°; BC = CA = AB
       m) x = 20; ∠A = 80°, ∠B = 60°, ∠C = 40°; BC > CA > AB
       n) x = 15; ∠A = 45°, ∠B = 60°, ∠C = 75°; AB > CA > BC

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: colour the matching parts of two triangles in the same colour and
  say the letters in order; for every congruence proof first list what is GIVEN,
  then look for a common side or vertically opposite angles; build triangles
  from straws or strips (three lengths fix the triangle; 3, 4, 8 will not
  close); for side-angle order, draw an arrow from each angle across the
  triangle to its opposite side. Harder: prove SSS from SAS (place the triangles
  back to back and use isosceles triangles); prove that the medians to the equal
  sides of an isosceles triangle are equal; show that a median is less than half
  the sum of the two sides next to it (AB + AC > 2AD); prove that the sum of the
  three medians is less than the perimeter; find all triangles with whole-number
  sides and perimeter 15.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.22 — QUADRILATERALS: PARALLELOGRAM THEOREMS, MID-POINT THEOREM
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - ANGLE SUM: the angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360° (a diagonal splits
    it into two triangles, 2 × 180°).
  - A PARALLELOGRAM is a quadrilateral with BOTH pairs of opposite sides
    parallel. THEOREMS: a diagonal divides it into two CONGRUENT triangles
    (ASA); opposite sides are EQUAL; opposite angles are EQUAL; consecutive
    angles add up to 180°; the diagonals BISECT each other.
  - CONVERSES (tests for a parallelogram): a quadrilateral is a parallelogram if
    (i) both pairs of opposite sides are equal, or (ii) both pairs of opposite
    angles are equal, or (iii) the diagonals bisect each other, or (iv) ONE pair
    of opposite sides is both EQUAL and PARALLEL.
  - SPECIAL PARALLELOGRAMS: a RECTANGLE has a right angle (then all four are
    right angles) and its diagonals are EQUAL; a RHOMBUS has equal adjacent
    sides (so all four sides are equal) and its diagonals bisect each other at
    RIGHT ANGLES; a SQUARE is both, with equal diagonals that are perpendicular
    bisectors of each other.
  - Tests: a parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle; with
    perpendicular diagonals it is a rhombus; with equal AND perpendicular
    diagonals it is a square.
  - MID-POINT THEOREM: the segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a
    triangle is PARALLEL to the third side and HALF of it. If E, F are the
    mid-points of AB, AC then EF ∥ BC and EF = ½BC.
  - CONVERSE: the line through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel
    to another side, BISECTS the third side.
  - Consequences: the three mid-points of a triangle's sides form a triangle
    with HALF the perimeter and a QUARTER of the area; the mid-points of the
    sides of ANY quadrilateral form a parallelogram whose perimeter equals the
    sum of the diagonals; the segment joining the mid-points of the legs of a
    trapezium is parallel to the parallel sides and equals half their sum.
  - INTERCEPT THEOREM: if three or more parallel lines cut off equal intercepts
    on one transversal, they cut off equal intercepts on every transversal.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that the angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°. The angles of a
    quadrilateral are in the ratio 3 : 5 : 9 : 13. Find them.
                 D ------------------ C
                 |  \                /
                 |       \         /
                 |            \   /
                 A ------------- B
            (diagonal BD splits ABCD into ΔABD and ΔBCD)
    Answer: Each of the two triangles has angle sum 180°, so the total is 360°.
    The angles are 36°, 60°, 108° and 156°.
    Teacher explains: Draw the diagonal BD. It splits ∠B into ∠ABD + ∠DBC and ∠D
    into ∠ADB + ∠BDC.
            Statement                                 Reason
            ∠A + ∠ABD + ∠ADB = 180°                   angle sum of ΔABD
            ∠C + ∠DBC + ∠BDC = 180°                   angle sum of ΔBCD
            ∠A + (∠ABD + ∠DBC) + ∠C + (∠ADB + ∠BDC) = 360°    add
            ∠A + ∠B + ∠C + ∠D = 360°                  the parts make ∠B, ∠D
    Ratio: 3 + 5 + 9 + 13 = 30 parts make 360°, so one part is 12°: the angles
    are 3 × 12 = 36°, 5 × 12 = 60°, 9 × 12 = 108° and 13 × 12 = 156°. Check:
    36 + 60 + 108 + 156 = 360. The proof works for every CONVEX quadrilateral
    (and, with the right diagonal, for a concave one too). Common mistake: using
    180° for a quadrilateral. Now you try: three angles of a quadrilateral are
    75°, 90° and 110°. Find the fourth. (85°)

D2. ABCD is a parallelogram. Prove that the diagonal AC divides it into two
    congruent triangles, and deduce that AB = CD, AD = CB and ∠B = ∠D. If AB = 9
    cm, BC = 6 cm and ∠B = 110°, find CD, AD, ∠D, ∠A and ∠C.
                D ----------------------- C
               /                 .-'     /
              /            .-'          /
             /       .-'               /
            /  .-'                    /
           A ----------------------- B
    Answer: ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA by ASA, so AB = CD, BC = DA and ∠B = ∠D. CD = 9 cm,
    AD = 6 cm, ∠D = 110°, ∠A = ∠C = 70°.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            ∠BAC = ∠DCA                 alternate angles (AB ∥ DC)
            AC = CA                     common side
            ∠BCA = ∠DAC                 alternate angles (BC ∥ AD)
            ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA                 ASA rule
            AB = CD, BC = DA, ∠B = ∠D   CPCT
    Using the other diagonal BD in the same way gives ∠A = ∠C. So in a
    parallelogram the opposite sides are equal and the opposite angles are
    equal. Also ∠A + ∠B = 180° (co-interior angles, AD ∥ BC). Numbers:
    CD = AB = 9 cm, AD = BC = 6 cm, ∠D = ∠B = 110°, ∠A = 180° − 110° = 70° and
    ∠C = ∠A = 70°. Check: 70 + 110 + 70 + 110 = 360. Take care with the letter
    order: ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA, not ΔADC, because A ↔ C, B ↔ D, C ↔ A. Now you try: a
    parallelogram has one angle of 58°. Find the others. (122°, 58°, 122°)

D3. Prove the converse: if both pairs of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are
    equal, it is a parallelogram. Why does the ironing-board or "lazy tongs"
    mechanism keep its top parallel to the floor?
    Answer: With AB = CD and AD = CB, ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB by SSS, so ∠ABD = ∠CDB and
    ∠ADB = ∠CBD; these are alternate angles, so AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC. In a
    mechanism with rods of fixed equal opposite lengths, the quadrilateral stays
    a parallelogram whatever the angle, so the top stays parallel to the bottom.
    Teacher explains: Draw the diagonal BD.
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = CD                     given
            AD = CB                     given
            BD = DB                     common side
            ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB                 SSS rule
            ∠ABD = ∠CDB                 CPCT
            AB ∥ DC                     equal alternate angles (converse)
            ∠ADB = ∠CBD                 CPCT
            AD ∥ BC                     equal alternate angles (converse)
    Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so ABCD is a parallelogram. A
    parallelogram with fixed side lengths is NOT rigid: its angles can change.
    But because opposite sides stay equal, the figure stays a parallelogram, and
    so one side always stays parallel to the opposite side. This is used in
    parallel rulers, car jacks, some desk lamps and folding gates. Common
    mistake: thinking ONE pair of equal opposite sides is enough; an isosceles
    trapezium has one pair of equal (non-parallel) sides but is not a
    parallelogram. Now you try: a quadrilateral has sides AB = 7, BC = 4,
    CD = 7, DA = 4 (in cm). Is it a parallelogram? (yes: both pairs of opposite
    sides equal)

D4. Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, and state the
    converse. In parallelogram ABCD the diagonals meet at O with OA = (3x − 1)
    cm, OC = (x + 7) cm, OB = (2y) cm and OD = (y + 5) cm. Find x, y, AC and BD.
                D ----------------------- C
               /  `-.               .-'  /
              /      `-.       .-'      /
             /           ` O .         /
            /        .-'      `-.     /
           /    .-'              `-. /
          A ----------------------- B
    Answer: OA = OC and OB = OD. x = 4, y = 5, AC = 22 cm, BD = 20 cm. Converse:
    if the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, it is a
    parallelogram.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = CD                     opposite sides of a parallelogram
            ∠OAB = ∠OCD                 alternate angles (AB ∥ DC)
            ∠OBA = ∠ODC                 alternate angles (AB ∥ DC)
            ΔOAB ≅ ΔOCD                 ASA rule
            OA = OC, OB = OD            CPCT
    Numbers:
            3x − 1 = x + 7,  2x = 8,  x = 4:   OA = OC = 11, AC = 22 cm
            2y = y + 5,  y = 5:                OB = OD = 10, BD = 20 cm
    The converse is proved with vertically opposite angles: if OA = OC and
    OB = OD, then ΔOAB ≅ ΔOCD (SAS), so ∠OAB = ∠OCD, which gives AB ∥ DC;
    similarly AD ∥ BC. Common mistake: setting OA = OB; the diagonals bisect
    EACH OTHER, but they are not equal to each other (except in a rectangle).
    Now you try: in a parallelogram AC = 18 cm; find OA. (9 cm)

D5. Prove that if one pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral is equal AND
    parallel, it is a parallelogram. Use it: ABCD is a parallelogram and E, F
    are the mid-points of AB and CD. Show that AECF is a parallelogram.
                D ---------- F ---------- C
               /       .-'             .'/
              /   .-'              .-'  /
             /.-'              .-'     /
            A ---------- E ---------- B
    Answer: With AB = DC and AB ∥ DC, ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA (SAS) gives ∠BCA = ∠DAC, so BC
    ∥ AD. For AECF: AE = ½AB = ½DC = FC and AE ∥ FC, so AECF is a parallelogram.
    Teacher explains: Let AB = DC and AB ∥ DC. Draw the diagonal AC.
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = CD                     given
            ∠BAC = ∠DCA                 alternate angles (AB ∥ DC)
            AC = CA                     common side
            ΔBAC ≅ ΔDCA                 SAS rule
            ∠BCA = ∠DAC                 CPCT
            BC ∥ AD                     equal alternate angles
    For AECF: AE and FC lie along AB and DC, so AE ∥ FC. AE = ½AB and FC = ½DC,
    and AB = DC, so AE = FC (Axiom 7). One pair of opposite sides is equal and
    parallel, so AECF is a parallelogram, and therefore AF ∥ EC. This test is
    often the QUICKEST, because it needs only one pair of sides. Common mistake:
    "equal" alone or "parallel" alone is not enough (think of an isosceles
    trapezium, or any trapezium). Now you try: if AB = 10 cm in the figure, how
    long is EB? (5 cm)

D6. In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = (3x + 10)° and ∠B = (5x − 30)°. Find all four
    angles. Then prove that the bisectors of ∠A and ∠B meet at a right angle.
    Answer: x = 25; ∠A = ∠C = 85°, ∠B = ∠D = 95°. If the bisectors meet at P,
    then ∠PAB + ∠PBA = ½(∠A + ∠B) = 90°, so ∠APB = 90°.
    Teacher explains: ∠A and ∠B are CONSECUTIVE angles, which are co-interior
    angles between the parallel sides AD and BC, so they add up to 180°:
            (3x + 10) + (5x − 30) = 180
                         8x − 20 = 180
                              x = 25
            ∠A = 3 × 25 + 10 = 85°,  ∠B = 5 × 25 − 30 = 95°
    Opposite angles are equal: ∠C = 85° and ∠D = 95°. Check:
    85 + 95 + 85 + 95 = 360. For the bisectors, in ΔAPB:
            ∠PAB + ∠PBA = ½∠A + ½∠B = ½ × 180° = 90°
            ∠APB = 180° − 90° = 90°        (angle sum of ΔAPB)
    With the numbers: 42.5° + 47.5° = 90°. Doing this at all four corners shows
    that the four angle bisectors of a parallelogram (not a rhombus) form a
    RECTANGLE. Common mistake: setting consecutive angles EQUAL (that would give
    x = 20 and angles of 70°, which do not add up to 180°). Now you try:
    ∠A = (2x)° and ∠C = (x + 40)° in a parallelogram. (opposite angles: x = 40,
    ∠A = 80°, ∠B = 100°)

D7. Prove that a parallelogram with one right angle is a rectangle, and that the
    diagonals of a rectangle are equal. Conversely, show that a parallelogram
    with equal diagonals is a rectangle. How does a carpenter use this to check
    a door frame?
            D ---------------------- C
            |                        |
            |                        |
            A ---------------------- B
    Answer: If ∠A = 90° then ∠B = 180° − 90° = 90°, ∠C = ∠A = 90°,
    ∠D = ∠B = 90°. ΔABC ≅ ΔBAD by SAS, so AC = BD. Conversely equal diagonals
    give ΔABC ≅ ΔBAD by SSS, so ∠A = ∠B, and since ∠A + ∠B = 180°, each is 90°.
    The carpenter measures both diagonals: if they are equal, the frame is
    rectangular.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = BA                     common side
            ∠DAB = ∠CBA = 90°           angles of a rectangle
            AD = BC                     opposite sides of a parallelogram
            ΔDAB ≅ ΔCBA                 SAS rule
            BD = AC                     CPCT
    For the converse, if AC = BD then ΔABC ≅ ΔBAD by SSS (AB common, BC = AD,
    AC = BD), so ∠ABC = ∠BAD. These are consecutive angles of a parallelogram,
    which add up to 180°, so each is 90°. A carpenter or mason cannot easily
    measure a 90° angle on a big frame, but can measure two diagonals with a
    tape: equal diagonals (together with equal opposite sides) guarantee right
    angles. Common mistake: thinking ANY quadrilateral with equal diagonals is a
    rectangle; an isosceles trapezium also has equal diagonals. The
    quadrilateral must first be a parallelogram. Now you try: a rectangle has
    sides 6 cm and 8 cm. Find each diagonal. (√(36 + 64) = 10 cm)

D8. Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular bisectors of each
    other. A rhombus has diagonals 16 cm and 12 cm. Find its side. Which
    parallelograms are squares?
                      D
                    /   \
                  /       \
                A --- O --- C
                  \       /
                    \   /
                      B
    Answer: In rhombus ABCD, ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOB by SSS, so ∠AOB = ∠COB = 90°. The side
    is 10 cm. A parallelogram is a square if its diagonals are equal AND
    perpendicular (or: it is both a rectangle and a rhombus).
    Teacher explains: A rhombus is a parallelogram, so its diagonals bisect each
    other: OA = OC and OB = OD.
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = CB                     sides of a rhombus
            OA = OC                     diagonals of a parallelogram bisect
            OB = OB                     common side
            ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOB                 SSS rule
            ∠AOB = ∠COB                 CPCT
            ∠AOB = ∠COB = 90°           linear pair of equal angles
    Numbers: OA = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm and OB = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm, and ∠AOB = 90°, so by
    Pythagoras AB = √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 cm. The perimeter is 40 cm. Summary
    of the special parallelograms:
            rectangle:  equal diagonals
            rhombus:    perpendicular diagonals (they also bisect the angles)
            square:     equal AND perpendicular diagonals
    Common mistake: thinking the diagonals of a rhombus are equal; they are
    equal only in a square. Now you try: rhombus diagonals 10 cm and 24 cm.
    Side? (√(25 + 144) = 13 cm)

D9. Prove the mid-point theorem: if E and F are the mid-points of sides AB and
    AC of ΔABC, then EF ∥ BC and EF = ½BC. If BC = 14 cm, find EF.
                        A
                      /   \
                    /       \
                E /-----------\F
                /               \
              /                   \
            B-----------------------C
    Answer: EF ∥ BC and EF = ½BC = 7 cm.
    Teacher explains: Through C draw a line parallel to BA, meeting EF produced
    at G.
            Statement                   Reason
            AF = CF                     F is the mid-point of AC
            ∠EAF = ∠GCF                 alternate angles (AB ∥ GC)
            ∠AFE = ∠CFG                 vertically opposite angles
            ΔAEF ≅ ΔCGF                 ASA rule
            AE = CG, EF = FG            CPCT
            BE = AE = CG                E is the mid-point of AB
            BE ∥ CG and BE = CG         construction and the line above
            EBCG is a parallelogram     one pair of opposite sides equal and ∥
            EG ∥ BC and EG = BC         opposite sides of a parallelogram
            EF = ½EG = ½BC              EF = FG
    So EF ∥ BC and EF = ½BC. With BC = 14 cm, EF = 7 cm. The theorem connects
    all the earlier results: congruence, alternate angles and the parallelogram
    tests. It gives a quick way to measure a length you cannot reach: to find
    the width BC of a pond, measure the distance EF between the mid-points of AB
    and AC on dry land and double it. Common mistake: halving the wrong side; EF
    is half of the side it does NOT touch. Now you try: EF = 4.5 cm. Find BC. (9
    cm)

D10. Prove the converse of the mid-point theorem: the line through the mid-point
     of one side of a triangle parallel to another side bisects the third side.
     Use it: in trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC, AB = 12 cm and DC = 8 cm, E is the
     mid-point of AD and the line through E parallel to AB meets BC at F. Show
     that F is the mid-point of BC and find EF.
                    D --------- C
                   /             \
                E ------------------ F
                 /                   \
                A ------------------- B
     Answer: F is the mid-point of BC, and EF = (12 + 8)/2 = 10 cm.
     Teacher explains: CONVERSE. In ΔABC let E be the mid-point of AB and let
     the line through E parallel to BC meet AC at F. Let F' be the mid-point of
     AC. By the mid-point theorem EF' ∥ BC. But through E there is only ONE line
     parallel to BC (Playfair's axiom), so EF and EF' are the same line and
     F = F': F is the mid-point. TRAPEZIUM: draw the diagonal AC, meeting EF at
     G.
             In ΔADC: E is the mid-point of AD and EG ∥ DC,
                      so G is the mid-point of AC and EG = ½DC = 4 cm
             In ΔCAB: G is the mid-point of CA and GF ∥ AB,
                      so F is the mid-point of CB and GF = ½AB = 6 cm
             EF = EG + GF = 4 + 6 = 10 cm = (AB + DC)/2
     The segment joining the mid-points of the non-parallel sides of a trapezium
     is parallel to the parallel sides and equals HALF THEIR SUM. It is the
     "average width" of the trapezium, which is why the area of a trapezium is
     (average of parallel sides) × height. Common mistake: taking EF = ½AB or
     ½DC. Now you try: a trapezium has parallel sides 15 cm and 9 cm. Length of
     the mid-segment? (12 cm)

D11. (a) ΔABC has sides 8 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm. D, E, F are the mid-points of its
     sides. Find the sides and the perimeter of ΔDEF, and compare the areas. (b)
     P, Q, R, S are the mid-points of the sides of a quadrilateral ABCD with
     diagonals AC = 9 cm and BD = 7 cm. What kind of figure is PQRS and what is
     its perimeter?
     Answer: (a) 4, 5 and 6 cm; perimeter 15 cm, half of 30 cm; area of ΔDEF is
     a quarter of the area of ΔABC. (b) PQRS is a parallelogram with perimeter
     9 + 7 = 16 cm.
     Teacher explains: (a) Each side of ΔDEF joins two mid-points, so it is HALF
     the side it does not touch:
             sides of ΔABC:   8     10     12     perimeter 30
             sides of ΔDEF:   4      5      6     perimeter 15
     The three segments cut ΔABC into FOUR triangles; each is congruent to ΔDEF
     (SSS: all have sides 4, 5, 6), so area(ΔDEF) = ¼ area(ΔABC). (b) In ΔABC, P
     and Q are mid-points of AB and BC, so PQ ∥ AC and PQ = ½AC. In ΔADC, S and
     R are mid-points of AD and DC, so SR ∥ AC and SR = ½AC. Hence PQ = SR and
     PQ ∥ SR: PQRS is a parallelogram (one pair of opposite sides equal and
     parallel). This is VARIGNON'S theorem, true for EVERY quadrilateral.
             PQ = SR = ½ × 9 = 4.5,   QR = PS = ½ × 7 = 3.5
             perimeter = 2(4.5 + 3.5) = 16 = AC + BD
     If the diagonals are equal, PQRS is a rhombus; if they are perpendicular,
     it is a rectangle. Common mistake: expecting PQRS to have the same shape as
     ABCD. Now you try: the mid-points of the sides of a rectangle with
     diagonals 10 cm. What figure, and what perimeter? (a rhombus with side 5
     cm; perimeter 20 cm)

D12. State the intercept theorem. Three parallel lines l, m, n cut a transversal
     p at A, B, C with AB = BC = 3 cm, and another transversal q at D, E, F with
     DE = 4.5 cm. Find EF. How can ruled notebook paper be used to divide a
     strip of card into 5 equal parts?
             l  -----A--------D--------
                      \        \
             m  -------B--------E------
                        \        \
             n  ---------C--------F----
     Answer: If parallel lines make equal intercepts on one transversal, they
     make equal intercepts on every transversal; so EF = DE = 4.5 cm. Lay the
     strip across the notebook so that its ends are on two ruled lines 5 spaces
     apart; the lines in between cut it into 5 equal parts.
     Teacher explains: Proof: join A to F, meeting m at G.
             In ΔACF: B is the mid-point of AC and BG ∥ CF,
                      so G is the mid-point of AF   (converse of the mid-point
                                                           theorem)
             In ΔFAD: G is the mid-point of FA and GE ∥ AD,
                      so E is the mid-point of FD, and DE = EF
     The notebook lines are parallel and EQUALLY spaced, so they make equal
     intercepts on a line perpendicular to them; by the theorem they make equal
     intercepts on ANY slanting line, including the strip of card. Tilt the
     strip until one end is on line 0 and the other on line 5: the lines 1, 2,
     3, 4 mark the division points. This is also the idea behind dividing a
     segment in a given ratio with ruler and compass (topic 7.28). Common
     mistake: using the theorem when the lines are NOT parallel, or when the
     intercepts on the first transversal are not equal. Now you try: four
     parallel lines cut p into three equal parts of 2 cm and cut q with the
     first part 3.2 cm. Length on q from the first to the fourth line?
     (3 × 3.2 = 9.6 cm)

       l) DE = 4.5
       m) AC = 12
       n) AQ = 4

M12. True or false?
     a) The angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°.
     b) A diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles.
     c) The diagonals of a parallelogram are equal.
     d) The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
     e) Consecutive angles of a parallelogram are equal.
     f) Every rectangle is a parallelogram.
     g) Every rhombus is a square.
     h) Every square is a rhombus.
     i) The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.
     j) The diagonals of a rectangle are perpendicular.
     k) A quadrilateral with equal diagonals is a rectangle.
     l) A parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle.
     m) A quadrilateral with one pair of sides equal and parallel is a
        parallelogram.
     n) A trapezium has two pairs of parallel sides.
     o) The mid-point segment of a triangle is half the third side.
     p) The mid-point triangle has half the area of the triangle.
     q) Joining the mid-points of any quadrilateral gives a parallelogram.
     r) The mid-segment of a trapezium equals half the sum of the parallel
        sides.
     s) A parallelogram can have exactly three right angles.
     t) The bisectors of two consecutive angles of a parallelogram meet at 90°.
     Answers: a) true   b) true   c) false   d) true   e) false   f) true
              g) false   h) true   i) true   j) false   k) false   l) true
              m) true   n) false   o) true   p) false (a quarter)   q) true
              r) true   s) false   t) true

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make a family tree of quadrilaterals (quadrilateral → trapezium →
  parallelogram → rectangle / rhombus → square) and list the properties each
  inherits; build parallelograms from Meccano strips or straws and push them to
  see what changes and what stays the same; fold a paper triangle so that the
  apex touches the base to see the mid-point segment; for each proof, mark the
  parallel sides with arrows first. Harder: prove that the quadrilateral formed
  by the angle bisectors of a parallelogram is a rectangle; prove that the
  medians of a triangle meet at a point two-thirds of the way along each (use
  the mid-point theorem twice); show that the line joining the mid-points of the
  diagonals of a trapezium is parallel to the parallel sides and equals half
  their difference; explore Varignon's parallelogram in GeoGebra by dragging the
  vertices.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.23 — AREAS OF PARALLELOGRAMS AND TRIANGLES ON SAME BASE
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Two figures are ON THE SAME BASE AND BETWEEN THE SAME PARALLELS when they
    share a side (the base) and the vertices (or side) opposite the base lie on
    one line parallel to the base. We write ar(ABCD) for the area of ABCD.
  - THEOREM 1: parallelograms on the same base (or on equal bases) and between
    the same parallels are equal in area. Proof by congruent triangles: cut a
    triangle off one end and add a congruent triangle at the other end. So area
    of a parallelogram = base × height, for EITHER pair of sides:
    b₁ × h₁ = b₂ × h₂.
  - A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles. Hence if a
    triangle and a parallelogram are on the same base and between the same
    parallels, ar(triangle) = 1/2 × ar(parallelogram), which gives area of a
    triangle = 1/2 × base × height.
  - THEOREM 2: triangles on the same base (or equal bases) and between the same
    parallels are equal in area. CONVERSE: triangles on the same base and on the
    same side of it with equal areas lie between the same parallels (their
    heights are equal).
  - Triangles with the same height have areas in the ratio of their bases. A
    MEDIAN divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area; the two
    diagonals of a parallelogram divide it into four triangles of equal area; in
    a trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC, ar(ABD) = ar(ABC), ar(ADC) = ar(BDC) and
    ar(AOD) = ar(BOC), where O is the meeting point of the diagonals.
  - In proofs write each step with a reason (same base and same parallels,
    median, diagonal of a parallelogram, congruent triangles) and add or
    subtract areas of pieces.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels
    are equal in area.
        A-------E-------B-------F      line AF ∥ DC
          \   /           \   /
            D---------------C
         parallelograms ABCD and EFCD on the same base DC
    Answer: ΔADE ≅ ΔBCF, so
    ar(ABCD) = ar(ADE) + ar(EDCB) = ar(BCF) + ar(EDCB) = ar(EFCD).
    Teacher explains: Both parallelograms stand on DC and their top sides AB and
    EF lie on the same line AF, parallel to DC. Compare the two triangles at the
    ends:
       Statement                    Reason
       AD = BC                      opposite sides of ∥gm ABCD
       ∠DAE = ∠CBF                  corresponding angles, AD ∥ BC
       ∠AED = ∠BFC                  corresponding angles, ED ∥ FC
       ΔADE ≅ ΔBCF                  AAS
       ar(ADE) = ar(BCF)            congruent figures, equal areas
    Now add the same piece EDCB to both:
    ar(ABCD) = ar(ADE) + ar(EDCB) = ar(BCF) + ar(EDCB) = ar(EFCD). The
    parallelogram has only been cut and re-glued: a triangle moved from one end
    to the other. So every parallelogram on base DC between these parallels has
    the same area as the RECTANGLE on DC between them, namely base × height.
    Common mistake: thinking the "slanting" parallelogram is bigger because its
    sides are longer. Its perimeter is bigger; its area is not. Now you try: a
    parallelogram and a rectangle stand on the same base 12 cm between the same
    parallels 5 cm apart. Area of each? (60 cm²)

D2. In parallelogram ABCD, AB = 16 cm, the height AE onto DC is 8 cm and the
    height CF onto AD is 10 cm. Find AD.
    Answer: AD = 12.8 cm.
    Teacher explains: A parallelogram has TWO base-height pairs, one for each
    pair of sides, and both give the same area:
       area = DC × AE = 16 × 8 = 128 cm²      (DC = AB = 16 cm)
       area = AD × CF = AD × 10
       AD × 10 = 128,  AD = 128 ÷ 10 = 12.8 cm
    Rule: b₁ × h₁ = b₂ × h₂. The height must be PERPENDICULAR to the base it is
    paired with: AE goes with DC (or AB), CF goes with AD (or BC). Check: the
    longer side has the shorter height (16 > 12.8 and 8 < 10). Common mistake:
    multiplying AB by CF, which mixes a base with the wrong height. Now you try:
    AB = 12 cm, height onto AB is 7 cm, AD = 10 cm. Find the height onto AD.
    (8.4 cm)

D3. Prove that triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are
    equal in area. Then find the area of every triangle whose base is AB = 10 cm
    and whose third vertex lies on a line parallel to AB at a distance of 6 cm.
    Answer: Each such triangle is half of a parallelogram on AB between the same
    parallels, so all have the same area: 1/2 × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².
    Teacher explains: Let ΔABP and ΔABQ have P and Q on a line l ∥ AB. Through B
    draw BE ∥ AP and BF ∥ AQ, meeting l at E and F.
       Statement                          Reason
       ABEP, ABFQ are parallelograms      both pairs of sides ∥
       ar(ABEP) = ar(ABFQ)                same base AB, same ∥s
       ar(ABP) = 1/2 ar(ABEP)             diagonal BP halves ∥gm
       ar(ABQ) = 1/2 ar(ABFQ)             diagonal BQ halves ∥gm
       ar(ABP) = ar(ABQ)                  halves of equal areas
    So sliding the top vertex along the parallel line never changes the area:
    the base and the height stay the same. With AB = 10 cm and height 6 cm:
    area = 1/2 × 10 × 6 = 30 cm² for every position. Common mistake: taking the
    slanting side AP as the height. The height is the perpendicular distance
    between the parallels. Now you try: base 9 cm, parallels 8 cm apart. Area of
    each triangle? (36 cm²)

D4. ABCD is a parallelogram of area 84 cm² and P is any point on side CD. Find
    ar(APB) and ar(APD) + ar(BPC). Does the answer depend on where P is?
    Answer: ar(APB) = 42 cm² and ar(APD) + ar(BPC) = 42 cm², wherever P is on
    CD.
    Teacher explains: ΔAPB and parallelogram ABCD are on the same base AB and
    between the same parallels AB and DC. So
       ar(APB) = 1/2 × ar(ABCD) = 1/2 × 84 = 42 cm²
       ar(APD) + ar(BPC) = ar(ABCD) − ar(APB) = 84 − 42 = 42 cm²
    Why half? Area of the triangle = 1/2 × AB × h and area of the
    parallelogram = AB × h, with the SAME h. Moving P along CD changes the two
    side triangles (one grows while the other shrinks) but never their total.
    Common mistake: thinking P must be the midpoint of CD. It does not matter.
    Now you try: a parallelogram of area 50 cm², P on CD. ar(APB)? (25 cm²)

D5. Prove that a median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of equal
    area. In ΔABC, AD is a median and E is the midpoint of AD. If
    ar(ABC) = 64 cm², find ar(BED).
    Answer: ar(ABD) = ar(ACD); ar(BED) = 1/4 × ar(ABC) = 16 cm².
    Teacher explains: Draw AN ⟂ BC. Then ar(ABD) = 1/2 × BD × AN and
    ar(ACD) = 1/2 × DC × AN. Since D is the midpoint of BC, BD = DC, so the two
    areas are equal: EQUAL BASES, SAME HEIGHT.
       ar(ABD) = 1/2 ar(ABC) = 1/2 × 64 = 32     (AD is a median)
       BE is a median of ΔABD                    (E is mid AD)
       ar(BED) = 1/2 ar(ABD) = 1/2 × 32 = 16 cm²
    So ar(BED) = 1/2 × 1/2 × ar(ABC) = 1/4 × 64 = 16 cm². The same idea is used
    over and over: every time a median is drawn, the area is halved. Common
    mistake: halving the length but forgetting that the triangles must also have
    the same height (they do, because they share the vertex opposite the halved
    side). Now you try: ar(ABC) = 36 cm². Find ar(BED). (9 cm²)

D6. Itwaari has a four-sided field ABCD. The panchayat asks him to give up the
    corner at D for a health centre and take equal land on the other side so
    that his field becomes a TRIANGLE of the same area. How can it be done? If
    ar(ABC) = 180 m² and ar(ACD) = 120 m², what is the area of the new
    triangular field?
    Answer: Join AC. Through D draw DE ∥ AC meeting BC produced at E. Then
    ar(ACD) = ar(ACE), so ar(ABE) = ar(ABCD) = 300 m².
    Teacher explains: Step 1: join the diagonal AC. Step 2: draw DE ∥ AC to meet
    BC extended at E. Step 3: ΔACD and ΔACE are on the same base AC and between
    the same parallels AC and DE, so they have EQUAL areas. Hence
       ar(ABE) = ar(ABC) + ar(ACE)
               = ar(ABC) + ar(ACD) = ar(ABCD)
               = 180 + 120 = 300 m²
    Itwaari gives up the corner piece near D and gains an equal piece near E;
    the total is unchanged. Common mistake: drawing DE parallel to a SIDE
    instead of the diagonal AC. Now you try: ar(ABC) = 250 m² and
    ar(ACD) = 170 m². Area of the new triangle? (420 m²)

D7. Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram divide it into four triangles of
    equal area. A tile ABCD in the shape of a parallelogram has area 96 cm². Its
    diagonals meet at O. Find ar(AOB) and ar(AOB) + ar(COD).
    Answer: Each of the four triangles has area 24 cm²;
    ar(AOB) + ar(COD) = 48 cm².
    Teacher explains: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so O
    is the midpoint of AC and of BD.
       BO is a median of ΔABC  →  ar(AOB) = ar(BOC)
       CO is a median of ΔBCD  →  ar(BOC) = ar(COD)
       DO is a median of ΔCDA  →  ar(COD) = ar(DOA)
    So all four are equal, each 1/4 of the parallelogram: 96 ÷ 4 = 24 cm², and
    ar(AOB) + ar(COD) = 24 + 24 = 48 cm². Notice: the four triangles are NOT all
    congruent (AOB and BOC have different shapes unless ABCD is a rhombus), yet
    their areas are equal. Equal area does not mean congruent. Now you try: a
    parallelogram of area 70 cm². Area of ΔBOC? (17.5 cm²)

D8. ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC. Its diagonals AC and BD meet at O. Prove
    that ar(AOD) = ar(BOC). If ar(ABC) = 40 cm² and ar(AOB) = 25 cm², find
    ar(AOD).
    Answer: ar(ABD) = ar(ABC) (same base AB, same parallels); subtracting
    ar(AOB) gives ar(AOD) = ar(BOC) = 40 − 25 = 15 cm².
    Teacher explains:
            A +---------+ B
             /  \     /  \
            /     O       \       AB ∥ DC
           /   /     \     \
        D +-----------------+ C
       Statement                          Reason
       ar(ABD) = ar(ABC)                  same base AB, AB ∥ DC
       ar(ABD) − ar(AOB)                  subtract the common
           = ar(ABC) − ar(AOB)            piece ΔAOB
       ar(AOD) = ar(BOC)
    Numbers: ar(BOC) = ar(ABC) − ar(AOB) = 40 − 25 = 15 cm², and so
    ar(AOD) = 15 cm². The two side triangles of a trapezium are always equal in
    area, even when the trapezium is not isosceles. Common mistake: saying ΔAOD
    ≅ ΔBOC. They are equal in area but usually not congruent. Now you try:
    ar(BDC) = 54 cm², ar(DOC) = 36 cm². Find ar(AOD). (18 cm²)

D9. D and E are points on the sides AB and AC of ΔABC such that
    ar(DBC) = ar(EBC). Prove that DE ∥ BC.
    Answer: ΔDBC and ΔEBC are on the same base BC, on the same side, with equal
    areas, so they are between the same parallels: DE ∥ BC.
    Teacher explains: This is the CONVERSE of theorem 2. Proof: let the heights
    of D and E above BC be h₁ and h₂.
       1/2 × BC × h₁ = ar(DBC) = ar(EBC) = 1/2 × BC × h₂
       so h₁ = h₂
    D and E are on the same side of BC at the same distance from it, so the line
    DE is parallel to BC (two points at equal heights above a line lie on a
    parallel line). Converses need care: the triangles must be on the SAME side
    of the base; if D were below BC, equal areas would not give DE ∥ BC. Now you
    try: ΔPQR and ΔPQS are on the same side of PQ = 8 cm and both have area
    28 cm². What is the distance between the parallels PQ and RS? (7 cm)

D10. ABCD is a parallelogram of area 120 cm² and E is the midpoint of CD. Find
     ar(ABE), ar(ADE) and ar(BCE).
     Answer: ar(ABE) = 60 cm², ar(ADE) = 30 cm², ar(BCE) = 30 cm².
     Teacher explains:
          D +------E------+ C
           /  .       .  /
          /     .   .   /
       A +-------------+ B          E is the midpoint of DC
     ΔABE and ABCD are on the same base AB and between AB ∥ DC, so
     ar(ABE) = 1/2 × 120 = 60 cm². The rest, 120 − 60 = 60 cm², is shared by
     ΔADE and ΔBCE. They have equal bases DE = EC and the same height (the
     distance between AB and DC), so each is 60 ÷ 2 = 30 cm².
     Another way: with base b and height h, bh = 120 and
     ar(ADE) = 1/2 × (b/2) × h = bh/4 = 30. Check: 60 + 30 + 30 = 120. Now you
     try: the area is 88 cm² and E is the midpoint of CD. ar(ADE)? (22 cm²)

D11. Budhia wants to divide her triangular field ABC of area 1,350 m² equally
     among herself and her two sons, each piece being a triangle with a vertex
     at the well at A. How can she do it?
     Answer: Divide BC into three equal parts at D and E and join AD and AE.
     Each of ΔABD, ΔADE and ΔAEC has area 1,350 ÷ 3 = 450 m².
     Teacher explains: All three triangles have their vertex at A, so they have
     the SAME height h (the perpendicular from A to BC). Their bases BD, DE, EC
     are equal, so their areas 1/2 × base × h are equal.
                         A
                      / / \ \
                    /  /   \  \
                  /   /     \   \
                B----D-------E----C      BD = DE = EC
     General rule: triangles with the same height have areas in the ratio of
     their bases. If instead BD : DC = 2 : 3, then ar(ABD) : ar(ADC) = 2 : 3, so
     ar(ABD) = 2/5 × 1,350 = 540 m². Common mistake: dividing the ANGLE at A
     into three equal parts; equal angles do not give equal areas. Now you try:
     divide a triangle of area 1,000 m² into 4 equal parts from one vertex. Area
     of each? (250 m²)

D12. P is any point inside parallelogram ABCD. Prove that
     ar(APB) + ar(PCD) = 1/2 ar(ABCD). If ar(ABCD) = 150 cm², ar(APB) = 40 cm²
     and ar(APD) = 48 cm², find ar(PCD) and ar(PBC).
     Answer: ar(PCD) = 35 cm² and ar(PBC) = 27 cm².
     Teacher explains: Through P draw EF ∥ AB, with E on AD and F on BC. Then
     ABFE and EFCD are parallelograms.
        ar(APB) = 1/2 ar(ABFE)      same base AB, AB ∥ EF
        ar(PCD) = 1/2 ar(EFCD)      same base DC, DC ∥ EF
        add:  ar(APB) + ar(PCD) = 1/2 [ar(ABFE) + ar(EFCD)]
                                = 1/2 ar(ABCD)
     The same argument with a line through P parallel to AD gives
     ar(APD) + ar(PBC) = 1/2 ar(ABCD). Numbers: half of 150 is 75, so
     ar(PCD) = 75 − 40 = 35 cm² and ar(PBC) = 75 − 48 = 27 cm². Check:
     40 + 35 + 48 + 27 = 150. Now you try: ar(ABCD) = 90 cm², ar(APB) = 20 cm².
     Find ar(PCD). (25 cm²)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Area of a parallelogram A = b × h (lengths in cm, areas in cm²). Find the

    a) b = 12, h = 7      b) b = 9, h = 8       c) b = 15, h = 6

M2. A parallelogram has sides b₁ and b₂ with the heights h₁ and h₂ onto them, so

M5. D is a point on side BC of ΔABC (1 : 1 means AD is a median). In a) to l)
    find ar(ABD) and ar(ADC). In m) to t) find BD : DC in simplest form.
    a) BD : DC = 1 : 1, ar(ABC) = 64     b) BD : DC = 1 : 1, ar(ABC) = 90
    c) BD : DC = 1 : 1, ar(ABC) = 37     d) BD : DC = 1 : 2, ar(ABC) = 60
    e) BD : DC = 2 : 3, ar(ABC) = 100    f) BD : DC = 3 : 1, ar(ABC) = 48
    g) BD : DC = 3 : 5, ar(ABC) = 72     h) BD : DC = 1 : 4, ar(ABC) = 45
    i) BD : DC = 5 : 2, ar(ABC) = 84     j) BD : DC = 4 : 7, ar(ABC) = 132
    k) BD : DC = 2 : 1, ar(ABC) = 25.5   l) BD : DC = 1 : 3, ar(ABC) = 10
    m) ar(ABD) = 20, ar(ADC) = 30        n) ar(ABD) = 18, ar(ADC) = 18
    o) ar(ABD) = 12, ar(ADC) = 36        p) ar(ABD) = 45, ar(ADC) = 27
    q) ar(ABD) = 14, ar(ADC) = 35        r) ar(ABD) = 50, ar(ADC) = 20
    s) ar(ABD) = 16, ar(ADC) = 40        t) ar(ABD) = 9, ar(ADC) = 21
    Answers: a) 32, 32   b) 45, 45   c) 18.5, 18.5   d) 20, 40   e) 40, 60
             f) 36, 12   g) 27, 45   h) 9, 36   i) 60, 24   j) 48, 84
             k) 17, 8.5   l) 2.5, 7.5   m) BD : DC = 2 : 3   n) BD : DC = 1 : 1
             o) BD : DC = 1 : 3   p) BD : DC = 5 : 3   q) BD : DC = 2 : 5
             r) BD : DC = 5 : 2   s) BD : DC = 2 : 5   t) BD : DC = 3 : 7

     q) ar(APS) = 9: ar(ABCD)      r) ar(ARQ) = 15: ar(ABCD)
