M12. True or false? Correct the false ones.
     a) Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels have
        equal areas.
     b) Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels have
        equal perimeters.
     c) A triangle and a parallelogram on the same base and between the same
        parallels have equal areas.
     d) A median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area.
     e) A median divides a triangle into two congruent triangles.
     f) The diagonals of a parallelogram divide it into four triangles of equal
        area.
     g) Triangles with equal areas are congruent.
     h) Congruent triangles have equal areas.
     i) In trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC, ar(ABD) = ar(ABC).
     j) In trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC, ar(ABD) = ar(BDC).
     k) Triangles with the same height have areas in the ratio of their bases.
     l) Two triangles on the same base with equal areas always lie between the
        same parallels.
     m) A rectangle and a parallelogram on the same base and between the same
        parallels have equal areas.
     n) Area of a parallelogram = product of two adjacent sides.
     o) The triangle formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of a triangle
        has 1/4 of its area.
     p) Joining the midpoints of the sides of a parallelogram gives a
        quadrilateral with 1/2 of its area.
     Answers: a) true   b) false (the slanting one has a longer perimeter)
              c) false (the triangle is half)   d) true
              e) false (equal area only, unless the triangle is isosceles with
                 the median from the apex)   f) true   g) false   h) true
              i) true   j) false (true only if AB = DC)   k) true
              l) false (they must be on the same side of the base)   m) true
              n) false (base × perpendicular height)   o) true   p) true

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: cut a paper parallelogram along a height and slide the triangle to
  the other end to make a rectangle; shade the pieces in colour; draw both
  parallel lines heavily and mark the height in every figure; for each new
  triangle say aloud "same base? same parallels? same height?"; use squared
  paper and count squares to see that sliding the top vertex keeps the area.
  Harder: prove that the four triangles cut off by the diagonals of a
  quadrilateral satisfy ar(AOB) × ar(COD) = ar(BOC) × ar(AOD); prove that
  joining the midpoints of any quadrilateral gives half its area; show how to
  turn any pentagon into a triangle of equal area by two parallel-line steps;
  and investigate with GeoGebra by dragging P along the top line and watching
  the area stay fixed.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.24 — CIRCLE THEOREMS: CHORDS, ARCS, ANGLES SUBTENDED, CYCLIC
             QUADRILATERALS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Words: a CHORD joins two points of the circle (a diameter is the longest
    chord); an ARC is a piece of the circle (minor arc less than a semicircle,
    major arc more); a SEGMENT is the region between a chord and an arc; the
    angle a chord SUBTENDS at a point is the angle between the lines from its
    ends to that point.
  - EQUAL CHORDS subtend EQUAL ANGLES at the centre (proof: SSS) and,
    conversely, chords that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal. Equal
    chords cut off equal arcs, and equal arcs have equal chords.
  - The PERPENDICULAR from the centre to a chord BISECTS the chord (proof: RHS),
    and the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to
    it. With radius r, chord c and distance d from the centre: r² = d² + (c/2)².
    Equal chords are EQUIDISTANT from the centre (and conversely); a longer
    chord is nearer to the centre.
  - There is exactly ONE circle through three non-collinear points: its centre
    is where the perpendicular bisectors of the joining segments meet. No circle
    passes through three collinear points.
  - ANGLE AT THE CENTRE = TWICE the angle at the circumference standing on the
    same arc. Hence ANGLES IN THE SAME SEGMENT are equal, and the ANGLE IN A
    SEMICIRCLE is 90°. An angle standing on a major arc is acute; on a minor arc
    it is obtuse.
  - CYCLIC QUADRILATERAL (all four vertices on a circle): OPPOSITE angles add up
    to 180°; conversely, if a pair of opposite angles adds up to 180°, the
    quadrilateral is cyclic. An EXTERIOR angle equals the INTERIOR OPPOSITE
    angle. A cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle.
  - In angle chasing write a REASON for every step: radii equal (isosceles
    triangle), angle at centre, same segment, semicircle, cyclic quadrilateral,
    exterior angle, angle sum of a triangle.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre. In a
    circle with centre O, AB = CD = 6 cm and ∠AOB = 70°. Find ∠COD and ∠OCD.
    Answer: ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD by SSS, so ∠COD = ∠AOB = 70°;
    ∠OCD = (180° − 70°) ÷ 2 = 55°.
    Teacher explains:
       Statement                  Reason
       OA = OC                    radii
       OB = OD                    radii
       AB = CD                    given
       ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD                SSS
       ∠AOB = ∠COD                CPCT
    Every chord together with the two radii to its ends makes an ISOSCELES
    triangle, because radii are equal. So in ΔOCD the base angles are equal:
    ∠OCD = ∠ODC = (180° − 70°) ÷ 2 = 55°. The converse is proved the same way
    with SAS: if ∠AOB = ∠COD, then ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD and AB = CD. Common mistake:
    forgetting that the proof needs the SAME circle (or equal circles); a 6 cm
    chord in a bigger circle subtends a smaller angle. Now you try: equal chords
    PQ and RS, ∠POQ = 84°. Find ∠ORS. (48°)

D2. Prove that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects
    the chord. A chord of a circle of radius 13 cm is 24 cm long. How far is it
    from the centre?
    Answer: ΔOMA ≅ ΔOMB by RHS, so AM = MB. Distance = 5 cm.
    Teacher explains:
                   O
                 / | \          OM ⟂ AB
            13 /   |d  \ 13
              /    |     \
            A------M------B
               12     12
       Statement                  Reason
       ∠OMA = ∠OMB = 90°          given OM ⟂ AB
       OA = OB                    radii (hypotenuses)
       OM = OM                    common
       ΔOMA ≅ ΔOMB                RHS
       AM = MB                    CPCT
    Now use Pythagoras in ΔOMA: AM = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm, so
    d² = 13² − 12² = 169 − 144 = 25 and d = 5 cm. The key triangle is always:
    radius as hypotenuse, HALF the chord and the distance as the legs,
    r² = d² + (c/2)². Common mistake: using the whole chord 24 instead of 12.
    Now you try: radius 10 cm, chord 6 cm from the centre. Length of the chord?
    (16 cm)

D3. Water flows in a pipe of inner diameter 52 cm. The water surface is 48 cm
    wide. How deep is the water?
    Answer: 16 cm deep if the pipe is less than half full (36 cm if it is more
    than half full).
    Teacher explains: Draw the cross-section: a circle of radius 26 cm, and the
    water surface is a chord of length 48 cm. The perpendicular from the centre
    bisects it, giving half-chord 24 cm.
       d² = 26² − 24² = 676 − 576 = 100,   d = 10 cm
       depth = r − d = 26 − 10 = 16 cm     (surface above the
                                            bottom, below centre)
       or depth = r + d = 26 + 10 = 36 cm  (surface above centre)
    The distance d is measured from the CENTRE, so to get the depth we must go
    from the surface down to the bottom of the pipe: r − d or r + d. Always ask
    which side of the centre the chord lies. Common mistake: giving d = 10 cm as
    the depth. Now you try: diameter 10 cm, surface width 8 cm, less than half
    full. Depth? (2 cm)

D4. AB and CD are parallel chords of a circle of radius 13 cm, with AB = 10 cm
    and CD = 24 cm. Find the distance between them when they are (a) on the same
    side of the centre, (b) on opposite sides.
    Answer: (a) 7 cm, (b) 17 cm.
    Teacher explains: Both chords are perpendicular to the same line through the
    centre, so their distances from O lie along one straight line.
       AB: d₁² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144,   d₁ = 12 cm
       CD: d₂² = 13² − 12² = 169 − 144 = 25,  d₂ = 5 cm
       same side:      12 − 5 = 7 cm
       opposite sides: 12 + 5 = 17 cm
    Notice the longer chord (24 cm) is NEARER the centre (5 cm) than the shorter
    one (12 cm). Draw both pictures; one problem has two answers unless the
    position is stated. Common mistake: halving the distance instead of the
    chord. Now you try: radius 5 cm, parallel chords 6 cm and 8 cm. Distance
    between them? (1 cm or 7 cm)

D5. Prove that equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre. In a
    circle of radius 17 cm, which is nearer to the centre: a chord of 30 cm or a
    chord of 16 cm?
    Answer: If AB = CD then AB/2 = CD/2 and ΔOMA ≅ ΔONC (RHS), so OM = ON. The
    30 cm chord is 8 cm from the centre, the 16 cm chord 15 cm: the longer chord
    is nearer.
    Teacher explains: Let M and N be the feet of the perpendiculars from O to AB
    and CD. They bisect the chords, so AM = CN (halves of equal chords).
       Statement                  Reason
       ∠OMA = ∠ONC = 90°          perpendiculars
       OA = OC                    radii
       AM = CN                    halves of equal chords
       ΔOMA ≅ ΔONC                RHS
       OM = ON                    CPCT
    Numbers: 17² − 15² = 289 − 225 = 64, so the 30 cm chord is 8 cm away;
    17² − 8² = 289 − 64 = 225, so the 16 cm chord is 15 cm away. Since
    d² = r² − (c/2)², a bigger chord leaves a smaller d. The converse (chords
    equidistant from the centre are equal) also holds. Now you try: radius
    25 cm, chords of 48 cm and 14 cm. Distances? (7 cm and 24 cm)

D6. Prove that the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle
    it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle. If
    ∠AOB = 100°, find ∠ACB for C on the major arc and for C on the minor arc.
    Answer: ∠AOB = 2∠ACB. For C on the major arc ∠ACB = 50°; on the minor arc
    ∠ACB = 130°.
    Teacher explains:
                     C
                   / | \
                 /   |   \         join CO and extend to D
               /     O     \
             /    /  |  \    \
            A  /     D     \  B
    Join CO and extend it to D. OA = OC (radii), so ΔOAC is isosceles:
    ∠OAC = ∠OCA = x. The exterior angle ∠AOD = x + x = 2x. In the same way
    ∠BOD = 2y where y = ∠OCB. Adding: ∠AOB = 2x + 2y = 2(x + y) = 2∠ACB.
    Numbers: C on the major arc: ∠ACB = 100° ÷ 2 = 50°. C on the minor arc: that
    angle stands on the MAJOR arc, whose central angle is the reflex angle
    360° − 100° = 260°, so ∠ACB = 260° ÷ 2 = 130°. Check: 50° + 130° = 180°: the
    two angles are opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral. Common mistake:
    halving the wrong central angle. Always look at WHICH arc the angle stands
    on. Now you try: ∠AOB = 140°. Angle at a point on the major arc? (70°)

D7. Explain why angles in the same segment are equal and why the angle in a
    semicircle is 90°. A carpenter has a circular table top and a set square.
    How can she find a diameter? If AB is a diameter of length 10 cm and
    AC = 6 cm, find BC.
    Answer: Each angle in the segment is half the same central angle, so they
    are equal; for a semicircle the central angle is 180°, so the angle is 90°.
    BC = 8 cm.
    Teacher explains: Same segment: ∠ACB and ∠ADB both stand on arc AB, so each
    equals 1/2 ∠AOB. They are equal. Semicircle: when AB is a diameter,
    ∠AOB = 180° (a straight angle), so ∠ACB = 180° ÷ 2 = 90°.
    Carpenter: put the right-angled corner of the set square ON the edge of the
    table; where its two arms cross the edge are the ends of a diameter (the
    converse: a chord subtending 90° at the circle is a diameter). Do it twice;
    the diameters cross at the centre.
       ∠ACB = 90°  (angle in a semicircle)
       BC² = AB² − AC² = 10² − 6² = 100 − 36 = 64,   BC = 8 cm
    Common mistake: putting the right angle anywhere except ON the circle. Now
    you try: diameter 13 cm, one chord from its end is 5 cm. The other chord to
    the same point? (12 cm)

D8. Prove that the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°. In
    cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A = (2x + 10)° and ∠C = (3x − 5)°. Find the
    angles.
    Answer: x = 35, ∠A = 80°, ∠C = 100°.
    Teacher explains: Let O be the centre. ∠BAD stands on arc BCD and ∠BCD
    stands on arc BAD. The two central angles on these arcs together make a full
    turn:
       ∠BAD = 1/2 × (central angle on arc BCD)
       ∠BCD = 1/2 × (central angle on arc BAD)
       ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 1/2 × 360° = 180°
    In the same way ∠B + ∠D = 180° (or: all four add up to 360°).
       (2x + 10) + (3x − 5) = 180
                 5x + 5 = 180
                      x = 35
       ∠A = 2 × 35 + 10 = 80°,   ∠C = 3 × 35 − 5 = 100°
    Consequence: a cyclic parallelogram is a RECTANGLE, since its opposite
    angles are equal AND add up to 180°, so each is 90°. Common mistake: adding
    ADJACENT angles (∠A + ∠B) to 180°. That is true for a parallelogram, not for
    a cyclic quadrilateral. Now you try: ∠B = (4y)° and ∠D = (y + 30)°. Find ∠B.
    (120°)

D9. ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. AB is produced to E and ∠CBE = 75°. Find
    ∠ADC, and give reasons. If also ∠BAD = 95°, find ∠BCD.
    Answer: ∠ADC = 75°; ∠BCD = 85°.
    Teacher explains:
       Statement                  Reason
       ∠ABC = 180° − 75° = 105°   angles on a straight line
       ∠ADC = 180° − 105° = 75°   opposite angles, cyclic quad
       ∠BCD = 180° − 95° = 85°    opposite angles, cyclic quad
    So the EXTERIOR angle ∠CBE equals the INTERIOR OPPOSITE angle ∠ADC. This is
    always true: both equal 180° − ∠ABC. It is a quick shortcut in angle
    chasing, but in a proof write the two steps. Converse: if an exterior angle
    equals the interior opposite angle, the quadrilateral is cyclic. Common
    mistake: taking the interior angle NEXT to the exterior angle. Now you try:
    ABCD cyclic, DC produced to F, ∠BCF = 68°. Find ∠BAD. (68°)

D10. A, B, C and D lie on a circle; the chords AC and BD meet at E. If
     ∠BEC = 130° and ∠ECD = 20°, find ∠BAC.
     Answer: ∠BAC = 110°.
     Teacher explains:
        Statement                  Reason
        ∠BEC = ∠EDC + ∠ECD         exterior angle of ΔCDE
        ∠EDC = 130° − 20° = 110°
        ∠BDC = ∠EDC = 110°         (E lies on BD)
        ∠BAC = ∠BDC = 110°         angles in the same segment
     Both ∠BAC and ∠BDC stand on chord BC, on the same side of it, so they are
     equal. Plan for angle chasing: mark every given angle, look for isosceles
     triangles (radii), same-segment pairs, cyclic quadrilaterals, and write one
     reason per line. Check: in ΔCDE, 110 + 20 + 50 = 180, where
     ∠CED = 180 − 130 = 50. Now you try: ∠BEC = 120°, ∠ECD = 35°. Find ∠BAC.
     (85°)

D11. Three villages A, B and C are not in a straight line. The panchayat wants a
     water tank equally far from all three. Where should it go? If the villages
     form a right-angled triangle with sides 6 km, 8 km and 10 km, how far is
     the tank from each village?
     Answer: At the meeting point of the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC
     (the circumcentre). For the right-angled triangle it is the midpoint of the
     10 km side, 5 km from each village.
     Teacher explains: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is
     equally far from A and B. The perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet at
     one point O, which is then equally far from A, B and C: the centre of the
     ONLY circle through A, B and C. (If A, B, C were collinear the two
     bisectors would be parallel and never meet, so no circle exists.)
     Right-angled triangle: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10², so the angle opposite
     the 10 km side is 90°. An angle of 90° on a circle stands on a DIAMETER
     (converse of the semicircle theorem), so the 10 km side is a diameter and
     the centre is its midpoint: radius 10 ÷ 2 = 5 km. Now you try: villages
     forming a 5-12-13 km triangle. Distance of the tank from each? (6.5 km)

D12. A chord of a circle is equal to the radius. Find the angle it subtends (a)
     at the centre, (b) at a point on the major arc, (c) at a point on the minor
     arc. Repeat for a chord of length r√2.
     Answer: Chord = r: 60°, 30°, 150°. Chord = r√2: 90°, 45°, 135°.
     Teacher explains: Chord AB = r: triangle OAB has OA = OB = AB = r, so it is
     EQUILATERAL and ∠AOB = 60°. On the major arc: 60° ÷ 2 = 30°. On the minor
     arc: (360° − 60°) ÷ 2 = 150°, or 180° − 30° = 150° (cyclic quadrilateral).
        chord r√2:  OA² + OB² = r² + r² = 2r² = AB²
        so ∠AOB = 90° (converse of Pythagoras)
        major arc: 90° ÷ 2 = 45°,  minor arc: 180° − 45° = 135°
     The two inscribed angles on opposite sides of a chord always add up to
     180°, because together with the chord they form a cyclic quadrilateral. Now
     you try: a chord subtends 120° at the centre. Angles at points on the major
     and minor arcs? (60° and 120°)

M12. True or false? Correct the false ones.

     b) The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
     c) A longer chord is farther from the centre.
     d) Through three collinear points there is exactly one circle.
     e) The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the
        same arc.
     f) Angles in the same segment are equal.
     g) The angle in a semicircle is 180°.
     h) An angle in the minor segment is acute.
     i) Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal.
     j) The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior
        opposite angle.
     k) Every parallelogram is cyclic.
     l) An isosceles trapezium is cyclic.
     m) A rhombus that is not a square can be cyclic.
     n) Equal arcs of a circle have equal chords.
     o) If a chord subtends 90° at a point of the circle, the chord is a
        diameter.
     p) The diameter is the longest chord.

              d) false (there is none)   e) true   f) true   g) false (90°)
              h) false (it is obtuse; it stands on the major arc)

              k) false (only rectangles)   l) true   m) false   n) true
              o) true   p) true

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw a big circle with a compass for every question and mark the
  centre; mark radii with ticks at once (every chord with two radii gives an
  isosceles triangle); for chord questions always draw the perpendicular from
  the centre and label r, d and HALF the chord; for angle questions shade the
  arc the angle stands on, then look for the angle at the centre on the same
  arc; cut out a cyclic quadrilateral and tear off opposite corners to see them
  make a straight angle. Harder: prove that the angle subtended by an arc at the
  centre is double the angle at the circumference when the centre lies OUTSIDE
  the angle; prove the converse of the cyclic quadrilateral theorem by
  contradiction; prove that the bisectors of the angles of any quadrilateral
  form a cyclic quadrilateral; find the radius of the circle through (0, 0),
  (8, 0) and (0, 6); and investigate with GeoGebra how ∠ACB stays fixed as C
  moves on the arc.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.25 — TANGENTS TO A CIRCLE; NUMBER OF TANGENTS FROM A POINT
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A TANGENT is a line that meets the circle at exactly ONE point, the POINT OF
    CONTACT. A SECANT meets it at two points. A line may also miss the circle
    altogether.
  - THEOREM: the tangent at any point of a circle is PERPENDICULAR to the radius
    through the point of contact (proof: the radius is the shortest distance
    from the centre to the tangent). Conversely, the line through the end of a
    radius perpendicular to it is a tangent.
  - NUMBER OF TANGENTS from a point P at distance d from the centre of a circle
    of radius r: none if P is inside (d < r), exactly one if P is on the circle
    (d = r), exactly two if P is outside (d > r).
  - THEOREM: the two tangents from an external point are EQUAL in length (proof:
    RHS). The centre lies on the bisector of the angle between them. Tangent
    length t = √(d² − r²), from the right angle between radius and tangent.
  - If PA and PB are the tangents, then ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180° (quadrilateral OAPB
    has two right angles), ∠OPA = 1/2 ∠APB, and triangle PAB is isosceles.
    Tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel.
  - A quadrilateral circumscribing a circle (all four sides tangents) has
    AB + CD = AD + BC. For the INCIRCLE of a triangle with sides a, b, c and
    semi-perimeter s, the tangent lengths from A, B, C are s − a, s − b, s − c;
    in a right triangle the inradius is r = (a + b − c)/2.
  - ALTERNATE SEGMENT THEOREM (introduction): the angle between a tangent and a
    chord through the point of contact equals the angle the chord subtends in
    the alternate (opposite) segment.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the
    radius through the point of contact.
    Answer: Every point of the tangent other than P lies outside the circle, so
    OP is the shortest segment from O to the tangent, and the shortest segment
    from a point to a line is the perpendicular. Hence OP ⟂ tangent.
    Teacher explains:
                      O
                      |  \
                      |     \ R
                      |        \
       -------------- P -------- Q ------   tangent at P
    Take any point Q on the tangent other than P. If Q were inside or on the
    circle, the line would cut the circle again, and it would be a secant, not a
    tangent. So Q is OUTSIDE, and OQ is longer than the radius: OQ > OR = OP,
    where R is where OQ crosses the circle.
    So OP is shorter than every other segment from O to the line: it is the
    SHORTEST distance, and the shortest distance from a point to a line is along
    the perpendicular. Therefore OP ⟂ PQ. Common mistake: "proving" it by
    measuring one drawing. Now you try: the tangent at P has a point Q with
    PQ = 12 cm; the radius is 5 cm. Find OQ. (13 cm)

D2. A circle has radius 5 cm. How many tangents can be drawn to it from a point
    P at distance (a) 3 cm, (b) 5 cm, (c) 8 cm from the centre? Explain.
    Answer: (a) none, (b) exactly one, (c) exactly two.
    Teacher explains: (a) d = 3 < 5: P is INSIDE. Every line through P crosses
    the circle twice (it is a secant), so no tangent is possible.
    (b) d = 5 = r: P is ON the circle. There is exactly one line through P
    perpendicular to OP, and it is the only tangent at P.
    (c) d = 8 > 5: P is OUTSIDE. Imagine a line through P turning: it misses the
    circle, then just touches it, cuts it, and just touches it again on the
    other side. So there are exactly TWO tangents, symmetric about the line OP.
       position of P      d compared with r     tangents
       inside             d < r                 0
       on the circle      d = r                 1
       outside            d > r                 2
    Real life: a bicycle wheel standing on a flat road touches it at exactly one
    point; the road is a tangent and the spoke to that point is vertical. Now
    you try: r = 7 cm, d = 7.5 cm. How many tangents? (2)

D3. Prove that the lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a
    circle are equal. Show also that the centre lies on the bisector of the
    angle between them.
    Answer: ΔOAP ≅ ΔOBP by RHS, so PA = PB and ∠OPA = ∠OPB.
    Teacher explains:
                 A
               /    \
             O        P       PA, PB tangents; OA ⟂ PA, OB ⟂ PB
               \    /
                 B
       Statement                     Reason
       ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°             tangent ⟂ radius
       OP = OP                       common hypotenuse
       OA = OB                       radii
       ΔOAP ≅ ΔOBP                   RHS
       PA = PB                       CPCT
       ∠OPA = ∠OPB, ∠AOP = ∠BOP      CPCT
    So OP bisects both the angle between the tangents at P and the angle AOB
    between the radii. A kite OAPB is formed: two pairs of equal adjacent sides
    (OA = OB, PA = PB). This result is behind almost every tangent problem.
    Common mistake: using SAS; the right angle is NOT between the two known
    sides, so the correct test is RHS. Now you try: PA = 9 cm. Find PB. (9 cm)

D4. A point P is 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Find the
    length of the tangent from P. Then: a person stands on a hill 0.5 km high.
    Taking the radius of the Earth as 6400 km, how far away is the horizon (the
    tangent length)?
    Answer: 12 cm; about 80.0 km.
    Teacher explains: The radius to the point of contact T is perpendicular to
    the tangent, so ΔOTP has its right angle at T and OP is the hypotenuse:
       PT² = OP² − OT² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144,   PT = 12 cm
    For the hill: OP = 6400 + 0.5 = 6400.5 km and OT = 6400 km.
       PT² = 6400.5² − 6400²
           = (6400.5 − 6400)(6400.5 + 6400)     (difference of squares)
           = 0.5 × 12800.5 = 6400.25
       PT = √6400.25 ≈ 80.0 km
    The difference of squares saves a lot of work with big numbers. Common
    mistake: adding the squares (d² + r²). The DISTANCE to the centre is the
    hypotenuse, the longest side. Now you try: d = 25 cm, r = 7 cm. Tangent
    length? (24 cm)

D5. PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O, and ∠APB = 80°.
    Find ∠AOB, ∠OPA, ∠PAB and ∠OAB.
    Answer: ∠AOB = 100°, ∠OPA = 40°, ∠PAB = 50°, ∠OAB = 40°.
    Teacher explains:
       Statement                      Reason
       ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°              tangent ⟂ radius
       ∠AOB = 360° − 90° − 90° − 80°  angle sum of quad OAPB
            = 100°
       ∠OPA = 80° ÷ 2 = 40°           OP bisects ∠APB
       ∠PAB = (180° − 80°) ÷ 2 = 50°  PA = PB, isosceles ΔPAB
       ∠OAB = 90° − 50° = 40°         ∠OAP = 90°
    Remember: ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°, because the other two angles of the
    quadrilateral OAPB are right angles. Notice ∠OAB = ∠OPA = 40° and ∠PAB = 1/2
    ∠AOB = 50°, the angle in the alternate segment. Common mistake: taking
    ∠AOB = 80° (the same as ∠APB). Now you try: ∠APB = 60°. Find ∠AOB. (120°)

D6. Two concentric circles have radii 5 cm and 3 cm. Find the length of the
    chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller circle, and prove that
    it is bisected at the point of contact.
    Answer: 8 cm; the radius of the small circle to the point of contact is
    perpendicular to the chord, and a perpendicular from the centre bisects a
    chord.
    Teacher explains:
       AB touches the small circle at M:  OM ⟂ AB  (tangent ⟂ radius)
       OM is also ⟂ to a chord of the big circle, so AM = MB
       AM² = OA² − OM² = 5² − 3² = 25 − 9 = 16,   AM = 4 cm
       AB = 2 × 4 = 8 cm
    Two theorems work together: the tangent-radius theorem for the SMALL circle
    and the perpendicular-bisector-of-a-chord theorem for the BIG circle. Every
    such chord has the same length, because it is always 3 cm from the centre.
    Common mistake: using the difference of radii 5 − 3 = 2. Now you try: radii
    13 cm and 5 cm. Length of the chord? (24 cm)

D7. A quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle (all four sides touch
    it). Prove that AB + CD = AD + BC. If AB = 6 cm, BC = 7 cm and CD = 4 cm,
    find AD.
    Answer: Adding equal tangent lengths gives AB + CD = AD + BC; AD = 3 cm.
    Teacher explains: Let the tangent lengths from A, B, C, D be a, b, c, d (the
    two tangents from each vertex are equal). Each side is made of two tangent
    pieces:
       AB = a + b      BC = b + c      CD = c + d      DA = d + a
       AB + CD = a + b + c + d = AD + BC
    So in every circumscribed quadrilateral the two pairs of OPPOSITE sides have
    equal sums. Numbers: 6 + 4 = AD + 7, so AD = 10 − 7 = 3 cm. Common mistake:
    adding ADJACENT sides. Now you try: AB = 9 cm, BC = 8 cm, CD = 5 cm. Find
    AD. (6 cm)

D8. Prove that a parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
    Answer: AB + CD = AD + BC, and in a parallelogram AB = CD and AD = BC, so
    2AB = 2BC, AB = BC: all four sides are equal.
    Teacher explains:
       AB + CD = AD + BC        circumscribed quadrilateral
       AB = CD, AD = BC         opposite sides of a parallelogram
       AB + AB = BC + BC        substitute
       AB = BC                  so all four sides are equal
    A parallelogram with all sides equal is a RHOMBUS. This is a typical short
    proof: combine a property of the circle (tangent lengths) with a property of
    the figure (opposite sides equal). The circle is then centred where the
    diagonals of the rhombus meet. Common mistake: starting from "a rhombus has
    equal sides" — that is what we must prove. Now you try: a rectangle
    circumscribes a circle. What kind of rectangle must it be? (a square)

D9. The incircle of ΔABC touches AB, BC, CA at P, Q, R. If AB = 12 cm, BC = 8 cm
    and CA = 10 cm, find the tangent lengths AP, BQ and CR.
    Answer: AP = 7 cm, BQ = 5 cm, CR = 3 cm.
    Teacher explains: Let AP = AR = x, BP = BQ = y, CQ = CR = z (equal
    tangents).
       x + y = 12      (AB)
       y + z = 8       (BC)
       z + x = 10      (CA)
       add: 2(x + y + z) = 30,   x + y + z = 15 = s
       x = 15 − 8 = 7,   y = 15 − 10 = 5,   z = 15 − 12 = 3
    The shortcut: the tangent length from a vertex is s − (the side OPPOSITE
    that vertex), where s is the semi-perimeter. Check: 7 + 5 = 12, 5 + 3 = 8,
    3 + 7 = 10. Common mistake: subtracting the side next to the vertex. Now you
    try: AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm, CA = 6 cm. Tangent length from A? (4 cm)

D10. A right-angled triangle has legs 5 cm and 12 cm. Find the radius of its
     incircle.
     Answer: r = 2 cm.
     Teacher explains: Hypotenuse: √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 cm. Let the incircle
     touch the legs at E and F near the right angle C. OE ⟂ CE and OF ⟂ CF, and
     ∠C = 90°, so OECF is a square: the tangent lengths from C are both r.
        tangents from A: 5 − r     tangents from B: 12 − r
        hypotenuse = (5 − r) + (12 − r) = 13
        17 − 2r = 13,   r = 2 cm
        formula: r = (a + b − c)/2 = (5 + 12 − 13)/2 = 2
     Check with areas: joining O to the vertices splits the triangle into three
     triangles of height r, so area = r × s. Area = 1/2 × 5 × 12 = 30 and
     s = (5 + 12 + 13)/2 = 15, so r = 30 ÷ 15 = 2. Both methods agree. Now you
     try: legs 8 cm and 15 cm. Inradius? (3 cm)

D11. Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are
     parallel. A round table top of diameter 1.2 m is pushed between two
     parallel walls so that it touches both. How far apart are the walls?
     Answer: Both tangents are perpendicular to the same line AB, so they are
     parallel; the walls are 1.2 m apart.
     Teacher explains: Let AB be a diameter, with tangents l at A and m at B.
        l ⟂ OA and m ⟂ OB         tangent ⟂ radius
        OA and OB lie on AB        AB is a diameter
        ∠(l, AB) = ∠(m, AB) = 90°  so l ∥ m (alternate angles)
     The distance between the parallel tangents is the length of AB, the
     diameter. So the walls are 1.2 m apart. The converse also holds: if the
     tangents at A and B are parallel, then AB is a diameter. Common mistake:
     thinking any two tangents can be parallel; only those at the ends of a
     diameter are. Now you try: two parallel tangents of a circle are 14 cm
     apart. Radius? (7 cm)

D12. AT is the tangent at A to a circle with centre O, and AB is a chord with
     ∠TAB = 65°. C is a point on the major arc and D on the minor arc. Find
     ∠ACB, ∠AOB and ∠ADB.
     Answer: ∠ACB = 65°, ∠AOB = 130°, ∠ADB = 115°.
     Teacher explains: ALTERNATE SEGMENT THEOREM: the angle between the tangent
     and the chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. Why? Draw the
     diameter AE.
        ∠EAT = 90°                     tangent ⟂ radius
        ∠ABE = 90°                     angle in a semicircle
        ∠TAB = 90° − ∠EAB = ∠AEB       angle sum of ΔABE
        ∠AEB = ∠ACB                    same segment
     Numbers: ∠ACB = ∠TAB = 65°; ∠AOB = 2 × 65° = 130° (angle at the centre);
     ∠ADB = 180° − 65° = 115° (ACBD is cyclic). Also OA ⟂ AT gives
     ∠OAB = 90° − 65° = 25°, and in isosceles ΔOAB: 180 − 25 − 25 = 130. The
     same answer. Now you try: ∠TAB = 50°. Angle in the alternate segment? (50°)

M11. PA and PB are tangents from P. A third tangent touches the minor arc AB at
     C and meets PA at Q and PB at R, so QC = QA and RC = RB. Find what is asked
     (cm).
     a) PA = 12: perimeter of ΔPQR
     b) PA = 7.5: perimeter of ΔPQR
     c) PA = 20: perimeter of ΔPQR
     d) PA = 9: perimeter of ΔPQR
     e) PA = 3.2: perimeter of ΔPQR
     f) PA = 15: perimeter of ΔPQR
     g) perimeter of ΔPQR = 30: PA
     h) perimeter of ΔPQR = 18: PA
     i) perimeter of ΔPQR = 50: PA
     j) perimeter of ΔPQR = 7: PA
     k) OP = 13, r = 5: perimeter of ΔPQR
     l) OP = 10, r = 6: perimeter of ΔPQR
     m) OP = 25, r = 7: perimeter of ΔPQR
     n) OP = 17, r = 8: perimeter of ΔPQR
     o) OP = 5, r = 3: perimeter of ΔPQR
     p) OP = 26, r = 10: perimeter of ΔPQR
     Answers: a) 24   b) 15   c) 40   d) 18   e) 6.4   f) 30   g) 15   h) 9
              i) 25   j) 3.5   k) 24   l) 16   m) 48   n) 30   o) 8   p) 48

M12. True or false? Correct the false ones.
     a) A tangent meets a circle at exactly one point.
     b) A secant meets a circle at exactly one point.
     c) The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius through it.
     d) From a point inside a circle, one tangent can be drawn.
     e) From a point on a circle, exactly one tangent can be drawn.
     f) From a point outside a circle, exactly two tangents can be drawn.
     g) The two tangents from an external point are equal in length.
     h) If PA and PB are tangents, ∠APB = ∠AOB.
     i) Tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel.
     j) Tangents at the ends of any chord are parallel.
     k) For a circumscribed quadrilateral, AB + BC = CD + DA.
     l) A parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
     m) The tangent length from P is √(d² + r²).
     n) The centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents
        from a point.
     o) The inradius of a 3-4-5 triangle is 1.
     p) A line perpendicular to a radius at its outer end is a tangent.
     Answers: a) true   b) false (two points)   c) true   d) false (none)
              e) true   f) true   g) true   h) false (∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°)
              i) true   j) false (only for a diameter)
              k) false (AB + CD = BC + DA)   l) true   m) false (√(d² − r²))
              n) true   o) true   p) true

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: roll a coin along a ruler to see a tangent touch at one point;
  always draw the radius to the point of contact and mark the right angle first;
  mark equal tangent lengths with the same letter (x, y, z) from each vertex;
  for the tangent length say "distance to the centre is the hypotenuse, subtract
  the squares"; build the kite OAPB from straws. Harder: prove the alternate
  segment theorem fully; prove that ∠APB = 2∠OAB for tangents PA and PB; given
  BD = 8, DC = 6 and inradius 4 in a triangle, find the other sides (13 cm and
  15 cm, using area = r × s); find the length of the common external tangent of
  two circles; and prove that the tangents at the ends of a chord meet on the
  perpendicular bisector of the chord.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.26 — SIMILAR TRIANGLES: BASIC PROPORTIONALITY (THALES) THEOREM,
             AA/SSS/SAS SIMILARITY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Two triangles are SIMILAR (ΔABC ~ ΔPQR) if their corresponding angles are
    equal AND their corresponding sides are in the same ratio:
    AB/PQ = BC/QR = CA/RP. The ORDER of letters gives the correspondence A ↔ P,
    B ↔ Q, C ↔ R. All congruent triangles are similar (ratio 1); all equilateral
    triangles are similar.
  - BASIC PROPORTIONALITY THEOREM (BPT, Thales): a line parallel to one side of
    a triangle, cutting the other two sides at D and E, divides them in the same
    ratio: AD/DB = AE/EC. Also AD/AB = AE/AC = DE/BC (ΔADE ~ ΔABC). Proof: by
    areas of triangles with the same height.
  - CONVERSE of BPT: if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same
    ratio, it is parallel to the third side.
  - SIMILARITY CRITERIA. AAA (or AA): two pairs of equal angles (the third pair
    then follows from the angle sum). SSS: all three pairs of sides in the same
    ratio. SAS: one pair of equal angles and the sides INCLUDING those angles in
    the same ratio. (SSA is not a test.)
  - To match vertices: equal angles correspond; for SSS match smallest with
    smallest, middle with middle, largest with largest; the vertex shared by two
    matched sides corresponds.
  - Applications: heights from shadows (sun rays are parallel, so AA), lamp-post
    shadows, trapezium diagonals (AO/OC = BO/OD = AB/CD), and the altitude to
    the hypotenuse of a right triangle, which splits it into two triangles
    similar to the whole and to each other.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove the Basic Proportionality Theorem: if DE ∥ BC in ΔABC, with D on AB
    and E on AC, then AD/DB = AE/EC. Then find EC when AD = 2 cm, DB = 3 cm and
    AE = 3 cm.
                    A
                   / \
                  /   \
               D +-----+ E        DE ∥ BC
                /       \
               /         \
            B +-----------+ C
    Answer: Using areas: ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB and ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = AE/EC,
    while ar(BDE) = ar(DEC). EC = 4.5 cm.
    Teacher explains: Join BE and CD. Triangles with the SAME HEIGHT have areas
    in the ratio of their bases (topic 7.23).
       ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB     same height from E to AB
       ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = AE/EC     same height from D to AC
       ar(BDE) = ar(DEC)           same base DE, between DE ∥ BC
       so AD/DB = AE/EC            equal fractions with equal
                                   denominators
    Numbers: 2/3 = 3/EC, so 2 × EC = 9 and EC = 4.5 cm. Common mistake: writing
    AD/DB = AE/AC, mixing a PART-to-PART ratio with a part-to-WHOLE ratio. Both
    sides must be of the same kind. Now you try: AD = 2 cm, DB = 3 cm,
    AE = 4 cm. Find EC. (6 cm)

D2. State and prove the converse of the BPT. In ΔABC, D is on AB and E is on AC.
    Is DE ∥ BC when (a) AD = 3, DB = 4.5, AE = 4, EC = 6; (b) AD = 5, DB = 7,
    AE = 6, EC = 8 (all in cm)?
    Answer: If AD/DB = AE/EC then DE ∥ BC. (a) 3/4.5 = 2/3 = 4/6, so DE ∥ BC.
    (b) 5/7 ≠ 6/8, so DE is not parallel to BC.
    Teacher explains: Proof by contradiction: suppose AD/DB = AE/EC but DE is
    NOT parallel to BC. Draw DE′ ∥ BC with E′ on AC. By the BPT,
    AD/DB = AE′/E′C. So AE/EC = AE′/E′C. Add 1 to both sides:
    (AE + EC)/EC = (AE′ + E′C)/E′C, that is AC/EC = AC/E′C, so EC = E′C and
    E′ = E. Then DE is the parallel line after all: a contradiction.
       (a) AD/DB = 3/4.5 = 2/3      AE/EC = 4/6 = 2/3     equal: ∥
       (b) AD/DB = 5/7 ≈ 0.714      AE/EC = 6/8 = 0.75    not ∥
    Always SIMPLIFY or turn both ratios into decimals before comparing.
    Cross-multiplying also works: 3 × 6 = 18 = 4.5 × 4 in (a), but 5 × 8 = 40 ≠
    42 = 7 × 6 in (b). Now you try: AD = 1.5, DB = 3, AE = 1, EC = 2. Parallel?
    (yes, both ratios are 1/2)

D3. In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. If AD = x, DB = x − 2, AE = x + 2
    and EC = x − 1, find x.
    Answer: x = 4.
    Teacher explains:
       AD/DB = AE/EC                      BPT
       x/(x − 2) = (x + 2)/(x − 1)
       x(x − 1) = (x − 2)(x + 2)          cross-multiply
       x² − x = x² − 4
       −x = −4,   x = 4
    Check: AD = 4, DB = 2, AE = 6, EC = 3 and 4/2 = 2 = 6/3. The x² terms
    cancel, leaving a LINEAR equation. Always check that every length comes out
    POSITIVE; a value making a length negative or zero is rejected. Common
    mistake: cross-multiplying wrongly as x(x + 2) = (x − 2)(x − 1). Now you
    try: AD = 4, DB = x − 4, AE = 8, EC = 3x − 19. Find x. (x = 11)

D4. An A-frame ladder has legs AB = AC = 2.4 m and its feet B and C are 1.6 m
    apart. A crossbar DE, parallel to the floor, is fixed with AD = AE = 1.8 m.
    How long is the crossbar?
    Answer: DE = 1.2 m.
    Teacher explains: DE ∥ BC, so ΔADE ~ ΔABC (corresponding angles are equal:
    AA), and the ratio of the small triangle to the big one is AD/AB:
       DE/BC = AD/AB
       DE/1.6 = 1.8/2.4 = 3/4
       DE = 1.6 × 3/4 = 1.2 m
    Common mistake: using DE/BC = AD/DB = 1.8/0.6 = 3, which would make the
    crossbar longer than the floor gap! For the THIRD side we must compare with
    the WHOLE side: DE/BC = AD/AB. The BPT ratio AD/DB works only for the two
    cut sides. Now you try: AD = 2 cm, AB = 5 cm, BC = 7.5 cm, DE ∥ BC. Find DE.
    (3 cm)

D5. ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC, AB = 12 cm and DC = 8 cm. Its diagonals
    meet at O and AC = 15 cm. Prove that AO/OC = BO/OD and find AO and OC.
    Answer: ΔAOB ~ ΔCOD (AA), so AO/OC = BO/OD = AB/CD = 3/2; AO = 9 cm,
    OC = 6 cm.
    Teacher explains:
       Statement                  Reason
       ∠OAB = ∠OCD                alternate angles, AB ∥ DC
       ∠OBA = ∠ODC                alternate angles, AB ∥ DC
       ΔAOB ~ ΔCOD                AA
       AO/CO = BO/DO = AB/CD      corresponding sides
    AB/CD = 12/8 = 3/2, so AC is split in the ratio 3 : 2. AO = 3/5 × 15 = 9 cm
    and OC = 2/5 × 15 = 6 cm. Check: 9/6 = 3/2. (Another proof: draw OE ∥ AB
    through O meeting AD at E and use the BPT in ΔDAB and ΔADC.) Now you try:
    AB = 10 cm, DC = 5 cm, BD = 12 cm. Find BO. (8 cm)

D6. Explain why two pairs of equal angles are enough for similarity. In ΔABC,
    ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 70°; in ΔPQR, ∠P = 60° and ∠Q = 50°. Are the triangles
    similar? Write the correspondence and the equal ratios.
    Answer: Yes. ∠C = 60° and ∠R = 70°, so A ↔ Q, B ↔ R, C ↔ P: ΔABC ~ ΔQRP and
    AB/QR = BC/RP = CA/PQ.
    Teacher explains: If two angles match, the third angles match too, because
    each is 180° minus the other two. Triangles with equal angles have the same
    shape (the AAA criterion); so AA is enough.
       ΔABC: ∠A = 50°, ∠B = 70°, ∠C = 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°
       ΔPQR: ∠P = 60°, ∠Q = 50°, ∠R = 180° − 60° − 50° = 70°
       match equal angles: A ↔ Q (50°), B ↔ R (70°), C ↔ P (60°)
    So ΔABC ~ ΔQRP. Sides: AB ↔ QR, BC ↔ RP, CA ↔ PQ. Common mistake: writing
    ΔABC ~ ΔPQR just because the letters are in alphabetical order; that would
    pair A (50°) with P (60°). Now you try: ∠D = 35°, ∠E = 95° and ∠X = 95°,
    ∠Y = 50°. Correspondence? (ΔDEF ~ ΔZXY)

D7. ΔABC has AB = 4 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 8 cm and ΔPQR has PQ = 9 cm, QR = 12 cm,
    RP = 6 cm. Are they similar? If so, write the similarity with the vertices
    in the right order and the scale factor.
    Answer: Yes (SSS), ΔABC ~ ΔRPQ with scale factor 3/2.
    Teacher explains: Arrange each set of sides in order and divide:
       ΔABC:  AB = 4    BC = 6    CA = 8
       ΔPQR:  RP = 6    PQ = 9    QR = 12
       ratio: 6/4 = 1.5   9/6 = 1.5   12/8 = 1.5    all equal
    So the triangles are similar by SSS with scale factor 1.5 = 3/2. To name the
    vertices: AB ↔ RP and BC ↔ PQ share B and P, so B ↔ P; then A ↔ R and C ↔ Q.
    Write ΔABC ~ ΔRPQ. Common mistake: comparing sides in the order they happen
    to be listed (4 with 9, 6 with 12). Now you try: sides 3, 4, 6 and 4.5, 6,
    9. Similar? (yes, scale factor 1.5)

D8. In ΔPQR, S is on PQ and T is on PR with PS = 4 cm, PQ = 10 cm, PT = 6 cm and
    PR = 15 cm. Prove that ΔPST ~ ΔPQR and find ST if QR = 12.5 cm. Is ST ∥ QR?
    Answer: PS/PQ = PT/PR = 2/5 and ∠P is common, so ΔPST ~ ΔPQR (SAS);
    ST = 5 cm; yes, ST ∥ QR.
    Teacher explains:
       PS/PQ = 4/10 = 2/5,   PT/PR = 6/15 = 2/5
       ∠SPT = ∠QPR            common angle, INCLUDED between the sides
       ΔPST ~ ΔPQR            SAS similarity
       ST/QR = 2/5,  ST = 2/5 × 12.5 = 5 cm
    The equal angle must lie BETWEEN the two pairs of proportional sides. Here
    ∠P is between PS and PT, and between PQ and PR. From the similarity,
    ∠PST = ∠PQR, and these are corresponding angles, so ST ∥ QR (another route
    to the converse of the BPT). Common mistake: using an angle that is not
    included (SSA is not a test). Now you try: PS = 3, PQ = 9, PT = 4, PR = 12,
    QR = 15. Find ST. (5)

D9. A vertical pole 6 m high casts a shadow 4 m long on the ground. At the same
    time a tower casts a shadow 28 m long. How tall is the tower? Why are the
    triangles similar?
    Answer: 42 m. The sun's rays are parallel, so the angle of elevation of the
    sun is the same for both, and both triangles have a right angle: AA.
    Teacher explains:
       height/shadow is the same for both:
       h/28 = 6/4
       h = 28 × 6/4 = 42 m
    Each object, its shadow and the sun's ray form a right-angled triangle. The
    right angles are equal, and the angles at the tip of the shadow are equal
    because the rays are parallel. Two angles are equal, so the triangles are
    similar (AA) and corresponding sides are in proportion. Common mistake:
    setting height/shadow equal to shadow/height (upside down). Put the same
    kind of quantity on top on both sides. Now you try: a 1.5 m girl casts a 2 m
    shadow; a building casts a 40 m shadow. Height of the building? (30 m)

D10. A girl 90 cm tall walks away from the base of a lamp-post at 1.2 m/s. The
     lamp is 3.6 m above the ground. Find the length of her shadow after
     4 seconds.
     Answer: 1.6 m.
     Teacher explains:
        L  (lamp)
        |\
        |  \
        |    \  G (girl's head)
        |     |\
        +-----+--+
        B     D   S         BD = 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 m,  DS = x
     ΔSDG ~ ΔSBL (common angle at S and right angles at D and B: AA).
        GD/LB = DS/BS
        0.9/3.6 = x/(4.8 + x)
        3.6x = 0.9 × (4.8 + x) = 4.32 + 0.9x
        2.7x = 4.32,   x = 1.6 m
     Convert to the same unit first (90 cm = 0.9 m). The big triangle includes
     BOTH the distance walked and the shadow: BS = 4.8 + x. Common mistake:
     using BD = 4.8 as the base of the big triangle. Now you try: a boy 1.5 m
     tall stands 7 m from a 5 m lamp-post. Length of his shadow? (3 m)

D11. ΔABC is right-angled at A and AD ⟂ BC. Prove that ΔDBA ~ ΔABC and ΔDAC ~
     ΔABC. If BD = 9 cm and DC = 16 cm, find AB, AC and AD.
     Answer: AB = 15 cm, AC = 20 cm, AD = 12 cm.
     Teacher explains:
                  A
                 /|\
                / | \          ∠BAC = 90°, AD ⟂ BC
               /  |  \
             B ---D----- C
        ΔDBA and ΔABC:  ∠B common,  ∠BDA = ∠BAC = 90°   AA
        ΔDAC and ΔABC:  ∠C common,  ∠ADC = ∠BAC = 90°   AA
        so also ΔDBA ~ ΔDAC (both similar to ΔABC)
     From ΔDBA ~ ΔABC: BD/AB = AB/BC, so AB² = BD × BC = 9 × 25 = 225,
     AB = 15 cm. From ΔDAC ~ ΔABC: AC² = DC × BC = 16 × 25 = 400, AC = 20 cm.
     Area two ways: AB × AC = BC × AD, so AD = 15 × 20 ÷ 25 = 12 cm. Check:
     15² + 20² = 225 + 400 = 625 = 25². Now you try: BD = 1.8, DC = 3.2. Find
     AB. (3)

D12. Which pairs are ALWAYS similar: (a) two equilateral triangles, (b) two
     isosceles triangles, (c) two right-angled triangles, (d) two isosceles
     right-angled triangles, (e) two congruent triangles? Riya says: "In ΔABC
     and ΔPQR, ∠A = ∠Q and ∠B = ∠P, so ΔABC ~ ΔPQR." Is she right?
     Answer: (a) yes, (b) no, (c) no, (d) yes, (e) yes. Riya is wrong about the
     order: it is ΔABC ~ ΔQPR.
     Teacher explains: (a) All angles are 60°: AA. (b) One can have angles 80°,
     50°, 50° and another 20°, 80°, 80°: different shapes. (c) Angles 90°, 30°,
     60° and 90°, 45°, 45°: different. (d) Always 90°, 45°, 45°: AA. (e)
     Congruent means same shape AND size: similar with ratio 1.
     Riya found the right triangles to compare, but A matches Q and B matches P,
     so the statement must be ΔABC ~ ΔQPR. With her order she would write
     AB/PQ = BC/QR, which pairs the wrong sides and gives wrong lengths. The
     order of letters IS the correspondence. Now you try: ∠X = ∠N, ∠Y = ∠L.
     Complete ΔXYZ ~ Δ__. (ΔNLM)

M1. In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC, so AD/DB = AE/EC. Find the

    a) AD = 2, DB = 3, AE = 3: EC         b) AD = 2, DB = 3, AE = 4: EC

M3. D is on AB and E is on AC of ΔABC. Is DE ∥ BC? Compare the ratios in

    a) AD = 3, DB = 4.5, AE = 4, EC = 6

    e) AD = 6, DB = 9, AE = 4, EC = 7
    f) AD = 8, DB = 2, AE = 12, EC = 3
    g) AD = 4, DB = 4, AE = 5, EC = 5

             i) yes, AD/DB = AE/EC = 1/3   j) no, 5/2 ≠ 7/3
             k) yes, AD/AB = AE/AC = 1/4   l) no, 1/3 ≠ 3/8

M4. DE ∥ BC in ΔABC. Find x (reject any value that makes a length zero or
    negative) and give AD, DB, AE, EC.
    a) AD = x, DB = x − 2, AE = x + 2, EC = x − 1
    b) AD = 4, DB = x − 4, AE = 8, EC = 3x − 19

             c) x = 13 (10, 18, 5, 9)   d) x = 14 (19, 18, 38, 36)

             g) x = 14 (8, 12, 10, 15)   h) x = 5 (10, 9, 10, 9)

M12. True or false? Correct the false ones.
     a) All equilateral triangles are similar.
     b) All isosceles triangles are similar.
     c) All right-angled triangles are similar.
     d) All congruent triangles are similar.
     e) All similar triangles are congruent.
     f) If DE ∥ BC in ΔABC, then AD/DB = AE/EC.
     g) If DE ∥ BC in ΔABC, then DE/BC = AD/DB.
     h) If AD/DB = AE/EC, then DE ∥ BC.
     i) Two triangles with two pairs of equal angles are similar.
     j) Two triangles with sides 3, 4, 5 and 6, 8, 10 are similar.
     k) Two sides in proportion and any one pair of equal angles prove
        similarity.
     l) If ΔABC ~ ΔPQR, then AB/PQ = BC/QR = CA/RP.
     m) If ΔABC ~ ΔQRP, then ∠A = ∠P.
     n) All squares are similar.
     o) All rhombuses are similar.
     p) The altitude to the hypotenuse divides a right triangle into two
        triangles similar to it.
     Answers: a) true   b) false   c) false   d) true
              e) false (only if the ratio is 1)   f) true
              g) false (DE/BC = AD/AB)   h) true   i) true   j) true
              k) false (the angle must be included)   l) true
              m) false (∠A = ∠Q)   n) true   o) false (angles can differ)
              p) true

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the small and the big triangle SEPARATELY, the same way up,
  and colour matching angles the same colour before writing any ratio; write the
  ratio as "small over big" for every pair; for SSS sort both sets of sides from
  shortest to longest; for BPT say "part over part, or part over whole, never
  mixed"; measure real shadows at school with a metre stick. Harder: prove the
  angle bisector theorem (the bisector of ∠A divides BC in the ratio AB : AC)
  using the BPT; prove that the line joining the midpoints of two sides is
  parallel to the third and half of it; show that in the trapezium figure the
  line through O parallel to AB has length 2 × AB × DC/(AB + DC); and use
  similar triangles to find the height of a tree with a mirror on the ground.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.27 — AREAS OF SIMILAR TRIANGLES; PYTHAGORAS VIA SIMILARITY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - THEOREM: the ratio of the areas of two similar triangles equals the SQUARE
    of the ratio of their corresponding sides. If ΔABC ~ ΔPQR with AB/PQ = k,
    then ar(ABC)/ar(PQR) = k². Proof: the altitudes are in the same ratio k, and
    area = 1/2 × base × height.
  - All corresponding LENGTHS (sides, altitudes, medians, angle bisectors,
    perimeters) are in the ratio k; AREAS are in the ratio k². Going back: side
    ratio = √(area ratio).
  - Special cases: the triangle joining the midpoints of the sides has 1/4 of
    the area; if DE ∥ BC and AD : DB = m : n, then ar(ADE) : ar(ABC) = m² :
    (m + n)²; in a trapezium with AB = k × CD, ar(AOB) : ar(COD) = k² : 1.
  - In a right triangle ABC with ∠A = 90° and AD ⟂ BC, the three triangles are
    similar, so AB² = BD × BC, AC² = DC × BC and AD² = BD × DC.
  - PYTHAGORAS BY SIMILARITY: adding AB² = BD × BC and AC² = DC × BC gives
    AB² + AC² = BC × (BD + DC) = BC². CONVERSE: if the square of one side equals
    the sum of the squares of the other two, the angle opposite the first side
    is a right angle (proof by constructing a right triangle and using SSS).
  - Applications: ladders, poles, distances travelled at right angles, the
    rhombus (sum of the squares of the sides = sum of the squares of the
    diagonals), and the equilateral triangle (altitude² = 3/4 × side²).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that the ratio of the areas of two similar triangles is equal to the
    square of the ratio of their corresponding sides.
    Answer: If ΔABC ~ ΔPQR, then
    ar(ABC)/ar(PQR) = (AB/PQ)² = (BC/QR)² = (CA/RP)².
    Teacher explains:
                A                          P
               /|\                        /|\
              / | \                      / | \
             /  |  \                    /  |  \
            B---M---C                  Q---N---R
            AM ⟂ BC                    PN ⟂ QR
       ar(ABC)/ar(PQR) = (1/2 × BC × AM)/(1/2 × QR × PN)
                       = (BC/QR) × (AM/PN)                (1)
       ΔABM ~ ΔPQN: ∠B = ∠Q (given), ∠M = ∠N = 90°      AA
       so AM/PN = AB/PQ = BC/QR                         (2)
       (1) and (2): ar(ABC)/ar(PQR) = (BC/QR) × (BC/QR) = (BC/QR)²
    The area has TWO lengths multiplied (base and height), and both are scaled
    by k, so the area is scaled by k × k = k². Common mistake: saying the areas
    are in the same ratio as the sides. Doubling every side makes the area FOUR
    times as big. Now you try: sides in the ratio 2 : 3. Ratio of the areas? (4
    : 9)

D2. ΔABC ~ ΔDEF, ar(ABC) = 64 cm² and ar(DEF) = 121 cm². If EF = 15.4 cm, find
    BC.
    Answer: BC = 11.2 cm.
    Teacher explains:
       (BC/EF)² = ar(ABC)/ar(DEF) = 64/121
       BC/EF = √(64/121) = 8/11
       BC = 15.4 × 8/11 = 1.4 × 8 = 11.2 cm
    Two steps: first take the SQUARE ROOT of the area ratio to get the side
    ratio, then scale. Check: the smaller area goes with the smaller side (64 <
    121 and 11.2 < 15.4). Common mistake: using 64/121 directly as the side
    ratio, which would give BC ≈ 8.1 cm. Now you try: ar(ABC) = 16 cm²,
    ar(PQR) = 25 cm², QR = 10 cm. Find BC. (8 cm)

D3. D, E, F are the midpoints of the sides BC, CA, AB of ΔABC. Find the ratio of
    the areas of ΔDEF and ΔABC.
    Answer: 1 : 4.
    Teacher explains: By the midpoint theorem each side of ΔDEF is half of a
    side of ΔABC: EF = 1/2 BC, FD = 1/2 CA, DE = 1/2 AB.
       EF/BC = FD/CA = DE/AB = 1/2    so ΔDEF ~ ΔABC (SSS)
       ar(DEF)/ar(ABC) = (1/2)² = 1/4
    Picture: the three midpoints cut ΔABC into FOUR congruent triangles (each
    similar to ΔABC with ratio 1/2), and ΔDEF is one of them. The similarity
    theorem and the picture agree. Common mistake: answering 1 : 2 because the
    sides are halved. Now you try: ar(ABC) = 60 cm². Find ar(DEF). (15 cm²)

D4. In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB, E on AC and AD : DB = 2 : 3. Find ar(ADE) :
    ar(ABC) and ar(ADE) : ar(DECB). If ar(ABC) = 75 cm², find ar(ADE) and the
    area of the trapezium DECB.
    Answer: 4 : 25 and 4 : 21; ar(ADE) = 12 cm², ar(DECB) = 63 cm².
    Teacher explains: DE ∥ BC gives ΔADE ~ ΔABC. The ratio of sides is AD/AB,
    NOT AD/DB:
       AD/AB = 2/(2 + 3) = 2/5
       ar(ADE)/ar(ABC) = (2/5)² = 4/25,  that is 4 : 25
       ar(DECB) = 25 − 4 = 21 parts,  so ar(ADE) : ar(DECB) = 4 : 21
       ar(ADE) = 4/25 × 75 = 12 cm²,  ar(DECB) = 75 − 12 = 63 cm²
    Common mistake: squaring 2 : 3 to get 4 : 9. The two triangles are ADE and
    ABC, whose corresponding sides are AD and AB. Now you try: AD : DB = 1 : 2.
    Find ar(ADE) : ar(ABC). (1 : 9)

D5. ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC and AB = 2 CD. The diagonals meet at O.
    Find ar(AOB) : ar(COD). If ar(COD) = 9 cm², find the areas of the other
    three triangles and of the trapezium.
    Answer: 4 : 1; ar(AOB) = 36 cm², ar(AOD) = ar(BOC) = 18 cm², trapezium
    81 cm².
    Teacher explains:
       ΔAOB ~ ΔCOD (AA, alternate angles), ratio AB/CD = 2
       ar(AOB)/ar(COD) = 2² = 4,  ar(AOB) = 4 × 9 = 36 cm²
       AO/OC = 2, and ΔAOD, ΔCOD have the same height from D:
       ar(AOD)/ar(COD) = AO/OC = 2,  ar(AOD) = 18 cm²
       ar(BOC) = ar(AOD) = 18 cm²     (topic 7.23)
       trapezium = 36 + 18 + 18 + 9 = 81 cm²
    Two different tools: SIMILAR triangles (AOB and COD) give the ratio k² = 4;
    triangles with the SAME HEIGHT (AOD and COD) give the ratio of bases k = 2.
    Pattern: ar(AOB) : ar(AOD) : ar(COD) = k² : k : 1. Now you try: AB = 3 CD
    and ar(COD) = 5 cm². Find ar(AOB). (45 cm²)

D6. The areas of two similar triangles are 25 cm² and 36 cm². The altitude of
    the first is 4 cm. Find the corresponding altitude of the second, and the
    ratio of their perimeters and of their medians.
    Answer: Altitude 4.8 cm; perimeters 5 : 6; medians 5 : 6.
    Teacher explains:
       side ratio k = √(25/36) = 5/6
       altitude: 4 ÷ (5/6) = 4 × 6/5 = 4.8 cm
    Every LENGTH in similar triangles is in the ratio k: altitudes (shown in D1
    by ΔABM ~ ΔPQN), perimeters (add three sides, each multiplied by k), and
    medians. For medians AD and PM: AB/PQ = BC/QR gives AB/PQ = BD/QM (halves),
    and ∠B = ∠Q, so ΔABD ~ ΔPQM (SAS) and AD/PM = AB/PQ = k.
    Only AREAS use k². Common mistake: writing the altitude ratio as 25 : 36.
    Now you try: areas 81 cm² and 49 cm². Ratio of the medians? (9 : 7)

D7. Prove Pythagoras' theorem using similar triangles: in ΔABC with ∠A = 90°,
    BC² = AB² + AC².
    Answer: Draw AD ⟂ BC. ΔDBA ~ ΔABC gives AB² = BD × BC; ΔDAC ~ ΔABC gives
    AC² = DC × BC. Adding: AB² + AC² = BC × (BD + DC) = BC².
    Teacher explains:
                 A
                /|\
               / | \
              /  |  \
            B ---D---- C        ∠BAC = 90°, AD ⟂ BC
       ΔDBA ~ ΔABC   (∠B common, ∠BDA = ∠BAC = 90°)
       BD/AB = AB/BC       so AB² = BD × BC
       ΔDAC ~ ΔABC   (∠C common, ∠CDA = ∠CAB = 90°)
       DC/AC = AC/BC       so AC² = DC × BC
       AB² + AC² = BD × BC + DC × BC = BC × (BD + DC) = BC × BC
    This proof uses only similar triangles, not area rearrangements. It also
    gives useful extra formulas for the altitude figure. Now you try: BD = 4 cm
    and DC = 5 cm. Find AB. (6 cm, since AB² = 4 × 9 = 36)

D8. Prove the converse of Pythagoras' theorem. Is a triangle with sides 7 cm,
    24 cm and 25 cm right-angled? At which vertex?
    Answer: Yes: 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². The right angle is opposite
    the 25 cm side.
    Teacher explains: Suppose in ΔABC, AC² = AB² + BC². Construct ΔPQR with
    ∠Q = 90°, PQ = AB and QR = BC.
       PR² = PQ² + QR²       Pythagoras in ΔPQR
           = AB² + BC² = AC²     so PR = AC
       ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR           SSS (AB = PQ, BC = QR, AC = PR)
       ∠B = ∠Q = 90°         CPCT
    To test a triangle, square the LONGEST side and compare with the sum of the
    squares of the other two: equal means right-angled, and the right angle is
    OPPOSITE the longest side. Common mistake: adding the wrong pair of squares.
    Now you try: sides 9, 40, 41. Right-angled? (yes: 81 + 1600 = 1681 = 41²)

D9. A 10 m ladder reaches a window 8 m above the ground. How far is its foot
    from the wall? Two vertical poles 6 m and 11 m high stand 12 m apart on
    level ground. How far apart are their tops?
    Answer: 6 m; 13 m.
    Teacher explains:
       ladder: foot² = 10² − 8² = 100 − 64 = 36,  foot = 6 m
       poles: difference in height = 11 − 6 = 5 m
              distance² = 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169,  distance = 13 m
    For the poles, draw a horizontal line from the top of the short pole to the
    tall pole: it makes a right triangle with legs 12 m (the gap) and 5 m (the
    DIFFERENCE of heights). Common mistake: using 11 m or 6 m as a leg. Always
    draw the right triangle first and label its hypotenuse. Now you try: a 13 m
    ladder with its foot 5 m from the wall. Height reached? (12 m)

D10. In ΔABC, ∠A = 90° and AD ⟂ BC. Prove that AD² = BD × DC. A semicircular
     arch has a diameter of 10 m. How high is the arch at a point 3 m from one
     end of the diameter?
     Answer: ΔDBA ~ ΔDAC gives BD/AD = AD/DC; the height is √21 ≈ 4.58 m.
     Teacher explains:
        ΔDBA ~ ΔDAC    (both are similar to ΔABC)
        ∠DBA = ∠DAC,  ∠BDA = ∠ADC = 90°
        BD/DA = DA/DC   so AD² = BD × DC
     The arch: take the diameter as BC and the top point of the arch as A. The
     angle in a semicircle is 90°, so ∠BAC = 90° and the vertical height AD
     satisfies AD² = BD × DC = 3 × 7 = 21, AD = √21 ≈ 4.58 m. Check at the
     middle: 5 × 5 = 25, height 5 m = the radius. Correct. Now you try:
     BD = 2 cm, DC = 8 cm. Find AD. (4 cm)

D11. Prove that the area of the equilateral triangle drawn on a side of a square
     is half the area of the equilateral triangle drawn on its diagonal. Also
     show that in an equilateral triangle ABC with altitude AD, 3AB² = 4AD².
     Answer: All equilateral triangles are similar, and diagonal = side × √2, so
     the ratio of areas is 1 : 2, since (√2)² = 2. AD² = AB² − (AB/2)² = 3/4
     AB².
     Teacher explains:
        square of side a:  diagonal² = a² + a² = 2a²
        area ratio = (side of small)² : (side of big)² = a² : 2a²
                   = 1 : 2
     We never needed the actual areas: similar figures, ratio of the squares of
     the sides. For the altitude: D is the midpoint of BC, so BD = AB/2 and
     AD² = AB² − AB²/4 = 3/4 AB², that is 4AD² = 3AB². So the altitude of an
     equilateral triangle of side a is (√3/2) a. Now you try: side 6 cm.
     Altitude? (3√3 ≈ 5.20 cm)

D12. Two aeroplanes leave an airport at the same time, one flying north at
     1000 km/h and the other west at 1200 km/h. How far apart are they after
     1.5 hours? A rhombus has diagonals 16 cm and 30 cm; find its side and show
     that the sum of the squares of the sides equals the sum of the squares of
     the diagonals.
     Answer: 300√61 ≈ 2343.1 km; side 17 cm, and 4 × 17² = 1156 = 16² + 30².
     Teacher explains:
        north: 1000 × 1.5 = 1500 km,   west: 1200 × 1.5 = 1800 km
        distance² = 1500² + 1800² = 2,250,000 + 3,240,000 = 5,490,000
        distance = √5,490,000 = 300√61 ≈ 2343.1 km
     North and west are at right angles, so the two paths are the legs of a
     right triangle. Tip: take out the common factor 300 first: 1500 = 300 × 5,
     1800 = 300 × 6, and √(25 + 36) = √61.
     Rhombus: the diagonals bisect each other at right angles, giving four right
     triangles with legs 8 and 15: side² = 64 + 225 = 289, side = 17 cm. Sum of
     squares of sides 4 × 289 = 1156; of diagonals 256 + 900 = 1156. Equal. Now
     you try: rhombus with diagonals 10 cm and 24 cm. Side? (13 cm)
