M12. True or false? Correct the false ones.
     a) The ratio of the areas of similar triangles equals the ratio of their
        sides.
     b) If the sides are doubled, the area is doubled.
     c) The ratio of the perimeters of similar triangles equals the ratio of
        their sides.
     d) The ratio of the medians of similar triangles equals the square root of
        the ratio of their areas.
     e) If the areas of two similar triangles are equal, the triangles are
        congruent.
     f) The midpoint triangle has half the area of the triangle.
     g) In a right triangle with ∠A = 90° and AD ⟂ BC, AD² = BD × DC.
     h) In the same figure, AB² = BD × DC.
     i) Sides 6, 8, 10 form a right-angled triangle.
     j) Sides 5, 6, 7 form a right-angled triangle.
     k) The right angle is opposite the longest side.
     l) If AB² + BC² = AC², then ∠A = 90°.
     m) For a rhombus, the sum of the squares of the sides equals the sum of the
        squares of the diagonals.
     n) The altitude of an equilateral triangle of side a is a√3/2.
     o) If ar(ADE) : ar(ABC) = 1 : 4 with DE ∥ BC, then D is the midpoint of AB.
     p) If AD : DB = 1 : 2 and DE ∥ BC, then ar(ADE) : ar(ABC) = 1 : 4.
     Answers: a) false (the square of the ratio)
              b) false (it is multiplied by 4)   c) true   d) true   e) true
              f) false (one quarter)   g) true   h) false (AB² = BD × BC)
              i) true   j) false (25 + 36 = 61 ≠ 49)   k) true
              l) false (∠B = 90°)   m) true   n) true   o) true
              p) false (1 : 9)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw a triangle on squared paper and its enlargement with sides
  doubled, then count squares to SEE the area become 4 times; keep the rule
  "lengths k, areas k²" on the board; always write the side ratio first and
  square it last (or square-root the area ratio first); for DE ∥ BC write AD :
  AB before squaring; label the hypotenuse before any Pythagoras calculation.
  Harder: prove that the ratio of the areas equals the square of the ratio of
  the angle bisectors; prove that in any triangle with AD ⟂ BC and BD = 3CD,
  2AB² = 2AC² + BC²; prove Apollonius' theorem AB² + AC² = 2AD² + 2BD² for the
  median AD; and find the ratio in which a line parallel to the base must cut a
  triangle to halve its area (AD : AB = 1 : √2, that is AD : DB = 1 : (√2 − 1)).


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.28 — CONSTRUCTIONS: DIVIDING A SEGMENT, TANGENTS, SIMILAR TRIANGLES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Constructions use only an unmarked ruler and compasses (a ruler is used for
    measuring given lengths). Every construction needs STEPS and a JUSTIFICATION
    (why it works), usually by the BPT, similar triangles, the angle in a
    semicircle or the tangent-radius theorem.
  - DIVIDING AB INTERNALLY IN THE RATIO m : n. Draw a ray AX making an acute
    angle with AB; with the same compass width mark m + n points A₁, A₂, ... on
    it; join the last point to B; through Aₘ draw a line parallel to it, cutting
    AB at P. Then AP : PB = m : n (BPT). Other method: draw parallel rays AX and
    BY on opposite sides, mark m points on AX and n on BY, join Aₘ to Bₙ
    (similar triangles).
  - A TRIANGLE SIMILAR TO ΔABC WITH SCALE FACTOR m/n. On a ray BX below BC mark
    the larger of m and n points; join Bₙ to C; through Bₘ draw a line parallel
    to BnC to meet BC (or BC extended) at C′; through C′ draw a line parallel to
    CA to meet BA (or BA extended) at A′. Then ΔA′BC′ ~ ΔABC with ratio m/n
    (smaller if m < n, larger if m > n).
  - TANGENT AT A POINT P OF A CIRCLE: draw the radius OP and the line through P
    perpendicular to OP.
  - TANGENTS FROM AN EXTERNAL POINT P: bisect OP at M; draw the circle with
    centre M and radius MO; it cuts the given circle at Q and R; PQ and PR are
    the tangents, because ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90° (angles in a semicircle). Their
    length is √(OP² − r²). If the centre is unknown, find it first as the
    meeting point of the perpendicular bisectors of two chords.
  - A PAIR OF TANGENTS INCLINED AT AN ANGLE θ: draw two radii OA and OB with
    ∠AOB = 180° − θ, and draw perpendiculars to them at A and B; they meet at P
    with ∠APB = θ.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Divide a line segment AB of length 7.6 cm internally in the ratio 5 : 8.
    Write the steps, justify the construction and find the two lengths.
    Answer: AP = 7.6 × 5/13 ≈ 2.92 cm and PB = 7.6 × 8/13 ≈ 4.68 cm.
    Teacher explains:
       Steps of construction
       1. Draw AB = 7.6 cm.
       2. Draw a ray AX making an acute angle with AB.
       3. With one compass width mark 5 + 8 = 13 points A₁, ..., A₁₃
          on AX, so that AA₁ = A₁A₂ = ... = A₁₂A₁₃.
       4. Join A₁₃B.
       5. Through A₅ draw a line parallel to A₁₃B (copy the angle at
          A₁₃), meeting AB at P.  Then AP : PB = 5 : 8.
    Justification: in ΔAA₁₃B, A₅P ∥ A₁₃B, so by the BPT AP/PB = AA₅/A₅A₁₃ = 5/8,
    because AA₅ is 5 equal steps and A₅A₁₃ is 8 steps. Measuring would give the
    same answer only approximately; the construction is exact. The lengths:
    7.6 × 5 ÷ 13 = 38/13 ≈ 2.92 cm and 7.6 − 2.92 = 4.68 cm (check:
    7.6 × 8/13 ≈ 4.68). Common mistake: marking only 8 points, or drawing the
    parallel through A₈ (that gives 8 : 5). Now you try: to divide AB in the
    ratio 3 : 7, how many points are marked and through which point is the
    parallel drawn? (10 points; through A₃)

D2. Describe a second way to divide AB = 10 cm in the ratio 3 : 2 using two
    parallel rays, and justify it.
    Answer: AP = 6 cm, PB = 4 cm.
    Teacher explains:
       1. Draw a ray AX making an acute angle ∠BAX with AB.
       2. Draw a ray BY on the other side of AB with ∠ABY = ∠BAX,
          so that AX ∥ BY (alternate angles).
       3. Mark A₁, A₂, A₃ on AX and B₁, B₂ on BY, all steps equal.
       4. Join A₃B₂; it cuts AB at P.  Then AP : PB = 3 : 2.
    Justification: ∠PAA₃ = ∠PBB₂ (alternate angles, AX ∥ BY) and ∠APA₃ = ∠BPB₂
    (vertically opposite), so ΔAPA₃ ~ ΔBPB₂ (AA). Hence AP/BP = AA₃/BB₂ = 3/2.
    Lengths: 10 × 3/5 = 6 cm and 10 × 2/5 = 4 cm. This method needs only m
    points on one ray and n on the other, and no parallel line through a marked
    point. Common mistake: putting both rays on the SAME side of AB (they would
    not give crossing lines). Now you try: in this method for 4 : 5, how many
    points on each ray? (4 on AX, 5 on BY; join A₄B₅)

D3. Divide a segment of 12 cm into 5 equal parts, and explain why the
    construction is better than measuring when a segment of 10 cm is to be
    divided into 3 equal parts.
    Answer: 12 cm: each part 2.4 cm. 10 cm: each part is 3 1/3 cm, which a ruler
    cannot mark exactly, but the construction can.
    Teacher explains: Mark 5 equal steps A₁ to A₅ on a ray AX, join A₅B and draw
    lines through A₁, A₂, A₃, A₄ parallel to A₅B. They cut AB into 5 equal
    parts, each 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4 cm. Why equal? By the BPT (repeatedly) the parallel
    lines cut AB in the same proportions as they cut AX, where the steps are
    equal.
    For 10 cm into 3 parts: 10 ÷ 3 = 3 1/3 cm, a recurring decimal. The ruler
    can only give an approximation (3.3 cm leaves 0.1 cm over), but the
    construction divides the segment EXACTLY, because it never uses the decimal
    at all. This is the power of geometry over measurement. Now you try: a
    segment of 9 cm into 4 equal parts. Length of each? (2.25 cm)

D4. Construct a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm, and then a triangle
    similar to it whose sides are 3/4 of the corresponding sides of the first.
    Find the new sides.
    Answer: New sides 3.75 cm, 4.5 cm and 5.25 cm.
    Teacher explains:
       1. Construct ΔABC with BC = 6 cm, AB = 5 cm, AC = 7 cm.
       2. Draw a ray BX making an acute angle with BC, on the side
          opposite to A.
       3. Mark 4 points B₁, B₂, B₃, B₄ on BX (4 = the larger of 3
          and 4), with BB₁ = B₁B₂ = B₂B₃ = B₃B₄.
       4. Join B₄C.
       5. Through B₃ draw a line parallel to B₄C meeting BC at C′.
       6. Through C′ draw a line parallel to CA meeting BA at A′.
       ΔA′BC′ is the required triangle.
    Justification: B₃C′ ∥ B₄C gives BC′/BC = BB₃/BB₄ = 3/4 (BPT). C′A′ ∥ CA
    gives ΔA′BC′ ~ ΔABC (AA), so every side is 3/4 of the original:
    5 × 3/4 = 3.75 cm, 6 × 3/4 = 4.5 cm, 7 × 3/4 = 5.25 cm. Common mistake:
    joining B₃C and drawing the parallel through B₄, which gives 4/3 (an
    enlargement). Now you try: scale factor 2/3 for sides 6, 9, 12 cm. New
    sides? (4, 6, 8 cm)

D5. Construct a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm, and a triangle similar
    to it with scale factor 5/3. What changes in the construction when the scale
    factor is greater than 1?
    Answer: New sides 6 2/3 ≈ 6.67 cm, 8 1/3 ≈ 8.33 cm and 10 cm. The parallel
    lines now meet BC and BA EXTENDED beyond C and A.
    Teacher explains:
       1. Construct ΔABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 4 cm, AC = 6 cm.
       2. Draw a ray BX below BC; mark 5 equal steps B₁, ..., B₅
          (5 = the larger of 5 and 3).
       3. Join B₃C (the DENOMINATOR point).
       4. Through B₅ (the NUMERATOR point) draw a line parallel to
          B₃C, meeting BC produced at C′.
       5. Through C′ draw a line parallel to CA, meeting BA
          produced at A′.  ΔA′BC′ ~ ΔABC with ratio 5/3.
    Justification: BC′/BC = BB₅/BB₃ = 5/3 (BPT in ΔBB₅C′), and C′A′ ∥ CA makes
    the triangles similar (AA). New sides: 4 × 5/3 = 20/3 = 6 2/3,
    5 × 5/3 = 25/3 = 8 1/3 and 6 × 5/3 = 10 cm. Rule for any scale factor m/n:
    mark max(m, n) points, JOIN Bₙ to C, draw the PARALLEL through Bₘ. Now you
    try: scale factor 7/5. Which point is joined to C, and through which is the
    parallel drawn? (B₅; B₇)

D6. An isosceles triangle has base 8 cm and altitude 4 cm. Construct a triangle
    similar to it with scale factor 1 1/2. Find the base, altitude, equal sides
    and area of both triangles.
    Answer: Original: base 8, altitude 4, equal sides 4√2 ≈ 5.66 cm, area
    16 cm². New: base 12, altitude 6, equal sides 6√2 ≈ 8.49 cm, area 36 cm².
    Teacher explains: Construct the original: draw BC = 8 cm, its perpendicular
    bisector, mark A on it 4 cm from BC, and join AB and AC. Each equal side is
    √(4² + 4²) = √32 = 4√2 ≈ 5.66 cm.
    Scale factor 1 1/2 = 3/2: mark 3 points on BX, join B₂C, draw the parallel
    through B₃ to meet BC produced at C′, then the parallel to CA through C′.
    Every length is multiplied by 3/2:
       base 8 × 3/2 = 12 cm,  altitude 4 × 3/2 = 6 cm
       equal sides 4√2 × 3/2 = 6√2 ≈ 8.49 cm
       area 1/2 × 12 × 6 = 36 cm² = 16 × (3/2)² = 16 × 9/4
    Lengths scale by k, areas by k² (topic 7.27). Common mistake: writing 1 1/2
    as 1/2 or 11/2. Change it to an improper fraction first. Now you try: scale
    factor 1/2 for the same triangle. New base and altitude? (4 cm and 2 cm)

D7. Draw a circle of radius 4 cm and take a point P on it. Construct the tangent
    at P (a) using the centre, (b) without using the centre.
    Answer: (a) Draw OP and the perpendicular to OP at P. (b) Draw a chord PQ,
    take R on the major arc, and make ∠QPT = ∠PRQ on the other side of PQ; PT is
    the tangent.
    Teacher explains:
       (a) 1. Join OP.
           2. Construct the line through P perpendicular to OP
              (e.g. extend OP to S with PS = OP and draw the
              perpendicular bisector of OS).
       (b) 1. Draw any chord PQ and join PR, RQ for R on the major
              arc.
           2. At P construct ∠QPT = ∠PRQ, with T on the side of PQ
              away from R.
    Justification: (a) a line perpendicular to a radius at its outer end is a
    tangent (converse of the tangent-radius theorem). (b) by the converse of the
    alternate segment theorem, a line through P making with the chord an angle
    equal to the angle in the alternate segment is the tangent. Method (b) is
    useful when the centre is not marked. Common mistake: drawing the
    perpendicular to the CHORD instead of the radius. Now you try: what angle
    does the tangent at P make with the radius OP? (90°)

D8. Draw a circle of radius 6 cm and a point P 10 cm from its centre O.
    Construct the pair of tangents from P, justify the construction and find
    their length.
    Answer: Each tangent is 8 cm long.
    Teacher explains:
       1. Draw the circle, centre O, radius 6 cm, and mark P with
          OP = 10 cm.
       2. Bisect OP (perpendicular bisector); let M be its midpoint.
       3. With centre M and radius MO = 5 cm draw a circle; it cuts
          the given circle at Q and R.
       4. Join PQ and PR: these are the required tangents.
    Justification: OP is a diameter of the circle through Q centred at M, so
    ∠OQP = 90° (angle in a semicircle). A line PQ perpendicular to the radius OQ
    at Q is a tangent. The same holds for R. Length:
    PQ² = OP² − OQ² = 10² − 6² = 100 − 36 = 64, PQ = 8 cm; measure to check the
    construction. Common mistake: drawing the auxiliary circle with centre O or
    P instead of the MIDPOINT M. Now you try: radius 5 cm, OP = 13 cm. Tangent
    length? (12 cm)

D9. A circle has been drawn with a bangle, so its centre is not known. P is a
    point outside it. How can you construct the tangents from P?
    Answer: Find the centre first: draw two non-parallel chords, construct their
    perpendicular bisectors; they meet at the centre O. Then construct the
    tangents from P as usual.
    Teacher explains: The perpendicular bisector of every chord passes through
    the centre (topic 7.24). Two such bisectors that are not parallel meet at
    ONE point, which must be the centre O. After that: bisect OP at M, draw the
    circle on OP as diameter, and join P to the two points where it cuts the
    bangle circle.
       chord 1 → perpendicular bisector 1  \
                                            > meet at the centre O
       chord 2 → perpendicular bisector 2  /
    Common mistake: using two PARALLEL chords; their bisectors are the same line
    and do not fix the centre. Choose chords at a good angle to each other for
    accuracy. Now you try: what is the least number of chords needed to find the
    centre? (2)

D10. Draw a pair of tangents to a circle of radius 5 cm which are inclined to
     each other at an angle of 60°. Find the length of each tangent and the
     distance of their meeting point from the centre.
     Answer: Radii at 120°; tangent length 5√3 ≈ 8.66 cm; OP = 10 cm.
     Teacher explains:
        1. Draw the circle and a radius OA.
        2. Draw OB with ∠AOB = 180° − 60° = 120°.
        3. Draw lines perpendicular to OA at A and to OB at B;
           they meet at P.  PA and PB are the tangents, ∠APB = 60°.
     Justification: in quadrilateral OAPB, ∠A = ∠B = 90°, so
     ∠APB = 360° − 90° − 90° − 120° = 60°. Lengths: OP bisects ∠APB, so
     ∠OPA = 30° and ΔOAP is a 30-60-90 triangle with OA = 5 opposite the 30°
     angle: OP = 2 × 5 = 10 cm and PA = √(10² − 5²) = √75 = 5√3 ≈ 8.66 cm.
     Common mistake: drawing the radii at 60° (that gives tangents at 120°). Now
     you try: tangents inclined at 90°. Angle between the radii, and the length
     of each tangent for radius 5 cm? (90°; 5 cm, since OAPB is a square)

D11. Draw two concentric circles of radii 4 cm and 6 cm. Construct a tangent to
     the smaller circle from a point on the larger circle, and find its length.
     Answer: √20 = 2√5 ≈ 4.47 cm.
     Teacher explains:
        1. Draw both circles with centre O; mark P on the larger one.
        2. Bisect OP at M (OP = 6 cm, so MO = 3 cm).
        3. Draw the circle with centre M and radius 3 cm, cutting the
           smaller circle at Q and R.
        4. PQ and PR are the tangents to the smaller circle.
     Length: ∠OQP = 90° (semicircle), so
     PQ² = OP² − OQ² = 6² − 4² = 36 − 16 = 20 and PQ = √20 = 2√5 ≈ 4.47 cm. The
     larger circle only supplies the point P; the tangent is to the SMALLER
     circle, so the radius in Pythagoras is 4 cm. Now you try: radii 3 cm and
     5 cm. Tangent length from the outer circle? (4 cm)

D12. Spot the mistake. (a) To divide AB in the ratio 3 : 4, Sam marked 7 points
     on AX, joined A₇B and drew the parallel through A₄. (b) For a triangle
     similar to ΔABC with scale factor 7/5, Nita marked 5 points on BX. (c) Ravi
     marked the points on AX with a different compass width each time.
     Answer: (a) He gets 4 : 3; the parallel must go through A₃. (b) She needs 7
     points (the larger of 7 and 5); join B₅C and draw the parallel through B₇.
     (c) The steps must be EQUAL, otherwise the ratio is wrong.
     Teacher explains: (a) The parallel through Aₖ cuts off AP : PB = k :
     (7 − k). With k = 4 the ratio is 4 : 3, the reverse. The first number of
     the ratio tells which point: A₃.
     (b) A scale factor 7/5 > 1 needs the point B₇ to exist. Mark 7 points, join
     the DENOMINATOR point B₅ to C, and draw the parallel through the NUMERATOR
     point B₇; C′ lies on BC produced.
     (c) The BPT gives AP/PB = AAₘ/AₘA₇; this equals m/n only when all the steps
     are equal. Keep the compass width fixed.
        check list:  equal steps  |  join the LAST point to B
                     parallel through the m-th point  |  measure
     Always measure the final result as a check. Now you try: for a scale factor
     2/7, how many points are marked on BX? (7)

M7. Tangents are constructed from P to a circle of radius r, with OP = d. Find
    the radius of the auxiliary circle drawn on OP as diameter, and the tangent
    length (cm; surds exact and to 2 decimal places).
    a) r = 6, d = 10      b) r = 5, d = 13
    c) r = 3, d = 5       d) r = 8, d = 17
    e) r = 7, d = 25      f) r = 4, d = 6
    g) r = 3, d = 8       h) r = 5, d = 9
    i) r = 2.5, d = 6.5   j) r = 6, d = 7.5
    k) r = 4, d = 5       l) r = 1.5, d = 4
    m) r = 9, d = 15      n) r = 2, d = 3
    o) r = 12, d = 13     p) r = 10, d = 26
    Answers: a) 5; 8   b) 6.5; 12   c) 2.5; 4   d) 8.5; 15   e) 12.5; 24
             f) 3; √20 = 2√5 ≈ 4.47   g) 4; √55 ≈ 7.42
             h) 4.5; √56 = 2√14 ≈ 7.48   i) 3.25; 6   j) 3.75; 4.5   k) 2.5; 3
             l) 2; √13.75 ≈ 3.71   m) 7.5; 12   n) 1.5; √5 ≈ 2.24   o) 6.5; 5
             p) 13; 24

M8. A pair of tangents PA, PB is constructed by drawing radii OA, OB and
    perpendiculars at A and B. In a) to l) the angle ∠APB between the tangents
    is given: find ∠AOB. In m) to t) ∠AOB is given: find ∠APB.
    a) ∠APB = 60°    b) ∠APB = 90°    c) ∠APB = 120°   d) ∠APB = 45°
    e) ∠APB = 30°    f) ∠APB = 70°    g) ∠APB = 80°    h) ∠APB = 100°
    i) ∠APB = 135°   j) ∠APB = 150°   k) ∠APB = 55°    l) ∠APB = 36°
    m) ∠AOB = 120°   n) ∠AOB = 90°    o) ∠AOB = 60°    p) ∠AOB = 150°
    q) ∠AOB = 100°   r) ∠AOB = 45°    s) ∠AOB = 30°    t) ∠AOB = 165°
    Answers: a) 120°   b) 90°   c) 60°   d) 135°   e) 150°   f) 110°   g) 100°
             h) 80°   i) 45°   j) 30°   k) 125°   l) 144°   m) 60°   n) 90°
             o) 120°   p) 30°   q) 80°   r) 135°   s) 150°   t) 15°

M9. Tangents PA and PB to a circle of radius r are inclined at the given angle
    ∠APB. Find the tangent length PA and the distance OP (cm), exact and to 2
    decimal places.
    a) ∠APB = 60°, r = 5     b) ∠APB = 60°, r = 4
    c) ∠APB = 60°, r = 3     d) ∠APB = 60°, r = 2.5
    e) ∠APB = 60°, r = 7     f) ∠APB = 90°, r = 5
    g) ∠APB = 90°, r = 3     h) ∠APB = 90°, r = 6
    i) ∠APB = 90°, r = 4.5   j) ∠APB = 120°, r = 3
    k) ∠APB = 120°, r = 6    l) ∠APB = 120°, r = 9
    m) ∠APB = 120°, r = 4    n) ∠APB = 60°, r = 10
    o) ∠APB = 90°, r = 10    p) ∠APB = 120°, r = 1
    Answers: a) 5√3 ≈ 8.66; 10   b) 4√3 ≈ 6.93; 8   c) 3√3 ≈ 5.20; 6
             d) 5√3/2 ≈ 4.33; 5   e) 7√3 ≈ 12.12; 14   f) 5; 5√2 ≈ 7.07
             g) 3; 3√2 ≈ 4.24   h) 6; 6√2 ≈ 8.49   i) 4.5; 9√2/2 ≈ 6.36
             j) √3 ≈ 1.73; 2√3 ≈ 3.46   k) 2√3 ≈ 3.46; 4√3 ≈ 6.93
             l) 3√3 ≈ 5.20; 6√3 ≈ 10.39   m) 4√3/3 ≈ 2.31; 8√3/3 ≈ 4.62
             n) 10√3 ≈ 17.32; 20   o) 10; 10√2 ≈ 14.14
             p) √3/3 ≈ 0.58; 2√3/3 ≈ 1.15

M10. Two-ray method: AX and BY are parallel rays on opposite sides of AB. For AP
     : PB = m : n, how many points are marked on each ray and which two points
     are joined?
     a) 3 : 2   b) 4 : 5
     c) 1 : 3   d) 2 : 1
     e) 5 : 2   f) 3 : 7
     g) 6 : 5   h) 2 : 5
     i) 7 : 4   j) 1 : 1
     k) 5 : 9   l) 8 : 3
     m) 4 : 1   n) 3 : 5
     o) 9 : 2   p) 2 : 7
     Answers: a) 3 on AX, 2 on BY; A₃B₂   b) 4 on AX, 5 on BY; A₄B₅
              c) 1 on AX, 3 on BY; A₁B₃   d) 2 on AX, 1 on BY; A₂B₁
              e) 5 on AX, 2 on BY; A₅B₂   f) 3 on AX, 7 on BY; A₃B₇
              g) 6 on AX, 5 on BY; A₆B₅   h) 2 on AX, 5 on BY; A₂B₅
              i) 7 on AX, 4 on BY; A₇B₄   j) 1 on AX, 1 on BY; A₁B₁
              k) 5 on AX, 9 on BY; A₅B₉   l) 8 on AX, 3 on BY; A₈B₃
              m) 4 on AX, 1 on BY; A₄B₁   n) 3 on AX, 5 on BY; A₃B₅
              o) 9 on AX, 2 on BY; A₉B₂   p) 2 on AX, 7 on BY; A₂B₇

M11. The first figure is the original triangle and the second is the constructed
     similar triangle. Find the scale factor k in simplest form and say whether
     the new triangle is smaller, larger or congruent.
     a) BC = 6, B′C′ = 4.5     b) BC = 5, B′C′ = 7.5
     c) BC = 8, B′C′ = 6       d) BC = 4, B′C′ = 10
     e) BC = 12, B′C′ = 9      f) BC = 9, B′C′ = 12
     g) BC = 7, B′C′ = 3.5     h) BC = 3, B′C′ = 7
     i) areas 9 and 16         j) areas 25 and 4
     k) areas 16 and 25        l) areas 4 and 9
     m) areas 49 and 36        n) areas 1 and 4
     o) perimeters 30 and 24   p) perimeters 18 and 27
     q) perimeters 20 and 35   r) perimeters 40 and 16
     s) areas 36 and 36        t) BC = 5, B′C′ = 5
     Answers: a) 3/4, smaller   b) 3/2, larger   c) 3/4, smaller
              d) 5/2, larger   e) 3/4, smaller   f) 4/3, larger
              g) 1/2, smaller   h) 7/3, larger   i) 4/3, larger
              j) 2/5, smaller   k) 5/4, larger   l) 3/2, larger
              m) 6/7, smaller   n) 2, larger   o) 4/5, smaller   p) 3/2, larger
              q) 7/4, larger   r) 2/5, smaller   s) 1, congruent
              t) 1, congruent

M12. True or false? Correct the false ones.
     a) To divide AB in the ratio 2 : 5, seven equal steps are marked on AX.
     b) The steps marked on AX may have different lengths.
     c) The ray AX must make an acute angle with AB.
     d) The construction for dividing a segment is justified by the BPT.
     e) For scale factor 4/7, the parallel is drawn through B₇.
     f) For a scale factor greater than 1, C′ lies on BC produced.
     g) To draw tangents from P, a circle is drawn with centre P and radius PO.
     h) The tangent construction is justified by the angle in a semicircle.
     i) From a point inside a circle two tangents can be constructed.
     j) For tangents inclined at 60°, the radii are drawn at 60°.
     k) The centre of a circle can be found from two non-parallel chords.
     l) A triangle with scale factor 1 is congruent to the original.
     m) In the two-ray method the rays are drawn on the same side of AB.
     n) With scale factor 2/3 the area of the new triangle is 4/9 of the
        original.
     o) A segment of 10 cm can be divided exactly into 3 equal parts by
        construction.
     p) To construct the tangent at P on the circle, draw the perpendicular to
        the chord through P.
     Answers: a) true   b) false (they must be equal)   c) true   d) true
              e) false (through B₄; B₇ is joined to C)   f) true
              g) false (centre the midpoint of OP, radius half of OP)   h) true
              i) false (none)   j) false (at 120°)   k) true   l) true
              m) false (opposite sides, parallel)   n) true   o) true
              p) false (perpendicular to the radius OP)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: construct slowly with a sharp pencil, labelling every point as
  soon as it is made; write the steps as a numbered list before drawing; say the
  rule "mark the bigger number, join the denominator point, parallel through the
  numerator point"; check every construction by measuring and comparing with the
  calculated length; practise copying an angle (for parallel lines) separately
  first. Harder: divide a segment EXTERNALLY in the ratio 3 : 1 (find P on AB
  produced with AP : PB = 3 : 1); construct a triangle similar to a given one
  with area half of the original (scale factor 1/√2, using a √2 construction);
  construct the common tangents of two circles; and prove that the construction
  of tangents from P works even when OP is only slightly larger than r.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.29 — COORDINATE GEOMETRY: DISTANCE FORMULA, SECTION FORMULA, AREA OF
             TRIANGLE
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - DISTANCE FORMULA: the distance between P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) is
    PQ = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²), from Pythagoras on the right triangle with
    horizontal leg x₂ − x₁ and vertical leg y₂ − y₁. From the origin:
    √(x² + y²).
  - Using distances: three points are COLLINEAR when the two shorter distances
    add up to the longest; a triangle is isosceles if two sides are equal and
    right-angled if the squares satisfy Pythagoras; a quadrilateral with four
    equal sides is a rhombus, and a square if its diagonals are also equal;
    equal opposite sides with equal diagonals give a rectangle.
  - SECTION FORMULA (internal division): the point P dividing AB with A(x₁, y₁),
    B(x₂, y₂) in the ratio m : n is P((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)).
    MIDPOINT (m = n): ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). Points of trisection use the
    ratios 1 : 2 and 2 : 1.
  - To find the ratio in which a given point (or an axis) divides AB, take the
    ratio as k : 1 and solve one coordinate equation for k. On the x-axis y = 0;
    on the y-axis x = 0.
  - CENTROID (where the medians meet, dividing each in the ratio 2 : 1 from the
    vertex): G((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3).
  - AREA OF A TRIANGLE with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃):
    1/2 × |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|. The points are collinear
    exactly when this area is 0. Area of a quadrilateral: split it along a
    diagonal into two triangles and add.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Derive the distance formula. Two towns are at A(2, 3) and B(10, 9) on a map
    grid whose unit is 1 km. How far apart are they?
    Answer: AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²) = √(8² + 6²) = 10 km.
    Teacher explains:
            y
            |              B(x₂, y₂)
            |             /|
            |           /  |  y₂ − y₁
            |         /    |
            |   A(x₁, y₁)--C
            |      x₂ − x₁
            +-------------------- x
    Draw the horizontal line through A and the vertical line through B; they
    meet at C(x₂, y₁) with a right angle. AC = x₂ − x₁ and CB = y₂ − y₁, so by
    Pythagoras AB² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)².
       AB = √((10 − 2)² + (9 − 3)²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10 km
    The order does not matter, because (−8)² = 8². Negative coordinates need
    brackets: for (−1, 3) and (2, −1),
    AB = √((2 − (−1))² + (−1 − 3)²) = √(9 + 16) = 5. Common mistake: subtracting
    an x-coordinate from a y-coordinate. Now you try: distance between (−3, 2)
    and (3, 10)? (10)

D2. Find the point on the x-axis which is equidistant from A(2, −5) and
    B(−2, 9).
    Answer: (−7, 0).
    Teacher explains: A point on the x-axis has y = 0, so call it P(x, 0). Set
    PA² = PB² (squares avoid square roots):
       (x − 2)² + (0 + 5)² = (x + 2)² + (0 − 9)²
       x² − 4x + 4 + 25 = x² + 4x + 4 + 81
       −4x + 29 = 4x + 85
       −8x = 56,   x = −7
    Check: PA² = (−7 − 2)² + 5² = 81 + 25 = 106 and
    PB² = (−7 + 2)² + 9² = 25 + 81 = 106. Equal. The x² terms always cancel,
    leaving a linear equation. Common mistake: taking P as (0, y), which is on
    the y-axis. Now you try: the point on the y-axis equidistant from (6, 5) and
    (−4, 3). ((0, 9))

D3. Show by the distance formula that A(1, 5), B(2, 3) and C(−2, 11) are
    collinear.
    Answer: AB = √5, AC = 3√5, BC = 4√5 and AB + AC = BC, so the points lie on
    one line (A is between B and C).
    Teacher explains:
       AB = √((2 − 1)² + (3 − 5)²) = √(1 + 4) = √5
       AC = √((−2 − 1)² + (11 − 5)²) = √(9 + 36) = √45 = 3√5
       BC = √((−2 − 2)² + (11 − 3)²) = √(16 + 64) = √80 = 4√5
       AB + AC = √5 + 3√5 = 4√5 = BC
    If the three points made a triangle, the sum of any two sides would be
    LONGER than the third (triangle inequality). Equality means the triangle is
    flat: the points are collinear, and the point that is not an end of the
    longest segment lies between the other two. Simplifying the surds makes the
    comparison easy. (A quicker test comes later: area = 0.) Now you try: are
    (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 5) collinear? (yes: √5 + √5 = 2√5)

D4. Show that A(1, 7), B(4, 2), C(−1, −1) and D(−4, 4) are the vertices of a
    square. Why is checking four equal sides not enough?
    Answer: All sides are √34 and both diagonals are √68, so ABCD is a square.
    Teacher explains:
       AB² = 3² + 5² = 34      BC² = 5² + 3² = 34
       CD² = 3² + 5² = 34      DA² = 5² + 3² = 34
       AC² = 2² + 8² = 68      BD² = 8² + 2² = 68
    Four equal sides make a RHOMBUS; a rhombus with equal diagonals is a SQUARE.
    Also 34 + 34 = 68, so each angle is a right angle (converse of Pythagoras).
    Working with the squares of the distances avoids surds. Summary: rhombus: 4
    equal sides; square: + equal diagonals; parallelogram: opposite sides equal;
    rectangle: + equal diagonals. Common mistake: stopping after the four sides.
    Now you try: (−1, −2), (1, 0), (−1, 2), (−3, 0). What figure? (a square:
    sides √8, diagonals 4)

D5. Show that A(7, 10), B(−2, 5) and C(3, −4) are the vertices of an isosceles
    right-angled triangle.
    Answer: AB² = BC² = 106 and CA² = 212 = 106 + 106: isosceles with the right
    angle at B.
    Teacher explains:
       AB² = (−2 − 7)² + (5 − 10)² = 81 + 25 = 106
       BC² = (3 + 2)² + (−4 − 5)² = 25 + 81 = 106
       CA² = (7 − 3)² + (10 + 4)² = 16 + 196 = 212
    AB = BC: isosceles. AB² + BC² = 106 + 106 = 212 = CA²: by the converse of
    Pythagoras the angle opposite CA, at B, is 90°. The right angle is always at
    the vertex OPPOSITE the longest side. Now you try: (0, 0), (3, 0), (0, 4).
    Right-angled? (yes: 9 + 16 = 25)

D6. Derive the section formula and find the point dividing the join of (4, −3)
    and (8, 5) internally in the ratio 3 : 1.
    Answer: (7, 3).
    Teacher explains: Let P(x, y) divide AB in the ratio m : n, with A(x₁, y₁),
    B(x₂, y₂). Draw horizontals and verticals to make right triangles AQP and
    PRB; they are similar (AA, parallel lines), so
       AP/PB = AQ/PR:   m/n = (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x)
       mx₂ − mx = nx − nx₁   so   x = (mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n)
       likewise              y = (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)
    Numbers, m = 3, n = 1, A(4, −3), B(8, 5):
       x = (3 × 8 + 1 × 4)/(3 + 1) = 28/4 = 7
       y = (3 × 5 + 1 × (−3))/(3 + 1) = 12/4 = 3
    Memory aid: m goes with the FAR point B, "cross-multiply". Check: P must be
    closer to B (3 parts from A, 1 part from B), and 7 is closer to 8 than to 4.
    Now you try: (−1, 7) and (4, −3) in the ratio 2 : 3. ((1, 3))

D7. Find the midpoint and the points of trisection of the join of A(2, −2) and
    B(−7, 4). Then find x and y if (1, 2), (4, y), (x, 6) and (3, 5) are the
    vertices of a parallelogram taken in order.
    Answer: Midpoint (−2.5, 1); trisection points (−1, 0) and (−4, 2). x = 6,
    y = 3.
    Teacher explains:
       midpoint: ((2 − 7)/2, (−2 + 4)/2) = (−2.5, 1)
       P, ratio 1 : 2: ((1 × (−7) + 2 × 2)/3, (1 × 4 + 2 × (−2))/3)
                  = (−3/3, 0/3) = (−1, 0)
       Q, ratio 2 : 1: ((2 × (−7) + 1 × 2)/3, (2 × 4 + 1 × (−2))/3)
                  = (−12/3, 6/3) = (−4, 2)
    The two points of trisection divide AB into three equal parts: P is one
    third of the way from A, Q two thirds. Check: Q is the midpoint of PB:
    ((−1 − 7)/2, (0 + 4)/2) = (−4, 2).
    Parallelogram: the diagonals bisect each other, so the midpoint of AC equals
    the midpoint of BD: ((1 + x)/2, (2 + 6)/2) = ((4 + 3)/2, (y + 5)/2). So
    1 + x = 7, x = 6, and 8 = y + 5, y = 3. Now you try: the midpoint of (3, −5)
    and (−1, 9)? ((1, 2))

D8. In what ratio does the point (−4, 6) divide the join of A(−6, 10) and
    B(3, −8)?
    Answer: 2 : 7.
    Teacher explains: Let the ratio be k : 1. By the section formula the
    x-coordinate of the point is (3k − 6)/(k + 1). Set it equal to −4:
       (3k − 6)/(k + 1) = −4
       3k − 6 = −4k − 4
       7k = 2,   k = 2/7      so the ratio is 2 : 7
       check y: (2 × (−8) + 7 × 10)/(2 + 7) = (−16 + 70)/9 = 54/9 = 6
    Using k : 1 leaves only ONE unknown. Always check with the other coordinate:
    if it fails, the point is not on the line AB at all. A negative k would mean
    the point is outside the segment (external division). Now you try: in what
    ratio does (3, 4) divide the join of (1, 2) and (7, 8)? (1 : 2)

D9. Find the ratio in which the x-axis divides the join of A(1, −5) and
    B(−4, 5), and the point of division. In what ratio does the y-axis divide
    the join of (5, −6) and (−1, −4)?
    Answer: x-axis: 1 : 1 at (−1.5, 0). y-axis: 5 : 1 at (0, −13/3).
    Teacher explains: On the x-axis the y-coordinate is 0. With ratio k : 1:
       (5k − 5)/(k + 1) = 0   so 5k = 5,  k = 1     ratio 1 : 1
       x = (−4 + 1)/2 = −1.5     point (−1.5, 0)
    On the y-axis the x-coordinate is 0:
       (−k + 5)/(k + 1) = 0   so k = 5          ratio 5 : 1
       y = (5 × (−4) + 1 × (−6))/6 = −26/6 = −13/3
    Quick check: the x-axis can cut AB only if A and B are on opposite sides of
    it (y-coordinates of opposite signs: −5 and 5). The ratio is the ratio of
    the DISTANCES from the axis: 5 to 5, that is 1 : 1, and for the y-axis 5 :
    1. Now you try: ratio in which the x-axis divides (2, −3) and (5, 6)? (1 :
    2)

D10. Show that the centroid of the triangle with vertices A(x₁, y₁), B(x₂, y₂),
     C(x₃, y₃) is ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3). Find the centroid of
     A(4, −6), B(3, −2), C(5, 2).
     Answer: G(4, −2).
     Teacher explains: Let D be the midpoint of BC: D((x₂ + x₃)/2, (y₂ + y₃)/2).
     The centroid G divides the median AD in the ratio 2 : 1. By the section
     formula:
        x = (2 × (x₂ + x₃)/2 + 1 × x₁)/(2 + 1) = (x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3
        y = (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3   in the same way
     So the centroid is simply the AVERAGE of the three vertices. Numbers:
     x = (4 + 3 + 5)/3 = 12/3 = 4, y = (−6 − 2 + 2)/3 = −6/3 = −2. Using the
     other medians gives the same point, which PROVES that the three medians
     meet at one point. Now you try: centroid of (1, 2), (4, 6), (7, −2)?
     ((4, 2))

D11. Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(1, −1), B(−4, 6) and
     C(−3, −5).
     Answer: 24 square units.
     Teacher explains: The formula comes from enclosing the triangle with
     trapeziums whose parallel sides are vertical:
     area = 1/2 × |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.
        x₁(y₂ − y₃) = 1 × (6 + 5)        = 11
        x₂(y₃ − y₁) = (−4) × (−5 + 1)    = 16
        x₃(y₁ − y₂) = (−3) × (−1 − 6)    = 21
        area = 1/2 × (11 + 16 + 21) = 1/2 × 48 = 24
     Write the three products in a column, with the pattern of the indices
     1(2 − 3), 2(3 − 1), 3(1 − 2). If the bracket total is negative, take its
     absolute value: area is never negative. Common mistakes: dropping a minus
     sign in (−4) × (−4), forgetting the 1/2. Now you try: area of (2, 3),
     (−1, 0), (2, −4)? (10.5 square units)

D12. Find k if (7, −2), (5, 1) and (3, k) are collinear. Then find the area of
     the quadrilateral with vertices A(−4, −2), B(−3, −5), C(3, −2), D(2, 3).
     Answer: k = 4; area 28 square units.
     Teacher explains:
        collinear: 7(1 − k) + 5(k + 2) + 3(−2 − 1) = 0
                   7 − 7k + 5k + 10 − 9 = 0
                   8 − 2k = 0,   k = 4
     Three points are collinear exactly when the "triangle" has zero area. Check
     with slopes: from (7, −2) to (5, 1) the rise is 3 for a run of −2, and from
     (5, 1) to (3, 4) also 3 for −2.
     Quadrilateral: split along the diagonal AC.
        ar(ABC) = 1/2 × [−4(−5 + 2) + (−3)(−2 + 2) + 3(−2 + 5)]
                = 1/2 × (12 + 0 + 9) = 10.5
        ar(ACD) = 1/2 × [−4(−2 − 3) + 3(3 + 2) + 2(−2 + 2)]
                = 1/2 × (20 + 15 + 0) = 17.5
        ar(ABCD) = 10.5 + 17.5 = 28
     Take the vertices in order round the figure so that the diagonal lies
     INSIDE it. Now you try: find k if (8, 1), (k, −4), (2, −5) are collinear.
     (k = 3)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Find the distance between the two points. Surds: exact simplest form and 2
    decimal places.
    a) (2, 3), (10, 9)        b) (0, 0), (5, 12)
    c) (−1, 3), (2, −1)       d) (−3, 2), (3, 10)
    e) (4, −5), (−4, 1)       f) (0, 7), (0, −2)
    g) (−6, 0), (3, 0)        h) (1, 1), (4, 5)
    i) (−2, −3), (−7, −15)    j) (5, −2), (−3, 13)
    k) (0, 0), (1, 1)         l) (2, 5), (4, 9)
    m) (−1, −1), (2, 2)       n) (3, −4), (−2, 6)
    o) (0, −3), (4, 0)        p) (−5, 2), (1, −1)
    q) (7, 7), (7, 7)         r) (0.5, 1), (2, 3)
    s) (−4, 6), (4, −9)       t) (1, −2), (−1, 2)
    u) (−3, −3), (3, 3)       v) (2, 0), (0, −6)
    w) (1.5, −2), (−2.5, 1)   x) (−8, 5), (−1, 5)
    Answers: a) 10   b) 13   c) 5   d) 10   e) 10   f) 9   g) 9   h) 5   i) 13

              g) k = 0   h) k = −1   i) k = −2   j) k = −2   k) 10.5 + 17.5 = 28
              l) 6 + 6 = 12   m) 9 + 4.5 = 13.5   n) 22.5 + 25 = 47.5
              o) 10 + 10 = 20   p) 6.5 + 11 = 17.5   q) 13 + 7 = 20
              r) 12 + 12 = 24   s) 7.5 + 12.5 = 20   t) 20 + 7.5 = 27.5

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: plot every set of points on squared paper first, so the answer can
  be estimated; write the coordinates in a small table with columns x and y
  before substituting; put negative numbers in brackets; for the section formula
  say "m with the far point"; for the area formula write the three products in a
  column and add at the end. Harder: find the circumcentre of (0, 0), (8, 0),
  (0, 6) (it is (4, 3), the midpoint of the hypotenuse); prove with coordinates
  that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other and that the midpoint
  of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices; find the point
  dividing AB EXTERNALLY in a given ratio; and find the area of a pentagon by
  splitting it into triangles.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.30 — HERON'S FORMULA
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - HERON'S FORMULA finds the area of ANY triangle from its three sides a, b, c,
    with no height needed: area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), where
    s = (a + b + c)/2 is the SEMI-PERIMETER (half the perimeter).
  - Method: (1) find s; (2) find s − a, s − b, s − c (check: they add up to s);
    (3) multiply s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c); (4) take the square root. Factorise
    into primes before taking the root: √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) =
    √(2⁴ × 3² × 7²) = 2² × 3 × 7 = 84.
  - The answer may be a whole number (13, 14, 15 gives 84) or a surd (5, 6, 7
    gives 6√6 ≈ 14.70). Leave surds in simplest form and give a decimal when a
    measurement is wanted. Units: cm gives cm², m gives m².
  - Special cases: EQUILATERAL triangle of side a: area = (√3/4)a². ISOSCELES
    triangle with equal sides a and base b: area = (b/4)√(4a² − b²). Both follow
    from Heron and agree with 1/2 × base × height.
  - Each factor s − a, s − b, s − c must be POSITIVE; this is exactly the
    triangle inequality (each side is less than the sum of the other two). If a
    factor is 0 the "triangle" is flat (area 0); if one is negative there is no
    triangle.
  - ALTITUDES from the area: area = 1/2 × base × height, so the height to side a
    is h = 2 × area ÷ a. The shortest altitude is on the longest side.
  - QUADRILATERALS: split along a diagonal into two triangles whose three sides
    are known, use Heron (or 1/2 × base × height for a right triangle) on each,
    and add. A rhombus splits into two congruent triangles; a trapezium splits
    into a parallelogram and a triangle.
  - COST problems: cost = area × rate (₹ per m²) for painting, turfing or
    levelling; cost = perimeter × rate (₹ per m) for fencing. Check which one
    the question asks for.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A triangular plot of land has sides 13 m, 14 m and 15 m. No angle is a right
    angle and nobody knows the height. Find its area, and the cost of levelling
    it at ₹25 per m².
    Answer: Area = 84 m²; cost = 84 × 25 = ₹2,100.
    Teacher explains: Heron of Alexandria (about 60 CE) found a way to get the
    area from the three sides alone. Set out the working in a column:
       s = (13 + 14 + 15)/2 = 42/2 = 21
       s − a = 21 − 13 = 8
       s − b = 21 − 14 = 7
       s − c = 21 − 15 = 6        check: 8 + 7 + 6 = 21 = s
       area = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6)
            = √(3 × 7 × 2³ × 7 × 2 × 3)
            = √(2⁴ × 3² × 7²) = 2² × 3 × 7 = 84 m²
    Splitting each number into primes makes the square root easy: pair up equal
    factors. Then cost = 84 × 25 = ₹2,100. Common mistakes: using the full
    perimeter 42 instead of s = 21, and forgetting the square root
    (21 × 8 × 7 × 6 = 7,056 is the square of the area, not the area). Now you
    try: sides 5 m, 12 m and 13 m. (s = 15, area = √(15 × 10 × 3 × 2) =
    √900 = 30 m²)

D2. Find the area of a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Give the exact
    answer and the value to 2 decimal places.
    Answer: Area = 6√6 cm² ≈ 14.70 cm².
    Teacher explains:
       s = (5 + 6 + 7)/2 = 9
       s − a = 4,  s − b = 3,  s − c = 2
       area = √(9 × 4 × 3 × 2) = √216 = √(36 × 6) = 6√6
    The product 216 is not a perfect square, so the area is a SURD. Take out the
    largest square factor: 216 = 36 × 6, so √216 = 6√6. With a calculator
    √6 ≈ 2.449, so 6√6 ≈ 14.70 cm². Estimate to check: a triangle with base 6
    and height about 5 has area about 15, so 14.7 is sensible. Common mistake:
    writing √216 = 108 (halving is not square-rooting). Now you try: sides 4 cm,
    5 cm, 7 cm. (s = 8, √(8 × 4 × 3 × 1) = √96 = 4√6 ≈ 9.80 cm²)

D3. The sides of a triangular field are in the ratio 12 : 17 : 25 and its
    perimeter is 540 m. Find its area. Fencing costs ₹40 per metre; what does it
    cost to fence the field?
    Answer: Sides 120 m, 170 m, 250 m; area = 9,000 m²; fencing costs ₹21,600.
    Teacher explains: First find the sides. Let them be 12x, 17x, 25x. Then
    12x + 17x + 25x = 54x = 540, so x = 10 and the sides are 120 m, 170 m and
    250 m. Now Heron:
       s = 540/2 = 270
       s − a = 150,  s − b = 100,  s − c = 20
       area = √(270 × 150 × 100 × 20)
            = √81,000,000 = 9,000 m²
    Tip: 270 × 150 × 100 × 20 = (27 × 15 × 2) × 10⁵ = 810 × 10⁵ = 81 × 10⁶, and
    √(81 × 10⁶) = 9 × 10³. Fencing goes ROUND the field, so it uses the
    perimeter: 540 × 40 = ₹21,600. Common mistake: multiplying the area by the
    fencing rate. Now you try: ratio 3 : 4 : 5, perimeter 144 m. (sides 36, 48,
    60; area 864 m²)

D4. Show that Heron's formula gives the area of an equilateral triangle of side
    a as (√3/4)a². Use it for a triangle of side 8 cm and for a triangular
    traffic sign of side 90 cm.
    Answer: Side 8 cm: 16√3 ≈ 27.71 cm². Side 90 cm: 2,025√3 ≈ 3,507.40 cm².
    Teacher explains: All sides are a, so s = 3a/2 and s − a = a/2 three times:
       area = √(3a/2 × a/2 × a/2 × a/2)
            = √(3a⁴/16) = (√3/4)a²
    For a = 8: (√3/4) × 64 = 16√3 ≈ 16 × 1.732 = 27.712 ≈ 27.71 cm². For a = 90:
    (√3/4) × 8,100 = 2,025√3 ≈ 3,507.40 cm². Check with Pythagoras: the height
    of an equilateral triangle is √(a² − (a/2)²) = (√3/2)a, and 1/2 ×
    a × (√3/2)a = (√3/4)a² — the same. Common mistake: (√3/4)a is not an area
    (no square). Now you try: side 6 cm. (9√3 ≈ 15.59 cm²)

D5. An isosceles triangle has perimeter 30 cm and each of its equal sides is
    12 cm. Find its area.
    Answer: Base = 6 cm; area = 9√15 cm² ≈ 34.86 cm².
    Teacher explains: Base = 30 − 12 − 12 = 6 cm. Heron:
       s = 15,  s − a = 3,  s − b = 3,  s − c = 9
       area = √(15 × 3 × 3 × 9) = √1,215 = √(81 × 15) = 9√15
    Shortcut for isosceles triangles with equal sides a and base b:
    area = (b/4)√(4a² −
    b²) = (6/4)√(576 − 36) = (3/2)√540 = (3/2) × 6√15 = 9√15. Or drop the height
    onto the base: it bisects the base, so h = √(12² − 3²) = √135 = 3√15 and
    area = 1/2 × 6 × 3√15 = 9√15. Three methods, one answer. √15 ≈ 3.873, so
    area ≈ 34.86 cm². Now you try: equal sides 5 cm, base 8 cm. (s = 9,
    √(9 × 4 × 4 × 1) = 12 cm²)

D6. For the triangle with sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm (area 84 cm²), find the
    three altitudes. Which is the shortest?
    Answer: On 13: 168/13 ≈ 12.92 cm; on 14: 12 cm; on 15: 56/5 = 11.2 cm. The
    shortest is on the longest side.
    Teacher explains: Area = 1/2 × base × height, so height = 2 × area ÷ base.
    Here 2 × area = 168:
       base 13:  h = 168 ÷ 13 = 168/13 ≈ 12.92 cm
       base 14:  h = 168 ÷ 14 = 12 cm
       base 15:  h = 168 ÷ 15 = 11.2 cm
    The area is the same whichever side we call the base, so a LONGER base goes
    with a SHORTER height. Heron gives the area; the altitude comes for free
    afterwards. Common mistake: forgetting the 2 (84 ÷ 14 = 6 is half the
    height). Now you try: triangle 9, 10, 17 with area 36 cm²; find the altitude
    on the side of 9 cm. (72/9 = 8 cm)

D7. A school garden ABCD has AB = 9 m, BC = 40 m, CD = 28 m, DA = 15 m and
    ∠ABC = 90°. Find its area.
    Answer: AC = 41 m; area = 180 + 126 = 306 m².
    Teacher explains:
            D ______ C
           /  .     |
       15 /     .   | 40        diagonal AC splits ABCD
         /    28  . |           into two triangles
        A-----------B
              9
    Split along the diagonal AC. In the right triangle ABC, AC = √(9² + 40²) =
    √1,681 = 41 m and area ABC = 1/2 × 9 × 40 = 180 m². Triangle ACD has sides
    41, 28, 15, so Heron:
       s = (41 + 28 + 15)/2 = 42
       area = √(42 × 1 × 14 × 27) = √15,876 = 126 m²
    Total 180 + 126 = 306 m². (The diagram is not to scale.) A quadrilateral
    needs 5 measurements (4 sides and a diagonal, or an angle) — 4 sides alone
    do not fix its shape. Now you try: quadrilateral with AB = 3, BC = 4,
    CD = 4, DA = 5 cm and diagonal AC = 5 cm. (6 + 2√21 ≈ 15.17 cm²)

D8. The triangular side wall of a flyover is used for advertisements. Its sides
    are 122 m, 22 m and 120 m. The company earns ₹5,000 per m² per year. How
    much does it earn in 3 months?
    Answer: Area = 1,320 m²; earnings = ₹1,650,000 (₹16.5 lakh).
    Teacher explains:
       s = (122 + 22 + 120)/2 = 132
       s − a = 10,  s − b = 110,  s − c = 12
       area = √(132 × 10 × 110 × 12) = √1,742,400 = 1,320 m²
    Pair the numbers: 132 × 12 = 1,584 and 10 × 110 = 1,100, so the product is
    1,584 × 1,100 = 1,742,400 = 1,320². (In fact 22² + 120² = 122², so this is a
    right triangle: 1/2 × 22 × 120 = 1,320 — a good check.) One year:
    1,320 × 5,000 = ₹6,600,000. Three months = 3/12 of a year:
    6,600,000 × 3/12 = ₹1,650,000, which is ₹16.5 lakh in the Indian system.
    Common mistake: forgetting to scale the yearly rate to 3 months. Now you
    try: the same wall for 6 months at ₹2,000 per m² per year. (₹1,320,000)

D9. An umbrella is made by stitching 10 triangular pieces of cloth, 5 red and 5
    yellow. Each piece has sides 20 cm, 50 cm and 50 cm. How much cloth of each
    colour is needed?
    Answer: One piece = 200√6 ≈ 489.90 cm²; each colour needs
    1,000√6 ≈ 2,449.49 cm².
    Teacher explains:
       s = (20 + 50 + 50)/2 = 60
       s − a = 40,  s − b = 10,  s − c = 10
       area = √(60 × 40 × 10 × 10) = √240,000
            = √(40,000 × 6) = 200√6 cm²
    Five pieces of one colour: 5 × 200√6 = 1,000√6 cm². √6 ≈ 2.449490, so
    1,000√6 ≈ 2,449.49 cm². Keep the exact form until the last step and then
    round — rounding 489.90 first and multiplying by 5 gives 2,449.50, a small
    but avoidable error. Now you try: a kite made of 4 pieces of sides 13, 13,
    10 cm. (each 60 cm², total 240 cm²)

D10. A rhombus-shaped field has side 30 m and one diagonal 48 m. It is shared
     equally by 18 cows for grazing. How much area does each cow get?
     Answer: Area = 864 m²; each cow gets 48 m².
     Teacher explains: The diagonal of 48 m splits the rhombus into two
     CONGRUENT triangles with sides 30, 30, 48.
        s = (30 + 30 + 48)/2 = 54
        area = √(54 × 24 × 24 × 6) = √186,624 = 432 m²
        field = 2 × 432 = 864 m²;  864 ÷ 18 = 48 m² per cow
     Check with the rhombus rule: the diagonals bisect each other at right
     angles, so half the other diagonal is √(30² − 24²) = 18, the other diagonal
     is 36 and area = 1/2 × 48 × 36 = 864 m². Common mistake: using only one
     triangle. Now you try: rhombus of side 5 cm with one diagonal 8 cm.
     (24 cm²)

D11. A trapezium-shaped park has parallel sides 25 m and 10 m and the other two
     sides 14 m and 13 m. Find its area.
     Answer: Height = 11.2 m; area = 196 m².
     Teacher explains:
          D___10___C              D___C
          /|       \              |  |\
       13/ |h       \14    →      |  | \14
        /  |         \           13|  |h \
       A---+----------B            A--E---B
               25                  10    15
     Draw CE parallel to DA. Then AECD is a parallelogram (AE = 10, EC = 13) and
     triangle EBC has sides 15 (= 25 − 10), 14 and 13. Heron on EBC: s = 21,
     area = √(21 × 6 × 7 × 8) = 84 m². Its height to the base 15 is the height
     of the trapezium: h = 2 × 84 ÷ 15 = 11.2 m. Trapezium
     area = 1/2 × (25 + 10) × 11.2 = 196 m². Check: parallelogram
     10 × 11.2 = 112, and 112 + 84 = 196. Now you try: parallel sides 20 m and
     5 m, other sides 13 m and 14 m. (triangle 15, 13, 14 again, h = 11.2, area
     140 m²)

D12. Riya tries Heron's formula on "triangles" with sides (a) 3, 4, 7 and (b) 3,
     4, 8. What happens, and why? Also check that Heron agrees with 1/2 × base ×
     height for the right triangle 6, 8, 10.
     Answer: (a) s = 7 and s − c = 0, so area 0: the points are in a line. (b)
     s = 7.5 and s − c = −0.5, so s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c) < 0: no such triangle.
     For 6, 8, 10 both give 24.
     Teacher explains: s − c = (a + b − c)/2, so s − c > 0 exactly when a + b >
     c. The three factors s − a, s − b, s − c are positive precisely when the
     TRIANGLE INEQUALITY holds for every side. (a) 3 + 4 = 7: the "triangle" is
     squashed flat into a segment, and Heron correctly gives area 0. (b)
     3 + 4 < 8: the two short sides cannot reach each other, the product
     7.5 × 4.5 × 3.5 × (−0.5) is negative and has no real square root. For 6, 8,
     10: s = 12, area = √(12 × 6 × 4 × 2) = √576 = 24, and 1/2 × 6 × 8 = 24.
     Always test a + b > c (with c the longest side) before starting. Now you
     try: can 5, 6, 12 form a triangle? (no, 5 + 6 < 12)

M8. The sides are in the given ratio and the perimeter is given. Find the sides
    and then the area.
    a) 3 : 4 : 5, perimeter 36       b) 3 : 4 : 5, perimeter 120
    c) 5 : 12 : 13, perimeter 60     d) 13 : 14 : 15, perimeter 84
    e) 12 : 17 : 25, perimeter 540   f) 13 : 14 : 15, perimeter 168
    g) 1 : 1 : 1, perimeter 30       h) 5 : 5 : 6, perimeter 64
    i) 5 : 5 : 8, perimeter 36       j) 9 : 10 : 17, perimeter 144
    k) 7 : 24 : 25, perimeter 112    l) 25 : 17 : 12, perimeter 108
    m) 2 : 3 : 4, perimeter 18       n) 8 : 15 : 17, perimeter 200
    Answers: a) 9, 12, 15; 54   b) 30, 40, 50; 600   c) 10, 24, 26; 120
             d) 26, 28, 30; 336   e) 120, 170, 250; 9,000   f) 52, 56, 60; 1,344
             g) 10, 10, 10; 25√3 ≈ 43.30   h) 20, 20, 24; 192
             i) 10, 10, 16; 48   j) 36, 40, 68; 576   k) 14, 48, 50; 336
             l) 50, 34, 24; 360   m) 4, 6, 8; 3√15 ≈ 11.62

M9. Can the three lengths be the sides of a triangle? Answer "triangle"
    (and give the area), "flat" (a + b = c, area 0) or "no triangle"

    a) 3, 4, 5     b) 3, 4, 7     c) 3, 4, 8     d) 2, 2, 3     e) 1, 2, 3

M12. These are right-angled triangles (hypotenuse last). Find the area by Heron
     and check it with 1/2 × leg × leg.
     a) 6, 8, 10
     b) 5, 12, 13
     c) 8, 15, 17
     d) 7, 24, 25

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always set out s, s − a, s − b, s − c in a column and check that
  the last three add up to s; factorise into primes before taking the square
  root; start with right triangles (3, 4, 5; 5, 12, 13) where 1/2 × base ×
  height gives the same answer as a check; draw every quadrilateral and mark the
  diagonal before splitting. Harder: prove Heron's formula from Pythagoras by
  writing the height to side c in terms of a, b, c; show that 16 ×
  area² = 2a²b² + 2b²c² + 2c²a² − a⁴ − b⁴ − c⁴; find all triangles with
  whole-number sides and perimeter 12 and their areas; show that among triangles
  with perimeter 30 the equilateral one has the largest area; research
  Brahmagupta's formula √((s − a)(s − b)(s − c)(s − d)) for a cyclic
  quadrilateral.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.31 — MENSURATION: COMBINATIONS OF SOLIDS, FRUSTUM, AREAS OF SECTORS AND
             SEGMENTS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A SECTOR is the "pizza slice" between two radii and the arc; a SEGMENT is
    the region between a CHORD and its arc. For angle θ at the centre: arc
    length = (θ/360) × 2πr, sector area = (θ/360) × πr², perimeter of sector =
    arc + 2r. Also sector area = 1/2 × arc × r.
  - MINOR SEGMENT = sector − triangle OAB. Triangle OAB
    (two radii and the chord): θ = 90° gives r²/2; θ = 60° gives an equilateral
    triangle, (√3/4)r²; θ = 120° also gives (√3/4)r² (height r/2, chord r√3).
    MAJOR SEGMENT = circle − minor segment; MAJOR SECTOR = circle − minor
    sector.
  - SHADED REGIONS: area = (whole figure) − (parts removed), or the sum of
    simple pieces (squares, triangles, circles, semicircles, quadrants, sectors,
    rings π(R² − r²)). Draw and label each piece first.
  - Solids (from Stage 6): cylinder V = πr²h, CSA = 2πrh; cone V = (1/3)πr²h,
    CSA = πrl with slant l = √(r² + h²); sphere V = (4/3)πr³, SA = 4πr²;
    hemisphere V = (2/3)πr³, curved SA 2πr², total SA 3πr².
  - COMBINATIONS: VOLUMES ADD (toy = cone + hemisphere). For SURFACE area add
    only the surfaces you can SEE or touch from outside; the faces where two
    solids are joined are hidden. A cube with a hemisphere scooped out:
    SA = 6a² − πr² + 2πr².
  - CONVERSION (melting and recasting): the VOLUME stays the same. Number of
    small objects = volume of big solid ÷ volume of one small object. Earth dug
    out = earth piled up.
  - FRUSTUM (bucket, glass, lampshade): the piece of a cone between two parallel
    circles of radii R and r, height h. Slant height l = √(h² + (R − r)²);
    V = (1/3)πh(R² + Rr + r²); CSA = π(R + r)l; TSA = π(R + r)l + πR² + πr². A
    frustum is a big cone minus a small cone.
  - π: give EXACT answers in terms of π (e.g. 3328π cm³) and approximate answers
    with π = 22/7 (neat when radii are multiples of 7) or π ≈ 3.14; always say
    which value you used. Capacity: 1,000 cm³ = 1 litre, 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A car has two wipers which do not overlap. Each blade is 21 cm long and
    sweeps through an angle of 120°. Find the total area cleaned at each sweep.
    (π = 22/7)
    Answer: 2 × 462 = 924 cm².
    Teacher explains: Each blade sweeps a SECTOR of radius 21 cm and angle 120°,
    which is 120/360 = 1/3 of a full circle.
       sector area = θ/360 × πr²
                   = 120/360 × 22/7 × 21 × 21
                   = 1/3 × 22 × 3 × 21 = 462 cm²
       two wipers  = 2 × 462 = 924 cm²
    Cancel before multiplying: 21 ÷ 7 = 3 and 21 ÷ 3 = 7. In terms of π one
    sector is 147π cm² (1/3 × 441π). Common mistakes: using the arc formula
    (2πr) instead of the area formula (πr²), and forgetting the second wiper.
    Now you try: a sprinkler of range 14 m waters a sector of 90°. (154 m²)

D2. The bob of a pendulum 35 cm long swings along an arc of length 22 cm.
    Through what angle does the pendulum swing? What area does the string sweep?
    (π = 22/7)
    Answer: θ = 36°; area swept = 385 cm².
    Teacher explains: Arc length = θ/360 × 2πr. Put in the numbers and solve for
    θ:
       θ/360 × 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 22
       θ/360 × 220 = 22
       θ = 22 × 360/220 = 36°
    The swept region is a sector: area = 36/360 × 22/7 × 35 × 35 = 385 cm². A
    quick check uses area = 1/2 × arc × radius = 1/2 × 22 × 35 = 385 cm² (a
    sector is like a "triangle" with base = arc and height = r). Common mistake:
    writing θ = 22/220 = 0.1 and forgetting the 360. Now you try: a 21 cm
    pendulum swings through 60°. How long is the arc? (22 cm)

D3. A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends a right angle at the centre.
    Find the areas of the minor segment and the major segment. (Exact, then with
    π = 3.14.)
    Answer: Minor segment = 25π − 50 ≈ 28.5 cm²; major
    segment = 75π + 50 ≈ 285.5 cm² (π = 3.14).
    Teacher explains:
              O
             /|        OA = OB = 10 cm, ∠AOB = 90°
          10/ |10      minor segment = region between
           /__|        chord AB and the short arc AB
          A    B
    Minor segment = sector OAB − triangle OAB.
       sector   = 90/360 × π × 10² = 25π
       triangle = 1/2 × 10 × 10   = 50   (right angle at O)
       minor    = 25π − 50 ≈ 78.5 − 50 = 28.5 cm²
       major    = 100π − (25π − 50) = 75π + 50
                ≈ 235.5 + 50 = 285.5 cm²
    Check: minor + major = 28.5 + 285.5 = 314 = 3.14 × 100, the whole circle.
    Common mistake: major segment = circle − sector (that is the major SECTOR).
    Note the sign: subtracting a segment that already has "− 50" gives "+ 50".
    Now you try: radius 14 cm, right angle, π = 22/7. (minor 154 − 98 = 56 cm²)

D4. In a circle of radius 12 cm find the area of the minor segment cut off by a
    chord that subtends (a) 60° and (b) 120° at the centre.
    Answer: (a) 24π − 36√3 ≈ 13.04 cm²; (b) 48π − 36√3 ≈ 88.44 cm².
    Teacher explains: (a) With θ = 60°, triangle OAB has OA = OB and the angle
    between them 60°, so the other two angles are also 60°: it is EQUILATERAL
    with side 12. Area = (√3/4) × 12² = 36√3. Sector = 60/360 × π × 144 = 24π.
    Segment = 24π − 36√3 ≈ 75.398 − 62.354 = 13.044 ≈ 13.04 cm²
    (calculator values).
    (b) With θ = 120°, drop the perpendicular OM onto the chord. It bisects the
    angle, making two 30°-60°-90° triangles:
       OM = r/2 = 6,  AM = (√3/2)r = 6√3,  AB = 12√3
       triangle = 1/2 × 12√3 × 6 = 36√3
       sector   = 120/360 × π × 144 = 48π
       segment  = 48π − 36√3 ≈ 150.796 − 62.354
                = 88.442 ≈ 88.44 cm²
    So for BOTH 60° and 120° the triangle is (√3/4)r². Keep answers exact until
    the end. Now you try: radius 6 cm, θ = 60°. (6π − 9√3 ≈ 3.26 cm²)

D5. A square lawn ABCD has side 14 m. At each corner there is a flower bed in
    the shape of a quadrant of radius 7 m. Find the area of the lawn left for
    grass (π = 22/7). What if instead one circular bed of diameter 14 m is
    placed in the middle?
    Answer: 196 − 154 = 42 m² in both cases.
    Teacher explains:
       +-----------+      quadrants of radius 7 at the corners
       |.-'     '-.|      four quarter circles make
       |           |      one full circle of radius 7
       |   grass   |      grass = square − circle
       |           |
       |'-.     .-'|
       +-----------+
    Four quadrants (quarter circles) of the same radius make one whole circle:
    area = 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154 m². Grass = 14 × 14 − 154 = 196 − 154 = 42 m². The
    single central circle of diameter 14 m also has radius 7 m, so the grass is
    again 42 m²: different pictures, same pieces. Method for any shaded region:
    (1) name the outer shape, (2) list the pieces removed, (3) subtract. Now you
    try: a circle of radius 7 cm drawn inside a square of side 14 cm; find the
    area outside the circle but inside the square in terms of π. (196 − 49π cm²)

D6. A running track has two straight parts of 100 m and two semicircular ends.
    The inner radius of each end is 35 m and the track is 7 m wide. Find the
    distance round the inner edge, round the outer edge, and the area of the
    track. (π = 22/7)
    Answer: Inner 420 m; outer 464 m; area 3,094 m².
    Teacher explains:
         ______________100 m______________
       /   ____________________________   \
      |   /                            \   |   ends: semicircles
      |   \____________________________/   |   r = 35, R = 42
       \______________________________ ___/
    Two semicircles make one full circle, so each edge = 2 straights + one
    circumference. Inner: 2 × 100 + 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 200 + 220 = 420 m. Outer
    radius = 35 + 7 = 42 m: 2 × 100 + 2 × 22/7 × 42 = 200 + 264 = 464 m. Area =
    two rectangles 100 × 7 + one ring:
       area = 2 × 100 × 7 + 22/7 × (42² − 35²)
            = 1,400 + 22/7 × 539 = 1,400 + 1,694 = 3,094 m²
    That is why runners in outer lanes start further ahead: the outer edge is
    44 m longer. Common mistake: working out (42 − 35)² instead of 42² − 35².
    Now you try: the difference between outer and inner edges for a track 3.5 m
    wide. (2 × 22/7 × 3.5 = 22 m)

D7. A wooden toy is a cone standing on a hemisphere of the same radius 3.5 cm.
    The total height of the toy is 15.5 cm. Find its total surface area and its
    volume. (π = 22/7)
    Answer: Surface area = 214.5 cm²; volume = 1,463/6 ≈ 243.83 cm³.
    Teacher explains:
            /\
           /  \      cone: h = 15.5 − 3.5 = 12, r = 3.5
          /    \     slant l = √(12² + 3.5²) = √156.25 = 12.5
         /______\
         \      /    hemisphere: r = 3.5
          `-..-'
    SURFACE: the flat circle where the two parts meet is hidden, so add only the
    curved surfaces:
       SA = 2πr² + πrl = πr(2r + l)
          = 22/7 × 3.5 × (7 + 12.5) = 11 × 19.5 = 214.5 cm²
    VOLUME: volumes simply add:
       V = 2/3 × πr³ + 1/3 × πr²h = 1/3 × πr²(2r + h)
         = 1/3 × 22/7 × 12.25 × (7 + 12) = 1/3 × 38.5 × 19
         = 731.5/3 ≈ 243.83 cm³
    Common mistakes: using the total height 15.5 as the cone's height, using the
    height instead of the slant height in πrl, and adding the hidden base
    circles to the surface. Now you try: a cone of radius 7 cm and height 24 cm
    on a hemisphere of radius 7 cm; find its surface area.
    (2 × 154 + 22/7 × 7 × 25 = 858 cm²)

D8. A tent is a cylinder of diameter 4 m and height 2.1 m with a conical top of
    the same base and slant height 2.8 m. Find the canvas needed (no floor) and
    its cost at ₹500 per m². (π = 22/7)
    Answer: 14π ≈ 44 m² of canvas; cost ₹22,000.
    Teacher explains: Canvas covers the curved side of the cylinder and the
    curved surface of the cone; the floor is not covered and the join is hidden.
       cylinder: 2πrh = 2 × π × 2 × 2.1 = 8.4π
       cone:     πrl  = π × 2 × 2.8     = 5.6π
       total = 14π ≈ 14 × 22/7 = 44 m²
       cost  = 44 × 500 = ₹22,000
    Work in terms of π and substitute once at the end: fewer steps, fewer
    errors. Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 2 m — using 4 m by mistake would double
    every answer. Now you try: cylinder r = 3.5 m, h = 2 m, cone slant 5 m.
    (22/7 × 3.5 × (4 + 5) = 99 m²)

D9. A hemisphere of diameter 7 cm is scooped out of one face of a wooden cube of
    edge 7 cm. Find the surface area and the volume of the solid that is left.
    (π = 22/7)
    Answer: Surface area = 332.5 cm²; volume = 1,519/6 ≈ 253.17 cm³.
    Teacher explains: SURFACE: from the 6 faces (6 × 49 = 294) we lose a circle
    of radius 3.5 on the top face, but we gain the inside of the bowl, a curved
    hemisphere of area 2πr²:
       SA = 6a² − πr² + 2πr² = 294 + πr²
          = 294 + 22/7 × 12.25 = 294 + 38.5 = 332.5 cm²
    VOLUME: removing wood lowers the volume:
       V = a³ − 2/3 × πr³ = 343 − 2/3 × 22/7 × 42.875
         = 343 − 539/6 = 1,519/6 ≈ 253.17 cm³
    Interesting fact: if the hemisphere were stuck ON TOP instead, the surface
    area would also be 294 + πr² = 332.5 cm², but the volume would INCREASE to
    343 + 539/6. Scooping out makes the surface bigger even though the solid is
    smaller. Now you try: a cube of edge 14 cm with a hemisphere of radius 7 cm
    scooped out; find its surface area. (1,176 + 154 = 1,330 cm²)

D10. A solid metal cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 18 cm is melted and recast
     into small spheres of radius 1 cm. How many spheres are made? A metal
     sphere of radius 4.2 cm is melted and recast into a cylinder of radius
     6 cm. Find the height of the cylinder.
     Answer: 216 spheres; height 2.744 cm.
     Teacher explains: When a solid is melted and recast, the VOLUME does not
     change.
        cylinder: V = π × 4² × 18 = 288π
        one ball: V = 4/3 × π × 1³ = 4π/3
        number  = 288π ÷ (4π/3) = 288 × 3/4 = 216
     π cancels, so there is no need to choose a value for it. Second part:
     πR²h = (4/3)πr³, so 36h = 4/3 × 4.2³ = 4/3 × 74.088 = 98.784 and
     h = 98.784 ÷ 36 = 2.744 cm. Common mistakes: comparing surface areas
     instead of volumes, and forgetting to cube the radius. Now you try: how
     many balls of radius 0.5 cm can be made from a sphere of radius 3 cm?
     (3³ ÷ 0.5³ = 216)

D11. A bucket is a frustum of a cone with top radius 20 cm, bottom radius 8 cm
     and depth 16 cm. Find its capacity in litres and the area of metal sheet
     used (it has a bottom but no lid).
     Answer: Capacity = 3,328π ≈ 10,455.22 cm³ ≈ 10.46 litres;
     sheet = 624π ≈ 1,960.35 cm².
     Teacher explains:
        R = 20 ___________
              \         /     depth h = 16
               \_______/      R − r = 20 − 8 = 12
                 r = 8
        l = √(h² + (R − r)²) = √(16² + 12²) = √400 = 20
        V = 1/3 × πh(R² + Rr + r²)
          = 1/3 × π × 16 × (400 + 160 + 64)
          = 1/3 × π × 16 × 624 = 3,328π ≈ 10,455.22 cm³
     1,000 cm³ = 1 litre, so the bucket holds about 10.46 litres. Metal: curved
     surface π(R + r)l = π × 28 × 20 = 560π, plus the bottom πr² = 64π: total
     624π ≈ 1,960.35 cm². The slant height uses R − r (the difference of the
     radii), not R. Common mistake: including the top circle
     (the bucket is open). Now you try: a frustum with R = 7, r = 4, h = 4 cm:
     find l and the curved surface area. (l = 5, 55π ≈ 172.79 cm²)

D12. Explain where the frustum formula V = (1/3)πh(R² + Rr + r²) comes from.
     Check it on a cone of radius 10 cm and height 30 cm cut in half by a plane
     parallel to its base halfway up.
     Answer: A frustum is a big cone minus a small cone. For the example both
     ways give 875π cm³.
     Teacher explains: Complete the frustum to a cone of height H + h over the
     small circle. By similar triangles r/R = H/(H + h), so H = rh/(R − r) and
     H + h = Rh/(R − r). Then
        V = 1/3 × πR²(H + h) − 1/3 × πr²H
          = 1/3 × π × (R³ − r³) × h/(R − r)
          = 1/3 × πh(R² + Rr + r²)
     using R³ − r³ = (R − r)(R² + Rr + r²). Example: the whole cone has
     V = 1/3 × π × 10² × 30 = 1,000π. Halfway up the radius is 5
     (similar triangles), so the small cone on top has V = 1/3 ×
     π × 5² × 15 = 125π. Frustum = 1,000π − 125π = 875π. Formula: 1/3 ×
     π × 15 × (100 + 50 + 25) = 5π × 175 = 875π. Notice the frustum is 7/8 of
     the cone although it is only half the height. Now you try: check with
     R = 6, r = 3, h = 4 (full cone height 8). (1/3 × π × 4 × 63 = 84π;
     96π − 12π = 84π)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Find the arc length and the sector area (π = 22/7; r in cm). Answer: arc,
    area.
    a) r = 7, θ = 90°       b) r = 7, θ = 60°       c) r = 7, θ = 180°
    d) r = 14, θ = 45°      e) r = 14, θ = 90°      f) r = 14, θ = 30°
    g) r = 21, θ = 60°      h) r = 21, θ = 120°     i) r = 21, θ = 40°
    j) r = 21, θ = 240°     k) r = 28, θ = 45°      l) r = 28, θ = 270°
    m) r = 35, θ = 72°      n) r = 35, θ = 36°      o) r = 42, θ = 30°
    p) r = 42, θ = 150°     q) r = 3.5, θ = 90°     r) r = 10.5, θ = 120°
    s) r = 7, θ = 360°      t) r = 14, θ = 135°
    Answers: a) 11, 38.5   b) 22/3, 77/3   c) 22, 77   d) 11, 77   e) 22, 154
             f) 22/3, 154/3   g) 22, 231   h) 44, 462   i) 44/3, 154
             j) 88, 924   k) 22, 308   l) 132, 1,848   m) 44, 770   n) 22, 385
