TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw every figure and label r, h, l and θ on it; write the
  fraction θ/360 first and simplify it (90° is 1/4, 60° is 1/6, 120° is 1/3);
  keep a formula card for sector, segment, cone, sphere and frustum; for
  combined solids colour the surfaces you can see and cross out the hidden ones;
  for recasting write "volume before = volume after" as the first line. Harder:
  show that sector area = 1/2 × arc × r; find the area of the Reuleaux triangle
  on side a (π/2 − √3/2)a²; prove that the volume of a hemisphere, cone and
  cylinder of equal radius and height r are in the ratio 2 : 1 : 3; find the
  height of a frustum whose volume equals half the cone it was cut from; design
  a bucket that holds exactly 10 litres with R = 2r.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.32 — TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS IN RIGHT TRIANGLES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - In a right-angled triangle, name the sides FROM THE ANGLE you are using: the
    HYPOTENUSE is opposite the right angle (always the longest side); the
    OPPOSITE side is across from the angle A; the ADJACENT side is next to A
    (and is not the hypotenuse). Change the angle and opposite and adjacent
    swap.
  - The six TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS of an acute angle A: sin A =
    opposite/hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan A = opposite/adjacent
    (memory aid SOH CAH TOA), and their reciprocals cosec A = 1/sin A = hyp/opp,
    sec A = 1/cos A = hyp/adj, cot A = 1/tan A = adj/opp.
  - QUOTIENT relations: tan A = sin A/cos A and cot A = cos A/sin A. "sin A" is
    ONE symbol (the sine of angle A), never "sin × A".
  - The ratios depend only on the ANGLE, not on the size of the triangle:
    triangles with the same angles are SIMILAR, so their side ratios are equal.
  - Because the hypotenuse is the longest side, 0 < sin A < 1 and 0 < cos A < 1
    for acute A, so cosec A > 1 and sec A > 1; tan A and cot A can be any
    positive number (tan A > 1 when A > 45°).
  - Given ONE ratio, find the others: draw a right triangle, label the two known
    sides as multiples of k (sin A = 3/5: opposite 3k, hypotenuse 5k), find the
    third side by Pythagoras (4k), then read off every ratio. Given a ratio and
    a side, find the other sides by scaling.
  - COMPLEMENTARY ANGLES: in triangle ABC with ∠B = 90°, A + C = 90°, and the
    side opposite A is adjacent to C. So sin(90° − A) = cos A, cos(90° − A) =
    sin A, tan(90° − A) = cot A, cot(90° − A) = tan A, sec(90° − A) = cosec A,
    cosec(90° − A) = sec A. Example: sin 72° = cos 18°, so sin 72°/cos 18° = 1.
  - Notation: sin²A means (sin A)², not sin(A²). Leave surd answers
    rationalised: 1/√5 = √5/5.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. In triangle ABC, ∠B = 90°, AB = 4 cm, BC = 3 cm and AC = 5 cm. Name the
    hypotenuse, the opposite side and the adjacent side for angle A, and again
    for angle C. Then write sin A and sin C.
    Answer: For A: hypotenuse AC = 5, opposite BC = 3, adjacent AB = 4, so
    sin A = 3/5. For C: hypotenuse AC = 5, opposite AB = 4, adjacent BC = 3, so
    sin C = 4/5.
    Teacher explains:
          A
          |\
        4 | \ 5          hypotenuse: opposite the right angle
          |  \           opposite:   across from the angle
          |_  \          adjacent:   touches the angle
          |_|__\
          B  3  C
    Stand at the angle you are working with and look across the triangle: the
    side you see is the OPPOSITE side. Of the two sides touching the angle, the
    longer one (across from the right angle) is the HYPOTENUSE and the other is
    ADJACENT. The hypotenuse never changes, but opposite and adjacent SWAP when
    we move from A to C. That is why sin A = 3/5 but sin C = 4/5. Common
    mistake: calling the hypotenuse the adjacent side because it touches the
    angle. Now you try: in the same triangle, write cos A and cos C.
    (cos A = 4/5, cos C = 3/5)

D2. In triangle ABC right-angled at B, AB = 12 cm, BC = 5 cm and AC = 13 cm.
    Write all six trigonometric ratios of angle A.
    Answer: sin A = 5/13, cos A = 12/13, tan A = 5/12, cosec A = 13/5,
    sec A = 13/12, cot A = 12/5.
    Teacher explains: For angle A: opposite = BC = 5, adjacent = AB = 12,
    hypotenuse = AC = 13. Check first that the sides fit Pythagoras:
    5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². Then use SOH CAH TOA:
       sin A = opp/hyp = 5/13      cosec A = hyp/opp = 13/5
       cos A = adj/hyp = 12/13     sec A   = hyp/adj = 13/12
       tan A = opp/adj = 5/12      cot A   = adj/opp = 12/5
    The right-hand column is the left-hand column turned upside down: these are
    the RECIPROCAL ratios. Check a quotient relation: sin A ÷
    cos A = (5/13) ÷ (12/13) = 5/12 = tan A. Common mistake: pairing cosec with
    cos and sec with sin — it is the other way round (each pair has exactly one
    "co"). Now you try: AB = 8, BC = 15, AC = 17. (sin A = 15/17, cos A = 8/17,
    tan A = 15/8, cosec A = 17/15, sec A = 17/8, cot A = 8/15)

D3. Two wheelchair ramps rise at the same angle A. Ramp P rises 0.5 m over a
    sloping length of 6 m; ramp Q is 9 m long. How high does Q rise? Explain why
    sin A is the same for both.
    Answer: Q rises 0.75 m; sin A = 0.5/6 = 0.75/9 = 1/12 for both.
    Teacher explains: Drop a vertical from the top of each ramp: each ramp is
    the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the same angle A. Two right
    triangles with an equal acute angle have all three angles equal, so they are
    SIMILAR (AA), and corresponding sides are in the same ratio. Hence
    rise/length is the same number for both — and that number is sin A. So
    sin A = 0.5/6 = 1/12, and for Q: height = 9 × sin A = 9 × 1/12 = 0.75 m.
    This is why a trigonometric ratio is a property of the ANGLE alone: we can
    build tables of sin, cos and tan and use them for any triangle. Common
    mistake: thinking a bigger triangle with the same angle has a bigger sine.
    Now you try: a 4 m ramp at the same angle; how high? (1/3 m ≈ 0.33 m)

D4. If sin A = 3/5 (A acute), find the other five trigonometric ratios of A.
    Answer: cos A = 4/5, tan A = 3/4, cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 5/4, cot A = 4/3.
    Teacher explains: sin A = opp/hyp = 3/5 does NOT say that the sides are 3
    and 5, only that they are in the ratio 3 : 5. So take opposite = 3k and
    hypotenuse = 5k (k > 0). By Pythagoras:
       adjacent² = (5k)² − (3k)² = 25k² − 9k² = 16k²
       adjacent  = 4k
    Now every ratio: cos A = 4k/5k = 4/5, tan A = 3k/4k = 3/4, and the
    reciprocals cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 5/4, cot A = 4/3. The k always cancels,
    which is the similar-triangles idea again. Common mistake: finding the third
    side as 5 − 3 = 2. Now you try: cos A = 12/13. (sin A = 5/13, tan A = 5/12,
    cosec A = 13/5, sec A = 13/12, cot A = 12/5)

D5. If cot θ = 7/8, evaluate (1 + sin θ)(1 − sin θ) ÷ [(1 + cos θ)(1 − cos θ)].
    Answer: 49/64.
    Teacher explains: Take adjacent = 7k, opposite = 8k; hypotenuse =
    √(49k² + 64k²) = k√113. So sin θ = 8/√113 and cos θ = 7/√113. Use
    (1 + x)(1 − x) = 1 − x² on top and bottom:
       top    = 1 − sin²θ = 1 − 64/113 = 49/113
       bottom = 1 − cos²θ = 1 − 49/113 = 64/113
       value  = (49/113) ÷ (64/113) = 49/64
    Notice 49/64 = (7/8)² = cot²θ. That is no accident: next topic we prove 1 −
    sin²θ = cos²θ, so the expression is cos²θ/sin²θ = cot²θ. A surd hypotenuse
    such as √113 is common; keep it exact. Now you try: if tan θ = 3/4, evaluate
    (1 − sin²θ)/(1 − cos²θ). (16/25 ÷ 9/25 = 16/9)

D6. A ramp makes an angle A with the ground where sin A = 5/13. The top of the
    ramp is 1.5 m above the ground. How long is the ramp, and how far does it
    reach along the ground?
    Answer: Length 3.9 m; horizontal distance 3.6 m.
    Teacher explains: sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, and the opposite side
    (the height) is 1.5 m:
       1.5/L = 5/13   so   L = 1.5 × 13/5 = 3.9 m
       cos A = 12/13  (5-12-13 triangle)
       ground = L × cos A = 3.9 × 12/13 = 3.6 m
    Check with Pythagoras: 1.5² + 3.6² = 2.25 + 12.96 = 15.21 = 3.9². To find a
    side: write the ratio that contains the known side and the unknown side,
    then solve. Scale factor view: 5 parts = 1.5 m, so 1 part = 0.3 m, 13
    parts = 3.9 m, 12 parts = 3.6 m. Now you try: tan A = 3/4 and the ground
    distance is 20 m; find the height and the hypotenuse. (15 m, 25 m)

D7. A right triangle has legs 1 cm (opposite A) and 2 cm (adjacent to A). Find
    all six ratios of A, rationalising the denominators.
    Answer: sin A = √5/5, cos A = 2√5/5, tan A = 1/2, cosec A = √5, sec A =
    √5/2, cot A = 2.
    Teacher explains: Hypotenuse = √(1² + 2²) = √5. Then sin A = 1/√5 and
    cos A = 2/√5. To RATIONALISE, multiply top and bottom by √5:
       sin A = 1/√5 = √5/5         cosec A = √5
       cos A = 2/√5 = 2√5/5        sec A   = √5/2
       tan A = 1/2                 cot A   = 2
    Both forms are correct; the rationalised form is easier to compare and to
    add. Approximate check: √5 ≈ 2.236, so sin A ≈ 0.447 and cos A ≈ 0.894, both
    less than 1 as they must be. Now you try: legs 1 and 1. (sin = cos = √2/2,
    tan = cot = 1, cosec = sec = √2)

D8. Explain why tan A = sin A/cos A and why sec A × cos A = 1. If sin A = 0.6
    and cos A = 0.8, find the other four ratios.
    Answer: tan A = 0.75, cot A = 4/3, cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 1.25.
    Teacher explains: Write each ratio with its sides (o, a, h for opposite,
    adjacent, hypotenuse):
       sin A/cos A = (o/h) ÷ (a/h) = o/h × h/a = o/a = tan A
       sec A × cos A = h/a × a/h = 1
    So we never need the sides once we know sin and cos: tan A = 0.6/0.8 = 0.75,
    cot A = 0.8/0.6 = 4/3, cosec A = 1/0.6 = 5/3, sec A = 1/0.8 = 1.25. Each
    ratio has a partner that multiplies with it to give 1: sin with cosec, cos
    with sec, tan with cot. Common mistake: thinking that 1/0.6 is 1.6
    (it is 1.666...). Now you try: sin A = 0.28 and cos A = 0.96. (tan A = 7/24,
    cot A = 24/7, cosec A = 25/7, sec A = 25/24)

D9. In triangle ABC with ∠B = 90°, show that sin C = cos A and tan C = cot A.
    Deduce the six complementary-angle rules.
    Answer: Since A + C = 90°, C = 90° − A, and sin(90° − A) = cos A,
    cos(90° − A) = sin A, tan(90° − A) = cot A, cot(90° − A) = tan A,
    sec(90° − A) = cosec A, cosec(90° − A) = sec A.
    Teacher explains: Angle sum: A + 90° + C = 180°, so C = 90° − A: A and C are
    COMPLEMENTARY. The side BC is opposite A but adjacent to C; the side AB is
    adjacent to A but opposite C; AC is the hypotenuse for both.
       sin C = AB/AC = cos A      cos C = BC/AC = sin A
       tan C = AB/BC = cot A      cot C = BC/AB = tan A
       sec C = AC/BC = cosec A    cosec C = AC/AB = sec A
    Replace C by 90° − A to get the rules. The names tell the story: "co-sine"
    is the sine of the COmplement. Examples: sin 70° = cos 20°, tan 65° =
    cot 25°, sec 80° = cosec 10°. Now you try: write cos 58° and cot 85° as
    ratios of the complementary angles. (sin 32°, tan 5°)

D10. Without tables, evaluate (a) sin 18°/cos 72°, (b) tan 26°/cot 64°, (c)
     cos 48° − sin 42°, (d) cosec 31° − sec 59°. Also write sin 67° + cos 75°
     using angles between 0° and 45°.
     Answer: (a) 1 (b) 1 (c) 0 (d) 0; sin 67° + cos 75° = cos 23° + sin 15°.
     Teacher explains: Look for two angles that add to 90°, then change one
     ratio into its co-ratio:
        (a) cos 72° = sin(90° − 72°) = sin 18°, so the value is 1
        (b) cot 64° = tan 26°, so the value is 1
        (c) sin 42° = cos 48°, so the value is 0
        (d) sec 59° = cosec 31°, so the value is 0
     For the last part: 67° = 90° − 23°, so sin 67° = cos 23°; 75° = 90° − 15°,
     so cos 75° = sin 15°. A calculator check: sin 18° ≈ 0.3090 and
     cos 72° ≈ 0.3090. Common mistake: cancelling "sin" against "cos" or
     subtracting the angles. Now you try: tan 35° × tan 55°.
     (tan 35° × cot 35° = 1)

D11. Find the acute angle A if (a) tan 2A = cot(A − 18°), (b) sec 4A =
     cosec(A − 20°) where 4A is acute.
     Answer: (a) A = 36° (b) A = 22°.
     Teacher explains: Rewrite one side with the co-ratio and compare angles.
     (a) cot(A − 18°) = tan(90° − (A − 18°)) = tan(108° − A), so
        2A = 108° − A   →   3A = 108°   →   A = 36°
     Check: 2A = 72° and A − 18° = 18°, and tan 72° = cot 18° since
     72° + 18° = 90°. (b) sec 4A = cosec(90° − 4A), so 90° − 4A = A − 20°,
     giving 5A = 110° and A = 22°. Check: 4A = 88° and A − 20° = 2°, which add
     to 90°. Shortcut: if f(X) = co-f(Y) with X and Y acute, then X + Y = 90°.
     Now you try: sin 3A = cos(A − 26°). (A = 29°)

D12. Which of these are possible for an acute angle A? (a) sin A = 4/3 (b)
     cos A = 0.99 (c) tan A = 7 (d) sec A = 0.5 (e) cosec A = 1.2. Give reasons.
     Also: if 3 cot A = 4, check that (1 − tan²A)/(1 + tan²A) = cos²A − sin²A.
     Answer: (a) no (b) yes (c) yes (d) no (e) yes. Both sides of the check
     equal 7/25.
     Teacher explains: sin A and cos A are "side ÷ hypotenuse", and the
     hypotenuse is the LONGEST side, so they lie between 0 and 1: (a) 4/3 > 1 is
     impossible; (b) 0.99 is fine (a very small angle). tan A = opp/adj can be
     any positive number: (c) is fine (a steep angle). sec A = hyp/adj > 1
     always, so (d) 0.5 is impossible, and cosec A = 1.2 > 1 is possible. For
     the check: cot A = 4/3, so tan A = 3/4, and a 3-4-5 triangle gives
     sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5.
        (1 − 9/16)/(1 + 9/16) = (7/16)/(25/16) = 7/25
        cos²A − sin²A = 16/25 − 9/25 = 7/25
     Now you try: can cot A = 0.001? can cos A = 1.01? (yes; no)

     p) cos A = 8/17: sin²A + cos²A
     q) cos A = 8/17: (1 − tan²A)/(1 + tan²A)
     r) cos A = 8/17: sec A + tan A
     s) cot A = 7/24: cos²A − sin²A
     t) cot A = 7/24: sin²A + cos²A
     u) cot A = 7/24: (1 − tan²A)/(1 + tan²A)
     v) cot A = 7/24: sec A + tan A
     w) cot A = 7/24: (sin A − cos A)/(sin A + cos A)
     x) cot A = 7/24: cosec²A − cot²A
     Answers: a) 7/5   b) 24/25   c) −7/25   d) 1   e) −7/25   f) 3   g) 17/13
              h) 120/169   i) 119/169   j) 1   k) 119/169   l) 3/2   m) 23/17
              n) 240/289   o) −161/289   p) 1   q) −161/289   r) 4   s) −527/625
              t) 1   u) −527/625   v) 7   w) 17/31   x) 1

M12. Triangle PQR has ∠Q = 90°. Use PR² − QR² = PQ², so PR − QR =
     PQ² ÷ (PR + QR). Find QR and PR, then sin P, cos P, tan P.
     a) PQ = 5, PR + QR = 25    b) PQ = 8, PR + QR = 32
     c) PQ = 7, PR + QR = 49    d) PQ = 12, PR + QR = 18
     e) PQ = 9, PR + QR = 81    f) PQ = 20, PR + QR = 50
     g) PQ = 15, PR + QR = 25   h) PQ = 24, PR + QR = 36
     i) PQ = 6, PR + QR = 18    j) PQ = 3, PR + QR = 9
     k) PQ = 10, PR + QR = 50   l) PQ = 16, PR + QR = 32
     Answers: a) QR = 12, PR = 13; 12/13, 5/13, 12/5
              b) QR = 15, PR = 17; 15/17, 8/17, 15/8
              c) QR = 24, PR = 25; 24/25, 7/25, 24/7
              d) QR = 5, PR = 13; 5/13, 12/13, 5/12
              e) QR = 40, PR = 41; 40/41, 9/41, 40/9
              f) QR = 21, PR = 29; 21/29, 20/29, 21/20
              g) QR = 8, PR = 17; 8/17, 15/17, 8/15
              h) QR = 10, PR = 26; 5/13, 12/13, 5/12
              i) QR = 8, PR = 10; 4/5, 3/5, 4/3
              j) QR = 4, PR = 5; 4/5, 3/5, 4/3
              k) QR = 24, PR = 26; 12/13, 5/13, 12/5
              l) QR = 12, PR = 20; 3/5, 4/5, 3/4

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: label the sides O, A, H from the angle before writing any ratio;
  keep a SOH CAH TOA card and a "reciprocal pairs" card (sin with cosec, cos
  with sec, tan with cot); always check the triangle with Pythagoras first; for
  complementary angles draw the triangle and look from the other acute angle;
  use only Pythagorean triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17) until the method is
  secure. Harder: show that sin A < A (in radians) < tan A using areas of a
  sector and two triangles; prove that sin A + cos A ≤ √2; find sin 15° using a
  30-60-90 triangle with a 15° extension; if sin A = (p² − q²)/(p² + q²), find
  the other five ratios; explore with a spreadsheet how sin A and cos A change
  as A goes from 0° to 90°.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.33 — TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS OF STANDARD ANGLES (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The EXACT values below come from two triangles: the right isosceles triangle
    (45°-45°-90°, sides 1, 1, √2) and half of an equilateral triangle
    (30°-60°-90°, sides 1, √3, 2). Learn them; they are used in every later
    topic.
  - sin: 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1 for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° (pattern √0/2, √1/2,
    √2/2, √3/2, √4/2). cos: the same list backwards. tan = sin/cos: 0, 1/√3, 1,
    √3, not defined. cosec, sec, cot are the reciprocals.
  - tan 90°, sec 90°, cot 0° and cosec 0° are NOT DEFINED (division by zero).
    Never write them as 0 or "infinity".
  - As A increases from 0° to 90°: sin A increases from 0 to 1, cos A decreases
    from 1 to 0, tan A increases from 0 without limit. sin A = cos A only at
    45°.
  - EVALUATING: replace each ratio by its exact value in brackets, square where
    there is a ² (sin²60° = (√3/2)² = 3/4), then simplify fractions and surds.
    Rationalise at the end.
  - SOLVING: turn the value back into an angle using the table: sin 2θ = √3/2
    with 2θ acute gives 2θ = 60°, θ = 30°. For two unknowns, e.g. sin(A + B) = 1
    and cos(A − B) = √3/2, get A + B = 90° and A − B = 30°, then solve the pair
    of equations (A = 60°, B = 30°).
  - Ratios do NOT distribute: sin(A + B) ≠ sin A + sin B and sin 2A ≠ 2 sin A in
    general. Test claimed rules at standard angles; one failure disproves a
    rule.
  - Decimal values: √2/2 ≈ 0.707, √3/2 ≈ 0.866, √3 ≈ 1.732, √3/3 ≈ 0.577.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Use a right-angled isosceles triangle to find sin 45°, cos 45° and tan 45°.
    Answer: sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2 = √2/2, tan 45° = 1.
    Teacher explains:
          C
          |\
        a |  \  a√2      ∠A = ∠C = 45°
          |_   \         AB = BC = a
          |_|____\        AC² = a² + a² = 2a²
          B   a   A
    In triangle ABC with ∠B = 90° and AB = BC = a, the base angles are equal, so
    each is (180° − 90°)/2 = 45°. Pythagoras: AC = √(2a²) = a√2. For angle A:
    opposite = BC = a, adjacent = AB = a, hypotenuse = a√2.
       sin 45° = a/(a√2) = 1/√2 = √2/2
       cos 45° = a/(a√2) = 1/√2 = √2/2
       tan 45° = a/a = 1
    The a cancels: the size of the triangle does not matter. So cosec 45° =
    sec 45° = √2 and cot 45° = 1. Common mistake: writing 1/2 for sin 45°
    (1/2 is sin 30°). Now you try: check that sin²45° + cos²45° = 1.
    (1/2 + 1/2 = 1)

D2. Cut an equilateral triangle of side 2a in half to find the six ratios of 30°
    and 60°.
    Answer: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3 = √3/3; sin 60° =
    √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3.
    Teacher explains:
              A
             /|\          all angles of ABC are 60°
         2a /30|  \ 2a    AD ⊥ BC halves the base and ∠A
           /   |   \      BD = a,  ∠BAD = 30°
          /60° |    \     AD² = (2a)² − a² = 3a², AD = a√3
         B-----D-----C
            a     a
    Triangle ABD has angles 30°, 60°, 90° and sides BD = a, AD = a√3, AB = 2a
    (ratio 1 : √3 : 2; the shortest side is opposite 30°).
       angle 30° (at A): opp = a, adj = a√3, hyp = 2a
          sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3 = √3/3
       angle 60° (at B): opp = a√3, adj = a, hyp = 2a
          sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3
    Notice sin 30° = cos 60° and sin 60° = cos 30°, as the complementary rule
    says. Reciprocals: cosec 30° = 2, sec 30° = 2/√3 = 2√3/3, cot 30° = √3;
    cosec 60° = 2√3/3, sec 60° = 2, cot 60° = √3/3. Now you try: find tan 30° ×
    tan 60°. (1)

D3. Explain the values of the ratios at 0° and 90°, and why tan 90° is not
    defined.
    Answer: sin 0° = 0, cos 0° = 1, tan 0° = 0; sin 90° = 1, cos 90° = 0,
    tan 90° is not defined (as are sec 90°, cot 0° and cosec 0°).
    Teacher explains: Keep the hypotenuse at length 1 and let angle A shrink
    towards 0°. The opposite side shrinks to 0 and the adjacent side stretches
    to 1, so sin A = opp/1 → 0, cos A = adj/1 → 1, tan A = opp/adj → 0. We
    DEFINE sin 0° = 0, cos 0° = 1, tan 0° = 0. Now let A grow towards 90°: the
    opposite side approaches 1 and the adjacent side approaches 0, so
    sin 90° = 1 and cos 90° = 0. But tan 90° = sin 90°/cos 90° = 1/0, and
    division by 0 has no answer: tan 90° is NOT DEFINED. Likewise sec 90° = 1/0,
    cosec 0° = 1/0 and cot 0° = 1/0 are not defined, while cot 90° = 0/1 = 0. As
    A approaches 90°, tan A grows without limit (tan 89° ≈ 57.29). Common
    mistake: writing tan 90° = 0 or = 1. Now you try: find cosec 90° and sec 0°.
    (1 and 1)

D4. Give a quick way to remember the sin, cos and tan values of 0°, 30°, 45°,
    60°, 90°, and write the full table.
    Answer: sin = √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2; cos is the same list reversed;
    tan = sin ÷ cos. The table is below.
    Teacher explains: Write the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 under the angles, take
    square roots and divide by 2: this gives sin. Reverse the list for cos.
    Divide sin by cos for tan. Then turn each upside down for cosec, sec, cot.
       A       0°       30°      45°      60°      90°
       sin A   0        1/2      √2/2     √3/2     1
       cos A   1        √3/2     √2/2     1/2      0
       tan A   0        √3/3     1        √3       n.d.
       cosec A n.d.     2        √2       2√3/3    1
       sec A   1        2√3/3    √2       2        n.d.
       cot A   n.d.     √3       1        √3/3     0
       (n.d. = not defined; 1/√2 = √2/2, 1/√3 = √3/3, 2/√3 = 2√3/3)
    Check the table with two facts: sin A = cos(90° − A) (read the sin row
    backwards to get the cos row) and sin²A + cos²A = 1 in every column, e.g. at
    60°: 3/4 + 1/4 = 1. Common mistake: swapping tan 30° and tan 60° — remember
    tan increases, so tan 30° = √3/3 ≈ 0.577 is the smaller. Now you try: from
    memory, give cot 30°, sec 45° and cosec 60°. (√3, √2, 2√3/3)

D5. Evaluate 2 sin²30° + tan²60° − cos²45°.
    Answer: 3.
    Teacher explains: Replace each ratio by its value IN BRACKETS, then square:
       2 sin²30° + tan²60° − cos²45°
       = 2(1/2)² + (√3)² − (1/√2)²
       = 2 × 1/4 + 3 − 1/2
       = 1/2 + 3 − 1/2 = 3
    sin²30° means (sin 30°)² = (1/2)² = 1/4, NOT sin(900°) and not 2 × 1/2.
    Brackets make the squaring safe, especially with surds: (√3)² = 3 and
    (1/√2)² = 1/2. Common mistake: working out (2 × 1/2)² for 2 sin²30°; the 2
    multiplies AFTER squaring. Now you try: sin²60° + cos²60° + tan²45°.
    (3/4 + 1/4 + 1 = 2)

D6. Evaluate (5 cos²60° + 4 sec²30° − tan²45°)/(sin²30° + cos²30°).
    Answer: 67/12.
    Teacher explains:
       top    = 5(1/2)² + 4(2/√3)² − 1²
              = 5/4 + 16/3 − 1 = 15/12 + 64/12 − 12/12 = 67/12
       bottom = (1/2)² + (√3/2)² = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1
       value  = 67/12 ÷ 1 = 67/12
    Work out the top and the bottom SEPARATELY, then divide. The bottom is
    sin²30° + cos²30°, which is always 1 (next topic proves sin²A + cos²A = 1
    for every A). (2/√3)² = 4/3, so 4 sec²30° = 16/3. Use a common denominator
    of 12 to add the fractions. Now you try: (sin 30° + tan 45° −
    cosec 60°)/(sec 30° + cos 60° + cot 45°). (value (3√3 − 4)/(3√3 + 4), which
    rationalises to (43 − 24√3)/11)

D7. Solve for θ: (a) sin 2θ = √3/2, (b) 2 cos 3θ = 1, (c) √3 tan(θ − 15°) = 1.
    In each case the angle inside the ratio is between 0° and 90°.
    Answer: (a) θ = 30° (b) θ = 20° (c) θ = 45°.
    Teacher explains: First make the ratio stand alone, then read the angle from
    the table, then solve the simple equation:
       (a) sin 2θ = √3/2          → 2θ = 60°          → θ = 30°
       (b) cos 3θ = 1/2           → 3θ = 60°          → θ = 20°
       (c) tan(θ − 15°) = 1/√3    → θ − 15° = 30°     → θ = 45°
    Check (a): sin(2 × 30°) = sin 60° = √3/2. The condition "between 0° and 90°"
    matters: in Stage 8 you will meet angles beyond 90° and sin 120° is also
    √3/2, which would give a second answer θ = 60°. Common mistake: dividing the
    VALUE by 2 (sin θ = √3/4) instead of the ANGLE. Now you try: tan 2θ = √3
    with 2θ acute. (θ = 30°)

D8. Find A and B (0° < B < A, A + B ≤ 90°) if (a) sin(A + B) = 1 and
    cos(A − B) = √3/2; (b) tan(A + B) = √3 and tan(A − B) = 1/√3.
    Answer: (a) A = 60°, B = 30° (b) A = 45°, B = 15°.
    Teacher explains: Turn each equation into an equation between angles, then
    solve the pair by adding and subtracting:
       (a) A + B = 90°,  A − B = 30°
           add: 2A = 120°, A = 60°;  then B = 90° − 60° = 30°
       (b) A + B = 60°,  A − B = 30°
           add: 2A = 90°,  A = 45°;  then B = 60° − 45° = 15°
    Check (b): tan(45° + 15°) = tan 60° = √3 and tan(45° − 15°) =
    tan 30° = 1/√3. This is a trigonometry question that becomes a pair of
    linear equations (topic 7.8). Now you try: cos(A − B) = 1 and sin(A + B) =
    √3/2. (A − B = 0°, A + B = 60°: A = B = 30°)

D9. Check at standard angles: (a) is sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A true for A = 30°?
    (b) is sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B true for A = 30°, B = 60°? (c) is cos 2A =
    cos²A − sin²A true for A = 30° and 45°?
    Answer: (a) yes: both sides √3/2. (b) no: 1 on the left, (1 + √3)/2 on the
    right. (c) yes: 1/2 and 0 on both sides.
    Teacher explains:
       (a) sin 60° = √3/2;  2 × 1/2 × √3/2 = √3/2          equal
       (b) sin 90° = 1;     sin 30° + sin 60° = 1/2 + √3/2   not equal
       (c) A = 30°: cos 60° = 1/2; 3/4 − 1/4 = 1/2          equal
           A = 45°: cos 90° = 0;   1/2 − 1/2 = 0            equal
    A single counter-example PROVES that a rule is false, as in (b): sin does
    not "multiply out" over a sum. But agreement at a few angles does NOT prove
    a rule is true for all angles; (a) and (c) are true identities, proved in
    Stage 8. Checking at standard angles is still the best way to catch
    mistakes. Now you try: does cos(60° − 30°) equal cos 60° − cos 30°? (no:
    √3/2 on the left, (1 − √3)/2 on the right)

D10. A 6 m ladder leans against a wall making 60° with the ground. How high up
     the wall does it reach and how far is its foot from the wall?
     Answer: Height 3√3 ≈ 5.20 m; foot 3 m from the wall.
     Teacher explains:
           |`-.
           |   `-.   6 m
         h |      `-.
           |_        `-.  60°
           +---- d -------
     The ladder is the hypotenuse. Height h is OPPOSITE the 60° angle, the
     distance d is ADJACENT:
        sin 60° = h/6   →  h = 6 × √3/2 = 3√3 ≈ 5.196 ≈ 5.20 m
        cos 60° = d/6   →  d = 6 × 1/2 = 3 m
     Check: 3² + (3√3)² = 9 + 27 = 36 = 6². Choose the ratio that links the side
     you KNOW with the side you WANT. Now you try: the same ladder at 45°.
     (height = foot distance = 3√2 ≈ 4.24 m)

D11. In triangle ABC, ∠B = 90°, BC = 5 cm and ∠ACB = 30°. Find AB and AC.
     Answer: AB = 5/√3 = 5√3/3 ≈ 2.89 cm; AC = 10/√3 = 10√3/3 ≈ 5.77 cm.
     Teacher explains: For the 30° angle at C: AB is opposite, BC = 5 is
     adjacent, AC is the hypotenuse.
        tan 30° = AB/BC  →  AB = 5 × 1/√3 = 5√3/3
        cos 30° = BC/AC  →  AC = 5 ÷ (√3/2) = 10/√3 = 10√3/3
     Check with the 1 : √3 : 2 pattern of a 30°-60°-90° triangle: the side
     opposite 30° is the shortest (AB = 5√3/3), the hypotenuse is twice it
     (10√3/3), and the side opposite 60° is √3 times it (5). Now you try:
     ∠C = 60°, BC = 4 cm. (AB = 4√3 ≈ 6.93 cm, AC = 8 cm)

D12. State whether true or false, with a reason: (a) sin A increases as A
     increases from 0° to 90°; (b) cos A increases in the same range; (c)
     sin θ = cos θ for all θ; (d) cot A is not defined at A = 0°; (e) sin 30° +
     sin 60° = sin 90°.
     Answer: (a) T (b) F (c) F (d) T (e) F.
     Teacher explains: Read along the rows of the table. (a) sin: 0, 0.5, 0.707,
     0.866, 1 — increasing. (b) cos: 1, 0.866, 0.707, 0.5, 0 — DECREASING. (c)
     Only at 45° are they equal; at 30° they are 1/2 and √3/2. (d) cot 0° =
     cos 0°/sin 0° = 1/0: not defined. (e) 1/2 + √3/2 ≈ 1.366, but sin 90° = 1.
     For "true for all" statements one counter-example is enough to answer F.
     Common mistake: believing all ratios behave like sin. Now you try: true or
     false: tan A > sin A for 0° < A < 90°. (true: tan A = sin A/cos A and
     cos A < 1)

M4. Find θ, where 0° ≤ θ ≤ 90°.
    a) sin θ = 1/2        b) cos θ = √3/2       c) tan θ = 1
    d) sin θ = √3/2       e) cos θ = 1/2        f) tan θ = √3

M5. Find θ. The angle inside each ratio lies between 0° and 90°.
    a) sin 2θ = √3/2          b) tan 3θ = 1             c) cos 2θ = 1/2

    p) sin(90° − θ) = 1/2
    Answers: a) θ = 30°   b) θ = 15°   c) θ = 30°   d) θ = 30°   e) θ = 30°
             f) θ = 70°   g) θ = 10°   h) θ = 20°   i) θ = 30°   j) θ = 70°
             k) θ = 22.5°   l) θ = 25°   m) θ = 60°   n) θ = 90°   o) θ = 22.5°
             p) θ = 60°

M6. True or false? Check by putting in the exact values.
    a) sin 60° = 2 sin 30° cos 30°
    b) cos 60° = 1 − 2 sin²30°
    c) tan 60° = 2 tan 30°/(1 − tan²30°)
    d) sin(60° − 30°) = sin 60° − sin 30°
    e) cos 90° = 2 cos 45°
    f) sin 90° = 2 sin 45°
    g) cos 60° = 2 cos²30° − 1
    h) sin 30° + sin 60° = sin 90°
    i) sin²45° + cos²45° = 1
    j) 1 + tan²60° = sec²60°
    k) 1 + cot²30° = cosec²30°
    l) cos 30° = cos 60° × 2
    m) sin 60° cos 30° − cos 60° sin 30° = sin 30°
    n) cos 60° cos 30° − sin 60° sin 30° = cos 90°
    Answers: a) T   b) T   c) T   d) F   e) F   f) F   g) T   h) F   i) T   j) T
             k) T   l) F   m) T   n) T

M7. Find A and B, where A > B > 0° and A + B ≤ 90°.
    a) sin(A + B) = 1, cos(A − B) = √3/2
    b) tan(A + B) = √3, tan(A − B) = √3/3
    c) cos(A + B) = 1/2, sin(A − B) = 1/2
    d) sin(A + B) = √3/2, sin(A − B) = 1/2
    e) cos(A + B) = 0, cos(A − B) = 1/2
    f) tan(A + B) = 1, cos(A − B) = √3/2
    g) sin(A + B) = 1, tan(A − B) = √3/3
    h) cos(A − B) = √2/2, sin(A + B) = 1
    i) tan(A − B) = 1, sin(A + B) = √3/2
    j) sec(A + B) = 2, cosec(A − B) = 2
    k) cot(A + B) = 0, cot(A − B) = √3
    l) sin(A + B) = √2/2, cos(A − B) = √3/2
    Answers: a) A = 60°, B = 30°   b) A = 45°, B = 15°   c) A = 45°, B = 15°
             d) A = 45°, B = 15°   e) A = 75°, B = 15°   f) A = 37.5°, B = 7.5°
             g) A = 60°, B = 30°   h) A = 67.5°, B = 22.5°
             i) A = 52.5°, B = 7.5°   j) A = 45°, B = 15°   k) A = 60°, B = 30°
             l) A = 37.5°, B = 7.5°

M8. Rationalise the denominator and give the value to 3 decimal places.
    a) 1/√2                b) 1/√3                c) 2/√3
    d) √3/2                e) √2                  f) √3
    g) 3/√3                h) 4/√2                i) √3/√2
    j) 1/(2√3)             k) 6/√3                l) 1/(√3 + 1)

    p) 1/(2 − √3)
    Answers: a) √2/2 ≈ 0.707   b) √3/3 ≈ 0.577   c) 2√3/3 ≈ 1.155
             d) √3/2 ≈ 0.866   e) √2 ≈ 1.414   f) √3 ≈ 1.732   g) √3 ≈ 1.732
             h) 2√2 ≈ 2.828   i) √6/2 ≈ 1.225   j) √3/6 ≈ 0.289   k) 2√3 ≈ 3.464
             l) (√3 − 1)/2 ≈ 0.366   m) √6/3 ≈ 0.816   n) 2 − √3 ≈ 0.268
             o) √3 + 1 ≈ 2.732   p) √3 + 2 ≈ 3.732

M9. Which is larger? (Write "equal" if they are equal.)
    a) sin 30°, cos 30°             b) sin 60°, tan 60°
    c) cos 45°, sin 45°             d) tan 30°, sin 30°
    e) cos 60°, cos 30°             f) sin 90°, tan 45°
    g) sec 30°, sec 60°             h) cosec 30°, cosec 60°
    i) cot 30°, tan 30°             j) sin 45°, tan 30°
    k) cos 0°, sec 0°               l) sin 60°, cos 30°
    m) tan 60°, cosec 30°           n) sin 30° + sin 60°, sin 90°
    Answers: a) cos 30°   b) tan 60°   c) equal   d) tan 30°   e) cos 30°
             f) equal   g) sec 60°   h) cosec 30°   i) cot 30°   j) sin 45°
             k) equal   l) equal   m) cosec 30°   n) sin 30° + sin 60°

M10. A right triangle has acute angle A. Find the side opposite A, the side
     adjacent to A and the hypotenuse (exact).
     a) A = 30°, hyp = 10    b) A = 30°, opp = 4
     c) A = 30°, adj = 6     d) A = 60°, hyp = 12
     e) A = 60°, opp = 9     f) A = 60°, adj = 5
     g) A = 45°, hyp = 8     h) A = 45°, opp = 7
     i) A = 45°, adj = 3     j) A = 30°, hyp = 1
     k) A = 60°, adj = 1     l) A = 45°, hyp = 1
     m) A = 30°, adj = 2√3   n) A = 60°, opp = 3√3
     o) A = 45°, hyp = 6√2   p) A = 30°, opp = √3
     Answers: a) opp 5, adj 5√3, hyp 10   b) opp 4, adj 4√3, hyp 8
              c) opp 2√3, adj 6, hyp 4√3   d) opp 6√3, adj 6, hyp 12

              g) opp 4√2, adj 4√2, hyp 8   h) opp 7, adj 7, hyp 7√2
              i) opp 3, adj 3, hyp 3√2   j) opp 1/2, adj √3/2, hyp 1
              k) opp √3, adj 1, hyp 2   l) opp √2/2, adj √2/2, hyp 1
              m) opp 2, adj 2√3, hyp 4   n) opp 3√3, adj 3, hyp 6
              o) opp 6, adj 6, hyp 6√2   p) opp √3, adj 3, hyp 2√3

M11. Put in the value of θ and evaluate. Compare: which pairs always agree
     (they are identities) and which do not? (sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and
     cos 2θ = 1 − 2 sin²θ agree; sin 2θ and 2 sin θ do not.)
     a) θ = 0°: sin 2θ           b) θ = 0°: 2 sin θ cos θ
     c) θ = 0°: cos 2θ           d) θ = 0°: 1 − 2 sin²θ
     e) θ = 0°: 2 sin θ          f) θ = 30°: sin 2θ
     g) θ = 30°: 2 sin θ cos θ   h) θ = 30°: cos 2θ
     i) θ = 30°: 1 − 2 sin²θ     j) θ = 30°: 2 sin θ
     k) θ = 45°: sin 2θ          l) θ = 45°: 2 sin θ cos θ
     m) θ = 45°: cos 2θ          n) θ = 45°: 1 − 2 sin²θ
     o) θ = 45°: 2 sin θ
     Answers: a) 0   b) 0   c) 1   d) 1   e) 0   f) √3/2   g) √3/2   h) 1/2
              i) 1/2   j) 1   k) 1   l) 1   m) 0   n) 0   o) √2

M12. Evaluate exactly. (In Stage 8 you will see that each is a single ratio of
     one angle, such as sin 90° or cos 15°; here just compute.)
     a) sin 30° cos 60° + cos 30° sin 60°
     b) cos 45° cos 45° − sin 45° sin 45°
     c) cos 60° cos 30° + sin 60° sin 30°
     d) sin 45° cos 45° + cos 45° sin 45°
     e) (tan 45° + tan 30°)/(1 − tan 45° tan 30°)
     f) (tan 45° − tan 30°)/(1 + tan 45° tan 30°)
     g) sin 45° cos 30° + cos 45° sin 30°
     h) cos 45° cos 30° + sin 45° sin 30°
     i) sin 60° cos 45° − cos 60° sin 45°
     j) cos 45° cos 60° − sin 45° sin 60°
     k) 3 sin 30° − 4 sin³30°
     l) 4 cos³30° − 3 cos 30°

     n) sin 60°/(1 + cos 60°)
     Answers: a) 1   b) 0   c) √3/2   d) 1   e) √3 + 2   f) 2 − √3
              g) (√2 + √6)/4   h) (√2 + √6)/4   i) (√6 − √2)/4   j) (√2 − √6)/4

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build the table from the two triangles every day for a week until
  it can be written from memory in two minutes; always put values in brackets
  before squaring; practise rationalising 1/√2 and 1/√3 separately; use a
  calculator to check decimal values (sin 60° ≈ 0.866). Harder: find sin 15° and
  cos 15° exactly from the 45° − 30° values ((√6 − √2)/4, (√6 + √2)/4); find
  tan 22.5° from a right isosceles triangle with an extended leg (√2 − 1); prove
  that sin 18° = (√5 − 1)/4 using a 36°-72°-72° golden triangle; show that
  sin θ + cos θ is largest at 45°.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.34 — TRIGONOMETRIC IDENTITIES (sin² + cos² = 1 ETC.)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - An IDENTITY is an equation that is true for EVERY value of the angle for
    which both sides are defined (an equation such as sin θ = 1/2 is true only
    for some angles).
  - The three Pythagorean identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 (for all θ), 1 + tan²θ =
    sec²θ (0° ≤ θ < 90°), 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ (0° < θ ≤ 90°). Divide the first
    by cos²θ or by sin²θ to get the other two.
  - Useful rearrangements: sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ = (1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ);
    cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ; sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 = (sec θ − tan θ)(sec θ + tan θ);
    cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1.
  - Expressing in terms of one ratio (θ acute): cos θ = √(1 − sin²θ), tan θ =
    sin θ/√(1 − sin²θ), sec θ = √(1 + tan²θ), sin θ = tan θ/√(1 + tan²θ), and so
    on.
  - PROVING an identity: start from the MORE COMPLICATED side and change it step
    by step into the other side. Useful moves: write everything in sin and cos;
    combine fractions over a common denominator; factorise; multiply top and
    bottom by a conjugate such as (1 + cos θ); replace 1 by sin²θ + cos²θ. Never
    treat the identity as an equation to be "solved" by doing the same thing to
    both sides.
  - Algebra you need: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b², a³ −
    b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), and the rules
    for fractions.
  - CHECKING: test a claimed identity at a few angles (30°, 45°, 60°, or any
    angle on a calculator). If it fails at one angle, it is NOT an identity. If
    it passes, that is evidence, not a proof.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that sin²A + cos²A = 1 for every acute angle A, and check it at
    A = 30° and A = 0°.
    Answer: By Pythagoras (opp² + adj² = hyp²), dividing by hyp² gives sin²A +
    cos²A = 1. At 30°: 1/4 + 3/4 = 1; at 0°: 0 + 1 = 1.
    Teacher explains:
          C
          |\          ∠B = 90°: opp = BC, adj = AB, hyp = AC
          | \         BC² + AB² = AC²   (Pythagoras)
          |  \
          |_  \       divide every term by AC²:
          |_|__A      (BC/AC)² + (AB/AC)² = 1
          B           sin²A + cos²A = 1
    This is Pythagoras' theorem written in trigonometry. The argument works for
    EVERY right triangle, so the identity holds for every acute A, and the table
    shows it also holds at 0° and 90° (0 + 1 and 1 + 0). sin²A means (sin A)².
    Rearrangements used all the time: sin²A = 1 − cos²A and cos²A = 1 − sin²A.
    Common mistake: writing sin A + cos A = 1 (no squares); at 45° that gives
    √2/2 + √2/2 = √2, not 1. Now you try: check the identity at 60°.
    (3/4 + 1/4 = 1)

D2. Derive 1 + tan²A = sec²A and 1 + cot²A = cosec²A from sin²A + cos²A = 1. For
    which angles in 0° ≤ A ≤ 90° are they true?
    Answer: Divide by cos²A (allowed when A ≠ 90°) and by sin²A (when A ≠ 0°).
    So 1 + tan²A = sec²A for 0° ≤ A < 90° and 1 + cot²A = cosec²A for 0° <
    A ≤ 90°.
    Teacher explains:
       sin²A + cos²A = 1         ÷ cos²A:
       sin²A/cos²A + 1 = 1/cos²A  →  tan²A + 1 = sec²A
       sin²A + cos²A = 1         ÷ sin²A:
       1 + cos²A/sin²A = 1/sin²A  →  1 + cot²A = cosec²A
    We may only divide by something that is NOT zero: cos 90° = 0, so the first
    is not claimed at 90° (and indeed tan 90° and sec 90° are not defined);
    sin 0° = 0, so the second excludes 0°. Check at 60°: 1 + (√3)² = 4 = 2² =
    sec²60°. Rearranged forms: sec²A − tan²A = 1 and cosec²A − cot²A = 1. Now
    you try: check 1 + cot²A = cosec²A at 30°. (1 + 3 = 4 = 2²)

D3. Express cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A and cot A in terms of sin A only
    (A acute).
    Answer: cos A = √(1 − sin²A), tan A = sin A/√(1 − sin²A), cosec A = 1/sin A,
    sec A = 1/√(1 − sin²A), cot A = √(1 − sin²A)/sin A.
    Teacher explains: Start from cos²A = 1 − sin²A. For acute A, cos A > 0, so
    take the positive root: cos A = √(1 − sin²A). Then every other ratio follows
    from the quotient and reciprocal relations:
       tan A   = sin A/cos A = sin A/√(1 − sin²A)
       cosec A = 1/sin A
       sec A   = 1/cos A = 1/√(1 − sin²A)
       cot A   = cos A/sin A = √(1 − sin²A)/sin A
    Test with sin A = 3/5: √(1 − 9/25) = √(16/25) = 4/5 = cos A, and
    tan A = (3/5)/(4/5) = 3/4 — the 3-4-5 triangle again. Common mistake:
    √(1 − sin²A) = 1 − sin A (the root does not split). Now you try: express
    sin A and sec A in terms of tan A. (sin A = tan A/√(1 + tan²A), sec A =
    √(1 + tan²A))

D4. If tan A = 1/√7, find (cosec²A − sec²A)/(cosec²A + sec²A) using identities,
    without drawing a triangle.
    Answer: 3/4.
    Teacher explains: Use cosec²A = 1 + cot²A and sec²A = 1 + tan²A. With
    tan²A = 1/7 and cot²A = 7:
       cosec²A = 1 + 7   = 8
       sec²A   = 1 + 1/7 = 8/7
       value = (8 − 8/7)/(8 + 8/7) = (48/7)/(64/7) = 48/64 = 3/4
    Identities let us jump straight from tan to sec and cosec. Check with a
    triangle: opposite 1, adjacent √7, hypotenuse √8, so cosec²A = 8 and
    sec²A = 8/7 — the same. Common mistake: using cosec²A = 1 + tan²A (wrong
    pairing: cosec goes with cot). Now you try: if cot A = 2, find sec²A.
    (tan²A = 1/4, sec²A = 5/4)

D5. Prove that (sec θ − tan θ)(sec θ + tan θ) = 1. Hence, if sec θ + tan θ = 3,
    find sec θ − tan θ, sec θ and tan θ.
    Answer: LHS = sec²θ − tan²θ = 1. If sec θ + tan θ = 3 then sec θ −
    tan θ = 1/3, sec θ = 5/3 and tan θ = 4/3.
    Teacher explains:
       LHS = (sec θ − tan θ)(sec θ + tan θ)
           = sec²θ − tan²θ          (difference of two squares)
           = 1                       (since 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ)
           = RHS
    So sec θ + tan θ and sec θ − tan θ are RECIPROCALS. With sum 3, the
    difference is 1/3. Adding the two equations: 2 sec θ = 3 + 1/3 = 10/3,
    sec θ = 5/3; subtracting: 2 tan θ = 3 − 1/3 = 8/3, tan θ = 4/3. Check:
    1 + 16/9 = 25/9 = (5/3)². Write proofs as a column starting with "LHS =" and
    ending with "= RHS", one step per line. Now you try: prove
    (cosec θ − cot θ)(cosec θ + cot θ) = 1. (cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1)

D6. Prove (sin θ + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ. If sin θ + cos θ = √2, find
    sin θ cos θ and θ (acute).
    Answer: sin θ cos θ = 1/2 and θ = 45°.
    Teacher explains:
       LHS = (sin θ + cos θ)²
           = sin²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ + cos²θ
           = (sin²θ + cos²θ) + 2 sin θ cos θ
           = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ = RHS
    Similarly (sin θ − cos θ)² = 1 − 2 sin θ cos θ. With sin θ + cos θ = √2:
    2 = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ, so sin θ cos θ = 1/2. Then
    (sin θ − cos θ)² = 1 − 1 = 0, so sin θ = cos θ and θ = 45°. Common mistake:
    (sin θ + cos θ)² = sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 (the middle term is forgotten). Now you
    try: if sin θ + cos θ = 7/5, find sin θ cos θ. (49/25 = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ,
    so 12/25)

D7. Prove that (1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ) = (cosec θ − cot θ)².
    Answer: Start from the right-hand side and write it in sin and cos.
    Teacher explains:
       RHS = (cosec θ − cot θ)²
           = (1/sin θ − cos θ/sin θ)²
           = (1 − cos θ)²/sin²θ
           = (1 − cos θ)²/(1 − cos²θ)
           = (1 − cos θ)²/((1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ))
           = (1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ) = LHS
    The RHS looked more complicated, so we started there. Key moves: change
    cosec and cot into sin and cos; replace sin²θ by 1 − cos²θ; factorise the
    difference of squares; cancel the common factor (1 − cos θ). Numeric check
    at θ = 60°: LHS = (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3; RHS = (2/√3 − 1/√3)² = (1/√3)² = 1/3.
    Now you try: prove (1 + sin θ)/(1 − sin θ) = (sec θ + tan θ)². (same method,
    with cos²θ = (1 − sin θ)(1 + sin θ))

D8. Prove that sin θ/(1 + cos θ) + (1 + cos θ)/sin θ = 2 cosec θ.
    Answer: Combine the two fractions over a common denominator.
    Teacher explains:
       LHS = [sin²θ + (1 + cos θ)²] / [(1 + cos θ) sin θ]
           = [sin²θ + 1 + 2 cos θ + cos²θ] / [(1 + cos θ) sin θ]
           = [2 + 2 cos θ] / [(1 + cos θ) sin θ]
           = 2(1 + cos θ) / [(1 + cos θ) sin θ]
           = 2/sin θ = 2 cosec θ = RHS
    The step "sin²θ + cos²θ = 1" turns 1 + 1 into 2. Then factorise 2 and cancel
    (1 + cos θ). Adding fractions is exactly as in algebra: a/b +
    c/d = (ad + bc)/(bd). Check at 90°: 1/1 + 1/1 = 2 = 2 cosec 90°. Common
    mistake: adding tops and bottoms separately. Now you try: prove
    cos θ/(1 − sin θ) + cos θ/(1 + sin θ) = 2 sec θ. (common denominator 1 −
    sin²θ = cos²θ)

D9. Prove that √((1 + sin θ)/(1 − sin θ)) = sec θ + tan θ (θ acute).
    Answer: Multiply top and bottom inside the root by (1 + sin θ).
    Teacher explains:
       LHS = √[(1 + sin θ)(1 + sin θ) / ((1 − sin θ)(1 + sin θ))]
           = √[(1 + sin θ)² / (1 − sin²θ)]
           = √[(1 + sin θ)² / cos²θ]
           = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ          (both positive for acute θ)
           = 1/cos θ + sin θ/cos θ = sec θ + tan θ = RHS
    Multiplying by the CONJUGATE (1 + sin θ) makes the denominator a perfect
    square cos²θ, so the square root disappears. We need cos θ > 0 and 1 + sin θ
    > 0 to take the root, which is true for acute θ. Check at 30°:
    √((3/2)/(1/2)) = √3 and sec 30° + tan 30° = 2/√3 + 1/√3 = 3/√3 = √3. Now you
    try: prove √((1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ)) = cosec θ − cot θ.
    (multiply by 1 − cos θ)

D10. Prove that tan θ/(1 − cot θ) + cot θ/(1 − tan θ) = 1 + sec θ cosec θ.
     Answer: Write everything in sin θ and cos θ, then use the factorisation of
     a³ − b³.
     Teacher explains:
        LHS = sin²θ/[cos θ(sin θ − cos θ)] − cos²θ/[sin θ(sin θ − cos θ)]
            = (sin³θ − cos³θ)/[sin θ cos θ(sin θ − cos θ)]
            = (sin θ − cos θ)(sin²θ + sin θ cos θ + cos²θ)
              ÷ [sin θ cos θ(sin θ − cos θ)]
            = (1 + sin θ cos θ)/(sin θ cos θ)
            = 1/(sin θ cos θ) + 1 = 1 + sec θ cosec θ = RHS
     First line: tan θ/(1 − cot θ) = (sin θ/cos θ) ÷ ((sin θ − cos θ)/sin θ) =
     sin²θ/(cos θ(sin θ − cos θ)); in the second fraction 1 −
     tan θ = (cos θ − sin θ)/cos θ = −(sin θ − cos θ)/cos θ, which makes the
     minus sign. The cube identity is the key algebraic step. Check at 30°:
     LHS = (√3/3)/(1 − √3) + √3/(1 − √3/3) ≈ −0.789 + 4.098 = 3.309;
     RHS = 1 + (2/√3)(2) ≈ 3.309. Now you try: check the identity at 60°. (both
     sides 1 + 4/√3 ≈ 3.309)

D11. If sec θ + tan θ = p, show that sin θ = (p² − 1)/(p² + 1). Find sin θ when
     p = 2.
     Answer: sin θ = 3/5 when p = 2.
     Teacher explains: From D5, sec θ − tan θ = 1/p. Add and subtract:
        sec θ = (p + 1/p)/2 = (p² + 1)/(2p)
        tan θ = (p − 1/p)/2 = (p² − 1)/(2p)
        sin θ = tan θ/sec θ = (p² − 1)/(p² + 1)
     For p = 2: sin θ = (4 − 1)/(4 + 1) = 3/5, and sec θ = 5/4, tan θ = 3/4 —
     the 3-4-5 triangle. Notice sin θ = tan θ ÷ sec θ because
     (sin θ/cos θ) ÷ (1/cos θ) = sin θ. Common mistake: squaring sec θ + tan θ =
     p and forgetting the middle term. Now you try: p = 3. (sin θ = 8/10 = 4/5)

D12. Ravi claims sin θ + cos θ = 1 is an identity because it works at 0° and
     90°. Is he right? How should we test claimed identities?
     Answer: No. At 45°, sin 45° + cos 45° = √2 ≈ 1.414, not 1, so it is not an
     identity. One counter-example disproves; agreement at a few angles only
     supports a claim and a proof is needed.
     Teacher explains: An identity must hold for EVERY angle. Test several
     angles, including "ordinary" ones like 30°, 45°, 60°:
        θ       sin θ + cos θ          1 + tan²θ    sec²θ
        0°      0 + 1 = 1              1            1
        30°     (1 + √3)/2 ≈ 1.366     4/3          4/3
        45°     √2 ≈ 1.414             2            2
        60°     (√3 + 1)/2 ≈ 1.366     4            4
     The first column is not constant, so sin θ + cos θ = 1 is false in general
     (it is only an EQUATION with solutions 0° and 90°). The last two columns
     agree at every test angle, which supports 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ — and D2 proves
     it. A calculator at a strange angle like 37° is a good extra test. Now you
     try: test (sin θ + cos θ)² = sin²θ + cos²θ at 30°. (LHS = 1 + 2 × 1/2 ×
     √3/2 = 1 + √3/2 ≈ 1.866, RHS = 1: not an identity)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Simplify to a number or a single term.
    a) (1 − sin²θ) sec²θ
    b) (1 + tan²θ) cos²θ
    c) sin θ cot θ
    d) cos θ tan θ
    e) (sec²θ − 1) cot²θ
    f) (cosec²θ − 1) tan²θ
    g) sin²θ + cos²θ + tan²θ
    h) 9 sec²θ − 9 tan²θ
    i) (1 + cos θ)(1 − cos θ)(1 + cot²θ)
    j) sec θ (1 − sin θ)(sec θ + tan θ)
    k) tan θ/sec θ
    l) cot θ/cosec θ
    m) (sin θ + cos θ)² + (sin θ − cos θ)²
    n) sin θ sec θ
    o) (1 − cos²θ) cosec²θ
    p) cot²θ − cosec²θ
    q) tan²θ − sec²θ
    r) (sec θ + tan θ)(1 − sin θ)
    s) cos θ cosec θ
    t) sin⁴θ − cos⁴θ + cos²θ
    u) 1/(1 + sin θ) + 1/(1 − sin θ)
    v) (1 + tan²θ)/(1 + cot²θ)
    Answers: a) 1   b) 1   c) cos θ   d) sin θ   e) 1   f) 1   g) sec²θ   h) 9
             i) 1   j) 1   k) sin θ   l) cos θ   m) 2   n) tan θ   o) 1   p) −1
             q) −1   r) cos θ   s) cot θ   t) sin²θ   u) 2 sec²θ   v) tan²θ

M2. θ is acute. Express the first ratio in terms of the second only.
    a) cos θ in terms of sin θ     b) tan θ in terms of sin θ
    c) sec θ in terms of sin θ     d) cot θ in terms of sin θ
    e) sin θ in terms of cos θ     f) tan θ in terms of cos θ
    g) cosec θ in terms of cos θ   h) cot θ in terms of cos θ
    i) sec θ in terms of tan θ     j) cos θ in terms of tan θ

    m) sin θ in terms of cot θ     n) cos θ in terms of cot θ

             p) √(sec²θ − 1)/sec θ   q) √(cosec²θ − 1)

M5. Prove, starting from the left-hand side. Give each step (the answers show
    one correct chain).
    a) (sec θ − tan θ)(sec θ + tan θ) = 1
    b) (cosec θ − cot θ)(cosec θ + cot θ) = 1
    c) (sin θ + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ
    d) (sin θ − cos θ)² = 1 − 2 sin θ cos θ
    e) cos²θ(1 + tan²θ) = 1
    f) sin θ cot θ sec θ = 1
    g) tan θ + cot θ = sec θ cosec θ
    h) sin⁴θ − cos⁴θ = sin²θ − cos²θ
    i) sec⁴θ − sec²θ = tan⁴θ + tan²θ
    j) (1 − sin θ)(1 + sin θ) sec²θ = 1
    k) cos θ/(1 − sin θ) = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ
    l) 1/(sec θ − tan θ) = sec θ + tan θ
    Answers:
      a) LHS = sec²θ − tan²θ
             = 1 = RHS
      b) LHS = cosec²θ − cot²θ
             = 1 = RHS
      c) LHS = sin²θ + cos²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ
             = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ = RHS
      d) LHS = sin²θ + cos²θ − 2 sin θ cos θ
             = 1 − 2 sin θ cos θ = RHS
      e) LHS = cos²θ sec²θ
             = 1 = RHS
      f) LHS = sin θ × cos θ/sin θ × 1/cos θ
             = 1 = RHS
      g) LHS = sin θ/cos θ + cos θ/sin θ
             = (sin²θ + cos²θ)/(sin θ cos θ)
             = 1/(sin θ cos θ)
             = sec θ cosec θ = RHS
      h) LHS = (sin²θ − cos²θ)(sin²θ + cos²θ)
             = sin²θ − cos²θ = RHS
      i) LHS = sec²θ(sec²θ − 1)
             = (1 + tan²θ) tan²θ
             = tan²θ + tan⁴θ = RHS
      j) LHS = (1 − sin²θ) sec²θ
             = cos²θ sec²θ
             = 1 = RHS
      k) LHS = cos θ(1 + sin θ)/(1 − sin²θ)
             = cos θ(1 + sin θ)/cos²θ
             = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ = RHS
      l) LHS = (sec θ + tan θ)/(sec²θ − tan²θ)
             = sec θ + tan θ = RHS

M6. Prove (harder). Each answer shows one correct chain, starting from the side
    named.
    a) (1 + sin θ)/(1 − sin θ) = (sec θ + tan θ)²
    b) cos θ/(1 − tan θ) + sin θ/(1 − cot θ) = sin θ + cos θ
    c) (cosec θ − sin θ)(sec θ − cos θ) = sin θ cos θ
    d) (1 + cot θ − cosec θ)(1 + tan θ + sec θ) = 2
    e) (sin θ − 2 sin³θ)/(2 cos³θ − cos θ) = tan θ
    f) (sin θ + cosec θ)² + (cos θ + sec θ)² = 7 + tan²θ + cot²θ
    g) (1 + sec θ)/sec θ = sin²θ/(1 − cos θ)
    h) sin θ/(1 − cos θ) = cosec θ + cot θ
    i) 1/(cosec θ − cot θ) − 1/sin θ = 1/sin θ − 1/(cosec θ + cot θ)
    j) (cos θ − sin θ + 1)/(cos θ + sin θ − 1) = cosec θ + cot θ
    Answers:
      a) RHS = ((1 + sin θ)/cos θ)²
             = (1 + sin θ)²/cos²θ
             = (1 + sin θ)²/((1 − sin θ)(1 + sin θ))
             = (1 + sin θ)/(1 − sin θ) = LHS
      b) LHS = cos²θ/(cos θ − sin θ) + sin²θ/(sin θ − cos θ)
             = (cos²θ − sin²θ)/(cos θ − sin θ)
             = cos θ + sin θ = RHS
      c) LHS = ((1 − sin²θ)/sin θ)((1 − cos²θ)/cos θ)
             = (cos²θ/sin θ)(sin²θ/cos θ)
             = sin θ cos θ = RHS
      d) LHS = ((sin θ + cos θ − 1)/sin θ)((cos θ + sin θ + 1)/cos θ)
             = ((sin θ + cos θ)² − 1)/(sin θ cos θ)
             = (2 sin θ cos θ)/(sin θ cos θ)
             = 2 = RHS
      e) LHS = sin θ(1 − 2 sin²θ)/(cos θ(2 cos²θ − 1))
             = sin θ(1 − 2 sin²θ)/(cos θ(2(1 − sin²θ) − 1))
             = sin θ(1 − 2 sin²θ)/(cos θ(1 − 2 sin²θ))
             = tan θ = RHS
      f) LHS = sin²θ + 2 + cosec²θ + cos²θ + 2 + sec²θ
             = 5 + cosec²θ + sec²θ
             = 5 + (1 + cot²θ) + (1 + tan²θ)
             = 7 + tan²θ + cot²θ = RHS
      g) LHS = cos θ + 1
             = (1 − cos²θ)/(1 − cos θ)
             = sin²θ/(1 − cos θ) = RHS
      h) LHS = sin θ(1 + cos θ)/(1 − cos²θ)
             = sin θ(1 + cos θ)/sin²θ
             = (1 + cos θ)/sin θ
             = cosec θ + cot θ = RHS
      i) LHS = cosec θ + cot θ − cosec θ
             = cot θ
             = cosec θ − (cosec θ − cot θ)
             = 1/sin θ − 1/(cosec θ + cot θ) = RHS
      j) LHS = (cot θ − 1 + cosec θ)/(cot θ + 1 − cosec θ)
             = (cot θ + cosec θ − (cosec²θ − cot²θ))/(cot θ − cosec θ + 1)
             = (cosec θ + cot θ)(1 − cosec θ + cot θ)/(cot θ − cosec θ + 1)
             = cosec θ + cot θ = RHS

M7. Evaluate the left side and the right side at θ = 30°, 45° and 60°
    (as "left, right"). Decide: identity (proved in this topic or Stage 8) or
    not an identity?
    a) sin θ + cos θ = 1

             b) 30°: 4/3, 4/3; 45°: 2, 2; 60°: 4, 4 → identity
             c) 30°: −1/2, 1; 45°: 0, 1; 60°: 1/2, 1 → not an identity
             d) 30°: 16/3, 16/3; 45°: 4, 4; 60°: 16/3, 16/3 → identity
             e) 30°: 4√3/3, 2; 45°: 2, 2; 60°: 4√3/3, 2 → not an identity
             f) 30°: 1/2, 1/2; 45°: 0, 0; 60°: −1/2, −1/2 → identity
             g) 30°: (√3 + 2)/2, 1; 45°: 2, 1; 60°: (√3 + 2)/2, 1 → not an
                identity
             h) 30°: √3/3, √3/3; 45°: 1, 1; 60°: √3, √3 → identity
             i) 30°: √3/6, √3/6; 45°: √2/2, √2/2; 60°: 3/2, 3/2 → identity
             j) 30°: 3/2, 3/2; 45°: √2/2, √2/2; 60°: √3/6, √3/6 → identity

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep the three identities and their rearrangements on a card; in
  every proof first rewrite tan, cot, sec and cosec in sin and cos; practise the
  algebra (common denominators, difference of squares) with x and y before using
  sin and cos; after each proof check it at 30° with the table. Harder: prove
  (1 + cot θ − cosec θ)(1 + tan θ + sec θ) = 2 in two different ways; show that
  sin⁶θ + cos⁶θ = 1 − 3 sin²θ cos²θ; if cos θ + sin θ = √2 cos θ, prove cos θ −
  sin θ = √2 sin θ; find the minimum value of sin²θ + cosec²θ
  (answer 2, at θ = 90°) and of 4 sin²θ + cosec²θ; show that sec²θ + cosec²θ ≥
  4.


================================================================================
TOPIC 7.35 — HEIGHTS AND DISTANCES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The LINE OF SIGHT joins the observer's eye to the object. The ANGLE OF
    ELEVATION is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when we
    look UP; the ANGLE OF DEPRESSION is the angle between the horizontal and the
    line of sight when we look DOWN. Both are measured from the HORIZONTAL,
    never from the vertical.
  - The angle of depression of B seen from A equals the angle of elevation of A
    seen from B (alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines).
  - Method: (1) draw a clear diagram with the horizontal, the vertical object
    and the right angle; (2) mark the angle and the known length; (3) choose the
    ratio linking the known side and the wanted side — usually tan θ =
    height/horizontal distance (use sin or cos when the sloping length is
    involved); (4) solve and give the exact answer, then a decimal.
  - Standard values: tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = √3; sin 30° = 1/2,
    sin 60° = √3/2. Use √3 ≈ 1.732 and √2 ≈ 1.414 for decimals.
  - TWO OBSERVATION POINTS on the same side at distance d apart with angles α
    (far) and β (near): h cot α − h cot β = d, so h = d/(cot α − cot β). On
    OPPOSITE sides: h cot α + h cot β = d.
  - OBSERVER ABOVE THE GROUND (building, cliff, lighthouse): draw the horizontal
    through the eye; add the observer's height at the end. Flagstaff on a
    building: find the horizontal distance from the building first, then the
    full height, then subtract.
  - Moving objects: distance travelled = difference of the two horizontal
    distances; speed = distance ÷ time.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Explain angle of elevation and angle of depression with a picture. Riya
    stands on a balcony and sees her friend Sam on the ground at an angle of
    depression of 30°. At what angle of elevation does Sam see Riya?
    Answer: 30°. The angle of depression from Riya equals the angle of elevation
    from Sam.
    Teacher explains:
       R ------------------------ horizontal through Riya's eye
       |`-.   30° = angle of depression
       |   `-.
       |      `-.     line of sight
       |         `-.
       |            `-.   30° = angle of elevation
       +---------------`- S    ground (horizontal)
    Both angles are measured from a HORIZONTAL line: elevation when you look up
    from the lower point, depression when you look down from the higher point.
    The two horizontal lines are parallel and the line of sight cuts both, so
    the angles are ALTERNATE ANGLES and are equal. Common mistakes: measuring
    the depression from the vertical wall (that gives 60°, the complement), and
    putting the depression angle at the bottom of the diagram. Now you try: from
    the top of a cliff the angle of depression of a boat is 45°. What is the
    angle of elevation of the cliff top from the boat? (45°)

D2. From a point on the ground 30 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of
    elevation of the top is 60°. Find the height of the tower.
    Answer: h = 30√3 ≈ 51.96 m.
    Teacher explains:
         T
         |`-.
         |   `-.
       h |      `-.
         |_        `-.  60°
         B----- 30 ----- P
    We know the side ADJACENT to 60° (30 m) and want the OPPOSITE side (h), so
    use tan:
       tan 60° = h/30
       h = 30 × tan 60° = 30√3 ≈ 30 × 1.732 = 51.96 m
    Always write the exact answer first (30√3 m), then the decimal. Estimate:
    tan 60° is about 1.7, so the tower is a little less than twice the distance.
    Common mistake: using sin 60° = h/30 — but 30 m is not the hypotenuse. Now
    you try: distance 50 m, elevation 30°. (50/√3 = 50√3/3 ≈ 28.87 m)

D3. A kite is flying on a string 80 m long. The string is straight and makes 60°
    with the ground. How high is the kite? How far along the ground is it from
    the person?
    Answer: Height 40√3 ≈ 69.28 m; horizontal distance 40 m.
    Teacher explains: The string is the HYPOTENUSE, so use sin for the height
    and cos for the horizontal distance:
       sin 60° = h/80   →  h = 80 × √3/2 = 40√3 ≈ 69.28 m
       cos 60° = d/80   →  d = 80 × 1/2 = 40 m
    Check with Pythagoras: 40² + (40√3)² = 1600 + 4800 = 6400 = 80². Real kites
    fly higher when the string is steeper: at 30° the same string gives only
    80 × 1/2 = 40 m. Now you try: a 12 m ladder reaches a window when it makes
    60° with the ground. How high is the window? (6√3 ≈ 10.39 m)

D4. From the top of a lighthouse 75 m above the sea, the angle of depression of
    a boat is 30°. How far is the boat from the foot of the lighthouse?
    Answer: 75√3 ≈ 129.90 m.
    Teacher explains:
       L ------------------ horizontal
       |`-.  30°
       |    `-.
    75 |       `-.
       |          `-.
       |_         30° `-.
       F-------- d ------- B
    The angle of depression at L equals the angle of elevation at B
    (alternate angles), so the triangle has 30° at B. Opposite = 75, adjacent =
    d:
       tan 30° = 75/d
       d = 75/tan 30° = 75√3 ≈ 75 × 1.732 = 129.9 m
    Dividing by tan 30° = 1/√3 is the same as multiplying by √3. Common mistake:
    putting the 30° at the top between the vertical and the line of sight. Now
    you try: height 50 m, depression 45°. (50 m)

D5. The shadow of a tower is 40 m longer when the sun's altitude is 30° than
    when it is 60°. Find the height of the tower.
    Answer: h = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m.
    Teacher explains:
         T
         |\ `-.
       h | \    `-.
         |  \      `-.
         |_  \ 60°     `-. 30°
         B----C------------D
           x        40
    Let x be the shorter shadow. From the two right triangles:
       tan 60° = h/x          →  x = h/√3
       tan 30° = h/(x + 40)   →  x + 40 = h√3
       subtract: 40 = h√3 − h/√3 = 2h/√3
       h = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m,   x = 20 m
    The sun's altitude is its angle of elevation. The lower the sun, the longer
    the shadow. Eliminating x is the key step: write BOTH horizontal distances
    in terms of h. Now you try: the shadow of a pole is √3 times its height.
    Find the sun's altitude. (tan θ = 1/√3, θ = 30°)

D6. From a point P on level ground, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower
    is 30°. On walking 20 m towards the tower, it becomes 60°. Find the height
    of the tower and the distance of the second point from the tower.
    Answer: h = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m; the second point is 10 m from the tower.
    Teacher explains: Let the second point Q be x m from the foot B. Then:
       from Q: h = x tan 60° = x√3
       from P: h = (x + 20) tan 30° = (x + 20)/√3
       x√3 = (x + 20)/√3   →  3x = x + 20  →  x = 10
       h = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m
    Two unknowns (h and x) need two equations — one from each viewpoint. Notice
    triangle PQT is isosceles: its angle at P is 30° and the exterior angle at Q
    is 60°, so ∠PTQ = 30° and QT = PQ = 20 m; then h = 20 sin 60° = 10√3. Common
    mistake: using 20 as the distance from P to the tower. Now you try: angles
    45° and 60°, walk 30 m. (h = 15(3 + √3) ≈ 70.98 m)

D7. A flagstaff stands on top of a building 20 m high. From a point on the
    ground, the angles of elevation of the bottom and the top of the flagstaff
    are 45° and 60°. Find the length of the flagstaff.
    Answer: 20(√3 − 1) ≈ 14.64 m.
    Teacher explains:
            F  (top of flagstaff)
            |
            T  (top of building)
            |
         20 |       angles at P: 45° to T, 60° to F
            |_
            B-------- d -------- P
    First find the distance d from the 45° triangle BTP: tan 45° = 20/d, so
    d = 20 m. Then the full height BF from the 60° triangle:
       tan 60° = BF/20   →  BF = 20√3
       flagstaff = BF − BT = 20√3 − 20 = 20(√3 − 1)
                 ≈ 20 × 0.732 = 14.64 m
    Two triangles share the SAME horizontal distance d — that is the link.
    Common mistake: using tan(60° − 45°) for the flagstaff alone; angles cannot
    be subtracted like that. Now you try: building 10 m, angles 30° and 60°.
    (d = 10√3, flagstaff = 30 − 10 = 20 m)

D8. From the top of a 7 m high building, the angle of elevation of the top of a
    cable tower is 60° and the angle of depression of its foot is 45°. Find the
    height of the tower.
    Answer: 7(1 + √3) ≈ 19.12 m.
    Teacher explains:
                            C
                            |
       A ------ d --------- E       AE horizontal
       |  `-. 45°           |       ∠CAE = 60°, ∠EAD = 45°
     7 |      `-.           | 7
       |_         `-.       |
       B-------- d -------- D
    Draw the horizontal AE through the observer. Depression 45° to the foot D:
    tan 45° = 7/d, so d = 7 m. Elevation 60° to the top C: CE = d tan 60° = 7√3.
    Tower height = CE + ED = 7√3 + 7 = 7(√3 + 1) ≈ 7 × 2.732 ≈ 19.12 m. The part
    of the tower BELOW the observer's eye is equal to the building's height. Now
    you try: building 10 m, elevation 30°, depression 45°. (d = 10,
    tower = 10 + 10/√3 ≈ 15.77 m)

D9. A man on the top of a lighthouse 100 m high sees a ship sailing straight
    towards it. The angle of depression of the ship changes from 30° to 45°. How
    far did the ship travel? If this took 2 minutes, find its speed.
    Answer: 100(√3 − 1) ≈ 73.20 m; speed ≈ 36.6 m per minute.
    Teacher explains:
       first distance  = 100/tan 30° = 100√3
       second distance = 100/tan 45° = 100
       travelled = 100√3 − 100 = 100(√3 − 1) ≈ 73.20 m
       speed ≈ 73.2 ÷ 2 = 36.6 m per minute
    As the ship comes closer, the angle of depression INCREASES. Work out each
    horizontal distance separately and subtract. Using √3 ≈ 1.732:
    100 × 0.732 = 73.2 m. Common mistake: thinking the distance is proportional
    to the angle (it is not; tan is not linear). Now you try: cliff 60 m,
    depression 45° then 60°. (60 − 20√3 ≈ 25.36 m)

D10. An aeroplane flies horizontally at a height of 1500√3 m. From a point on
     the ground the angle of elevation changes from 60° to 30° in 15 seconds.
     Find its speed in km/h.
     Answer: 3000 m in 15 s = 200 m/s = 720 km/h.
     Teacher explains:
        A1 ----------------------- A2    plane, height 1500√3 m
        |                           |
        B1 ------------------------ B2   ground points below A1, A2
        observer P is on the line B1B2, before B1:
        PB1 = x1 (elevation 60°),  PB2 = x2 (elevation 30°)
        x1 = 1500√3/tan 60° = 1500√3/√3 = 1500 m
        x2 = 1500√3/tan 30° = 1500√3 × √3 = 4500 m
        distance flown = 4500 − 1500 = 3000 m
        speed = 3000 ÷ 15 = 200 m/s;  200 × 3.6 = 720 km/h
     The height is chosen so the surds cancel. To change m/s to km/h multiply by
     3.6 (3600 seconds per hour, 1000 m per km). Common mistake: giving the
     answer in m/s when km/h is asked. Now you try: height 1000 m, elevation
     changes from 45° to 30° in 10 s. (1000(√3 − 1) ≈ 732 m,
     73.2 m/s ≈ 263.52 km/h)

D11. Two poles of equal height stand on opposite sides of a road 80 m wide. From
     a point between them on the road, the angles of elevation of their tops are
     60° and 30°. Find the height of the poles and the position of the point.
     Answer: Height 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m; the point is 20 m from the first pole and
     60 m from the second.
     Teacher explains:
        A                              C
        |`-.                        .-'|
        |   `-.                  .-'   |
      h |      `-.  60°  30° .-'       | h
        |_________`-.___.-'____________|
        B      x      P       80 − x   D
        h = x tan 60° = x√3
        h = (80 − x) tan 30° = (80 − x)/√3
        3x = 80 − x  →  x = 20,  h = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m
     On OPPOSITE sides the two horizontal distances ADD to the width of the
     road; on the same side they SUBTRACT. The steeper angle (60°) belongs to
     the nearer pole. Now you try: road 100 m, both angles 45°. (point in the
     middle, h = 50 m)

D12. From a point 60 m above a still lake, the angle of elevation of a cloud is
     30° and the angle of depression of its reflection in the lake is 60°. Find
     the height of the cloud above the lake.
     Answer: 120 m.
     Teacher explains: The reflection is as far BELOW the water as the cloud is
     ABOVE it. Let the cloud be H m above the lake and x m away horizontally
     from the observer:
        cloud:      tan 30° = (H − 60)/x   →  x = √3(H − 60)
        reflection: tan 60° = (H + 60)/x   →  x = (H + 60)/√3
        √3(H − 60) = (H + 60)/√3
        3H − 180 = H + 60  →  2H = 240  →  H = 120 m
     The observer is 60 m up, so the cloud is H − 60 above eye level and the
     reflection is H + 60 below eye level. Setting the two expressions for x
     equal eliminates it. Now you try: observer 20 m above the lake, angles 30°
     and 60°. (H = 40 m)
